story.title: Omar and the Glowing Bike Chain
story.subtitle: A midnight ride through two hundred years of bicycles

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Running Machine
chapters.text:
Omar practiced his favorite BMX trick in the backyard, a wheelie down the ramp. A flashlight sat on the cooler. It was way past bedtime, but the trick needed one more try.

His bike's chain started to glow, silver and green, like it had swallowed a firefly. Omar froze. "Chains don't do that," he whispered.

The chain unspooled off the frame and stretched into a shining road of light. Omar grabbed his handlebars and rolled onto the glow.

WHOOSH! The yard melted away. Omar landed in a grassy field in Germany, back in **1817**. A man in a tall hat sat on a strange wooden two-wheeler with no pedals at all.

"Karl von Drais," the man said, tipping his hat. "Care to try my running machine?"

Omar stared at the wheels. "Wait — no pedals? How do you even go?"

"You push with your feet," Karl said, "like running, but sitting down."

Omar hopped on and pushed off, legs pumping fast. It wobbled, but it rolled. "This is basically a scooter with handlebars!" he laughed.

The glowing chain wrapped around his wrist like a bracelet, ready to pull him somewhere new.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker
chapters.text:
The chain tugged, and WHOOSH, Omar landed on a bumpy cobblestone street in France. A man was bolting metal pedals straight onto the front wheel of a bike.

"Pierre Michaux," he said. "Pedals go right on the front wheel now. We call it the velocipede."

Omar climbed on and rode it over the bumpy stones. His teeth rattled the whole way. "This should be called the BONESHAKER," Omar said, "because it's shaking my bones!"

Pierre laughed so hard he nearly fell over. "Good name. That's exactly what everyone is already calling it."

Omar rubbed his sore arms. "You need something squishy on those wheels," he said. "Something that soaks up the bumps."

Pierre scratched his head. "Someday, somebody will think of that."

Omar grinned, already wondering who.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant Wheel
chapters.text:
Next stop: a street in the **1870s**, with a wheel taller than Omar's dad. A rider wobbled way up high.

"The penny-farthing," the rider called down. "Big wheel up front, named after two old coins — a big penny and a tiny farthing."

Omar squinted up. "One pedal turn and you go way farther with a wheel that big?"

"That's the whole idea," the rider said. "But sit this high, and a sudden stop can send you flying over the handlebars. We call that 'taking a header.'"

Just then the rider hit a bump and started to tip. Omar's BMX instincts kicked in. "Lean back! Don't grab the brake!" he shouted.

The rider leaned back hard and straightened right out, safe and still way up high. "Thanks, kid!" he called, pedaling off.

Omar laughed with relief. "Tallest bike I've ever seen, for sure."
chapters.shout_line: LEAN BACK! DON'T GRAB THE BRAKE!

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Safety Bicycle
chapters.text:
The glow chain pulled Omar to England, **1885**. A man named John Kemp Starley stood beside a bike with two wheels the same size, joined to the back wheel by a chain.

Omar grinned. "That's basically my BMX bike!"

"I call it the safety bicycle," John said. "Same-size wheels, chain driving the back one. No more giant wheel, no more headers."

Omar hopped on and pedaled a smooth circle around the yard. "This feels so much better!"

"People everywhere will want one," John said. "This shape will become the one bikes are built like, forever after."

Omar lifted his glowing wrist-chain. "My bike has a chain too, see?"

John Kemp Starley's eyes went wide. "Looks like yours already learned a thing or two from mine."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Squishy Air Tires
chapters.text:
Next, a workshop in Scotland, **1888**. A man named John Boyd Dunlop knelt beside a tricycle, wrapping a rubber tube around its wheel.

"My son's tricycle rides too rough on solid rubber wheels," John said. "So I filled a rubber tube with air instead."

Omar poked the tire with his thumb. It squished and bounced back. "Like my BMX tires! Bouncy air inside!"

"Exactly," John said. "Air soaks up every bump in the road."

Omar remembered the boneshaker from before. "This is what that guy in France needed!" he said. "Squishy wheels, just like you said!"

John Boyd Dunlop smiled. "Good thing word travels fast. Soon every bike in the world will roll on air."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Golden Age
chapters.text:
WHOOSH, and Omar stood on a busy street in the **1890s**, with more bikes rolling by than he had ever seen in one place.

A woman pedaled past confidently, wearing baggy trousers instead of a long skirt.

"These are called bloomers," she called to Omar. "Long skirts get caught in bike chains and wheels, so we made something safer to wear instead."

Omar nodded. "Smart. Function over fashion."

"Bikes gave women a way to go wherever we want, whenever we want," she said. "A famous American named Susan B. Anthony even said riding a bike set women free more than almost anything else in the world."

Omar watched her roll off down the street. "Cool," he said. "A bike that changes more than just how fast you go."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Bike Shop That Learned to Fly
chapters.text:
The chain dropped Omar into a bike shop in Dayton, Ohio, in the **1890s**. Two brothers, Wilbur and Orville Wright, were fixing a customer's wheel.

"We fix bikes here," Wilbur said, "but we tinker with other ideas too."

Omar noticed thin metal tubes and spoked wheels stacked on a shelf. "Those look like airplane parts," he said.

Orville grinned. "Good eye. Light metal tubes and spoked wheels work great on bikes. Turns out they work great on flying machines too."

"You're going to build an airplane?" Omar asked, eyes wide.

"In **1903**," Orville said, "we plan to."

Omar laughed. "From bike shop to the sky. That's wild."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Ramp
chapters.text:
The chain glowed one more time, and WHOOSH, Omar landed on dirt hills in California, the **1970s**. Kids like him raced small, sturdy bikes down bumpy trails, popping jumps off the dirt.

"BMX bikes," one rider said, skidding to a stop. "Built tough, like motocross motorcycles, but for us kids."

Nearby, other riders bolted wide, bumpy tires onto their bikes for rough trails. "Mountain bikes," someone said. "Perfect for riding down hills like these."

Omar laughed. "I knew my BMX bike had an awesome family tree!"

The glow chain tugged one last time. WHOOSH! Omar landed back in his own backyard, flashlight still sitting on the cooler.

His bike chain looked like plain metal again, just a little sparkle left in the moonlight. Omar grinned. "Over a billion bikes in the whole world now," he whispered, "and mine's got the best story of all."

He wheeled his bike into the garage, yawning big.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Omar. Pedal on.

true_facts.text: In **1817**, a German inventor named Karl von Drais built a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals — riders pushed it along with their feet.
Karl's invention was called the running machine and steered with handlebars, just like bikes today.
In the **1870s**, people rode the penny-farthing, with a giant front wheel taller than a grown-up and a tiny back wheel.
The penny-farthing got its funny name from two old coins — a big penny and a tiny farthing.
Riding so high up was risky — a sudden stop could send a rider flying over the handlebars, called 'taking a header.'
In **1885**, John Kemp Starley invented the safety bicycle, with two same-size wheels and a chain driving the back wheel.
The safety bicycle was much easier to balance than the penny-farthing, so it became the bike everyone wanted.
In **1888**, John Boyd Dunlop invented air-filled rubber tires, making rides much smoother than hard rubber wheels.
In the **1890s**, bikes gave women new freedom, and Susan B. Anthony said riding a bike helped set women free more than almost anything else.
Because long skirts were dangerous near bike wheels and chains, riders started wearing looser pants called bloomers instead.
Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio in the **1890s**, before they built the first successful airplane.
The Wright brothers used bike-building tricks, like light metal tubes and spoked wheels, to help build their flying machine.
Today there are more than a billion bicycles in the world — more than any other kind of vehicle.

new_recurring.name: The Glow Chain
new_recurring.rule: A bicycle chain that glows silver-green, unspools into a road of light, and wraps around a child's wrist like a bracelet between stops. It pulls the child forward in time whenever they are ready for the next adventure, and returns them…

fact_pack.summary: Bicycles evolved over 200 years from a wooden walking machine with no pedals to today's lightweight, geared bikes ridden by billions of people. Along the way inventors added pedals, chains, air-filled tires, and gears, making bikes faster, safer, and more comfortable.

facts.text: In 1817, German inventor Karl von Drais built the 'Laufmaschine' or 'running machine,' a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals that riders pushed along with their feet.
Von Drais's invention was nicknamed the 'draisine' or 'hobby horse' and was steered with handlebars, much like a modern bike.

In the 1860s, French makers Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement added pedals directly to the front wheel, creating the 'velocipede,' nicknamed the 'boneshaker' for its rough ride on cobblestone streets.
Pierre Lallement patented a pedal-driven bicycle design in the United States in 1866.
In the 1870s, the 'penny-farthing' bicycle appeared, with a giant front wheel (sometimes taller than a person) and a tiny back wheel, letting riders go faster with one pedal turn.
Penny-farthings were named after two British coins of very different sizes, the large penny and the small farthing.
Riding a penny-farthing was risky because the rider sat high above the front wheel and could be thrown headfirst in a sudden stop, a fall nicknamed 'taking a header.'
In 1885, Englishman John Kemp Starley invented the 'Rover Safety Bicycle,' with two similarly sized wheels and a chain driving the back wheel, much closer to modern bikes.
The safety bicycle's lower, even wheels made it much easier and safer to ride than the penny-farthing, and it quickly became the standard design worldwide.
In 1888, Scottish inventor John Boyd Dunlop developed the practical pneumatic (air-filled) rubber tire, making bike rides much smoother than solid rubber tires.
Dunlop's tire company grew into the Dunlop Tyre brand, still famous today for tires on bikes and cars.
The 1890s bicycle craze, called the 'Golden Age of Bicycles,' saw millions of bikes sold across Europe and the United States.
Bicycles gave women new freedom to travel independently in the 1890s, and American reformer Susan B. Anthony said cycling 'has done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world.'
Because long skirts were dangerous around bike gears and wheels, the bicycle craze helped popularize more practical clothing for women, including bloomers.
Wilbur and Orville Wright, who later invented the first successful airplane in 1903, ran a bicycle repair and manufacturing shop in Dayton, Ohio in the 1890s.
The Wright brothers used bicycle-building skills, like lightweight metal tubing and spoked wheels, to help design their early flying machines.
Multi-speed gear systems, called derailleurs, became common on bikes in the 1930s, letting riders shift gears to handle hills more easily.
The Tour de France, the world's most famous long-distance cycling race, began in 1903 and today covers about 3,500 kilometers (2,175 miles) across France over about three weeks.
BMX bikes, small and sturdy for tricks and dirt racing, became popular in the United States in the 1970s, inspired by motocross motorcycles.
Mountain bikes with wide, knobby tires were developed in the 1970s in Marin County, California, by riders who wanted to bike down rough dirt trails.
Today, an estimated one billion or more bicycles exist worldwide, more than any other kind of vehicle.
The Netherlands and Denmark are famous today for having more bicycles than cars in some cities, with wide bike lanes built for everyday cyclists.
Modern bicycles are made from lightweight materials like aluminum and carbon fiber, letting racing bikes weigh less than 8 kilograms (about 17 pounds).

story.title: Tom and the Gear That Remembered
story.subtitle: A ride through two hundred years of bicycles.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Gear in the Toolbox (1817)
chapters.text:
Tom was flat on the garage floor, flashlight clenched in his teeth, hunting down why his derailleur — the little metal arm that shifts his chain between gears — kept skipping.

He dug past old tubes and patch kits and found a battered tin box he'd never seen before. Inside sat a single gear, dull bronze, bigger than his thumb. He picked it up.

It was warm. That wasn't right. Metal doesn't warm up by itself.

He turned it over again, and it hummed — a low metal note, like a wheel spinning fast. The garage light flickered green. The floor dropped away under him.

Tom landed hard on packed dirt. A man in a long coat was pushing a wooden two-wheeler along with his own feet, like a kid on a balance bike that had grown up. There were no pedals anywhere.

"You're staring," the man said, not unkindly. "Karl von Drais. This is my Laufmaschine — my running machine."

Tom checked again for pedals. Nothing. "How do you go anywhere?"

"You run," said Drais, "then lift your feet and glide." He demonstrated, scooting and coasting like it was obvious.

The gear buzzed in Tom's pocket. A small, precise voice rose out of it. "Correct date: **1817**. First two-wheeled riding machine in history. No pedals yet — just handlebars and balance."

Tom nearly dropped it. "You *talk*?"

"I'm a pinion," said the gear. "Small gear, big opinions. Call me Pinion."

Tom grinned despite himself, grabbed the handlebars — they steered exactly like his mountain bike's — and ran, then lifted his feet to glide. "It steers like mine does!"

"Keep that thought," said Pinion. "It gets better."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker (1860s)
chapters.text:
The gear hummed again, and the dirt path turned to cobblestones.

A man was bolting a metal crank straight onto a wheel. Pedals, finally — but welded right onto the front wheel itself.

"Pierre Michaux," the man said, "and my partner, Pierre Lallement. We call it the **velocipede**."

Tom climbed on and pedaled three feet before his teeth started chattering. Every cobblestone jumped straight up through the frame.

"This is brutal," Tom said, gripping the bars.

"People call it the **boneshaker**," Lallement said, grinning, "for reasons you've just discovered."

Tom studied the wheel — solid metal rim, no cushion at all. His engineer brain clicked. "You need something soft between the wheel and the road. Like... a tube of air?"

Lallement blinked. "An interesting notion. Patent one, why don't you."

Pinion buzzed in his pocket. "Hold that thought. In **1866**, Lallement actually does patent a pedal bicycle in America. Your soft-tube idea comes later — from someone else entirely."

Tom laughed, rattling over another stone. "Can't wait to meet him."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Taking a Header (1870s)
chapters.text:
The road sharpened into the 1870s, and the bicycle got ridiculous.

A front wheel towered over Tom, taller than he was. The back wheel looked like an afterthought, tiny and trailing behind.

"They call it a **penny-farthing**," Pinion said, "after two old British coins — one huge, one tiny. Guess which wheel is which."

A rider rolled past, perched high above the giant wheel like he was balancing on a unicycle with a seat.

"One turn of the pedals," the rider called down, "and you fly twice as far as on a small wheel!"

Tom squinted at the geometry. Pedals bolted straight to that huge front hub meant speed — but the rider's chin was a long way from the ground.

"What happens if you stop fast?" Tom asked.

"We call it **taking a header**," the rider said cheerfully. "You go over the front. Headfirst."

Tom pictured the physics — high center of gravity, barely any brakes — and kept both boots firmly on the dirt. "I'll admire this one from down here, thanks."

"Wise," said Pinion. "Very wise."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Shape That Stuck (1885)
chapters.text:
The gear hummed, and the giant wheel shrank.

Tom found himself looking at something nearly ordinary — two wheels, same size, a chain looping between them.

A man in shirtsleeves wiped grease from his hands. "John Kemp Starley," he said. "I call her the **Rover Safety Bicycle**."

Tom circled it slowly. Even wheels. Chain drive to the back wheel. A seat low enough to touch the ground.

"This is basically my bike," Tom said, surprised.

"That's rather the idea," Starley said. "Lower, steadier, safer. No headers."

"In **1885**," Pinion added, "this shape becomes the one that sticks. Give or take a hundred and forty years of tweaks, you're still riding it."

Tom swung a leg over and pedaled a slow circle. It felt instantly familiar — handlebars, chain, two matched wheels, nothing trying to throw him over the front.

"Finally," Tom said. "Something that isn't trying to kill me."

"Give it time," Starley laughed. "You'll want it smoother yet."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Vet's Idea (1888)
chapters.text:
One hum of the gear later, the road felt different before Tom even saw why.

A man knelt beside a small tricycle, wrapping a rubber tube around its wheel and pumping air into it with a hand pump.

"John Boyd Dunlop," he said, not looking up. "I'm a vet, not a bicycle man. But my son's tricycle rattled his teeth loose on this garden path."

"So you gave it air," Tom said, catching on fast.

"A **pneumatic tire**," Dunlop said. "Rubber, filled with air, instead of solid rubber on a metal rim."

"In **1888**," said Pinion, "this fixes the boneshaker problem for good."

Tom rode the tricycle across the gravel path. No rattle. No jolt. Just a soft, bouncy roll, like his own mountain bike tires eating up a rocky trail.

"This is basically what my tires do," Tom said, grinning. "Just newer rubber."

"Same idea," said Dunlop. "Smoother ride, happier teeth."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Everyone Gets a Bike (1890s)
chapters.text:
The gear hummed into a street crowded with bicycles — hundreds of them, ridden by kids, grandparents, everyone in between.

A woman rolled past in a long skirt, then swapped to looser, split trousers before climbing onto her bike. "Can't pedal safely in skirts," she told Tom. "Gears and long fabric don't mix."

"This is the **Golden Age of Bicycles**," Pinion said. "**1890s.** Millions of bikes sold, across Europe and America."

A sharp-eyed woman nearby nodded at the crowd of riders. "Susan B. Anthony," she introduced herself. "Cycling has done more to free women to travel on their own than almost anything else in the world."

Tom thought about that — a bike as a way to just *go*, without asking anyone's permission.

Down a side street, a small shop sign read BICYCLES REPAIRED. Two brothers were truing a wheel, spinning it and tapping spokes straight.

"Wilbur and Orville Wright," Pinion said quietly. "Bicycle men first."

Tom watched them bend lightweight metal tubing into a frame. "Bikes before planes," he said slowly. "The tubing, the spoked wheels — "

"Exactly the skills they'll use," said Pinion, "in **1903**, to build the first airplane that actually flies."

Tom looked at the thin, strong tubing in Orville's hands and understood, for the first time, that an engineer's best tricks move between inventions.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Up the Mountain (1903–1930s)
chapters.text:
The gear hummed twice, fast, and the street turned into open road — racers strung out in a long line, climbing a hill under a hot sun.

"The **Tour de France**," Pinion said. "First raced in **1903**. Today it's about **3,500 kilometers** — over two thousand miles — across three straight weeks."

Tom watched a rider's legs pump at the exact same speed, hill or flat.

"Doesn't he need lower gears for that climb?" Tom asked.

"Not yet," said Pinion. "Wait a few decades."

Another hum, smaller this time, and the hill was still there but the bike had changed — a small metal arm now hung by the back wheel, nudging the chain between different-sized gears.

"The **derailleur**," Pinion said. "**1930s.** Shift it, and the chain jumps to an easier gear for the hill."

Tom grinned — this was the exact part he'd been digging through his toolbox for, back home.

"That's literally what I was fixing," Tom said.

"Then you already know," said Pinion, "that a tiny moving part can save your whole ride."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Marin County, and Home (1970s)
chapters.text:
One more hum, and the road turned to dirt — steep, rutted, winding down a dry California hillside.

A group of riders stood at the top with heavy old bikes, fat tires, no fear on their faces.

"Marin County," Pinion said. "**1970s.** Riders wanting to bomb down rough trails built bikes tough enough to survive it."

One rider grinned at Tom's own bike — knobby tires, sturdy frame. "Looks familiar."

"That's basically mine," Tom said. Nearby, smaller, scrappier bikes popped off dirt jumps — **BMX**, built the same decade, inspired by motorcycle racing.

"This is where my bike comes from," Tom said, watching the trail riders drop in. "All of it. The chain, the gears, the tires — two hundred years, bolted onto one frame."

"One billion bicycles exist in the world today," Pinion said. "More than any other kind of vehicle, anywhere."

The gear pulsed warm one last time.

Tom blinked, and he was back on the garage floor, flashlight still between his teeth, the derailleur still in his hands.

In his palm sat the gear, cool now, ordinary bronze. On his workbench, the tool somehow sat already tightened, perfectly adjusted.

He turned the pedal. The chain shifted clean — no skip, no catch.

"Two hundred years," Tom murmured, "just to fix one gear."

He set Pinion carefully back in the tin box, next to the patch kits, and flicked off the garage light.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there was a trail waiting — and a bike finally ready for it.

story.title: Sam and the Gecko Who Could Climb Anything
story.subtitle: A sticky-footed trip up walls, glass, and one very steep mountain.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Gecko
chapters.text:
Sam lay on his bedroom floor. He held his rubber spider tight. It was way past bedtime.

On the shelf sat a little toy gecko. Sam had named him Gordon. Gordon never did anything.

Tonight, Gordon's eyes turned bright green. CLICK! His tiny feet twitched.

"Whoa," Sam whispered.

Gordon hopped down. He felt warm in Sam's hand. "Hello, Sam," he said. "Want to see how real geckos climb?"

Sam grinned. "Yes! Spiders and geckos are my favorites!"

A tiny green door opened in the wall. "Climb through," said Gordon.

They squeezed through. Suddenly everything was huge. The glass wall in front of them looked like a cliff.

A real gecko zoomed straight up it. No slipping. No sliding.

"How does he do that?" Sam asked. "He's not even falling!"

"Look close," said Gordon. He pointed at the gecko's toes.

Sam looked hard. He saw rows and rows of tiny lines, like little brushes.

"Those are hairs," said Gordon. "Millions of tiny hairs on every toe."

"Millions?!" Sam's eyes went wide.

"That many," said Gordon. "That's why he can run up glass. He can even walk upside down on a ceiling."

Sam touched the glass himself. His hand just slid off.

"No fair," he laughed.

"You don't have gecko feet," said Gordon, chuckling. "But stick around. There's more."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: No Glue, No Mess
chapters.text:
Sam looked at his own fingers. Once he touched tape. It stayed sticky and gross for hours.

"Does the gecko have glue feet?" Sam asked.

Gordon shook his tiny head. "No glue at all. Watch."

The gecko lifted one toe off the glass. Then another. Peel, peel, peel. Like pulling up tape, but clean.

"No mess!" said Sam. "His feet don't get yucky!"

"Exactly," said Gordon. "It's not glue. It's those tiny hairs again."

"Then how do they stick?" Sam asked.

"They get so close to the glass," said Gordon, "that something invisible grabs on. Too small to see. Even smaller than the hairs. We call those tiny bits molecules."

Sam squinted at the glass. "I still can't see them."

"Nobody can," said Gordon. "But each one holds on just a little. Millions of them together hold on a lot."

Sam thought about that. "So it's like... everybody pushes together?"

Gordon's whole face lit up. "That's it, Sam! Like a hundred hands. Each one holds a little. Together, they hold a lot."

The gecko flicked one foot. He skittered sideways, quick as a blink.

"And when he wants to stop sticking," said Gordon, "he just peels his toes up. One at a time. No glue to scrub off."

Sam clapped his hands. "I want sticky feet like that!"

"Maybe one day," laughed Gordon. "Humans copied this trick. I'll show you later."

Sam's eyes went wide. "Humans copied gecko feet?!"

"Later," said Gordon. "First, somebody else is waiting. Somebody with eight legs."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Spider's Secret
chapters.text:
A new door opened onto a garden wall. A fat, friendly spider sat right in the middle of it.

Sam gasped. "A spider! I love spiders!"

"This one climbs glass too," said Gordon. "Go on. Ask her how."

Sam leaned close, careful not to touch. "How do you climb straight up?" he asked.

The spider waved one leg. Gordon smiled. "She says: look at my feet."

Sam looked closely. Each tiny foot had rows of hairs. Just like the gecko's. Only even smaller.

"Spiders have their own tiny hairs too!" Sam said. "Thousands on every foot!"

"That's right," said Gordon. "That's why so many spiders can run up smooth glass windows."

The spider scuttled sideways, straight up the wall. She didn't wobble once.

Sam clapped. "Go, spider, go!"

The spider paused at the top. She waved one leg down at him, like a little hello.

Sam waved back, grinning ear to ear. "You pick up every bug in your own garden at home," said Gordon. "Next time, look at their feet too."

"I will," said Sam. "I bet ants have secrets too."

Gordon grinned. "Good guess. Let's go find out."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Buzzy Fly
chapters.text:
Buzzzzz! A fat fly landed on a window.

"Watch this one," said Gordon. "Totally different trick."

The fly's feet looked wet and shiny. Sam leaned in close. "Is he sticky too?"

"Sort of," said Gordon. "His feet ooze out tiny drops. Like little glue drops. Flies do this. So do some beetles."

"Goo!" Sam giggled. "Like when I eat jam and get it everywhere."

"A little like that," laughed Gordon. "Except his goo stays right on his own feet. It helps him stick to glass. Even to your ceiling."

The fly buzzed off the glass. He looped in the air. Then — SPLAT! He landed again, feet first.

Sam burst out laughing.

"He's fine," said Gordon quickly. "Flies land like that all the time. It's just how they fly."

Sam pressed close to the glass, but not too close. "His feet are so small. How does goo even fit?"

"Tiny pads," said Gordon. "Built just for this one job."

Sam nodded, very serious. "Spiders have hairs. Geckos have hairs. Flies have goo. Everybody's got their own trick."

"Everybody," agreed Gordon. "Come see the ones with claws."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sneakers and Slippers
chapters.text:
Next, Gordon led Sam to a crack in an old brick wall. An ant marched straight up it.

"Ants use two different tricks," said Gordon. "Watch what she does."

The ant dug in with tiny claws. Scritch, scritch, scritch, up the rough bricks she went.

Then she reached smooth glass at the top. Her claws stopped working there. She switched to sticky pads instead. She kept right on climbing.

Sam's mouth fell open. "She changed her shoes!"

Gordon laughed so hard his tail wiggled. "Sort of! Rough wall, sharp claws. Smooth wall, sticky pads. Ants do this. Cockroaches do this too."

"That's so smart," said Sam. "Like wearing sneakers AND slippers."

"Exactly like that," said Gordon.

The ant reached the very top. She gave a tiny wave with one leg, like she knew Sam was watching.

Sam waved back. "Good job, ant!"

"Ready for more climbers?" asked Gordon. "These ones live on a mountain."

Sam bounced on his toes. "A mountain! Let's go!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Goats and Squirrels
chapters.text:
The next door opened onto a rocky mountain, cold and windy.

A mountain goat stood on a cliff. It looked much too steep. Sam held his breath. "Is he going to fall?"

"Nope," said Gordon right away. "Watch his feet."

The goat's hooves had a hard rim on the outside. Inside was something softer. It squished around every little bump in the rock.

"His feet are hard outside, soft inside," said Sam. "Like a sneaker with a squishy middle!"

"Just like that," said Gordon.

The goat hopped from rock to rock. He never slipped, not once.

Then a squirrel zipped past them. Straight up a tree trunk.

"What about him?" Sam asked.

"Claws," said Gordon. "Sharp, curved claws. He digs them into tiny cracks. Cracks you and I can't even see."

Sam searched the tree trunk hard. He couldn't spot a single crack. "They must be really, really tiny."

"Tinier than tiny," said Gordon. "But his claws find them anyway."

The squirrel reached the top branch. He chattered loudly, like he was showing off.

Sam laughed and clapped. "Show-off squirrel!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Rain and Slime
chapters.text:
Next stop: a rainy garden, dark and damp.

A little green tree frog sat on a wet leaf. Then he hopped onto a window and stuck there.

"His feet are wet," said Sam. "Won't that make him slip?"

"Should," said Gordon. "But look closer."

Sam looked hard. The frog's toe pads were flat. They had tiny little shapes on them, like a honeycomb.

"Those special pads grip even wet, slippery places," said Gordon. "Wet leaves. Wet glass. No problem at all."

"Cool," breathed Sam.

Down on the ground, a snail glided up the very same window. Slow and steady.

"No hairs. No claws. No sticky pads," said Gordon. "Just slime."

Sam watched the shiny trail behind it. "He's climbing on slime?"

"His whole foot ripples underneath him," said Gordon. "Little waves, over and over. It's slow. But it always works."

"Slow and slimy wins the race," Sam giggled.

"Something like that," laughed Gordon.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Gecko Glove
chapters.text:
"Now," said Gordon, "remember how I said humans copied gecko feet?"

Sam bounced on his toes. "Yes! Show me!"

A new door opened onto a sunny room full of scientists. One of them pressed two small paddles against a tall glass wall. Sam spotted the same pattern from the gecko's toes.

"In **2014**, scientists built paddles just like this," said Gordon. "A whole person climbed a glass wall holding these."

Sam's jaw dropped. "A whole person?! Climbing glass?!"

"A whole person," said Gordon. "No ropes. Just a gecko trick."

The scientist reached the top of the wall. He waved down, grinning.

"People studied gecko feet," said Gordon. "They made new sticky tape. They even made gloves for climbing."

Sam grinned wide. "Geckos are basically inventors."

"Basically," Gordon agreed, laughing.

Then the little green door glowed bright. Sam felt himself grow big again. He blinked, and he was back on his bedroom floor. His rubber spider was still in his hand.

Gordon sat still on the shelf once more, just a toy again. But one eye glinted green, quick as a wink.

On the carpet beside Sam lay something small and shiny. A tiny gecko-foot sticker, like it had traveled home with him.

Sam smiled and held it tight. Tomorrow, he would show it to every bug in the garden.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Sam. Climb well.

fact_pack.summary: Lots of animals can climb smooth walls and even walk upside down on ceilings, using clever tricks like sticky pads, tiny hooked claws, or millions of microscopic hairs. Scientists who study these tricks have even copied them to invent new kinds of sticky tape and climbing gloves for people.

facts.text: Geckos can run up glass and walk across ceilings because their toes have millions of microscopic hairs called setae.
Each gecko seta splits into hundreds of even tinier tips called spatulae, which get so close to a surface that weak molecular attractions called van der Waals forces hold the foot in place.
A gecko's sticky grip is not glue, so its feet never get messy or leave residue, and it can lift its toes off instantly by peeling them, toe by toe, like pulling up tape.
Flies and some beetles climb using tiny pads on their feet that ooze a sticky liquid, acting like natural glue drops.
Spiders have thousands of microscopic hairs called setules on their feet, similar in idea to gecko hairs, which is why many spiders can climb smooth glass.
Ants and cockroaches use a combination of sharp claws for rough surfaces and sticky footpads for smooth ones, switching tools depending on the wall.
Mountain goats and some wild sheep climb near-vertical cliffs using hooves with a hard outer rim and a soft, grippy inner pad that molds to rock.
Squirrels climb trees and walls using sharp curved claws that dig into tiny cracks and bumps invisible to human eyes.
Tree frogs have special flattened, mucus-covered toe pads with tiny hexagon-shaped patterns that help them stick to wet leaves and glass.
Snails and slugs climb smooth walls by gliding on a layer of slime, which lets their muscular foot grip and move in rippling waves.
Some crabs and lobsters use small hooked bristles on their legs to cling to rocky, underwater walls against strong currents.
Bats cannot climb walls quickly like geckos, but they use curved claws on their feet to hang upside down from cave ceilings and cliff walls.
Woodpeckers climb straight up tree trunks using stiff tail feathers as a prop and two toes forward, two toes back for extra grip.
In 2014, scientists built a gecko-inspired handheld paddle that let a person climb a glass wall by pressing sticky synthetic pads against it.
Engineers have copied gecko foot structure to create reusable sticky tape and gripping robot feet that work in space, where regular glue fails in a vacuum.
A gecko's sticking ability is so strong that scientists calculated a gecko the size of a human could theoretically support its whole body weight from one finger, though real geckos are small.
Geckos keep their sticky feet clean and dust-free through a self-cleaning effect, where dirt particles roll off the tiny hairs as the gecko walks.
Praying mantises and stick insects use both small claws and sticky pads called arolia, choosing which one to use depending on the surface.
Some climbing animals, like certain ants, are so light compared to their sticky footpad area that they could theoretically hold many times their own body weight while hanging upside down.
Rock climbers sometimes study gecko and insect feet for ideas on new types of climbing shoes and gloves with better grip.
Many wall-climbing animals rely on physics tricks rather than suction, since true suction cups need airless pockets that are hard to maintain on rough or dusty surfaces.
Remoras, a type of fish, use a modified dorsal fin shaped like a suction pad to stick to sharks, whales, and boat hulls rather than walls.

story.title: Sam and the Gecko Who Climbed Everything
story.subtitle: A sticky, stuck-together bedtime adventure

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Gecko Light Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Sam lay on his bedroom floor. Past bedtime. Way past.

He lined up his toy spiders in a row. Eight legs each. He counted them every single night.

On the wall above his bed glowed a little green gecko sticker. It was his night-light. It always just glowed, quiet and still.

Tonight it blinked.

Sam sat up. "Did you just wink at me?"

The gecko sticker peeled off the wall. SPLORP! It landed on the carpet and grew legs that waved.

"Hiya," said the gecko. "I'm Tiko. Tokay gecko. Best climber you will ever meet."

Sam grinned so big his face hurt. "Climbers are my favorite thing. After spiders. And bugs. And also geckos."

"Good," said Tiko, "because tonight, you ARE a gecko."

WHOOOSH! The room spun. Sam shrank down, down, down, until the carpet looked like a giant green ocean.

He looked at his hands. Little sticky toes, just like Tiko's.

"Why are my toes sticky?" Sam asked.

"Toes have millions of teeny tiny hairs," said Tiko. "So many, you cannot even see one. They let us stick to glass. Even upside down!"

Sam looked up at his bedroom window. Smooth. Shiny. Straight up and down.

"Can I climb that?" Sam asked.

"Only one way to find out," said Tiko.

Sam pressed one sticky toe onto the glass. It held.

"It's holding!" Sam yelled. "IT'S HOLDING!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Up the Window Glass
chapters.text:
Sam climbed higher. Toe. Toe. Toe. Each one stuck like it meant it.

"This is the best thing I have ever done," Sam said. "Besides catching the roly-poly behind the shed."

Tiko laughed, a little clicking sound. "Wait till you want to come back DOWN."

Sam stopped. "Uh oh. Am I stuck?"

"Nope," said Tiko. "Watch me."

Tiko peeled one toe off the glass. Then another. Then another. Just like pulling up a piece of tape.

"It's not even glue," said Tiko. "No mess. Nothing sticky left behind. Just peel, peel, peel."

Sam tried it. He peeled his front toe. CLICK. Then the next one. CLICK. Then the next.

"IT PEELS LIKE TAPE!" Sam shouted.

"Grown-ups study stuff like this for their whole job," said Tiko. "They're called scientists. They liked our sticky toes so much, they copied them. In 2014, they made sticky pads for human hands. A real person climbed a real glass wall. A whole human, climbing just like us!"

Sam pictured his dad climbing up the living room window wearing sticky gloves. He laughed so hard he nearly peeled off all ten toes at once.

"Let's keep climbing," Sam said. "I want to meet more climbers."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Spider in the Corner
chapters.text:
Up near the ceiling, something moved. Eight legs. Fast.

Sam's eyes went wide. "A SPIDER!"

"Don't worry," said Tiko. "Just say hi."

Sam waved. "Hi! I pick up spiders in my yard all the time!"

The spider waved one leg back. "Nice to meet a fan," it said, in a tiny, scratchy voice.

"How do you climb glass?" Sam asked. "You don't even look sticky."

"Same trick as Tiko," said the spider. "Tiny hairs on my feet too. Thousands of them. That's how I walk straight up your window, and you can't."

Sam looked at his own gecko toes, then at the spider's feet. "We match!"

"Kind of," said Tiko. "Spiders got their own version, all by themselves."

The spider scuttled sideways along the glass, quick as a blink.

"Race you to the top!" Sam said.

He pushed off with his sticky toes. Toe, toe, toe, faster now.

The spider reached the top first. "Too slow, gecko boy!"

Sam laughed so hard he nearly slid back down. "SPIDERS STICK TOO! Rematch tomorrow!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Sticky, Drippy Fly
chapters.text:
Something landed on the glass next to Sam. BZZZZT.

A fly. Rubbing its front legs together.

"Watch this," said the fly. It took one more step and left a tiny wet footprint. SQUELCH.

"Ew," said Sam, delighted. "What IS that?"

"My feet drip a little goo," the fly said proudly. "Like tiny drops of glue. That's how I stick."

Sam leaned in close. "Can I touch it?"

"Sure," said the fly.

Sam poked the wet spot. His toe stuck fast. SPLAT.

"I'm STUCK!" Sam yelled, giggling the whole time.

"Peel it, like Tiko showed you," said the fly.

Sam peeled his toe off, slow and careful. It made a tiny squelchy sound coming free.

"Beetles do the same gooey trick," said Tiko. "Different bug. Same idea. A little drippy glue on the feet."

"Bugs are SO good at this," Sam said. "No wonder I like them so much."

He poked the wet spot one more time, just for fun. SPLAT. SQUELCH. Giggle.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Ants on the Brick Wall
chapters.text:
Tiko led Sam down to the garden, out past the window frame, onto a bumpy brick wall.

A line of ants marched straight up it, quick and tidy.

"How do THEY do it?" Sam asked. "This wall isn't even smooth."

"Ants carry two tools," said an ant marching past. "Sharp little claws for bumpy walls, like this brick. Sticky pads for smooth walls, like your window."

"You just pick whichever one you need?" Sam asked.

"Every single time," said the ant.

Sam looked closer at the bricks. Tiny holes. Tiny bumps. Too small to see before, but not too small now that he was ant-sized.

"The claws grab the little bumpy bits!" Sam said, pointing at one. "I found it!"

"You sure did," said Tiko. "Cockroaches do the very same two-tool trick too."

Sam dug his own toe into a bumpy brick. It held. Different from the sticky glass way. But it held.

"Two tricks are better than one," Sam decided, climbing on.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Goat on the Rocky Cliff
chapters.text:
WHOOOSH. Tiko hopped them onto Sam's old fish tank rock, now looming like a whole rocky mountain.

A fuzzy mountain goat stood on a steep rock, calm as anything.

"Aren't you scared?" Sam called up. "That's so steep!"

"Nope," said the goat. "My hooves do the work." It lifted one foot. "Hard edges around the outside. Soft, squishy middle. The soft part squishes flat onto the rock and grips."

Sam squinted. "Like a shoe that changes shape?"

"Exactly like that," said the goat.

The goat hopped from rock to rock, never slipping once. Not even a wobble.

"I want hooves," Sam said.

"You've got sticky toes instead," said Tiko. "Way better for glass."

"Fine," Sam said. "I'll trade you for a window, not a cliff."

The goat laughed, a funny little bleat, and bounced away up the rocks.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Squirrel in the Backyard Tree
chapters.text:
Back near Sam's own yard, a squirrel zipped straight up the big oak tree.

"Whoa, how is he not falling?" Sam asked.

"Claws," said Tiko. "Curved ones. They dig into teeny cracks in the bark. Cracks too small for you to even see."

The squirrel paused halfway up. "Little bumps, little dips. My claws grab every single one!"

Sam ran his tiny gecko fingers over the bark. Up close, it was not smooth at all. Bumpy. Crumbly. Full of tiny places to hold.

"It's like the ants," Sam said. "Everybody's got their own trick for their own wall!"

"Now you're getting it," said Tiko.

The squirrel flicked its tail and shot the rest of the way up. "Nuts don't collect themselves!"

Sam laughed so hard he nearly let go of the tree bark.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Frog on the Wet Leaf
chapters.text:
A raindrop plinked onto a leaf below them. Sitting right in the middle: a small green tree frog.

"How are you not sliding right off?" Sam asked. "That leaf is soaking wet!"

The frog lifted one foot. Its toe had a flat little pad on the end.

It was covered in slippery wet stuff called mucus. That's just slimy goo, kind of like frog snot.

"Gross," said Sam, grinning. "I love it."

"My pads have tiny little honeycomb shapes on them," the frog said. "They grip the wet leaf, even slippery as it is."

Sam looked closer. Tiny six-sided shapes, like a soccer ball, covered the frog's toes.

"You're sticky even when it's wet," Sam said. "Tiko can't even do that!"

"Different trick for a different job," Tiko agreed. "Wet leaves need a wet-sticking expert."

The frog gave a little bow, and hopped off into the dark garden.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Snail and the Walk Back Home
chapters.text:
Near the garden path, something very slow caught Sam's eye. A snail, gliding straight up the garden wall.

"No claws. No hairs. No goo," Sam said. "How?"

"Slime," said the snail, not speeding up one single bit. "I lay down a trail of slime. Then I ripple my foot along it, nice and slow."

Sam watched the snail's whole underside ripple like a tiny wave. "That is so cool AND so slow."

"Slow and sure beats fast and fallen," said the snail.

Tiko chuckled. "Every climber we met tonight had their own trick. Sticky hairs. Goo drops. Claws. Hooves. Slime. All different. All brilliant."

"I want to try every single one again tomorrow," Sam said.

WHOOOSH. The garden spun. The brick wall shrank. The oak tree shrank. Sam grew and grew, until he was lying on his own bedroom carpet again, toy spiders lined up right where he left them.

The green gecko sticker was back on the wall above his bed, glowing soft and quiet.

"Climb well, Sam," Tiko whispered, and the glow faded down to sleep.

Sam pulled his blanket up, smiling at the ceiling, already picking which bug to find tomorrow.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Sam. Climb well.

Spiders have thousands of their own tiny hairs on their feet, which is why many spiders can climb smooth glass.
Flies and some beetles climb using tiny drops of goo that ooze from their feet like little bits of glue.

Mountain goats climb steep, rocky cliffs using hooves that have hard edges on the outside and a soft, squishy middle.

Tree frogs have flat toe pads with tiny honeycomb shapes that grip wet, slippery leaves.
Snails climb walls by laying down a trail of slime and rippling their foot along it, slow and steady.
In 2014, scientists built sticky, gecko-style pads that let a real person climb a glass wall.

new_recurring.rule: A chatty, colorful gecko who lives as a glowing green sticker night-light on Sam's wall. He peels off the wall to guide Sam on nighttime adventures, shrinking Sam down to meet other animals, and always signs off with the words 'Climb well.'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Sam grew back to normal size on his own bedroom carpet, right next to his lined-up toy spiders, while the green gecko night-light glowed softly above his bed and Tiko whispered 'Climb well, Sam' before fading to sleep.

story.title: Rosa, Isla, and the Sticky-Toed Gecko
story.subtitle: A climbing adventure with ladybirds, spiders, and one very sticky lizard

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Ladybird
chapters.text:
Rosa lay on her tummy. She watched her ladybird nightlight. It glowed a soft green.

Isla sat on the top bunk. She drew a climbing wall on paper. She drew little hand holds.

Then the nightlight blinked twice. CLICK. CLICK.

It did not do that before.

Rosa poked it with one finger. "Hello, ladybird," she said.

POP! The light popped open. Out crawled a tiny lizard with big round eyes.

"Hello!" he said. "I'm Gordy the Gecko. I climb walls for fun."

Isla jumped off her bed. "Walls? Like rock climbing?"

"Just like that," said Gordy. "Want to see how animals climb? Even upside down?"

Rosa clapped her hands. "Ladybirds too?"

"Ladybirds too," said Gordy, winking. "Hold onto my tail. Here we go."

WHOOSH! The bedroom wall turned soft and green, like a jungle. Rosa and Isla tumbled through.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Gordy's Sticky Toes
chapters.text:
They landed by a big glass wall. It went straight up, up, up.

Gordy skittered right up it. He did not fall. Not even a little.

"How do you do that?" asked Isla. "Glass is so slippery!"

Gordy held up one tiny foot. "Look close," he said.

Isla looked close. She gasped. "Your toes have lines! Like tiny hairs!"

"**Millions of tiny hairs**," said Gordy proudly. "Each one grabs onto bumps so small you cannot see them."

Rosa reached out and touched the glass. "I don't feel bumps," she said.

"That's because they're tinier than a speck of dust," said Gordy.

Isla grinned. "So that's how geckos run up walls. And across ceilings?"

"Yep," said Gordy. "Upside down too!" He scurried across the ceiling to prove it.

Rosa laughed so hard she almost fell off her leaf. "Do it again!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: No Glue, No Mess
chapters.text:
Gordy stuck to the glass wall. Then he peeled one toe up at a time.

"Wait," said Isla. "Is that glue?"

"Nope," said Gordy. "**No glue at all**. My feet never get sticky and messy."

Rosa touched his foot. It felt clean and dry. "Not sticky!" she said, surprised.

"I can let go fast too," said Gordy. "Just like peeling off a sticker. Toe by toe."

He peeled his feet off the glass. Peel, peel, peel, peel!

"That's so cool," said Isla. "No glue, but it still grips?"

"Tiny hairs don't need glue," said Gordy. "They just grab on, then let go."

Rosa tried peeling her own fingers off the glass. "Peel, peel!" she giggled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Ladybird's Secret
chapters.text:
A little ladybird landed on the glass, right next to Rosa.

Rosa squealed. "A ladybird! My favorite!"

"Watch her feet," said Gordy. "She's a climber too."

The ladybird walked straight up the wall. She did not slip at all.

"Ladybirds are beetles," said Gordy. "Beetles and flies have **tiny sticky pads** on their feet."

"Sticky like glue?" asked Isla.

"A little bit like glue," said Gordy. "Tiny sticky drops help them hold on."

Rosa watched the ladybird climb higher and higher. "Go, ladybird, go!" she cheered.

The ladybird reached the top and flew away. Rosa waved. "Bye bye, climbing bug!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Eight Legs, Lots of Hairs
chapters.text:
Something dropped down on a thread. Rosa jumped. "What's that?!"

"Just a spider," said Gordy gently. "She's friendly. Watch her climb."

The spider climbed up the glass with all eight legs.

"She has hairs too," said Gordy. "**Thousands of tiny hairs** on her feet."

Isla leaned in close. "Like your hairs, Gordy?"

"Just like mine," said Gordy. "That's why spiders can climb glass too."

Rosa took a deep breath. "She's not scary. She's just climbing."

"That's right," said Gordy. "She's just going home to her web."

The spider disappeared over the top of the wall. Rosa waved goodbye too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Claws or Glue?
chapters.text:
Next, Gordy led them to a bumpy rock wall. Ants marched straight up it.

"Look at their tiny claws," said Gordy. "Perfect for rough, bumpy walls."

Then the ants reached smooth glass. They didn't stop at all.

"How?" asked Isla. "Their claws won't work on smooth glass!"

"They **switch tools**," said Gordy. "Sticky feet for smooth walls, claws for bumpy ones."

Rosa pointed. "Like changing shoes!"

"Exactly like changing shoes," laughed Gordy. "Smart little ants."

Isla nodded. "Cockroaches do that too, right?"

"You got it," said Gordy. "Claws and sticky pads, whichever works best."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Goats on a Cliff
chapters.text:
Suddenly the wall became a huge rocky cliff. Goats leaped from rock to rock.

"Whoa!" said Isla. "That cliff is almost straight up and down!"

"Mountain goats don't mind," said Gordy. "Look at their feet."

Rosa looked close. "Their feet are hard on the outside!"

"Right," said Gordy. "**Hard edges grip the rock**. But inside is soft and squishy."

"Squishy like a sponge?" asked Rosa.

"A bit like that," said Gordy. "The soft part molds around the bumpy rock."

Isla grinned. "Hard outside, soft inside. Perfect for climbing cliffs."

A goat leaped right past them and landed with a soft THUD. Rosa clapped.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Squirrel Speed
chapters.text:
A squirrel zoomed past them up a tall tree. Scritch scritch scritch!

"Whoa, he's fast!" said Rosa.

"Squirrels have **sharp, curvy claws**," said Gordy. "They dig into tiny cracks in the bark."

Isla touched the tree trunk. "I don't see any cracks."

"They're tiny," said Gordy. "Too small for us to see. But just right for claws."

The squirrel reached the top and sat down, nibbling a nut.

Isla laughed. "He made it look so easy."

"Climbing is easy," said Gordy, "when you have the right feet."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Froggy High Five
chapters.text:
Rain started to fall. A tiny tree frog hopped onto a wet leaf.

"Won't he slip?" asked Rosa. "The leaf is all wet!"

"Watch his toes," said Gordy. "They're flat and a little bit slimy."

Isla peered closer. "They look like tiny stamps!"

"Good eye," said Gordy. "Those **flat, slimy toes** stick to wet leaves and glass."

The frog hopped higher, never slipping once. Ribbit!

Rosa held up her hand. "High five, froggy!"

The frog lifted one sticky toe, as if waving back. Rosa giggled with delight.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Home Again
chapters.text:
"One more thing," said Gordy. "People wanted sticky feet too."

Isla's eyes lit up. "Like rock climbers?"

"Just like that," said Gordy. "Scientists are people who study how things work. They studied gecko feet. Then they made **sticky climbing gloves** for people."

Isla looked at her paper drawing of a climbing wall. "I want gloves like that!"

"Maybe someday," said Gordy, smiling.

WHOOSH! The green jungle faded. The bedroom wall came back.

Rosa was back on her tummy. Isla was back on her bunk.

The ladybird nightlight glowed softly green, just like before.

But on the carpet sat one tiny gecko-shaped sticker, shining faintly.

Rosa picked it up and stuck it on her hand. "Sticky toes," she whispered, yawning.

Isla smiled and tucked her climbing drawing under her pillow.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Rosa. Goodnight, Isla. Stick with it!

true_facts.text: Geckos can run up glass and walk across the ceiling. Their toes have **millions of tiny hairs** that grab tiny bumps.
A gecko's sticky grip isn't glue. He can **peel his toes off fast**, just like pulling up a sticker.
Ladybirds and flies have **tiny sticky pads** on their feet, with a little sticky liquid to help them climb.
Spiders have **thousands of tiny hairs** on their feet too, just like geckos, so they can climb smooth glass.
Ants and cockroaches **switch tools**: sharp claws for bumpy walls, sticky feet for smooth ones.
Mountain goats have hooves with **hard edges and soft, squishy insides**, perfect for steep rocky cliffs.
Squirrels have **sharp, curvy claws** that dig into tiny cracks in tree bark too small to see.
Tree frogs have **flat, slightly slimy toes** that help them stick to wet leaves and glass.
Scientists studied gecko feet and then made **sticky climbing gloves** for people.

new_recurring.name: Gordy the Gecko
new_recurring.rule: A cheerful, sticky-toed gecko who pops out of a glowing object in the children's room and guides them through nature's climbing tricks. Ends adventures with the phrase 'Stick with it!'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Rosa and Isla return to their bedroom to find a tiny glowing gecko sticker left on the carpet, and Isla tucks her climbing-wall drawing under her pillow before sleep.

fact_pack.summary: Lots of animals can climb smooth walls and even walk upside down on ceilings, using clever tricks like sticky pads, tiny hooked claws, or millions of microscopic hairs. Scientists who study these tricks have even copied them to invent new kinds of sticky tape and climbing gloves for people.

facts.text: Geckos can run up glass and walk across ceilings because their toes have millions of microscopic hairs called setae.
Each gecko seta splits into hundreds of even tinier tips called spatulae, which get so close to a surface that weak molecular attractions called van der Waals forces hold the foot in place.
A gecko's sticky grip is not glue, so its feet never get messy or leave residue, and it can lift its toes off instantly by peeling them, toe by toe, like pulling up tape.
Flies and some beetles climb using tiny pads on their feet that ooze a sticky liquid, acting like natural glue drops.
Spiders have thousands of microscopic hairs called setules on their feet, similar in idea to gecko hairs, which is why many spiders can climb smooth glass.
Ants and cockroaches use a combination of sharp claws for rough surfaces and sticky footpads for smooth ones, switching tools depending on the wall.
Mountain goats and some wild sheep climb near-vertical cliffs using hooves with a hard outer rim and a soft, grippy inner pad that molds to rock.
Squirrels climb trees and walls using sharp curved claws that dig into tiny cracks and bumps invisible to human eyes.
Tree frogs have special flattened, mucus-covered toe pads with tiny hexagon-shaped patterns that help them stick to wet leaves and glass.
Snails and slugs climb smooth walls by gliding on a layer of slime, which lets their muscular foot grip and move in rippling waves.
Some crabs and lobsters use small hooked bristles on their legs to cling to rocky, underwater walls against strong currents.
Bats cannot climb walls quickly like geckos, but they use curved claws on their feet to hang upside down from cave ceilings and cliff walls.
Woodpeckers climb straight up tree trunks using stiff tail feathers as a prop and two toes forward, two toes back for extra grip.
In 2014, scientists built a gecko-inspired handheld paddle that let a person climb a glass wall by pressing sticky synthetic pads against it.
Engineers have copied gecko foot structure to create reusable sticky tape and gripping robot feet that work in space, where regular glue fails in a vacuum.
A gecko's sticking ability is so strong that scientists calculated a gecko the size of a human could theoretically support its whole body weight from one finger, though real geckos are small.
Geckos keep their sticky feet clean and dust-free through a self-cleaning effect, where dirt particles roll off the tiny hairs as the gecko walks.
Praying mantises and stick insects use both small claws and sticky pads called arolia, choosing which one to use depending on the surface.
Some climbing animals, like certain ants, are so light compared to their sticky footpad area that they could theoretically hold many times their own body weight while hanging upside down.
Rock climbers sometimes study gecko and insect feet for ideas on new types of climbing shoes and gloves with better grip.
Many wall-climbing animals rely on physics tricks rather than suction, since true suction cups need airless pockets that are hard to maintain on rough or dusty surfaces.
Remoras, a type of fish, use a modified dorsal fin shaped like a suction pad to stick to sharks, whales, and boat hulls rather than walls.

timeline.event: Scientists begin seriously studying gecko feet with early microscopes
Researchers identify van der Waals forces as the true secret of gecko stickiness
DARPA-funded scientists demonstrate a human climbing a glass wall using gecko-inspired paddles

story.title: Milo, Juno and the Dinosaur Brick
story.subtitle: A WHOOOOSH back to the land before time

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick Glows Again
chapters.text:
Milo and Juno sat on the carpet. The big LEGO tower from last night stood tall. It still went CLICK and held tight.

Juno hugged his toy dinosaur. "I wish real dinosaurs were here," he said.

Then the red brick on top of the tower began to glow. It hummed like a sleepy bee.

"It's doing the thing again!" Milo said.

Juno poked it. CLICK! The brick lit up bright red.

WHOOOOSH! The room spun. The carpet turned into warm, squishy mud. Trees as tall as houses popped up around them.

"Whoa," Milo whispered. "Where are we?"

A deep voice rumbled. "You are a very, very long time ago."

Milo spun around. A big gray dinosaur with three horns stood smiling at them.

"I'm Terra," she said. "Dinosaurs like me started showing up about **230 million years ago**. That's so long ago, even your grandma's grandma's grandma wasn't born yet!"

Juno's eyes went wide. "That's SO many years."

"The very first dinosaurs were small," Terra said. "But some of us grew up big. Want to meet some?"

Milo grinned. "Yes! And can we see a shark dinosaur?"

Terra laughed, a sound like a trumpet. "No shark dinosaurs here. But I promise you'll love what we find."

She started walking, her big feet going THUMP, THUMP on the soft ground.

"Follow me," she said. "Play well, and watch your step!"

Juno giggled and ran after her, dinosaur toy still in his hand. Milo looked back at the glowing brick, now floating beside them like a little red moon, then ran to catch up.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Terra the Triceratops
chapters.text:
Terra stopped by a big rock. "Look at my face," she said. "What do you see?"

Juno counted. "One, two, three horns!"

"That's right," Terra said. "And see this big bony collar around my neck? We call it a **frill**. It's like a shield, to keep my neck safe."

Milo touched the frill gently. "It's so hard! Like a LEGO shield."

"Exactly," Terra said, pleased. "I use my horns and my frill to stay safe."

Juno gasped. "Does someone chase you?"

"Sometimes," Terra said calmly. "But I'm big and strong, and my horns do the job. No need to worry."

Milo thought for a second. "Could we build a frill out of LEGO bricks?"

Terra tilted her head. "What a good idea."

Milo pictured a wide curved plate, clicking onto a tiny LEGO dinosaur's neck. "We could make tiny horns too," he said. "Three of them, just like yours."

"Dinosaurs like me are called **Triceratops**," Terra said. "It basically means three-horned face."

Juno tried the word. "Try-SAIR-a-tops!"

"Close enough," Terra chuckled.

They walked on, Milo already planning his next LEGO build: a Triceratops with a snap-on frill. Juno marched behind, holding three fingers up to his own forehead like horns.

"Honk honk, I'm a dinosaur!" Juno yelled.

Terra laughed so hard her frill wobbled, and even the tall trees seemed to shake a little.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant Long-Neck
chapters.text:
THUD. THUD. THUD. The ground shook under their feet.

Juno grabbed Milo's hand. "Is it mad?"

Terra shook her head. "No, just big. Look up."

Milo tipped his head back, and back, and back. A dinosaur with a neck like a crane reached high into the trees.

"Whoa," Milo breathed. "That's the biggest thing I've ever seen."

"She might be the biggest dinosaur of all," Terra said. "Her kind is called **Argentinosaurus**. She could grow longer than **100 feet**."

Milo's jaw dropped. "That's SO long!"

Milo had an idea. "Let's measure her with our arms!"

He stretched his arms wide. Juno stretched his arms wide too. They stood end to end, trying to match the dinosaur's length.

"One Milo, two Milos, three Milos..." Juno counted, giggling.

They never got close to the end of her, and they both tumbled into the soft mud, laughing.

"Even sharks aren't that big," Milo said, thinking of his favorite ocean giants.

"Nothing swims this big," Terra said. "She eats leaves at the very top of the trees, where no one else can reach."

The giant dinosaur swung her long neck gently, like saying hello.

Juno waved both hands. "Hi, giant dinosaur!"

She blinked slowly, then kept munching leaves, not bothered one bit. A leaf fluttered down and landed right on Juno's head, and he laughed so hard he fell over again.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Terrible Lizard's Name
chapters.text:
A loud ROAR echoed through the trees. Juno jumped. "Who's that?"

Terra smiled. "Don't worry, he's full. That's just him saying hello."

A huge dinosaur stomped closer, his mouth full of enormous teeth.

Milo stared. "Those teeth are huge!"

"Each tooth is about **12 inches** long," Terra said. "That's as long as a ruler."

Juno hid behind Terra's leg, just for a second, then peeked back out. "Is he scary?"

"He looks scary," Terra said, "but right now he's just showing off his smile."

The big dinosaur opened his mouth wide, almost like a yawn, then flopped down in the mud with a SPLAT, perfectly happy.

Milo laughed with relief. "He's kind of silly."

"A scientist named **Richard Owen** looked at bones like these a long time ago," Terra said. "In **1842**, he made up a brand new word for animals like us: **dinosaur**. In an old language, it means 'terrible lizard.'"

Juno repeated it slowly. "Terrible lizard."

"That's a big name," Milo said, "for a guy who just naps in the mud."

"Names don't always tell the whole story," Terra chuckled.

Milo had an idea. "What if we gave him a nicer name? Like... Mud Muncher?"

The huge dinosaur let out a happy snort, as if he liked it just fine.

"Mud Muncher it is," Terra said.

Juno cheered. "MUD MUNCHER!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sue and the Lucky Dog
chapters.text:
Terra led them to a dusty, rocky place. SCRITCH SCRITCH. Something was digging.

"Who's digging?" Juno asked.

"People called **paleontologists**," Terra said. "They dig up old bones to learn how dinosaurs lived."

Milo watched them brushing dirt off a huge bone. "Is that a real dinosaur?"

"It's what's left of one," Terra said. "Bones that turned hard like rock over a very long time. We call them **fossils**."

Juno touched the ground carefully. "Like a dinosaur puzzle!"

"Exactly," Terra said. "One of the biggest T. rex puzzles ever found got the nickname **Sue**. People found her bones in **South Dakota** in **1990**."

"Sue found a T. rex?" Milo asked, confused.

"No, Sue is the dinosaur's nickname," Terra laughed. "Some people tell a fun story that a farmer's dog once dug up part of a famous dinosaur bone. That part might be a little bit made-up, but it's a fun tale to tell."

Milo grinned. "I like that story anyway."

Juno knelt down and started digging in the soft dirt with his hands, very gently.

"Can I find a fossil too?" he asked.

"Dig carefully," Terra said, "and let's see."

Juno brushed away dirt, and underneath was a curved, hard shape.

"I FOUND ONE!" Juno shouted.

Terra leaned in close. "Well look at that. You found a piece of old dinosaur bone."

Milo clapped. "Juno the fossil finder!"

Juno held it up proudly, grinning from ear to ear, and tucked it carefully into his pocket.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Tiny Turkey Dinosaur
chapters.text:
Something small rustled in the bushes. Juno froze. "What's that?"

A little dinosaur popped out, about the size of Juno's toy chicken.

"That's a Velociraptor," Terra said.

Milo blinked. "Wait, that's it? In my movies they're huge!"

"Movies make them bigger," Terra said. "Really, they were only about the size of a **turkey**."

Juno laughed. "That's not scary at all!"

The little dinosaur hopped closer, covered in soft fluff.

"Feathers?" Milo asked, surprised. "On a dinosaur?"

"Lots of dinosaurs had **feathers**," Terra said, "just like this one."

Juno reached out a careful hand, not touching, just watching. "Can I say hi?"

"You can wave," Terra said. "Let's not touch. Wild animals like to be watched, not grabbed."

Juno waved both hands. "Hi, little feathery dinosaur!"

The small dinosaur tilted its head, then darted off into the bushes, quick as a cat.

Milo giggled. "He's fast for someone so small."

"Small and speedy," Terra agreed. "Not every dinosaur was a giant."

Juno sat back on his heels. "I like this one best. He's turkey-sized, like Thanksgiving!"

Milo laughed so hard he nearly fell over. "Turkey-saurus!"

Terra joined in laughing, her frill shaking, and even Juno did a wobbly little turkey gobble, flapping his elbows like wings.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Spiky Tails and Plates
chapters.text:
CLACK. CLACK. CLACK. A strange sound came from behind a rock.

Milo peeked around. "Whoa, look at those plates!"

A dinosaur with big bony plates down its back walked slowly by.

"That's Stegosaurus," Terra said. "The plates run along her back, and spikes stick out of her tail."

Juno counted the plates. "One, two, three, four..."

"She swings that spiky tail to stay safe," Terra said. "Scientists even gave the tail a silly name: a **thagomizer**. It just means the spiky part of her tail."

Milo tried the word. "Thag-oh-mizer. That's a funny word!"

Juno giggled. "Thagomizer, thagomizer!"

The Stegosaurus swished her tail gently, and CLACK CLACK, the spikes knocked together like wind chimes.

Juno covered his ears, laughing. "It's like music!"

Milo had an idea. "We should build one out of LEGO, with plates that click on like puzzle pieces."

"Snap-on plates," Terra said. "I like how you think."

The Stegosaurus walked on, swishing her tail, CLACK CLACK, like she was waving goodbye with it.

Juno waved back with his whole arm. "Bye bye, thagomizer tail!"

Milo waved too, already sketching the snap-on plates in his head, brick by brick.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Brave Beach Hunter
chapters.text:
They reached a sunny beach cliff. Waves crashed below. WHOOSH, SPLASH.

A girl with a little hammer tapped at the rocks. "Hi!" she said. "I'm Mary."

Milo looked closer. "Are you looking for dinosaurs?"

"Not quite," Mary said, smiling. "I look for old sea creatures that lived back when dinosaurs did. They turn into **fossils** too, but they're big swimming reptiles, not dinosaurs at all."

Juno frowned. "Not dinosaurs? But they're old and giant?"

"That's right," Terra said. "Animals called **plesiosaurs** and **mosasaurs** swam in the ocean while dinosaurs walked on land. They just weren't dinosaurs themselves."

Mary tapped gently, and a curved shape appeared in the rock. "There we go."

"Whoa!" Milo leaned in. "How do you know where to look?"

"Lots of practice," Mary said. "I've been doing this since I was your age. People who study old bones when they grow up are called **paleontologists**. I was one of the very first."

Juno clapped. "You're so brave!"

"Thank you," Mary said, brushing dirt from the fossil. "It takes patience, and a little bit of luck."

Milo picked up a small rock and tapped it like Mary, very gently. "Can I try?"

"Of course," Mary said. "Just be gentle, and careful with the rocks."

Juno tapped too, giggling with each little knock. "Tap tap tap!"

Nothing turned up for the boys that day, but they didn't mind one bit. They had a beach, a hammer, and a brave new friend.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Dinosaurs Everywhere
chapters.text:
The sky began to turn orange. "It's almost time," Terra said.

Juno tugged her leg. "Do we have to go?"

"Not yet," Terra said. "One more thing first."

She led them to a quiet hill. "A very, very long time after the first dinosaurs, about **66 million years** later, something big changed on Earth. Most dinosaurs disappeared, all around the same time."

Juno's lip wobbled. "All of them? Forever?"

"Not quite all," Terra said gently. "Some small, feathery dinosaurs lived on. Over a very long time, they turned into something you know very well."

Milo thought hard. "Birds?"

"Birds," Terra said, smiling. "Every bird you've ever seen is a tiny bit dinosaur. So really, dinosaurs never totally left."

Juno looked up, and right then, a bird flew overhead, chirping.

"Hi, dinosaur bird!" Juno yelled, waving both arms.

Milo grinned. "That's so cool. Dinosaurs are still everywhere."

"Everywhere you look," Terra agreed.

The red brick floated closer, glowing warm and bright.

"Time to go home," Terra said. "Play well, you two."

Milo hugged her leg. "Bye, Terra! Thank you!"

Juno waved his little fossil bone. "Bye bye, Mud Muncher! Bye, turkey dinosaur!"

WHOOOOSH! The mud and trees spun away into warm, swirly light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
THUMP. They landed back on the soft carpet.

The LEGO tower stood right where they left it, still clicking tight.

Juno looked down at his hand. He was still holding the little fossil bone from the beach.

"Whoa," Milo whispered. "Juno, you brought something back!"

Juno turned it over, and over. "My very own dinosaur treasure."

Milo looked at his own hands, and an idea popped into his head. "Let's build a LEGO Triceratops. With a snap-on frill, just like Terra's."

Juno nodded hard. "And a thagomizer tail!"

They grabbed bricks and started clicking pieces together, right there on the carpet floor. CLICK. CLICK. CLICK.

The red brick on top of the tower glowed one last soft time, then went dark and still, waiting for the next adventure.

Milo yawned, holding up his half-built dinosaur. Juno yawned right back, still gripping his little fossil bone tight.

Outside the window, the moon was already up, round and quiet, like it had been watching the whole time.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: The very first dinosaurs lived about **230 million years ago**.
A Triceratops has **three horns** and a big bony collar called a **frill**.
Argentinosaurus might have grown longer than **100 feet** — that's really, really long!
A scientist named **Richard Owen** made up the word **dinosaur** in **1842**. It means 'terrible lizard.'
A T. rex tooth could be **12 inches** long, as long as a ruler.
One famous T. rex skeleton is nicknamed **Sue**, found in **South Dakota** in **1990**.
A story says a farmer's dog once dug up a dinosaur bone, but that part might be made up.
A Velociraptor was really only about the size of a **turkey**, not a giant like in movies.
Lots of dinosaurs, like Velociraptor, had soft **feathers**.
A Stegosaurus had bony plates on its back and a spiky tail called a **thagomizer**.
Old dinosaur bones that turned hard like rock are called **fossils**.
Big swimming reptiles called **plesiosaurs** and **mosasaurs** lived in the ocean at the same time as dinosaurs, but weren't dinosaurs themselves.
Birds today are related to dinosaurs, so dinosaurs never totally disappeared.
Most dinosaurs disappeared about **66 million years** after they first showed up.

new_recurring.name: Terra the Triceratops
new_recurring.rule: A calm, friendly Triceratops guide who appears whenever the magic brick glows for a dinosaur adventure. She explains facts gently, says 'Play well' like the kids, and leads them safely home at the end.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: The adventure ended with Juno still holding a tiny fossil bone he had found on the ancient beach, and the magic red brick glowing once more before going dark atop their LEGO tower.

fact_pack.summary: Dinosaurs were a group of reptiles that lived on Earth for over 160 million years, long before humans existed. They came in sizes from as small as a chicken to as big as a school bus, and today we learn about them from fossils dug up all over the world.

facts.text: Dinosaurs first appeared about 230 million years ago, during the Triassic period.
Most non-bird dinosaurs went extinct about 66 million years ago at the end of the Cretaceous period.
Many scientists believe a huge asteroid struck Earth near modern-day Mexico, causing the mass extinction that ended the age of dinosaurs.
The word 'dinosaur' means 'terrible lizard' in Greek, coined by scientist Richard Owen in 1842.
Argentinosaurus may have been the largest dinosaur, estimated to be over 30 meters (100 feet) long.
Tyrannosaurus rex had teeth up to 30 centimeters (12 inches) long, including the root.
Velociraptor was actually about the size of a turkey, much smaller than shown in movies.
Many dinosaurs, including Velociraptor, are now believed to have had feathers.
Birds are considered modern-day descendants of theropod dinosaurs, so dinosaurs never fully disappeared.
The Stegosaurus had bony plates along its back and spikes on its tail called a 'thagomizer.'
Triceratops had three horns on its face and a large bony frill to protect its neck.
Fossils form when an animal's remains are buried quickly and minerals slowly replace the bone over thousands of years.
Mary Anning, an English fossil hunter born in 1799, discovered important marine reptile fossils near Lyme Regis.
The first scientifically named dinosaur was Megalosaurus, described by William Buckland in 1824.
'Sue' is the nickname of one of the largest and most complete T. rex skeletons ever found, discovered in South Dakota in 1990.
Pterosaurs could fly but were not technically dinosaurs; they were flying reptiles related to them.
Plesiosaurs and Mosasaurs lived in the oceans at the same time as dinosaurs but were not dinosaurs themselves.
Some dinosaurs, like Maiasaura, cared for their babies in nests, which scientists learned from fossilized nesting sites in Montana.
The Spinosaurus is believed to be the largest known carnivorous dinosaur, possibly longer than T. rex, and may have spent time swimming.
Dinosaur footprints, called trace fossils, have been found preserved in hardened mud in places like Texas and China.
The Gobi Desert in Mongolia and China is one of the richest places in the world for finding dinosaur fossils.
Some dinosaurs, like Microraptor, had four wings and could glide between trees.
Paleontologists are scientists who study fossils to learn how dinosaurs lived, moved, and ate.
A popular story says a farmer's dog once dug up part of a famous dinosaur fossil; this detail is likely exaggerated folklore rather than confirmed history.
