story.title: Max, Sami, and the Brick That Started Everything
story.subtitle: A journey through ninety years of clicking plastic, with one competitive brother and one extremely patient one.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Carpenter in Billund (1932)
chapters.text:
Max was three gear ratios into building a robot arm out of LEGO Technic pieces, and Sami was on the floor beside him, drawing the next version before Max had even finished the first. That was how it always went. Max built. Sami designed something better. Max got competitive about it.

"I just need a stronger elbow joint," Max muttered, digging through the bin for a longer axle. His hand closed around something that wasn't an axle at all — a single old brick, gray and scratched, way heavier than plastic should be.

"Where'd that come from?" Sami asked, looking up from her sketchbook.

Neither of them knew. But when Max pressed it against one of Sami's bricks, just to see if it would even click, the brick went warm, then hot, then it lit up amber from the inside, like a tiny lightbulb had switched on under the studs — the little round bumps on top.

**WHOOOSH.**

The bedroom folded away like a page turning. When it unfolded again, Max and Sami were standing in a small wooden workshop that smelled like fresh-cut pine, sawdust drifting in a shaft of sunlight.

A man in a carpenter's apron looked up from a half-finished stepladder, not even surprised. "You're earlier than most," he said. "I'm Ole Kirk Christiansen. Welcome to Billund."

"Billund... Denmark?" Sami said. She'd seen the word on the bottom of a LEGO box.

"The very one," Ole Kirk said. "**1932.** I make wooden toys here. Ducks, mostly. And stepladders, because wooden ducks don't pay all the bills."

Max picked up a little wooden duck from the workbench and turned it over, checking the joints like he checked his Technic builds. "No wheels. No gears. Just... wood?"

"Just wood," Ole Kirk agreed. "For now."

Sami noticed he said *for now* like a man already thinking about his next idea. She liked that. It was the same look she got right before a drawing turned into something completely different from what she'd planned.

The brick in Max's pocket gave a small, impatient pulse of warmth, like it was saying: *keep going.*

"There's more, isn't there," Max said. It wasn't really a question.

Ole Kirk smiled and went back to his stepladder. "Oh, there's a lot more."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Play Well (1934)
chapters.text:
The workshop was the same, but the sign over the door was new — somebody had just finished painting it, and the paint still looked wet.

**LEGO**.

"That's a weird word," Sami said, head tilted, already imagining how she'd draw the letters bigger, bolder, with little bricks for serifs.

Ole Kirk clearly loved that question. "**1934.** I squashed together two Danish words — *leg godt*. It means **'play well.'**"

Max said it out loud a few times, the way you test a part before you trust it. "Leg-oh. Lego. Huh. That actually works."

"There's a rumor going around," Ole Kirk added, lowering his voice like he was sharing a secret, even though he was clearly enjoying this part, "that in Latin, an old language people used to use for serious things, *lego* means **'I put together.'** Some people think I planned that too."

"Did you?" Sami asked.

"I did not," Ole Kirk admitted, grinning. "But it's a good story, and I'm not about to correct anyone."

Max snorted. "So it's basically a happy accident."

"The best kind," Ole Kirk said.

Sami had already flipped to a blank page and was sketching the sign, the wet paint, the whole scene, the way she did whenever something felt worth keeping. Max watched her draw the letters and noticed something.

"You wrote it like it clicks together," he said. "The L locks into the E."

Sami looked down at her own drawing, surprised. She hadn't meant to do that. But now that Max said it, she couldn't unsee it, and she liked it better that way.

The brick in Max's pocket pulsed again, warmer this time, like it approved.

"Play well," Ole Kirk said again, like it was a promise he intended to keep for a very long time. "Now go on. Things are about to get a lot less wooden."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Plastic and the First Little Bricks (1947–1949)
chapters.text:
The next WHOOOSH dropped them into a workshop that buzzed and clanked, full of machines Max immediately wanted to take apart.

"**1947,**" said a voice, and this time it was a different, younger man wiping his hands on a rag — Ole Kirk's son, broad-shouldered, clearly the kind of person who liked fixing things himself. "I'm Godtfred. My father bought one of the first plastic-squirting machines in Denmark." He patted a hulking metal contraption that hissed steam. "It melts plastic and shoots it into a mold, and out comes whatever shape the mold is."

"That's basically a 3D printer's great-great-grandfather," Max said, impressed despite himself.

By **1949**, the machine was spitting out small hollow bricks with bumps on top — studs, Sami noted, just like in her drawing. Godtfred called them **Automatic Binding Bricks**, which Sami thought was a terrible name for something so good-looking.

"They don't bind anything," she said, picking one up. She pressed two together. They sat there. Unimpressed. Then she pulled, and they came apart with a soft, sad little pop.

"They're a little loose," Godtfred admitted, rubbing the back of his neck. "We're working on it."

Max, who had spent an entire weekend arguing with his robot arm's elbow joint until it finally held tight, understood the problem immediately. "You need something underneath. Not just bumps on top — something on the bottom that grabs them."

Godtfred went very still, the way people do right before a good idea lands on them. He grabbed a pencil and a scrap of paper. "Say that again."

"Something underneath," Max repeated, feeling, for one brief and extremely satisfying moment, like the smartest engineer in Denmark. "Tubes. Hollow tubes that hug the bumps on the brick below."

Godtfred stared at the sketch forming under his own pencil like he hadn't quite believed it would look that simple.

"Come back in a few years," he said. "I think you just saved me some time."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Click Heard Around the World (1958)
chapters.text:
When the brick pulsed them forward again, the workshop had grown into something closer to a real factory, and Godtfred was older, calmer, holding a single brick up to the light like a jeweler inspecting a diamond.

"**January 28th, 1958,**" he said. "Today I filed the **patent** — that's a kind of legal promise that says this design is mine, and nobody else gets to copy it without asking. Tubes underneath, studs on top. Take a look."

He flipped the brick over. Sami leaned in and gasped, delighted, because there they were — the exact tubes Max had described, hollow and round, waiting to grab the next brick's bumps.

"Try it," Godtfred said.

Max pressed two bricks together. **CLICK.** He pulled. Nothing happened. He pulled harder. Still nothing. He turned to Sami with the particular smugness of an older brother about to win an argument neither of them was having. "It holds."

"Everyone can hear that it holds, Max," Sami said, rolling her eyes, but she was grinning.

Godtfred reached into his coat pocket and pulled out something small and gray. He set it on the table next to a shiny new one, fresh off the machine.

"Try this one too," he said.

Max clicked the old scratched brick — the very same kind of brick that had started this whole adventure — onto the brand-new one. It locked in exactly the same way, snug and certain, like no time had passed between them at all.

"That old brick in your pocket," Godtfred said, nodding at the one Max had carried through three different years, "was made the same year as this one. And it still fits a brick made decades later, because the design barely changed. A **1958** brick clicks into a brick made this morning."

Sami looked down at the two bricks locked together and thought about how her sketchbook had a drawing from first grade and a drawing from last week, and how different they looked, and how nothing she owned fit together across that much time except, apparently, this.

"That's kind of amazing," she said quietly.

"IT CLICKS!" Max yelled, because somebody had to say it out loud, and it might as well be him.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Fire, Plastic, and a Park Full of Bricks (1960–1968)
chapters.text:
The next landing was colder. Sami smelled smoke before she saw anything, and her stomach dropped — but Godtfred was standing calmly in front of them, arms crossed, watching the last curls of smoke drift up from a burned-out warehouse a safe distance away. Nobody was near the building. Nobody was in danger.

"**1960,**" Godtfred said. "That warehouse held every wooden toy we had left in storage. Fire got it overnight. Everyone got out fine — it was just the toys."

"That's terrible," Sami said.

"It was," Godtfred agreed. "But it also made the decision easy. We stopped making wooden toys after that and put everything into the plastic bricks instead."

Max understood that kind of thing better than he expected to. "Like when your first robot design fails and you just... start the next one better."

"Exactly like that," Godtfred said.

By **1963**, the company had switched to a tougher plastic called **ABS** — it didn't crack as easily and it kept its color instead of fading, which Sami appreciated immediately, since faded colors were the enemy of any good drawing.

Then the brick pulsed them forward one more time, into bright sunshine and the sound of hundreds of kids laughing. A model windmill built entirely out of bricks spun lazily nearby, taller than Max.

"**1968,**" Godtfred said, spreading his arms. "Welcome to the first LEGOLAND, right here in Billund, built on the same ground as my father's old workshop."

Max looked around at kids running between giant brick sculptures and felt, for once, like competing with Sami over who built the better robot arm seemed delightfully small. "You built an entire park out of this stuff."

"We built an entire park out of *your* idea," Godtfred said, pointing at him, "roughly. The tubes. Don't let it go to your head."

"Too late," Max said, and Sami laughed so hard she nearly dropped her sketchbook.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Gears, Faces, and a New Boss (1969–1979)
chapters.text:
This time the brick deposited them in a nursery full of much bigger, chunkier bricks, clearly built for much smaller hands.

"**1969,**" Godtfred explained, handing Sami a fat plastic brick she could have worn as a bracelet. "**DUPLO** — sized for toddlers, but it still clicks onto regular bricks. Nobody gets left out."

Sami immediately pictured her baby cousin building alongside her someday and decided this was the single best invention so far, which was saying something.

Then — and this was the moment Max had secretly been hoping for the entire trip — the scene shifted to a table scattered with gears, axles, and long gray beams.

"**1977,**" said a new voice. A younger designer held up a beam with holes down its length. "We call it **Technic**. Real gears. Real moving parts. Bricks that do things, not just sit there looking good."

Max picked up a beam like he was greeting an old friend. "This is... this is literally what I build with. Every weekend. This exact stuff."

"Good," the designer said. "Then you already know what to do with it."

One table over, Sami found something even better: a little yellow figure with movable arms, a round head, and a separate hat that popped right off.

"**1978,**" the designer said. "First **minifigure**. Swap the hats, swap the faces, make a thousand different people out of the same little body."

Sami swapped the hat for a different one, then a third, already redesigning the figure's whole personality with each change. "I could draw a hundred different outfits for this guy."

"People have drawn a lot more than a hundred," the designer said.

Last stop: a confident young man shaking hands with half the factory floor at once. "**1979,**" he said. "Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen. Ole Kirk's grandson. I grew up playing with these exact bricks, and now I'm running the place."

"Family business," Max said approvingly.

"The best kind," Kjeld agreed, echoing his grandfather without knowing it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Tires, Space Battles, and a Very Close Call
chapters.text:
The brick's next jump skipped forward fast, like flipping through years instead of walking through them.

"Quick fact before we move on," Kjeld said, catching them mid-WHOOOSH. "Because the company makes so many tiny rubber tires for sets, some people say LEGO is one of the biggest tire makers in the world — just counting how many tires, not how big they are. We're not out there making truck tires. Just a lot of very, very small ones."

"That might be a slight exaggeration," Sami said, "but I love it anyway."

"**1999,**" Kjeld continued, as shelves around them filled with tiny spaceships and figures Max actually recognized. "First LEGO Star Wars sets. People went a little crazy for those."

Around the year 2000, a glowing newspaper headline floated past calling the LEGO brick a **Toy of the Century** — which Max thought was a fairly big claim for something that started as a wooden duck.

Then the mood shifted. The factory looked quieter, a little worried.

"Early 2000s," Kjeld said, more serious now. "We hit a hard time. Spent money on too many different things at once and nearly ran out. It was close."

"Did it... shut down?" Sami asked, and for a second the question hung there, genuinely uncertain.

"No," said a new man stepping forward, calm and direct. "I'm Jorgen. Became the person in charge — the **CEO** — in **2004**. We went back to basics. Focused on the bricks. It worked."

Max exhaled, surprised at how relieved he actually felt.

By **2014**, a giant screen lit up showing a movie theater packed with kids watching tiny plastic people have an enormous adventure.

"**The LEGO Movie**," Jorgen said, smiling now. "Turns out everyone still loved the bricks. They just needed reminding."

"I could've told you that," Max said, nodding at the Technic beam still in his pocket.

"Next time," Jorgen said, "call us first."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Bedroom Floor
chapters.text:
The final WHOOOSH was gentler than the rest, like the brick knew they were almost home.

Max and Sami landed back on the bedroom carpet exactly where they'd started, the half-built Technic arm still sitting between them, Sami's sketchbook still open to the page she'd been drawing on. No time had passed at all, as far as the clock on the wall was concerned.

But the old gray brick in Max's hand had gone cool and quiet now, like it was resting after a long trip.

"Headquarters is still in Billund," Sami said slowly, piecing it together out loud, the way she did when a drawing was finally coming together. "Same ground as the old workshop."

"And it's still a family thing," Max added. "Kirkbi — that's them, Ole Kirk's family — they still own most of it."

Sami looked down at the brick, then at the half-finished robot arm, then at her own sketchbook full of redesigns Max hadn't built yet.

"You know what's funny," she said. "Every single idea we saw back there started because somebody looked at a brick and thought, *this could be better.*"

Max picked up the old brick and clicked it onto the elbow joint of his robot arm, right where the weak spot had been bugging him for days. It held. Properly held, the way Godtfred's bricks had held sixty-some years ago, because apparently nothing about that part had ever really needed fixing.

"Elbow's done," Max said, testing it with a satisfied grin.

"Then draw me the next part," he added, nudging Sami's sketchbook toward her.

Sami was already uncapping her pencil.

Tomorrow, there was a shoulder joint to figure out — and, knowing the two of them, an argument about whose idea it had really been.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there was a shoulder joint to figure out.

true_facts.text: **Ole Kirk Christiansen** started the company in **Billund, Denmark**, in **1932**, making wooden toys and stepladders.
In **1934** the company got the name **LEGO**, short for two Danish words meaning **'play well.'**
People sometimes say *lego* means **'I put together'** in an old language called Latin — fun, but probably just a coincidence, not the real reason for the name.
In **1949** the company made **Automatic Binding Bricks** — early plastic bricks with bumps on top, but they didn't hold together very well yet.
**Godtfred Kirk Christiansen** added hollow tubes underneath the bricks to grip the bumps below, and that design was officially promised as his own — a **patent** — on **January 28, 1958**.
A brick made in **1958** still clicks perfectly onto a brand new brick today, because the design has barely changed.
A **1960** fire burned up the company's leftover wooden toys, and afterward they decided to make only plastic bricks from then on.
The very first LEGOLAND theme park opened in **Billund** in **1968**, right next to the original workshop.

fact_pack.summary: LEGO began as a small Danish carpenter's workshop in 1932 and grew into one of the world's best-loved toys, built around a simple plastic brick that clicks together and never goes out of style. Along the way the company survived a warehouse fire and a near-bankruptcy, while keeping every brick compatible with every other brick ever made.

facts.text: Carpenter Ole Kirk Christiansen founded the company in Billund, Denmark, in 1932, first making wooden toys and stepladders.
In 1934 Christiansen named his company LEGO, a shortening of the Danish phrase 'leg godt,' meaning 'play well.'
A popular story notes that 'lego' also happens to mean 'I put together' in Latin, though this seems to be a happy coincidence rather than the real reason for the name.
LEGO began working with plastic in 1947, becoming one of the first Danish companies to own a plastic injection-molding machine.
In 1949 the company produced 'Automatic Binding Bricks,' hollow studded plastic bricks that were the direct ancestor of the modern LEGO brick.
Ole Kirk's son Godtfred Kirk Christiansen redesigned the brick with hollow tubes underneath, and the new locking brick was patented on 28 January 1958.
A brick made in 1958 still fits perfectly with a LEGO brick made today because the tube-and-stud design has barely changed.
A 1960 fire destroyed the company's wooden-toy warehouse, and afterward the family decided to stop making wooden toys and focus only on plastic bricks.
In 1963 LEGO switched its brick material to ABS plastic, which resists cracking and keeps its color much better than the earlier plastic.
The first LEGOLAND theme park opened in Billund in 1968, right next to the original factory.
DUPLO bricks, sized just right for toddlers and still compatible with regular LEGO bricks, were introduced in 1969.
The LEGO Technic line, adding gears, axles and beams for more mechanical builds, launched in 1977.
The first LEGO minifigures, with movable arms and swappable heads and hats, appeared in 1978.
Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen, grandson of the founder, took over leadership of the company in 1979, keeping it in family hands for another generation.
Because so many tiny rubber tires are made for LEGO sets, the company is sometimes called one of the world's biggest tire producers by count, though it makes no full-size tires.
LEGO launched its first Star Wars sets in 1999, beginning a long line of licensed themes based on movies and games.
The Fortune Encyclopedia and other outlets named the LEGO brick a top 'Toy of the Century' around the year 2000.
In the early 2000s the LEGO Group ran into serious financial trouble and came close to bankruptcy.
Jorgen Vig Knudstorp became CEO in 2004 and led a turnaround that focused the company back on its core brick sets.
In 2014 The LEGO Movie brought LEGO characters to cinemas worldwide and became a major box-office success.
The LEGO Group is still headquartered in Billund, Denmark, on the same ground where Ole Kirk's workshop once stood.
The Kirkbi family, descendants of Ole Kirk Christiansen, remain the majority owners of the LEGO Group today.

story.title: Ada and the Magnet Robot
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip through pulling, pushing, and the giant magnet called Earth.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Fridge
chapters.text:
Ada lined up her fridge magnets into a wobbly robot shape on the kitchen fridge. She always built robots out of her favorite magnets before bed.

Tonight, one magnet buzzed under her finger. It felt warm, like a little heartbeat.

"Hello?" Ada whispered.

The magnet robot wiggled. Two tiny eyes blinked open. "Hello, Ada," it said in a clicky voice. "I'm Bolt. Want to see how I work?"

Ada grinned so big her cheeks hurt. "Yes!"

Bolt hummed, and the fridge door swirled like silver water. Ada stepped through — and landed somewhere humming with invisible pulls.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Push, Pull, Click!
chapters.text:
Two big magnets floated in front of Ada, sliding closer, then jumping apart.

"Why won't they touch?" Ada asked.

Bolt landed on one end. "Every magnet has two ends," he said. "We call them **poles** — a **north** end and a **south** end."

Ada poked the floating magnets. When she turned one around, it snapped straight to the other with a loud **CLICK!**

"Opposite poles **pull together**," Bolt said. "But two of the same kind **push apart**."

Ada flipped the magnet back and forth, giggling as it clicked and bounced, clicked and bounced.

"It's like a dance," she said. "A pulling, pushing dance!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Tiny Spinning Dancers
chapters.text:
Bolt pressed a button on his chest, and everything got tiny. Ada found herself standing inside a piece of metal.

Little dots spun everywhere, each one humming like a top.

"Those are **electrons**," Bolt said. "Tiny spinning bits inside every atom. When they spin the same way, they act like their own little magnets."

Ada watched clumps of electrons line up in neat rows, like kids holding hands.

"When lots of them point the same way," Bolt said, "the whole piece of metal becomes magnetic. We call each lined-up group a **domain**."

But in a wooden block nearby, the little dots pointed every which way, messy as scribbles.

"That's why wood isn't magnetic," Ada said. "Nobody's lining up!"

"Exactly," said Bolt, spinning with pride.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Invisible Hug
chapters.text:
Back at full size, Bolt set a magnet on the table. A paperclip zoomed across and stuck, even though nothing touched it.

"What's pulling it?" Ada asked.

"An invisible **magnetic field**," Bolt said. "It's the stretchy space around a magnet where its push and pull work."

"Can I see it?" Ada asked.

Bolt sprinkled tiny iron bits — like silver sugar — around the magnet. They curved into loops, swooping from one end to the other.

"Whoa," Ada breathed. "It's like the magnet is drawing itself!"

"That's the shape of its field," Bolt said, "from the north pole, curling all the way to the south."

Ada traced the loops with her finger, careful not to touch the magnet.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Rock That Pointed
chapters.text:
Bolt's fridge-door swirl opened onto a rocky hillside, long, long ago.

A traveler held up a strange black rock. It kept sticking to his iron knife.

"That's **lodestone**," Bolt said. "A rock from the ground that's already magnetic. People near a place called **Magnesia** found it first."

"Is that where the word magnet comes from?" Ada asked.

"Good guess," Bolt said. "Most people think so."

Later, Bolt showed her travelers floating a lodestone on a leaf in water. It turned, slow and steady, until it pointed the same direction every time.

"That's an early **compass**," Bolt said. "People used it to find their way, over two thousand years ago."

Ada spun the leaf herself, giggling as it swung back to the same spot, again and again.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Giant Magnet Called Earth
chapters.text:
Bolt zoomed them high into the sky. Below them, the whole Earth hung like a blue marble.

"Guess what," Bolt said. "This whole planet is a magnet too."

Ada's eyes went wide. "The whole Earth?"

"Deep, deep inside," Bolt said, "melted iron swirls around and around. That swirling makes Earth act like one giant bar magnet."

Bolt handed her a tiny compass. Its needle spun, wobbled, then settled, pointing the same way no matter how Ada turned around.

"The needle's north end gets pulled toward Earth's magnetic north," Bolt said.

Ada spun in a circle three times. The needle didn't budge. "It always knows the way!"

"That's how sailors never got lost," Bolt said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Magnet You Can Switch Off
chapters.text:
Bolt led Ada to a junkyard where a giant crane swung overhead.

CLUNK! It lifted a rusty old car straight off the ground, no hooks, no ropes.

Ada gasped. "How is it just staying up there?"

"That crane has an **electromagnet**," Bolt said. "Wrap wire in a coil, zap it with electricity, and it turns into a magnet — one you can switch on and off."

The crane operator flipped a switch. CLUNK! The car dropped gently onto a pile.

"On for pulling, off for letting go," Bolt said.

Then Bolt handed Ada a bar magnet and a tiny saw. "Cut it in half. Go on."

Ada did. Both halves instantly had their own north and south ends.

"Two whole magnets," Ada laughed, "out of one!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Trains That Float, Birds That Know the Way
chapters.text:
Next, Bolt showed Ada a sleek train gliding with no wheels touching the track.

"It's floating!" Ada shouted.

"Strong magnets push the whole train up," Bolt said. "Without rubbing on the rails, it can zoom super fast. We call that a **maglev** train."

Ada touched a gold ring and a penny nearby. Neither one stuck to her magnet.

"Gold and copper don't stick," Bolt said. "Only some metals, like iron, really answer a magnet's pull."

High above, a line of birds flew past in a V shape.

"Some birds, turtles, and fish," Bolt said, "can feel Earth's magnetic field too. It helps them find their way on long trips."

Ada waved at the birds. "Safe travels!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to the Fridge
chapters.text:
The silver swirl opened once more, and Ada stepped back into her kitchen.

Bolt shrank down onto the fridge, settling among the other magnets.

"One last thing," Bolt said. "Fridge magnets like me are made from bendy rubber mixed with magnet powder. That's why I can bend without falling off."

Ada pressed Bolt flat, then let him spring back, round and happy.

She lined her magnets into a smiling robot face, right where she'd started.

"Goodnight, Bolt," she whispered.

Bolt's eyes blinked slow, like a sleepy wink. "Goodnight, Ada. Pull in close, and dream away."

Ada climbed into bed, feeling the whole humming, clicking, pulling world tucked safely behind her, on the fridge door.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ada. Pull in close, and dream away.

A magnet has an invisible stretchy space around it called a **magnetic field**, where its pull works.
Sprinkling tiny iron bits near a magnet shows curvy loops — the shape of its magnetic field.
A naturally magnetic rock called **lodestone** was first found near a place called Magnesia.
People long ago floated a lodestone to make an early **compass**, which always pointed the same way.

fact_pack.summary: Magnets are objects that pull on iron and a few other metals using an invisible force called magnetism. This pack explains why magnets attract and repel, how Earth itself is a giant magnet, and the people and discoveries behind our understanding of magnetism.

facts.text: A magnet has two ends called poles, a north pole and a south pole, where the magnetic force is strongest.
Opposite poles attract each other (north pulls south), while like poles repel each other (north pushes north away).
Magnetism comes from the movement of tiny particles called electrons inside atoms, which act like tiny spinning magnets themselves.
In magnetic materials like iron, nickel, and cobalt, groups of atoms called magnetic domains can line up in the same direction to create a strong overall magnetic field.
In most materials the atoms' tiny magnetic fields point in random directions, which is why most objects, like wood or plastic, are not magnetic.
A magnetic field is the invisible area around a magnet where its force can push or pull on other magnetic objects.
You can see the shape of a magnetic field by sprinkling iron filings near a magnet; they line up in curved lines from pole to pole.
The ancient Greeks discovered a naturally magnetic rock called lodestone near a region called Magnesia, which is likely where the word 'magnet' comes from.
The Chinese used lodestones to make the first compasses more than 2,000 years ago, helping travelers find direction.
Earth itself acts like a giant bar magnet because of swirling liquid iron deep in its core, and this is called Earth's magnetic field.
A compass needle points north because it lines up with Earth's magnetic field, with its north pole attracted toward the planet's magnetic north.
Confusingly, Earth's magnetic north pole actually behaves like a magnetic south pole, which is why opposite-pole attraction pulls compass needles there.
In 1820, Danish scientist Hans Christian Oersted discovered that electricity flowing through a wire creates a magnetic field, linking electricity and magnetism for the first time.
English scientist Michael Faraday showed in 1831 that moving a magnet near a wire could create electric current, an idea now used in generators that make our electricity.
An electromagnet is a magnet made by wrapping wire into a coil and running electric current through it, and it can be switched on and off.
Electromagnets are used in everyday things like doorbells, loudspeakers, electric motors, and giant cranes that lift old cars in junkyards.
If you cut a bar magnet in half, you do not get a separate north piece and south piece; each new piece becomes its own smaller magnet with both a north and south pole.
Heating a magnet to a very high temperature, called its Curie point, can make it lose its magnetism because the heat jumbles up its lined-up atoms.
Not all metals are magnetic: for example, aluminum, gold, copper, and silver are not attracted to ordinary magnets.
Some of the strongest magnets made today are called neodymium magnets, made from a mix of iron, boron, and the rare-earth metal neodymium.
Maglev trains use powerful magnets to float above their tracks and glide forward without touching the rails, reducing friction and allowing very high speeds.
Hospitals use giant, extremely strong magnets inside MRI machines to take detailed pictures inside the human body without any cutting.
Some animals, like birds, sea turtles, and some fish, are believed to sense Earth's magnetic field to help them navigate during long migrations.
Refrigerator magnets are usually made from flexible rubber mixed with magnetic powder, which is why they can bend without losing their stick.

story.title: Nora and the Buried City of Pompeii
story.subtitle: A mosaic tile glows, and a whole Roman town wakes up under the ash.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Tile That Warmed Up
chapters.text:
Nora sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor, snapping tiny glass squares into a picture of a dolphin. It was almost bedtime, but one more tile wouldn't hurt.

She picked up a chip of blue glass. It was warm. Not sun-warm. Glowing-warm.

The tile hummed, soft and low, like a bee caught in a jar. Then the floor tilted, the dolphin picture spun into gold light, and Nora wasn't in her bedroom anymore.

She stood on a stone street, in bright sun, with the smell of bread and the sound of a hundred voices.

"Welcome," said a small voice. The blue tile floated at her shoulder, tiny and bright as a star. "I used to be part of a floor. Floors remember a lot."

"Where are we?" Nora asked.

"A town called **Pompeii**," said the tile. "Near a city called **Naples**, in what is now southern Italy." The word *southern* just meant the bottom part of the map.

Nora looked around. Shops lined the street. People carried baskets. A man sold olives from a big jar.

"How many people live here?" she asked, counting doorways until she lost track at twenty.

"Somewhere between **eleven thousand and fifteen thousand**," said the tile. "Shops, baths, theaters, temples — a whole busy town."

"That's more than my whole school!" Nora said, and the tile wobbled, which was its way of laughing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Stepping Stones and Secret Pipes
chapters.text:
Nora's shoe splashed in a puddle, and she hopped back with a squeak.

"Careful," said the tile. "But look down."

Across the street sat three flat stones, raised up like little islands, with gaps between them.

Nora hopped from stone to stone, dry the whole way. "It's a bridge for feet!"

"Exactly," said the tile. "The **stepping stones** kept people's sandals dry, while carts still rolled right through the gaps underneath."

A cart rumbled past, its wheels fitting the gaps perfectly, and Nora grinned.

At the corner, water trickled from a stone fountain shaped like a face. Nora cupped her hands and felt it splash cool.

"How does water get all the way up here?" she asked.

"**Pipes**," said the tile. "Long metal tubes carried water under the streets, all the way to fountains like this one."

"So Romans had their own secret water tunnels," Nora said, tracing the fountain's carved eyebrows with one finger. "Sneaky."

"Clever," the tile corrected, bobbing happily. "There's a difference."

Nora splashed one more handful at the tile just to see it dodge, and it did, which made her laugh out loud in the middle of the street.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Stone Bowl
chapters.text:
A roar rolled down the street, and Nora froze. Then she heard clapping, and cheering, and realized it was just a crowd.

Ahead stood a huge oval building, like a stone bowl turned on its side.

"What is THAT?" Nora asked, tipping her head all the way back.

"An **amphitheater**," said the tile. "A giant round stage for games, built about **70 years before the eruption** that buried this town. One of the oldest ever found."

"What kind of games?" Nora asked.

"Contests, called gladiator games," said the tile gently. "People came from all around to watch."

Nora climbed a few stone steps and sat down where thousands once sat. She imagined the noise, the fans, the sun on stone seats.

"It's like a stadium," she said.

"The very first kind," said the tile.

She traced a crack in the step with her finger. "Pompeii even had a nickname," the tile added. "Some people think its name may come from an old word meaning **'five,'** maybe for five little villages that joined together to make one town."

"Five friends who became one team," Nora said, and the tile glowed a little brighter, as if it liked that.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Mountain Wakes Up
chapters.text:
The ground gave a tiny shiver under Nora's shoes, and she grabbed the tile.

"It's all right," said the tile. "That mountain over there has woken up before."

Nora looked past the rooftops at a tall green mountain, smoke curling lazily from its top.

"That's **Mount Vesuvius**," said the tile. "A **volcano** — a mountain that can shoot out hot ash and rock."

"Is it going to do that now?" Nora asked, eyes wide.

"Not while we're standing here," said the tile. "But on **August 24th, in the year 79**, it did."

The sky in Nora's mind turned dark and strange, far across the water.

"A young Roman named **Pliny the Younger** watched it happen from across the bay," said the tile. "He wrote two long letters describing everything he saw — so carefully that scientists still use his words today to understand this kind of eruption."

"So he was like a news reporter," Nora said. "Before cameras."

"Before pencils were even common," said the tile. "Ash fell for two days, until it covered the whole town, as deep as **twenty feet** in places. Deeper than your house is tall."

Nora hugged her knees, quiet for a moment. "That's a lot of ash."

"It is," said the tile softly. "And it's why we can visit here at all."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Bread That Waited
chapters.text:
Nora smelled something warm and crusty, drifting from a little stone oven.

"Someone's baking," she said, stepping closer.

Inside the oven sat a round loaf, scored with lines like a pie, perfectly shaped.

"That loaf has been sitting there for a very long time," said the tile. "Almost **two thousand years**. The ash covered it so fast that it never burned, never crumbled. Diggers found it still marked with the baker's own stamp."

"It's still a bread shape," Nora whispered, leaning in without touching.

"That's the strange magic of ash," said the tile. "It sealed this town shut like a lid on a jar. Paintings on walls stayed bright. Even messages people scribbled stayed readable."

"Like a time capsule," Nora said.

"Like the biggest time capsule anyone ever opened," agreed the tile.

Nora peeked around the corner of the bakery and spotted words painted on the outside wall in faded red letters.

"What does that say?" she asked.

"An old advertisement," said the tile. "Romans painted messages right on their walls — ads for shops, even messages about elections. Like sidewalk chalk that never washed away."

Nora grinned. "I'm definitely painting my door when I get home."

"Please don't," said the tile, and Nora laughed so hard she nearly knocked over the bread.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Town by the Sea
chapters.text:
The tile led Nora along a path that curved toward the water, salty wind in her hair.

"There's another town near here," said the tile. "Smaller, right by the sea, called **Herculaneum**. The same eruption buried it too — but under a different kind of hot, heavy material."

"Different how?" Nora asked.

"It sealed things even tighter," said the tile. "Diggers there found wooden furniture that hadn't rotted away. Even scrolls of paper, still rolled up."

Nora pictured a whole wooden chair, waiting patiently for two thousand years.

"Wood doesn't usually last that long," she said.

"No," said the tile. "But sealed away from air and rain, it can."

They stood at the edge of a cliff, looking down at old stone archways near the water.

"A brave commander named **Pliny the Elder** sailed his ships toward this coast that very day," said the tile, "to try to help the people here."

"That's really brave," Nora said quietly. "Sailing toward the scary mountain instead of away from it."

"It is," agreed the tile. "Some of the bravest people run toward trouble to help, not away from it."

Nora nodded, and tucked that thought away like a little souvenir.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Pictures on the Wall
chapters.text:
Inside a grand house, Nora gasped. The walls were covered in paintings — deep red, bright gold, figures in flowing robes.

"These are called **frescoes**," said the tile. "Paintings made right into wet wall plaster, so they became part of the wall itself."

"They look almost new," Nora said, tracing the air near a painted dancer, careful not to touch.

"The ash protected the colors," said the tile. "This house is famous. People call it the **Villa of the Mysteries**, because nobody is completely sure what the paintings show — maybe a secret ceremony, maybe a celebration."

"A real mystery," Nora said, delighted. "In a house called Mysteries."

"Convenient, isn't it," said the tile.

Nora studied a tiny mosaic on the floor, little colored squares just like the ones in her own bedroom.

"Someone made this with tiles like you," she said.

"Long, long before I was a tile," said the tile, glowing proudly anyway. "Every tiny piece had its place. That's how a mosaic becomes a picture."

"Every tiny piece tells a big story," Nora said slowly, trying the words out.

The tile sparkled. "I like that. Keep it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Digging It Up Again
chapters.text:
The gold light swirled, and the busy street faded into quiet dirt and stone walls, half-buried under earth.

"Where did everyone go?" Nora asked.

"Time passed," said the tile. "For a very long while, this whole town slept under the ground, forgotten."

"Forever?" Nora asked.

"Not forever," said the tile. "In **1748**, workers digging nearby found old walls and objects poking up from the dirt. People realized a whole town was buried right underneath."

Nora watched shadowy figures with shovels, carefully brushing dirt from a painted wall.

"They dig so carefully," she noticed.

"People who study old places like this are called **archaeologists**," said the tile. "They brush away dirt slowly, so nothing gets broken."

"Like unwrapping a present you don't want to tear," Nora said.

"Exactly like that," said the tile. "And even now, only about **two-thirds** of the town has been uncovered. There's still more town waiting under the ground."

Nora's eyes went wide. "So there could be more bread ovens down there? More paintings?"

"Almost certainly," said the tile. "People find new rooms and new paintings still, every single year."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home, With a Tiny Piece
chapters.text:
The gold light swirled one more time, soft and slow, and Nora blinked.

She was back on her bedroom floor, mosaic dolphin still half-finished in front of her.

The little blue tile sat quietly in her palm, not glowing anymore, just an ordinary piece of glass.

"Are you still there?" Nora whispered.

A tiny warmth answered her, like a wink.

"That mountain is still there too," the tile murmured sleepily. "Scientists watch it closely, every day, because so many people live near it now."

"To make sure everyone stays safe," Nora said.

"Exactly," said the tile. "And the buried town you visited is now one of the most visited old places on Earth — millions of people come to walk its streets every single year, just like you did tonight."

Nora pressed the little blue tile into the last empty space of her dolphin mosaic. It clicked into place, perfectly, as if it had always belonged there.

She pulled her blanket up to her chin, thinking of stepping stones, secret pipes, and bread that waited two thousand years just to be found.

"Every tiny piece tells a big story," she murmured, eyes already closing.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Nora. Every tiny piece tells a big story.

story.title: Nora and the Tile from Pompeii
story.subtitle: One tiny mosaic piece opens a whole buried town.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Tile
chapters.text:
Nora sat on her bedroom floor, sorting bright mosaic tiles into piles. Blue, red, gold — she loved building little pictures from tiny squares. It was way past bedtime, but one more pattern wouldn't hurt.

Then she noticed it: a chipped red tile, warm under her finger. She tapped it once, twice, three times, like a knock on a door.

CLICK. The tile glowed like a tiny sun.

"Hello," said a small voice. "I'm a tessera — that's what Romans called a little mosaic tile. Want to see where I came from?"

Before Nora could answer, the glow swallowed the room.

She landed on a sunny street lined with stone buildings. Market sellers called out. Dogs barked. Everything smelled like fresh bread.

"Welcome to Pompeii," said the tessera. "A real Roman town, near where the city of Naples is today. About eleven to fifteen thousand people once lived right here."

"Pompeii," Nora whispered. "Why's it called that?"

"Some say it comes from an old word, *pompe*, meaning 'five' — maybe because five little villages joined to make one town."

Nora grinned. "Five pieces making one picture. Just like a mosaic."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Stones in the Street
chapters.text:
Nora skipped ahead and stopped. Big stone blocks crossed the road, with gaps on either side.

"What are these for?" she asked.

"Stepping stones," said the tessera. "People hopped across without getting muddy feet. Carts rolled right through the gaps between them."

Nora counted the gaps. "One, two... just enough for wheels!"

Nearby, water trickled from a stone fountain shaped like a face.

"Pompeii had pipes under the streets," the tessera said, "carrying water to fountains all over town. People filled their jugs right here."

Nora cupped her hands under the spout. Cool water splashed her fingers.

"Smart town," she said. "They thought of everything."

"They did," said the tessera. "Come on — I want to show you where people cheered the loudest."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Loudest Seats in Town
chapters.text:
A huge oval building rose ahead, bigger than any building Nora had seen.

"What's THAT?" she asked, tipping her head back.

"An amphitheater," said the tessera. "That's an open-air stadium. People built it almost one hundred fifty years before the town was buried — one of the oldest ever found."

Nora climbed onto a stone step. "What did they watch here?"

"Gladiator games," the tessera said. "Brave fighters, roaring crowds, lots of noise."

Nora cupped her hands and shouted into the empty rows. "GO TEAM!"

Her voice echoed back three times.

"I think they heard that one in Naples," laughed the tessera.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: A Strange Cloud
chapters.text:
The sky turned a strange grey-brown. Nora pointed at the mountain across the bay.

"Why is there smoke way up there?"

"That's Mount Vesuvius," said the tessera. "It's a volcano — a mountain that can blow out hot ash and rock. On **August 24th, in the year 79**, it erupted."

Nora felt a flutter of worry. "Are we safe?"

"We're just watching, like a boy named Pliny the Younger did," the tessera said gently. "He stood far across the bay and wrote down everything he saw, like a careful reporter. His letters are why scientists still call this kind of eruption 'Plinian' today."

"So writing can be brave too," Nora said.

"Very brave," said the tessera. "Let's see what the ash left behind."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Frozen in Time
chapters.text:
The glow shimmered, and years rushed by in a blink.

Ash and light rock called pumice had rained down, covering the whole town — as deep as a two-story house.

"That's SO much," Nora gasped.

"It happened fast," said the tessera, "fast enough to keep things exactly as they were. Come look."

Inside a stone bakery, Nora spotted a round loaf, still marked with the baker's own stamp, sitting in the oven.

"That bread is thousands of years old?" Nora asked.

"Baked the same day the ash fell," said the tessera. "Paintings on walls, even silly messages people scribbled outside shops — all kept safe too."

Nora touched the cool stone gently. "It's like a time capsule."

"Exactly like one," said the tessera.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Lost and Found
chapters.text:
The light flickered again. Now workers with shovels stood in a dusty field.

"Where are we now?" Nora asked.

"Many years later," said the tessera. "Pompeii was forgotten for a long, long time — until **1748**, when workers digging here found old walls and ancient things buried below."

Nora watched a worker brush dirt from a stone step — the very one she'd hopped across earlier.

"They found the stepping stones!" she said.

"People called archaeologists kept digging carefully after that," said the tessera. "That's what we call people who dig up the past to learn from it."

Nora clapped. "Pompeii came back."

"In a way," smiled the tessera, "it never really left."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Wooden Doors and Painted Walls
chapters.text:
The tessera led Nora to a smaller town by the sea.

"This is Herculaneum," it said. "Buried by the same eruption, but by a different kind of hot ash. Here, even wooden furniture and old scrolls survived."

Nora peeked into a doorway. "A whole wooden door, after all this time?"

"Amazing, right?" said the tessera.

Back near Pompeii, Nora found a wall covered in bright paintings.

"These are frescoes," said the tessera, "paintings made right onto wet walls. One famous set, in the Villa of the Mysteries, shows a mysterious ceremony nobody's fully explained."

Nora studied the colors — reds, golds, deep blues — and grinned.

"It's like a giant mosaic," she said, "just painted instead of tiled."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Whole Picture
chapters.text:
"One last stop," said the tessera, and the glow swirled again.

Now Nora stood above Pompeii, looking down at stone streets stretching far below.

"Millions of people visit here every year now," said the tessera. "It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site — that means a group of countries agreed to help protect it forever."

"Is it all dug up?" Nora asked.

"Only about two-thirds," said the tessera. "New paintings and rooms are still being found."

"And the volcano?"

"Still there," said the tessera. "Scientists watch it closely, every single day, to keep everyone nearby safe."

Nora nodded slowly. "Every tiny tile tells a story."

"Every tiny tile tells a story," the tessera agreed, and the glow folded back into the little red tile.

Nora blinked. She was back on her bedroom floor, her finished mosaic glowing faintly in the lamp light — tiny stepping stones, a fountain, a round loaf of bread, all pieced together.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Nora. Every tiny tile tells a story. Sleep well, and dream in mosaics.

Only about **two-thirds** of Pompeii has been dug up so far, and new rooms keep turning up.

story.title: Isla and the Lamp of Pompeii
story.subtitle: A midnight dig through the town the mountain buried

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Lamp That Woke Up
chapters.text:
Isla was supposed to be asleep.

Instead she was cross-legged on her bedroom floor at 11:47 p.m., headlamp on, sorting through the dusty cardboard box her grandfather had left her — the one marked, in his looping handwriting, FINDS. HANDLE WITH CARE. ASK QUESTIONS FIRST.

He had been an archaeologist, the real kind, the kind who dug holes in the ground for a living and got excited about broken pots. Isla liked to think she'd inherited at least the excited-about-broken-pots part.

Tonight's find was a lump of bronze the size of her fist — a cracked old oil lamp, the kind Romans used before electricity existed, with a worn thumbprint pressed into the handle where someone had held it, two thousand years ago, exactly the way she was holding it now.

She rubbed the dust from the grooves. The lamp went warm. Then warmer. Then it began, very softly, to hum.

"Okay," Isla said, to nobody. "That's new."

Light poured out of the crack in the spout in one long golden rope, and it did not stop at her bedroom wall. It kept going straight through, like the wall wasn't fully convinced it was a wall. Isla had about half a second to decide whether this was a problem, and then the light pulled her through it.

She landed — feet first, like the lamp had been practicing — on a stone street warm from somewhere she couldn't see the sun. A cart wheel rattled nearby. Someone was shouting about fish.

The street in front of her wasn't flat. Big square stones crossed it in a raised line, a hand's width above the road, with gaps between them just wide enough for a wheel to pass through.

She'd seen a photo of stones exactly like these in one of her grandfather's books. "This is a crossing," she said slowly. "For people, so you don't have to step in the—" she glanced at the stained gutter and decided not to finish that sentence. "And carts still get through, because the gaps are exactly cart-wheel width."

The lamp pulsed once, satisfied, like a small nod.

"You're not just a lamp, are you," Isla said.

It hummed again. Close enough to a yes.

She stood looking at red-tiled roofs and a mountain rising green and calm in the distance, in a town that was very much alive, and very much not supposed to still exist.

"Where—" she started.

"Pompeii," said a voice behind her, and it did not belong to the lamp.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Five Villages and a Painted Insult
chapters.text:
Isla turned to find a boy about seventeen, wax tablet under one arm, looking at her like she'd appeared out of thin air — which, fairly, she had.

"I'm Gaius," he said, then caught himself. "Gaius Plinius. People call me Pliny. The younger one. There are two of us."

Isla knew that name. It had sat under a photo in her grandfather's book, next to the words eyewitness account. "You wrote letters," she said. "About—" she stopped, unsure if that was a secret she was meant to know yet.

Pliny just looked pleased. "I write things down. Useful. You never know what's going to matter later."

He was, Isla would decide, dramatically right about that.

He walked her into the square, past a building with huge curved stone benches rising in rows, big enough to swallow thousands of people.

"The amphitheater," he said, waving a hand. "A giant oval stage, built for games. Big crowds. One of the oldest of its kind anywhere."

Painted on a nearby wall, in letters a foot tall, was a scrawl of red paint.

"What's that say?" Isla asked.

"An advertisement," said Pliny. "For rooms to rent. And someone's opinion, right next to it, about who should win the next election." He said it the way someone might say and here's the weather report, which told Isla that painted walls doing the job of flyers was just Tuesday here.

She studied the word carved above the gate they'd just come through. POMPEII. Something about it nagged at her.

"That doesn't sound Latin," she said slowly. "It sounds like it's doing something with numbers."

Pliny raised an eyebrow, surprised. "Go on."

"There's a word — I read it somewhere — from an older language people spoke here before Latin took over. It means five." She looked at the streets fanning outward. "Was this five towns that joined into one?"

Pliny didn't answer right away, which from a boy who enjoyed being the smartest person in most rooms was as good as a yes.

"Nobody is completely certain," he admitted. "But that's the best guess anyone has. Five villages, one town, one name." He looked at her with new interest. "You might be useful to have around."

Isla decided she liked Pompeii. It was a town that argued in paint, named itself after arithmetic, and had just complimented her thinking within ten minutes of her arrival.

"What's for breakfast around here?" she asked instead, because the smell drifting down the street was extraordinary.

Pliny grinned. "Follow me."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Bread Still in the Oven
chapters.text:
The smell belonged to a bakery wedged between two shops, where a man with flour to his elbows slid round loaves into a domed brick oven on a long wooden paddle.

Each loaf had a pattern pressed into the top — lines cutting it into eight wedges, with a small stamped mark near the crust.

"That's a signature," Isla said, pointing. "A maker's mark. So people know whose bakery it came from."

The baker, who did not speak English and had no reason to, looked pleased that someone had noticed his stamp anyway, and handed her a warm end-piece of dough.

"Every baker marks his own," Pliny confirmed. "No point making the best bread in the street if nobody knows it was yours."

Isla chewed and thought about her grandfather's box, and the thumbprint on the lamp, and decided people had been signing their work since approximately forever.

Outside, a public fountain gurgled at the corner, water running continuously from a carved stone spout into a trough.

"It never stops?" Isla asked, crouching to look.

"Why would it?" said Pliny, like this was an odd question. "Lead pipes bring water down from the hills into fountains all over town. Shops, baths, houses that can afford it. It just keeps coming."

Isla traced the pipe where it vanished into the wall. A whole town, she thought, plumbed like a single machine, water finding its way to a hundred spouts without anyone pumping a handle. It was the kind of engineering people usually assumed came much later than two thousand years ago, and here it was, running quietly in the background of somebody's Tuesday.

"You people are extremely organized," she said, "for a town that also paints insults on walls."

"We contain multitudes," said Pliny solemnly, and went back to his bread.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Room That Kept Its Secrets
chapters.text:
Pliny led her up a street of grand houses until they reached one with painted walls so bright Isla actually gasped — reds and golds, floor to ceiling, covering every inch of plaster.

"Frescoes," said Pliny, watching her face. "Painted straight into wet plaster, so the color sinks in and never fades. This house has some of the best in town."

One room stopped her completely. Life-sized figures wound around the walls in a painted procession — a woman with a whip, dancers, something being revealed beneath a cloth — a scene that clearly meant something, urgently, to whoever had paid for it.

"What is this showing?" Isla breathed.

Pliny shrugged, and for the first time all night, looked genuinely stumped. "Nobody who lives here will tell outsiders. A ceremony, maybe. People argue about it." He tilted his head at the room. "That's rather why everyone just calls it the room of mysteries."

Isla, who had been waiting her whole life for someone to hand her an actual unsolved mystery, felt something click into place behind her ribs. "So nobody ever figures out what it means?"

"Not that I've heard," said Pliny, with the easy honesty of someone who did not know he was talking to a girl who would, in roughly seventeen centuries, be very good at exactly this kind of question.

Under the house, the ground gave the faintest shiver — so small Isla nearly missed it. Pliny didn't even look up.

"Does that happen a lot?" she asked.

"Since the big one, seventeen years back, smaller ones all the time," he said, already moving on. "Everyone's used to it by now."

Isla looked back at the painted room over her shoulder, the dancers frozen mid-step, the mystery exactly as unsolved as it had been a minute ago. She didn't know yet it would stay that way for a very long time — long enough that she herself, one day, might be one of the people still arguing about it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Mountain Opens
chapters.text:
They were in the market square, Pliny haggling cheerfully over olives, when the sky did something wrong.

Isla saw it first — a column rising straight up from the mountain behind the town, fast, white and gray, climbing higher than anything had a right to climb.

"Pliny." Her voice came out flatter than she meant it to. "Look at the mountain."

He looked. He went very quiet.

"That's Vesuvius," he said, confirming it to himself as much as to her. The calm green mountain Isla had noticed on arrival wasn't calm anymore.

Isla's brain, unhelpfully, chose that exact moment to supply a fact. "You write about this," she said. "In letters. People study your words for two thousand years because you're the only one who wrote down exactly what this looked like." She grabbed his sleeve. "That means you need to leave. Now. With your mother. That's what you do."

Pliny stared at her, and for once asked no clever question. He ran.

Isla watched the date settle around her like a fact finally becoming a place she stood in: August 24th, in the year 79. The mountain on every postcard, the one everyone called a gentle old neighbor, was erupting in front of her, exactly the way the letters said it would.

Ash began to fall — fine, gray, endless, drifting down like dirty snow, settling on rooftops and the painted wall still advertising rooms to rent. Mixed in were small, pale stones that bounced rather than thudded when they landed.

"That's pumice," Isla murmured, catching one — rock so full of trapped air bubbles it was nearly light enough to float.

The ash and pumice kept falling, that day and the next, until it had piled up over the whole town — eventually as deep as thirteen to twenty feet, burying streets, burying roofs, burying the oven with its bread still inside.

Thousands of people in and around the town died that day. But thousands more got out — including the boy who had just sprinted off toward his mother's house, who would live another forty years and write it all down so carefully that scientists, nineteen centuries later, would name this exact kind of eruption after him: a Plinian eruption.

Isla didn't move. The lamp in her pocket was warm against her leg, steady, like it was waiting for her to decide something.

"We're not done yet," she said. "Are we."

It hummed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Sailing Toward the Smoke
chapters.text:
The lamp pulled her sideways this time, not forward — across the bay, to a coastline where warships sat moored, crews staring, like everyone else, at the impossible cloud over the water.

A heavyset man in uniform stood at the rail of the largest ship, watching through narrowed eyes, utterly unbothered, while his sailors looked considerably more bothered.

"That's the other one," Isla guessed. "Pliny the Elder. His uncle."

The man turned at the sound of his own family name, raised an eyebrow at the girl who had apparently materialized on his deck, and decided — with the brisk practicality Isla was starting to recognize as a family trait — that there were more urgent matters than how she'd gotten there.

"People along that shore need boats," he said, mostly to his crew, but loud enough for her benefit. "So we will be the boats."

"You're sailing toward it," Isla said. "Not away."

"Famous last words tend to be more interesting that way," he said, which Isla chose to find reassuring rather than alarming, mostly because his crew were already hauling the oars and did not look like they planned on dying about it.

She watched the ships push across water gone the color of wet ash, sails cutting through floating pumice like it was sea foam, aimed straight at a coast everyone else was desperate to leave. It was, she thought, the single bravest thing she had ever personally watched — a man steering his ships toward danger on purpose, because people on the other side needed somewhere to stand.

"Will they make it?" she asked the lamp quietly.

The lamp didn't answer that one. Some things, apparently, even a magic oil lamp knows better than to promise.

What she did know, holding the rail as the fleet pulled away from view, was that because of ships like this one, people who'd have had nowhere to go got pulled out of the ash and onto a deck instead. She chose to hold onto that part.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Other Town
chapters.text:
The light shifted again, gentler this time, and set her down in a town that looked, at first glance, almost identical to the one she'd just left — same red roofs, same stone streets, same mountain looming behind it.

"Herculaneum," hummed the lamp, somehow managing to sound like a word despite not having a mouth. "Smaller than Pompeii. Same mountain. Same day."

But something here was different, and it took Isla a minute of walking to spot it.

In Pompeii, everything wooden had burned or rotted away over the centuries, leaving only holes where beams and furniture used to be. Here, through a doorway, she saw an actual wooden bed frame, scorched black but still standing, and on a shelf nearby, something that might once have been a scroll, rolled tight and blackened like a stick of charcoal.

"That's wood," Isla said slowly. "Actual wood. After two thousand years."

"Different kind of burying," the lamp hummed. "Pompeii got ash and stone from the sky. This town got something hotter and faster, moving along the ground — it buried things so completely, so fast, there was no air left to rot anything. Furniture. Scrolls. Even loaves, here too."

Isla crouched by the doorway, turning the idea over. Same volcano, same afternoon, two towns captured by two different kinds of disaster, like two photographs taken with completely different cameras.

"So the thing that destroyed it," she said slowly, "is also the reason we still have it."

The lamp didn't need to confirm that one. She could tell, by its warmth in her hand, she'd gotten it exactly right.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Found Again
chapters.text:
The light swirled a final time, and when it cleared, centuries had gone with it. Pompeii lay in front of her again, quiet now in a completely different way — no carts, no shouting fish-sellers, just low stone walls half-buried in soft earth, and tourists in sun hats taking photographs behind a rope.

"Nobody remembered this was even here," the lamp hummed, "for almost seventeen hundred years. Buried. Forgotten. Just a hill people planted grapes on."

"Until?" Isla asked, already knowing there had to be an until.

"1748," said the lamp. "Workers digging nearby hit stone where there shouldn't have been stone. Walls. Pots. A whole town, exactly where they left it."

Isla walked the quiet street slowly, past the same stepping stones, the same gutter, the same gate stamped POMPEII. It was unmistakably the place she had stood that morning — if that morning was even the right way to describe something that had happened nearly two thousand years ago and also several hours ago, depending who was counting.

A sign near the entrance, printed in six languages, named the place a UNESCO World Heritage Site — Isla had seen the term on a poster in her school library, and finally understood it properly: a place the whole world had formally agreed was too important to lose twice.

"How much of it has even been dug up?" she asked.

"About two-thirds," said the lamp. "The rest is still down there. Every year, somewhere under all that dirt, someone finds a fresco nobody's seen since the day it was painted."

Isla looked out at the green, ordinary-looking mountain still standing patiently behind the ruins — the same one that had done all of this, the same one people still lived beside today, the same one scientists still watched, every single day, because it had never actually stopped being a volcano.

"It's still active," she said. It wasn't really a question.

"Still watched. Closely," the lamp confirmed. "Just in case."

The light rose around her one more time, the ruins folding away like a page turning, and Isla landed — feet first, same as before — back on her own bedroom carpet, headlamp still on, the box from her grandfather still open beside her.

The lamp in her hand had gone cool and ordinary again, bronze and cracked and quiet. Except — she turned it over — where there had only been a worn thumbprint before, there was now a second mark pressed faintly beside it. Small. Fresh. Shaped exactly like her own thumb.

Isla sat very still, looking at the two prints side by side, separated by two thousand years and about four hours.

Then she reached for her notebook, because she had several hundred questions, and tomorrow she intended to start answering them.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she had an entire town's worth of questions to ask the dust.

Avoid graphic descriptions of people dying or suffering in the ash; mention that many people were killed, but center the story on discovery and learning rather than the disaster itself.

fact_pack.summary: Pompeii was a busy Roman town near the Bay of Naples that was buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD. Ash and pumice covered the town so completely that it was preserved for almost 1,700 years, giving us an amazing snapshot of everyday Roman life.

facts.text: Pompeii was a Roman town in what is now southern Italy, near the modern city of Naples.
On August 24, 79 AD, the nearby volcano Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii in ash and pumice.
Before the eruption, Pompeii was a lively town of about 11,000 to 15,000 people with shops, bathhouses, theaters, and temples.
The eruption buried Pompeii under as much as 4 to 6 meters (13 to 20 feet) of volcanic ash and rock.
Many people in Pompeii escaped, but historians believe around 2,000 residents of the town died, with thousands more dying in nearby areas like Herculaneum.

A Roman writer named Pliny the Younger watched the eruption from across the bay and wrote two letters describing it in detail, which is why scientists call this kind of violent eruption a 'Plinian eruption'.
Pliny the Younger's uncle, Pliny the Elder, was a famous naval commander and author who sailed toward Pompeii to help people and died during the rescue attempt.
The eruption happened so fast that it froze the town in time, preserving bread in ovens, paintings on walls, and even graffiti on buildings.
Ash hardened around the bodies of victims, and later excavators poured plaster into the hollow spaces to make detailed casts showing their shapes and poses.
Pompeii was mostly forgotten for centuries until it was rediscovered in 1748, when workers digging in the area found ancient walls and artifacts.
Nearby Herculaneum, a smaller seaside town, was also buried by the same eruption but under a different kind of volcanic material that preserved even wooden furniture and scrolls.
Archaeologists have found colorful wall paintings called frescoes, including the famous 'Villa of the Mysteries' paintings showing mysterious rituals.
Pompeii had an advanced water system with public fountains and lead pipes bringing water throughout the town.
The town had a large amphitheater built around 70 BC, one of the oldest known Roman amphitheaters, used for gladiator games.
Archaeologists found a loaf of bread, still shaped and marked by its baker, preserved in a Pompeii oven.
A plaster cast of a dog, apparently chained and unable to escape, was found and is one of the most famous and sad discoveries from the site.
Pompeii's streets had raised stepping stones so people could cross without stepping in mud or water, while carts still passed through gaps in the stones.
Mount Vesuvius is still an active volcano today, and scientists continue to study and monitor it because millions of people live nearby.
Pompeii is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Italy's most visited archaeological parks, drawing millions of visitors each year.
Only about two-thirds of Pompeii has been excavated so far, and new discoveries, like freshly uncovered frescoes, are still being made.
Some buildings in Pompeii had advertisements and political slogans painted on their outside walls, an ancient form of public messaging.
The name 'Pompeii' likely comes from an ancient Oscan word 'pompe', meaning 'five', possibly referring to five original villages that joined together.

timeline.event: Early settlement grows near Mount Vesuvius
A strong earthquake damages Pompeii, foreshadowing later eruption
Mount Vesuvius erupts and buries Pompeii
Rediscovery and first organized excavations begin
Pompeii named a UNESCO World Heritage Site
