story.title: Isla and the Trowel That Remembers Pompeii
story.subtitle: A dig through the ash, one layer at a time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Trowel That Hums (Tonight)
chapters.text:
Isla knelt on her bedroom carpet, bent over a shoebox of broken pottery.

Not real pottery. A birthday kit called *Junior Archaeologist*, full of plaster shards she was supposed to glue back into a vase. She had ignored the instructions days ago. Instead she treated it like a crime scene: each shard numbered, each one laid out on a sticky note, a case file nobody else in the house knew existed.

Her real trowel sat beside the box. She had found it at a flea market last spring, small and brass, with letters scratched into the handle that nobody — not her, not the man who sold it to her — could quite read anymore. It was the only true thing about the whole case.

Midnight had come and gone. She knew because her alarm clock said so, twice.

Then the trowel's handle went warm in her hand.

Isla froze. The dust on her desk, old eraser crumbs and pencil shavings, began to glitter — gray-gold, soft, patient, the way she imagined real volcanic ash might look if it ever caught the light just right.

She touched the trowel's tip to the dust.

The floor under her desk did not open. It unfolded, like a page turning sideways, into a glowing wall of layers stacked on top of each other, each one labeled in soft gold script: TODAY. 1997. 1748. 79 AD.

"That's not how geology works," Isla said, which was the sort of thing she said instead of screaming.

The deepest label pulsed brighter than the rest, like it wanted picking. She reached out and touched **79 AD**.

The gold light swallowed her whole, and when it let go, Isla was standing on a sunlit street that smelled like bread and the sea.

She blinked. Stalls. Shouting. A cart rattling over stone. This was not her bedroom.

The trowel hummed in her hand, steady, like it was waiting for her to ask the first real question. She crouched and brushed two fingers of dust off a low wall at the street's edge, and the stone answered the only way old stone can: with a glow.

Faint gold letters rose out of the rock, there and gone, like heat off a road in summer: a name, a number, a place.

"Pompeii," she read aloud. "Near the **Bay of Naples**, in what's now southern Italy."

She looked around at the shuttered shops, the people haggling over fish, the steam curling off a public bathhouse on the corner. This did not look like a place anyone would ever forget.

More letters rose, as if the wall had more to say once it realized someone was finally brushing it off properly.

"**Eleven to fifteen thousand people**," Isla read, and whistled low. "Shops, baths, theaters, temples. This place is busy."

She had expected ruins. She had gotten rush hour.

Somewhere behind her, a mountain sat green and quiet against the sky. Nobody in the street so much as glanced at it.

Isla did. She had read ahead, once, for a school project. She knew a secret this whole lively street did not know yet, and for a second it sat strangely in her stomach, like a spoiler she hadn't asked for.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Stones That Step Around Puddles (79 AD, an Ordinary Morning)
chapters.text:
Isla heard the water before she saw it — a fountain on the corner, spilling loud and constant, like someone had left a tap running for two thousand years.

She followed the sound and found a line of large flat stones laid across the street, spaced out like stepping stones over a puddle that never seemed to dry.

"Why would you need these in the middle of a road?" she muttered, crouching to look closer.

The trowel warmed in her palm, patient as ever. It wanted her to guess first.

She noticed something tucked between each stone: gaps, just wide enough for a cart wheel to roll through without the whole cart tipping sideways.

"They're not in the way," Isla said slowly. "They're for walking — and the gaps are so carts can still get through."

The nearest stone glowed gold, confirming it, the way a teacher nods when you finally crack the hard problem.

Pompeii's streets flooded with water, and worse, whenever it rained, so the Romans had built a crossing that worked for walking *and* driving — two thousand years before anyone argued about bike lanes.

Further down the street, she found the fountain's source: a line of pipes running along a wall, dull gray metal, humming faintly with water even now.

"**Lead pipes**," she read, brushing dust from a seam in the stone beside them. "Carrying water to fountains all over town."

It was, she thought, a town with better plumbing than some houses she had visited on actual school trips.

She passed a wall being patched by two men balanced on a wobbly ladder, plaster dripping, muttering about cracks that kept reopening no matter how many times they smoothed them over. The wall behind them still bore the pale scar of an old break, stitched together with new mortar.

Isla paused. "Rough few years?" she asked, though neither man could hear her.

The trowel, for once, didn't glow. Some questions, apparently, you just had to carry with you and figure out later.

She tucked the thought away like a shard in her sticky-note pile and walked on, toward the harbor, past a baker calling out prices, past a dog asleep in a doorway that had clearly claimed the whole street as its own.

The mountain behind the rooftops still hadn't said a word. Isla decided, for now, to let it keep its secret a little longer.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Letter Across the Bay (August 24, 79 AD)
chapters.text:
The gold light dropped her this time on a balcony across the water, where a boy not much older than she was sat hunched over a wax tablet, writing fast.

Smoke rose from the mountain behind the bay, a column climbing so high it looked less like smoke and more like a tree made of ash, spreading wide and flat at the top.

Isla had seen that shape before, in photographs of other volcanoes doing exactly this.

"That's today," she said quietly. "**August 24, 79 AD**."

The boy writing didn't look up, but the trowel pulsed once, soft and sure, the way it did when she'd gotten something exactly right.

His name, the glowing script told her as she leaned carefully over his shoulder, was **Pliny the Younger**. He was watching the eruption from across the bay and writing it all down, letter by letter, detail by detail: the color of the cloud, the shaking ground, the ash drifting down like snow that never cooled.

"He's basically live-tweeting a volcano," Isla muttered.

Out on the water, she could just make out a ship pushing *toward* the mountain instead of away from it. The trowel's glow supplied the name before she even asked: **Pliny the Elder**, the boy's uncle, sailing straight at the danger because there were people on that shore who needed help.

Isla watched the ship until it rounded the point and was gone from view.

Not everyone that day got rescued. Pompeii was buried fast, and many of the people living there did not get out in time. Isla felt that settle in her chest for a moment, quiet and real, and she let it, instead of rushing past it.

But the letters the boy on the balcony was writing right now would survive for almost two thousand years. Scientists still use his careful descriptions today to study this exact kind of eruption — they even named it after him: a **Plinian eruption**, loud and fast and towering, just like the one turning the sky orange in front of her.

"You're not just writing a letter," Isla told him, even though he couldn't hear her either. "You're writing the first weather report anyone ever wrote for a volcano."

The boy dipped his stylus and kept going, steady, unhurried, like someone who understood that getting the details right mattered more than getting them fast.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Bakery Under the Ash (Buried, 79 AD)
chapters.text:
The light dropped lower this time, and darker, until Isla was standing somewhere that felt less like a street and more like the inside of a sealed jar.

Everything around her sat frozen mid-motion: a cart with one wheel still turned, a shutter half closed, fine dust hanging in the air as if it hadn't decided yet whether to fall.

"This is the ash," she whispered, and the trowel glowed in answer, slow and steady, confirming it.

Not just a sprinkle, either. Isla paced the layer as it climbed past her knees, her waist, over her head — somewhere between **thirteen and twenty feet** of ash and rock, a glowing mark on the wall told her, burying the whole town in a single afternoon.

It should have felt like the saddest place she had ever stood. Instead it felt like someone had hit pause on an entire town and simply forgotten to press play again — which, she realized, was more or less exactly what had happened, for almost **1,700 years**.

She found the oven first by its smell, which made no sense at all, since nothing here should have smelled like anything in centuries. Inside sat a round, scored loaf of bread, still shaped by the baker's hands, a small stamp pressed into its crust like a signature nobody ever came back to claim.

"Someone made this and never picked it up," Isla said, and it was somehow the most human thing she had seen all night.

Paintings covered the walls nearby, bright reds and blues that should have faded to nothing centuries ago, kept instead as if the ash had tucked them in for a very long nap.

And scratched beside a doorway, in handwriting as careless as anything in her own school planner, was an advertisement for a shop — and right beneath it, someone's loud opinion about a local election, scrawled like a two-thousand-year-old sticky note stuck to a locker.

"They had **ads and political signs painted on their walls**," Isla laughed. "Some things never change."

She brushed the last of the dust from the baker's loaf, gently, the way you'd wake someone up on purpose rather than by accident. The trowel glowed brighter than it had all night, as if it approved of being careful with the small, ordinary things.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Town the Mountain Treated Differently (Herculaneum)
chapters.text:
The next layer smelled different before Isla even saw it — sharper, like a campfire that had been rained on and never quite gone out.

She stepped onto a street in a smaller town, tucked right against the water, where the walls weren't covered in the soft gray ash of Pompeii, but in something darker and harder, almost like stone poured straight from a pot.

"Herculaneum," she read off a door frame, brushing it clean. "Same volcano. Same day. Totally different leftovers."

Here the heat had come first and fast, baking everything solid before it had time to rot — which meant things survived that never should have: wooden shelves, wooden beams, even scrolls of old paper-like material, their edges charred but their shapes still whole.

Isla crouched by a bookshelf, if you could still call it that, and felt something close to awe. Wood simply did not last two thousand years. Except, apparently, when a volcano insisted otherwise.

Further up the street she found a villa with a name worth stopping for: the **Villa of the Mysteries**, its walls covered in painted pictures almost life-sized — people in deep red robes, caught mid-ceremony, in a ritual nobody today has ever fully explained.

She leaned close. A woman mid-gesture. A winged figure. A whip raised and never lowered.

"What *is* this?" Isla asked the wall directly.

The trowel stayed quiet. No glow, no gold letters rising to answer.

Which, for a girl who loved mysteries more than answers, was somehow the best possible response. Not every case gets solved. Archaeologists still argue about what the painted ceremony even shows — a wedding, a ritual, a secret club that never wrote down its own rules.

"I'll take it," Isla said, grinning at the silent painting. "Leave something for the rest of us to figure out."

She traced the edge of the **fresco** — a fancy word, she reminded herself, for a picture painted straight onto wet wall plaster — one more time before the gold light began to tug at her feet again, pulling her down toward the next layer.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Five Villages and a Shovel (1748)
chapters.text:
The next drop landed her in mud.

Real mud, cold and present-day-ish, under a gray sky, where a group of workers dug with shovels instead of trowels, muttering every time their spades hit stone instead of soil.

A glowing label hovered over the whole scene like a caption: **1748**.

"You found walls," Isla said, watching one worker drop to his knees and start brushing dirt away with his bare hands, exactly the way she brushed a plaster shard back home. "You found an entire town and you don't even know it yet."

Pompeii had been buried so completely that for almost seventeen centuries, most people had simply forgotten it ever existed. Then these workers, digging for something else entirely, hit the top of a wall that hadn't seen daylight in all that time.

She followed the dig as the gold light fast-forwarded it, weeks compressing into seconds, walls becoming streets becoming a whole town rising back out of the ground like a photograph slowly developing.

One building came up bigger than the rest: a huge oval structure with rows of stone seats circling a flat, open center.

"An **amphitheater**," Isla read, brushing dust from a stone archway — a fancy word, she reminded herself, for a big oval stadium built for crowds to watch games. This one went up around **70 BC**, making it one of the oldest ever found. "Gladiator games happened right here."

She stood in the stone seats and tried to imagine the roar of a crowd instead of the quiet mud.

One last puzzle nagged at her before she left: the name itself. *Pompeii.* Where had it even come from?

The trowel warmed, and old, worn letters surfaced on a nearby stone, in a language that wasn't quite Latin.

"**Pompe**," Isla sounded out, slow. "An old word from before Latin took over around here — it means *five*. Maybe because five little villages joined up to make one town."

She counted on her fingers anyway, just to feel it land. "Five villages. One case. I'll allow it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Mountain That Never Stopped Watching (Today)
chapters.text:
One more drop, and the light turned bright and ordinary, full of sunscreen smells and a hundred camera clicks.

Isla stood at the edge of a wide stone street, except now there were railings, little signs in six languages, and crowds of tourists photographing a bakery oven she'd watched get uncovered minutes ago, depending on how you counted minutes.

"**TODAY**," read the gold label overhead, and for once it didn't need confirming.

Pompeii, she learned, brushing dust off an information sign like it was any other piece of evidence, was now a place the whole world had agreed was too important to lose — a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**, visited by millions of people every single year.

And yet, for all those millions of visitors, only about **two-thirds** of the town had actually been dug out of the ground. The rest was still down there, waiting, probably holding more bread ovens, more unsolved paintings, more graffiti about elections nobody remembers voting in.

"New stuff gets found *all the time*," Isla said, delighted, reading about a fresco uncovered just recently, its colors still sharp enough to argue with the paint on her own bedroom wall. "This case is never actually closed."

She looked up, past the railings and the signs, at the mountain itself — still there, still green, still quietly impossible to ignore.

Mount Vesuvius had never stopped being a volcano. It was still active, she read, and scientists kept instruments watching it around the clock, because millions of people now lived in its shadow, same as before.

It wasn't scary, exactly. It was more like meeting a very old suspect who had gone quiet for a long time, but whom everyone sensibly kept an eye on anyway.

Isla touched the railing — the same stone, she was fairly sure, she'd once stood beside two chapters and two thousand years ago, back when it was alive and lively and far too busy to notice her.

"Thanks for the case file," she told the mountain.

It did not answer. Mountains rarely do. But the trowel, warm in her hand, gave one long, golden pulse, as if it agreed completely.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Carpet (Tonight, Later)
chapters.text:
The gold light folded itself back up the way it had come, layer by layer — 1997, 1748, 79 AD — sliding past like pages closing in a book, until the very last page set her down exactly where she'd started: cross-legged on her own bedroom carpet, shoebox of plaster shards still scattered in front of her.

The clock said it was later than before, though she was fairly sure that wasn't how time was supposed to work either.

Her trowel sat cool and ordinary in her hand now, brass and worn and scratched, no glow left in it anywhere.

Except — she looked closer — a thin line of fine gray dust had settled along its blade, the kind that wouldn't shake off with just a sleeve.

Isla smiled and left it exactly where it was.

She picked up her sticky notes, the ones numbering her plaster shards, and crossed out her old guess about what the broken vase used to look like. A town could sit buried for seventeen hundred years and still have two-thirds of its story left to dig up. Her vase, she decided, could wait one more night.

Tomorrow she had a trowel to clean, a shard puzzle to finish, and an awful lot of new questions to write down before she forgot a single one of them.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow she had a trowel to clean, a shard puzzle to finish, and a whole list of new questions to write down.

story.title: Isla and the Stone of Vesuvius
story.subtitle: A dig kit, a grey rock, and a city buried for seventeen hundred years.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Grey Stone on the Shelf
chapters.text:
Isla was supposed to be asleep. Instead she was lying on her bedroom floor, labeling pretend pottery shards with a tiny paintbrush, the way real archaeologists do. A lamp with a cracked shade threw long shadows across her dig tray.

On her shelf sat a rock the size of a fist. Her aunt had brought it back from a trip to Italy, light as a sponge and full of little holes, like it had been frozen mid-bubble. Isla had never thought much about it. Tonight, it hummed.

She froze. The rock was buzzing, faintly, like a phone on silent. She picked it up. It was warm.

"Okay," she whispered. "That's new."

The hum got louder. The holes in the stone began to glow a dull orange, like the last coals of a fire. Isla's bedroom wall rippled like water, and through it she could see sunlight, white stone, and a street full of people in togas, shouting over each other to sell bread and fish and wine.

"Go on, then," said a voice behind her — dry, polite, faintly amused, like someone reading out loud from a letter. "You wanted a mystery. I happen to have one that's been waiting seventeen hundred years."

Isla turned. Nobody was there. Just the stone, glowing in her palm.

"Are you... in the rock?" she asked.

"I'm in the story," said the voice. "The rock is just the door. Call me your guide. Or don't call me anything — I'll still show up."

Isla, who had read every mystery book in her school library twice, was not about to say no to an actual door. She stepped through the rippling wall and the glow swallowed her whole.

She landed on warm stone, in bright sun, in the middle of a street that smelled like baking bread and horses. A cart rattled past over raised stepping-stones laid across the road, with gaps underneath just wide enough for its wheels. People walked across the tops of the stones to keep their sandals out of the mud and water running down the gutters.

"Where," Isla said carefully, "and also *when*, am I?"

"Pompeii," said the voice, now walking beside her as a tall young man in a plain white tunic, ink-stained fingers, and the look of someone who always carried a notebook. "A real town, near a city you'd call **Naples**, in what's now southern **Italy**. And the *when* is the good part. You've got a little under two thousand years to go before you were born."

Isla grinned. A real place. A real time. This was, officially, the best Tuesday night of her life — and it was turning into the best Wednesday morning in Roman history, too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Five Villages and a Name
chapters.text:
The young man introduced himself as he walked. "Pliny," he said. "Pliny the Younger, to be exact. There's an older Pliny too — my uncle. Try to keep us straight, it matters later."

Isla filed that away the way she filed every clue. A name mentioned twice in one sentence was never an accident in a mystery book.

The street opened into a square crowded with shoppers, stray dogs, and a man shouting about olive oil prices. Isla counted doorways as they passed — bakery, bathhouse, another bakery, a shop selling little clay oil lamps.

"How many people even live here?" she asked.

"Somewhere between **eleven and fifteen thousand**,
 depending who's counting," Pliny said. "Nobody kept perfect records. But it's a real town. Shops, theaters, temples. Not a backwater."

Isla noticed something painted across a wall in faded red letters, words she couldn't read. "What does that say?"

"An advertisement," Pliny said. "And next to it, a bit of political campaigning — someone wants their friend voted into office. Walls were the internet of their day. People painted ads and slogans right on the outside of buildings for everyone to see."

Isla laughed. "So Pompeii had billboards."

"Pompeii had everything," Pliny said. "Which brings me to your first real clue. Nobody's entirely sure where the name *Pompeii* comes from. But one good guess involves an old local word, *pompe*, which might mean **'five.'** As if five small villages joined together to make one town."

Isla stopped walking. "Might. You said might twice now."

"I did," Pliny said, not even a little embarrassed. "Some of history is a fact you can hold in your hand. Some of it is a very good guess wearing a fact's coat. Part of your job tonight is telling which is which."

Isla liked that. A mystery where even the guide admitted he didn't know everything — that was more honest than most.

"Five villages," she said, testing the idea out loud. "Count the hills. Maybe I can find five of something."

Pliny's mouth twitched, almost a smile. "Now you're doing this properly."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Water, Baths, and the Big Stone Bowl
chapters.text:
They turned a corner and Isla heard it before she saw it: water, splashing steadily into a stone basin at chest height, right in the middle of the street.

"A public fountain," Pliny said. "There are dozens across town. Pompeii had a proper water system — pipes made of lead, running under the streets, feeding fountains and bathhouses and private homes that could afford the fee."

Isla dipped two fingers in. Cold, clean, and still running, nearly two thousand years before her own kitchen tap. "That's better plumbing than some old houses back home," she said.

"Rome was proud of its water," Pliny said. "Follow it, and it usually leads somewhere interesting."

It led them to a long, low building with steam curling out of a doorway. Inside, men lounged in warm pools, scraping oil off their skin with curved tools, chatting like it was any other Tuesday. "Bathhouse," Pliny explained. "Part gym, part spa, part the place you went to hear the town gossip."

Further on, the street climbed toward a huge oval building, stone seats rising in rings around a sandy floor. Isla's stomach did a small flip of recognition. "Is that—"

"An amphitheater," Pliny said. "A big open stadium for watching shows. This one went up around **70 BC**. One of the oldest of its kind that's survived anywhere. People packed in to watch gladiator contests."

Isla climbed a few stone steps and sat, imagining the roar of a crowd where now there was only wind. "How many seats?"

"Thousands," Pliny said. "Enough for most of the town, if everyone showed up at once."

Isla looked out at the oval floor, then back at the stepping-stones, the fountain, the bathhouse steam. "This isn't a sleepy little village," she said. "This is a whole working city. Shops, baths, sports, water on tap. People here had actual lives."

"That," Pliny said, "is exactly the point I was hoping you'd land on. Everyone remembers how Pompeii ended. Almost nobody stops to notice how ordinary it was right up until it wasn't."

The sentence hung there, a little heavier than the ones before it. Isla noticed. She was good at noticing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Walls Talk Back
chapters.text:
"You said 'right up until it wasn't,'" Isla said, catching up to Pliny on a narrow side street. "That's a mystery-book sentence if I ever heard one. What aren't you telling me?"

Pliny kept walking, hands behind his back. "Seventeen years before the end, in **62 AD**, the ground shook. Hard. A strong earthquake cracked walls, knocked statues flat, scared half the town into rebuilding."

"And nobody figured out why?" Isla asked.

"Nobody connected it to the mountain," Pliny said, nodding toward a dark peak rising green and calm over the rooftops. "Vesuvius hadn't erupted in living memory. People thought it was just a mountain. A good one for grapevines, actually."

Isla studied the wall beside her — more painted words, half-faded. "More ads?"

"Read it as a clue, not decoration," Pliny said. "A mix. Some advertising, some politics, some just graffiti someone scratched for fun. People here left their fingerprints everywhere, on purpose and by accident. That's a gift for anyone who shows up later wanting to understand them."

Isla crouched by a patch of plaster with faint scratches in it — a name, a joke, maybe a complaint about dinner. She couldn't read the words, but she understood the impulse. People two thousand years ago left notes on walls for the same reason she doodled in the margins of her homework: because they were there, and they wanted someone to know it.

"So the earthquake was a warning," she said slowly, "and nobody read it right."

"Warnings are only obvious afterward," Pliny said. "That's not a flaw in the Romans. That's just how warnings work."

He glanced at the mountain again, and for just a second his dry, amused voice went quiet and careful. "Keep that earthquake in your notes, though. It matters for what's coming. I promise you this part of the story doesn't dwell where it doesn't need to."

Isla nodded. She trusted him on that. Mostly because he'd already admitted, twice, when he wasn't sure of something — and a guide who admits his doubts is usually the one telling you the truth about the rest.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Letter-Writer on the Hill
chapters.text:
The stone in Isla's hand flickered, and the street dissolved into a hillside across the bay, grass underfoot, the sea glittering far below. Pliny stood beside her, older now by a heartbeat, a scroll and stylus in hand instead of a lounging stroll.

"This is where I actually was," he said. "Watching from across the water, on **August 24th, in the year 79**, when the mountain let go."

Isla looked toward Vesuvius. A column of ash rose from its top like a tree made of smoke, spreading flat at the crown, climbing impossibly high into the blue sky.

"I wrote two letters about it afterward," Pliny said. "Described it carefully — the shape of the cloud, the ash falling like snow, the ground trembling. I was trying to get every detail right, the way a careful witness should. Scientists still use my description today. They even named a whole kind of eruption after it — a **Plinian eruption** — any time a volcano blasts ash that high, that fast."

Isla stared at the cloud, caught somewhere between awed and unsettled. "Were you scared?"

"A little," Pliny admitted. "My uncle wasn't, though. He commanded ships nearby, and when word came that people needed rescuing, he sailed *toward* the mountain instead of away from it, to help bring people to safety by boat. That's the kind of brave I'd like to be, if I'm honest."

Isla watched the ash column a moment longer. "Is this the scary part?" she asked, direct, the way she liked mysteries to be direct with her.

"It's the serious part," Pliny said. "Many people did not get away in time, and that's simply true. But plenty did. My uncle's ships carried people to safer shores that same day. We're not going to sit here and watch the worst of it — that's not what this stone is for. We're going to go see what it left behind. That's where your kind of mystery actually lives."

Isla nodded, grateful, and let the stone pull them forward through the ash cloud — not into the moment itself, but past it, the way you'd skip the saddest page of a book to find out how the story turned out.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: What the Ash Kept Safe
chapters.text:
They landed in quiet. No carts, no shouting, no splashing fountains — just still air and soft grey ground, crunching faintly underfoot like old snow.

"The eruption buried the whole town," Pliny said, "under as much as **four to six meters of ash and rock** — that's roughly as deep as a two-story house. It happened fast enough to seal the place like a jar."

Isla crouched and brushed ash off something pale. A loaf of bread, round and scored into eight wedges, sitting exactly where a baker had left it in an oven nearly two thousand years ago. "It's still got the baker's mark on it," she whispered.

"Baked, scored, and never eaten," Pliny said. "Preserved mid-bake. The ash fell so thick and so fast it froze ordinary moments exactly as they were — bread in ovens, paintings on walls, jokes scratched into plaster. A town interrupted, not erased."

Further along, inside a grand house with painted columns, Isla found a wall of figures in deep red, dancing, holding strange ritual objects she didn't recognize. "What is this place?"

"They call it the **Villa of the Mysteries**," Pliny said, and Isla's whole face lit up at the word. "These wall paintings — **frescoes**, made by painting straight onto wet plaster so the color sinks in and lasts — show some kind of ceremony. Nobody today is entirely certain what it means. It's one of archaeology's genuine open questions."

"A mystery nobody's solved," Isla said, delighted. "That's basically the best kind."

She traced the edge of a painted figure's robe, still vivid red after all this time, and thought about how strange it was that a disaster could also be the reason something survived. The ash that buried Pompeii in silence had also locked its secrets in a box nobody could open — until somebody eventually would.

"Who found it, in the end?" Isla asked. "Who opens the box?"

Pliny's eyes glinted. "Patience. That's a later chapter. Right now, there's a second buried town you should see first — smaller, by the sea, and preserved in an even stranger way."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Town Next Door
chapters.text:
The stone carried them along the coast to a quieter town, tucked close to the water, with houses that still had their rooftops.

"**Herculaneum**," Pliny said. "Smaller than Pompeii, and caught by the same eruption — but buried under a different kind of volcanic material, more like a thick, fast-moving flow instead of falling ash."

Isla stepped inside a doorway and stopped. The wood was still there. An actual wooden bed frame, a shutter on its hinges, even a wooden screen, dark and brittle but unmistakably furniture, not dust.

"Pompeii kept bread and paintings," she said slowly. "Herculaneum kept... wood?"

"And scrolls," Pliny said. "Rolled-up books made of a material like paper, charred black on the outside, but with the writing still trapped inside, layer after layer. People are still working out clever ways to read them without unrolling them, since unrolling would crumble them to nothing."

Isla turned slowly in the little room, taking it in — a house, basically untouched, just... paused. "It's like two different photographs of the same terrible day," she said. "One town got ash. The other got something else. And together they show you different pieces of the same story."

"That's precisely it," Pliny said, sounding genuinely pleased, like a teacher whose best student had just shown their work. "Disasters aren't tidy. They don't preserve everything the same way. Which is exactly why archaeologists need both towns, not just one."

Isla ran a hand along the edge of the wooden shutter, careful not to press too hard. It felt impossibly fragile and impossibly real at the same time, like touching a held breath.

"Okay," she said. "Now I really want to know who found all this. Somebody had to be the one who looked at a buried wall and went, wait a second."

Pliny smiled, properly this time. "Finally," he said. "The part where someone does the finding."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Found Again
chapters.text:
The stone's glow shifted, warmer now, and the scene around them changed to workers in old-fashioned clothes, digging carefully with shovels and brushes in a dusty field.

"**1748**," Pliny said. "Workers digging in this area struck old walls and strange objects underground. Word got around. People realized there was an entire ancient town sitting quietly beneath the dirt, waiting."

"After how long?" Isla asked, though she could already do the math.

"Nearly **seventeen hundred years**," Pliny said. "Forgotten, then found again."

Isla watched the diggers work, slow and careful, brushing dust from a curved shape that might have been a jar, might have been a roof tile. It looked exactly like her own dig tray at home, just scaled up to the size of a city. "That's basically what I do with my pretend shards," she said. "Except real. And huge."

"It's still going," Pliny said. "Only about **two-thirds of Pompeii** has ever been properly dug up. The rest is still under there, waiting its turn. People find new frescoes, new rooms, new surprises most years."

"So it's an unfinished mystery," Isla said. "Still open."

"In **1997**, the whole site was named a place the world agreed to protect and care for forever — a list for the planet's most important places," Pliny said. "Millions of people visit every year now, to walk the same stepping-stones you walked tonight."

"And the mountain?" Isla asked, looking one last time at Vesuvius, calm and green against the sky.

"Still there. Still active," Pliny said. "Scientists watch it closely today, because a great many people live nearby now. Nobody's taking their eyes off it again."

The stone pulsed warm in Isla's palm, and the hillside folded away like a page turning. She landed back on her bedroom carpet, dig tray still scattered beside her, lamp still humming its ordinary electric hum.

She looked down. On top of her plastic pottery shards sat one new thing: a small, curled scrap of blackened material, thin as old paper, with the faintest ghost of writing pressed into it.

A message, it seemed, from a town that had never quite finished telling its story.

Isla picked it up carefully, the way you'd hold something that had waited seventeen hundred years to be noticed, and set it beside the grey stone on her shelf. Two mysteries now, side by side, both patiently unfinished.

Tomorrow, she had some reading to do.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she had some reading to do.

Pliny the Younger's uncle, Pliny the Elder, was a famous naval commander and author who sailed toward Pompeii to help people and died during the rescue attempt.
The eruption happened so fast that it froze the town in time, preserving bread in ovens, paintings on walls, and even graffiti on buildings.
Ash hardened around the bodies of victims, and later excavators poured plaster into the hollow spaces to make detailed casts showing their shapes and poses.
Pompeii was mostly forgotten for centuries until it was rediscovered in 1748, when workers digging in the area found ancient walls and artifacts.
Nearby Herculaneum, a smaller seaside town, was also buried by the same eruption but under a different kind of volcanic material that preserved even wooden furniture and scrolls.
Archaeologists have found colorful wall paintings called frescoes, including the famous 'Villa of the Mysteries' paintings showing mysterious rituals.
Pompeii had an advanced water system with public fountains and lead pipes bringing water throughout the town.
The town had a large amphitheater built around 70 BC, one of the oldest known Roman amphitheaters, used for gladiator games.
Archaeologists found a loaf of bread, still shaped and marked by its baker, preserved in a Pompeii oven.
A plaster cast of a dog, apparently chained and unable to escape, was found and is one of the most famous and sad discoveries from the site.
Pompeii's streets had raised stepping stones so people could cross without stepping in mud or water, while carts still passed through gaps in the stones.
Mount Vesuvius is still an active volcano today, and scientists continue to study and monitor it because millions of people live nearby.
Pompeii is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Italy's most visited archaeological parks, drawing millions of visitors each year.
Only about two-thirds of Pompeii has been excavated so far, and new discoveries, like freshly uncovered frescoes, are still being made.
Some buildings in Pompeii had advertisements and political slogans painted on their outside walls, an ancient form of public messaging.
The name 'Pompeii' likely comes from an ancient Oscan word 'pompe', meaning 'five', possibly referring to five original villages that joined together.

story.title: Ivy and the Rainbow in the Puddle
story.subtitle: A splashy, colorful bedtime adventure

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Puddle Paint
chapters.text:
Rain tap-tapped on Ivy's window. Tap, tap, tap!

Ivy painted big puddle shapes on her paper. Purple puddles, orange puddles, even a polka-dot one.

Then the real puddle on her windowsill started to glow. It glowed pink, then blue, then gold.

Ivy leaned close. "Ooooh," she said.

A tiny drop of water popped up and winked. "Hello, Ivy! I'm Splash," it said. "Want to see how rainbows are made?"

Ivy grabbed her paintbrush like a magic wand. "Yes, yes, YES!" she said.

Splash giggled. "Hop in, then. SPLOOSH!" And the puddle pulled her right in.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Inside a Raindrop
chapters.text:
Everything went quiet and round. Ivy and Splash were inside a raindrop!

Sunshine beamed through the clear, wobbly wall.

"Watch what happens," Splash said. The sunshine bent, just like a straw looks bendy in a glass of water.

Ivy gasped. "It's bending!"

"That's right," said Splash. "Light bends when it goes inside a raindrop."

Ivy touched the light with her paintbrush. It left a tiny rainbow smear in the air.

"I made rainbow paint!" Ivy cheered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Bouncy Light
chapters.text:
Inside the drop, the light didn't stop. It bounced off the back wall. BOING!

Ivy giggled. "Like a ball!"

"Just like a ball," said Splash. "Then it bends again on its way back out."

Out came colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple.

Ivy counted them on her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five, six!"

She pointed her paintbrush at each color, one by one.

"I want to paint every single one," she said.

Splash laughed so hard he nearly splashed right out of the raindrop. "Then let's go find more."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Turn Around
chapters.text:
Outside the drop, the sky was bright. But Ivy saw no rainbow yet.

"Where did the colors go?" she asked.

Splash floated beside her. "Turn around, Ivy."

Ivy turned her back to the sun. Now the rain was right in front of her, like a sparkly curtain.

WHOOSH — a rainbow arched across the sky!

"You have to have the sun behind you," said Splash. "And rain out in front."

Ivy clapped her paint-covered hands, leaving little rainbow handprints in the air.

"I found it! I found the rainbow!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sun and Rain Together
chapters.text:
A little cloud drifted close and sprinkled rain. At the same time, the sun peeked out.

"Both at once?" Ivy asked.

"Yes!" said Splash. "Rainbows need sun AND rain together, in the very same moment."

"That's why they pop up after a rain shower," Splash said, "when the sun comes out to say hello."

Ivy held up her brush like a little sun. She waved it over an imaginary puddle.

"Hello, sun! Hello, rain!" she sang.

The rainbow glowed brighter, like it was smiling right back at her.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Color Mixer
chapters.text:
A sparkly triangle of glass floated by, catching the light.

"That belonged to a clever thinker named Isaac Newton," said Splash. "He shined sunlight through glass like this."

"Out came all the colors, hiding inside plain white light!"

Ivy mixed her paints on her palette. Red and yellow became orange. Blue and yellow became green.

"I'm a color mixer too!" she said.

Splash clapped his watery hands. "Just like sunlight, hiding colors until they come out to play."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Puddle Detectives
chapters.text:
Two more friends waved from a tiny, drifting cloud.

"I'm Ibn al-Haytham," said one. "I studied how light moves, a long, long time ago."

"I'm Kamal al-Din," said the other. "I used round glass balls to copy raindrops."

Ivy's eyes went wide. "Like pretend raindrops?"

"Exactly," said Kamal al-Din. "That's how I found the rainbow's secret."

Ivy pulled a round bead from her pocket. She held it up to the light, just like he did.

A little rainbow shimmer danced on her hand.

"I'm a puddle detective too!" she cheered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
Splash took Ivy's hand. "Time to go home."

SPLOOSH! They popped back into her bedroom puddle.

Outside, the rain had stopped. The whole yard looked washed and shiny.

Ivy looked out her window. A real rainbow stretched over the grass.

She had the sun behind her, just like Splash showed her.

Ivy grabbed her paintbrush and painted the whole arch. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple — every color in its place.

She set her painting on the windowsill, right next to the puddle.

Splash winked from the water. "Goodnight, Ivy. Paint bright dreams."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ivy. Sleep tight, and paint bright dreams.

true_facts.text: Sunshine goes into a little raindrop and it **bends**.
Inside the drop, the light **bounces**, just like a bouncy ball.
Then the light **bends again** and comes out as colors.
To see a rainbow, the **sun has to be behind you**.
The **rain has to be out in front of you**, like a curtain.
Rainbows need the **sun and the rain at the same time**.
That's why rainbows often show up **right after a rain shower**.
A rainbow appears when the **sun peeks out from behind the clouds**.

new_recurring.rule: A tiny, cheerful raindrop who appears in puddles, rain, or spray to guide Ivy on gentle science adventures. Speaks in short, happy sentences, always says 'SPLOOSH!' when traveling between worlds, and signs off with 'Paint bright dreams.'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Ivy returns to her bedroom puddle, paints the rainbow she saw over her yard, and sets the painting beside the puddle as the real rain stops outside.

fact_pack.summary: Rainbows appear when sunlight passes through raindrops and gets bent, split into colors, and bounced back to our eyes. They are a science-and-wonder topic: a physics lesson dressed up as a beautiful arc in the sky, with plenty of fun details for kids to explore.

facts.text: A rainbow forms when sunlight enters a raindrop, bends, reflects off the inside back of the drop, and bends again as it exits.
This bending of light is called refraction, and it happens because light slows down and changes direction when it moves from air into water.
White sunlight is actually made of many colors mixed together, and raindrops separate them because each color bends by a slightly different amount.
The classic rainbow color order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet, often remembered with the name 'Roy G. Biv'.
Red always appears on the outer edge of a rainbow and violet on the inner edge because red bends the least and violet bends the most.
To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you and rain (or spray) must be in front of you.
Rainbows are actually full circles, but we usually only see an arc because the ground blocks the bottom half.
From an airplane, people sometimes see a complete circular rainbow because there is no ground in the way.
Every person actually sees a slightly different rainbow, made from different raindrops, because the angle of light to your eyes is unique to your position.
A rainbow always appears in the part of the sky directly opposite the sun, centered on a point called the antisolar point.
Sometimes a fainter second rainbow appears above the main one, with its colors reversed, caused by light bouncing twice inside the raindrops.
The dark strip of sky between a primary and secondary rainbow is called Alexander's band, named after the ancient Greek philosopher Alexander of Aphrodisias who described it around 200 AD.
Rainbows can also form in mist, waterfalls, garden hose spray, and even moonlight, where they are called moonbows.
Moonbows are usually so faint that they look white or gray to human eyes, though cameras can capture their colors.
The scientist Isaac Newton showed in the 1660s that a glass prism could split white light into the same rainbow of colors, proving light itself contains all the colors.
The Persian scientist Ibn al-Haytham and later Kamal al-Din al-Farisi studied light and rainbows in raindrops centuries before Newton, around the 1000s and 1300s.
Many cultures have myths about rainbows, such as the Norse story of Bifrost, a rainbow bridge connecting Earth to the home of the gods.
In the Bible, the rainbow appears as a sign of a promise from God to Noah after a great flood.
Many cultures tell of a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow, especially in Irish folklore involving leprechauns, though a rainbow's end is never a real fixed spot since it moves as you move.
Because a rainbow depends on where the viewer stands, you can never actually walk up to or touch one.
Rainbows need both sunlight and water droplets at the same time, which is why they often appear during or right after a rain shower when the sun peeks out.
A rainbow's size in the sky is always about the same, spanning roughly 42 degrees from the antisolar point for the primary bow.
The rainbow flag, created by artist Gilbert Baker in 1978, uses rainbow colors as a symbol of pride and diversity.
Rainbows are studied in a branch of science called optics, which explores how light behaves, bends, and reflects.

story.title: Priya, Dev, and the Rainbow That Wouldn't Sit Still
story.subtitle: A fizzy, splashy trip through sunbeams and raindrops

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Squirt That Started It All
chapters.text:
It was almost bedtime. Priya was drawing rainbows on her sketchpad. Dev was spraying his water pistol at absolutely nothing, because that is what water pistols are for.

"Dev! You got my paper wet!" Priya said.

"Oops," said Dev, not sorry at all.

The sun was low and orange outside the window. Dev aimed one more squirt into the last sunbeam — and the spray lit up in every color at once.

A tiny droplet popped out of the mist, glowing like a marble made of light, with a round, giggly face.

"Hiya!" it said. "I'm Fizzle."

"You need two things to make a rainbow," Fizzle said. "**Sunshine**, and water in the air — rain, or spray from a pistol works great. The sun has to be behind you, with the water out in front."

Dev spun around so the sun was on his back and squirted again. A perfect rainbow bent across the mist.

"WHOA," said Dev.

"Want to see how it really works?" Fizzle asked. "Climb in."

Priya laughed. "Climb into a water pistol?"

"Climb into the rainbow," Fizzle said, and the room filled with mist and light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Inside a Raindrop
chapters.text:
They shrank down, down, until they floated inside one single raindrop, round as a tiny glass ball.

"Light comes in here," Fizzle said, pointing at a beam of sunlight hitting the drop's curved wall. The beam bent sideways the moment it touched the water.

"Hey, it turned!" Priya said. "Why?"

"Light moves slower in water than in air," Fizzle said. "When it slows down, it bends. Scientists call that **refraction** — a fancy word for light taking a turn."

Dev ran in a sharp zigzag, pretending to be the beam. "REFRACTION!" he yelled, bumping a beanbag.

Inside the drop, the beam bounced off the back wall, then bent again on its way out, heading straight for Priya's eyes.

"It bends twice!" Priya said. "In, bounce, and out!"

"Exactly," said Fizzle. "Every raindrop does that little dance."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Secret Inside Sunlight
chapters.text:
Outside the drop, Fizzle held up a glass prism, shaped like a triangle.

"Sunlight looks white," Fizzle said. "But it's secretly hiding every color at once, all squished together."

"No way," said Priya. "That's like saying my white sock is secretly full of socks."

Fizzle shone a sunbeam through the glass. Out the other side came a stripe of color, stretched like a tiny painted rainbow on the wall.

"A scientist named **Isaac Newton** did this exact trick, back in the **1660s**," Fizzle said. "He proved sunlight is made of every color, mixed together."

Dev squirted his pistol right through the beam, just to see what happened. The colors wobbled and danced.

"Each color bends a slightly different amount," Fizzle said. "That's what pulls them apart so we can see them."

Priya grabbed her sketchpad. "I need to draw this."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Roy G. Biv Moves In
chapters.text:
Priya lined up her colored pencils on the floor. "If I was a rainbow," she said, "what order would I go in?"

"Red first," Fizzle said, "then orange, yellow, green, blue, and two purples called indigo and violet. People remember it with a name: **Roy G. Biv**."

"Like a guy who's really into crayons," Priya said, and Dev snorted.

"Red always sits on the outside edge of a rainbow," Fizzle added, "and violet always sits on the inside. Red bends the least going through a drop, and violet bends the most."

Dev squinted at the colors. "Red's on the outside 'cause it's shy," he decided.

"Close enough," said Fizzle, laughing.

Priya arranged her pencils, red to violet, in a perfect little arc on the carpet, matching the glowing one still hanging in the misty air above them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Rainbow That Never Ends
chapters.text:
"Can I ask something weird?" Priya said. "Does a rainbow have a bottom?"

Fizzle grinned. "Good question. A rainbow is actually a whole **circle**. We just can't see the bottom half, because the ground gets in the way."

Dev got down on his belly to peek underneath the misty arc, as if he might spot the missing half.

"From way up in an airplane, with no ground blocking anything, people sometimes see the whole circle, round as a hula hoop," Fizzle said.

"I'm gonna see a circle rainbow from a plane someday," Dev announced.

"Write it on your list," said Priya, patting his head.

The misty rainbow floated higher, curling almost all the way around them, before the bottom faded into the carpet like always.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Nobody Else's Rainbow
chapters.text:
Dev reached out to grab a handful of the glowing colors. His hand went straight through.

"Hey! Rude," he said to the rainbow.

"You can't ever touch one," Fizzle said. "A rainbow isn't really sitting in one spot. It only shows up at a certain angle between the sun, the water, and your own eyes."

"So if I moved over there," Priya said, pointing, "would I see a different one?"

"You'd see your very own rainbow," Fizzle said. "Nobody else sees the exact same one. Not even Dev, standing right next to you."

"We're rainbow twins who never match," Priya said. "Typical."

"Old stories say there's a pot of gold waiting at the end of one," Fizzle added. "That's probably just a fun old tale, since a rainbow's end keeps moving whenever you do."

"Story of my life," said Dev, chasing the drifting colors and never once catching them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Two for the Price of One
chapters.text:
A second, fainter arc shimmered into view above the first.

"Whoa, a copy!" Dev shouted.

"That's a second rainbow," Fizzle said. "It happens when light bounces twice inside the drops instead of once. Look close — its colors are flipped."

Priya squinted. "Violet's on the outside this time!"

"You got it," said Fizzle. "Rainbows can show up anywhere water and light team up — waterfall mist, garden hose spray, even moonlight."

"A nighttime rainbow?" Priya asked.

"A **moonbow**," Fizzle said. "They're usually so pale they look white or gray. But a camera can catch the colors hiding inside."

Dev squirted his pistol straight up, hoping for a midnight moonbow. Nothing happened — the moon wasn't out yet.

"Patience," said Priya, patting his shoulder. "Rainbows don't do requests."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
"People have told rainbow stories forever," Fizzle said, as the mist began to settle. "Some say it's a bridge for gods to cross. Some say it's a sign of a promise after a storm — a happy ending painted across the sky."

"I like that," Priya said softly. "A happy ending you can actually see."

The glow dimmed. "Sparkle on!" Fizzle said, and popped away like a soap bubble, leaving one small, ordinary drop sitting on the tip of Dev's water pistol.

Priya and Dev were back on the bedroom carpet, right where they'd started.

Priya's sketchpad lay open. Where a blank page had been, there was now a perfect rainbow, every color in order, red on the outside, violet tucked in close.

"I didn't draw that," Priya whispered.

"Rainbows don't always wait for pencils," said Dev, grinning, and gave his water pistol one last, happy squirt.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Dev. Sparkle on!

story.title: Milo, Juno and the Brick That Found Sharks
story.subtitle: A swim through five hundred million years of fins

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick That Turned Blue
chapters.text:
Milo and Juno sat on the carpet. They were building a brick tower. It was the tallest one yet.

Suddenly, one brick glowed red. It was the very same brick from last week. The one that went CLICK and held.

"It's doing the thing!" Juno shouted.

The brick buzzed in Milo's hand. Then it turned bright blue, like the sea.

CLICK! A tiny brick shark popped up. He had a big smile and shiny eyes.

"Hello!" he said. "I'm Finn. Want to see real sharks?"

"YES!" said Juno.

Finn's tail spun like a little propeller. WHOOOOSH! The carpet melted into blue water.

Milo reached out and touched Finn's back. It felt bumpy, like sandpaper.

"Real shark skin feels like that too," said Finn. "Rough, like sandpaper. It helps sharks zoom through the water."

Then Milo noticed something else. "Finn, your bones feel bendy. Not hard, like mine."

"Good catch!" said Finn. "Shark bones are made of cartilage. That's bendy stuff, like the bendy part of your ear. Squish your ear and feel it!"

Milo squished his own ear. "Whoa, bendy!"

"Exactly," grinned Finn. "Ready to swim?"

"READY!" yelled Juno.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: So Many Shark Friends
chapters.text:
They swam through the blue water. Little fish zipped past them.

"Look!" said Milo. "A spotted one! A stripy one! A tiny one!"

Juno counted on her fingers. "One, two, three... I runned out of fingers!"

Finn laughed, a bubbly laugh. "You'll need way more fingers. There are more than **500 different kinds of sharks** swimming in our oceans."

Milo's mouth popped open. "Five hundred?! That's more than all my LEGO bricks!"

"Some are tiny as your hand," said Finn. "Some are longer than a school bus."

Juno spotted a shark with a flat, wide head zooming by. "That one looks funny!"

"We'll meet him later," said Finn, winking.

Milo spun in the water like a happy fish. "Five hundred shark friends. We better say hi to lots of them!"

"SPLOOSH!" yelled Juno, splashing her hands.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Older Than Dinosaurs
chapters.text:
Juno loved dinosaurs more than anything. "Finn, were there sharks when dinosaurs were alive?"

Finn gave a big shark smile. "Even older than that, Juno! Sharks swam in the ocean more than **400 million years ago**. That's before dinosaurs. Before even trees!"

Juno's eyes went wide as dinner plates. "Sharks are OLDER than my dinosaurs?!"

"Way older," said Finn.

Milo thought hard about it. "So sharks saw the very first dinosaur ever hatch?"

"They might have!" laughed Finn.

Juno did a happy dino-stomp dance in the water. Little bubbles popped up around her feet.

"Sharks win! Sharks win!" she cheered.

Milo high-fived her floaty fin. "Dinosaurs are still cool, though."

"Everyone here is cool," said Finn. "Follow me. Next stop is a BIG one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
A shadow fell over them. Milo looked up. And up. And up.

"That's the **whale shark**," said Finn. "The biggest fish in the whole sea. Longer than **40 feet** — longer than a school bus!"

Juno hid behind Milo's arm, just for one second. "Is it scary?"

The whale shark opened its huge mouth. Tiny bits of food floated in and got slurped right up.

"Nope!" said Finn. "He only eats teeny tiny bits of food floating in the water. Smaller than a crumb!"

Milo relaxed all over. "He's like a big gentle vacuum cleaner!"

Juno giggled and waved at the giant shark. The whale shark blinked slowly and swam on by.

"Bye, big buddy!" Juno shouted.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Smile Wide
chapters.text:
Next they met a sleek gray shark with a toothy grin.

"This is the **great white shark**," said Finn. "He can grow as long as **20 feet**. Look at those teeth!"

Milo leaned in close. The teeth were shaped like little triangles, with bumpy edges like a saw.

"Why are they bumpy?" asked Milo.

"Good question," said Finn. "That shape helps him eat his dinner."

Then Milo noticed something wobbly. "Finn, is that tooth loose?"

"Sharp eyes!" said Finn. "Sharks lose teeth all the time. A new one always slides forward to take its place. Sharks grow thousands of teeth in one whole life!"

Juno gasped. "Thousands?! I only have baby teeth and grown-up teeth!"

"Sharks are extra fancy," laughed Finn.

The great white gave one more toothy grin and swam off, happy as can be.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Tooth as Big as a Hand
chapters.text:
They swam down, down, past old rocks and sand.

Milo spotted something shiny in the sand. He picked it up. It was a giant tooth, as big as his whole hand!

"Whoa! Whose tooth is THIS?" Milo asked.

"That," said Finn, "belonged to **Megalodon**. A giant shark who lived long, long ago."

"Where is he now?" asked Juno.

"He isn't around anymore," said Finn gently. "That's called **extinct**. It means he's all gone now."

"Like... gone gone?" asked Juno softly.

"Gone gone," said Finn. "But we still know about him because of teeth like this one. Old teeth left behind in rock are called **fossils**. They're like clues from long ago."

Milo held the tooth up proudly. "I found a clue!"

"You sure did," said Finn. "Great big discovery, Milo."

Juno patted the tooth softly. "Night night, old shark."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Wraparound Eyes and the Shark Lady
chapters.text:
The funny flat-headed shark from before swam closer.

"This is a **hammerhead shark**," said Finn. "His head is wide and flat, like a hammer. That means his eyes are far apart."

Juno giggled. "His head IS a hammer!"

"Why's that good?" asked Milo.

Finn grinned wide. "Wide eyes mean he can see almost all the way around himself. A wraparound view!"

Milo tried spreading his arms out wide like a hammerhead's head, wobbling through the water.

Finn chuckled. "There once was a scientist named **Eugenie Clark**. People called her the Shark Lady. She studied sharks for years and years. She showed everyone that sharks are curious, and can even learn tricks — just like a puppy!"

"Sharks are smart!" said Milo.

"Smart AND friendly," said Finn. "Now, little swimmers — time to go home."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
Finn's tail spun again. WHOOOOSH! The water swirled into carpet and lamps and pillows.

CLICK! Milo and Juno landed softly on their bedroom floor.

Milo opened his hand. The giant tooth was gone. In its place sat a small, shiny gray LEGO brick, shaped just like a tooth.

"A souvenir!" said Milo, grinning.

Juno yawned a big dinosaur yawn. "Sharks are older than dinosaurs... and I waved at a whale shark..."

Finn, now a tiny brick again, gave one last wink before going still and quiet on the carpet.

Milo placed the new tooth-shaped brick on top of their tower. It clicked right into place and held.

"Goodnight, sharks," whispered Juno, snuggling into her blanket.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

story.title: Milo, Juno, and the Brick Full of Sharks
story.subtitle: A WHOOOOSH, a whale shark, and one very old tooth named Chomper

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick Goes WHOOOOSH
chapters.text:
Milo stacked one more brick on top of his tall LEGO tower. It had held strong since last week, every single brick still clicked tight. Juno lined up her dinosaur toys beside it, making them roar.

The little red brick on top gave a tiny wink. Then it glowed bright red, like a stoplight at night. CLICK. CLICK. CLICK.

"It's doing the thing again!" Milo whispered.

WHOOOOSH! The whole room spun like a washing machine.

When it stopped spinning, Milo and Juno were floating in cool blue water. Bubbles tickled their noses. A huge gray shadow glided close, bigger than their whole living room.

Juno squeaked and grabbed Milo's arm.

Then the shadow turned sideways, showing a friendly, spotty face and a mouth wider than their front door.

"It's just a big fish!" Milo said. "A whale shark, I bet!"

The little brick, glowing softly on a string around his neck, gave one happy click, like it was saying yes. The whale shark swam slow circles around them, gentle as a balloon floating in air.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Biggest Fish in the Sea
chapters.text:
The whale shark opened its huge mouth wide, wider than a garage door. Milo peeked inside, careful to keep his hands tucked close. No teeth chomped at him. Instead, tiny bits of food floated in, like soup pouring through a strainer.

"It eats tiny floaty bits called plankton," the brick clicked softly, "even though it's over forty feet long!"

That's longer than a whole school bus! Juno counted on her fingers. "One, two, three... that's a LOT of feet!"

Milo held his hand near the shark's side, close but not touching. "It feels like it would be bendy," he said, "like my ear, not hard like a bone!"

The brick blinked yes, twice. "Sharks don't have hard bones inside like you do. They have soft, bendy stuff called cartilage, just like the squishy part of your ear."

"So if it bumped into my LEGO tower," Milo grinned, "it would just bounce right off!"

Juno giggled so hard she got the hiccups. The whale shark swam onward, slow and gentle as a passing cloud.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Five Hundred Shark Cousins
chapters.text:
A tiny shark, no bigger than a crayon, zipped right past Milo's nose. Then a much bigger shape slid by, teeth and all, moving slow and calm.

"Whoa, sharks come in ALL sizes!" Milo said.

The brick glowed brighter. "There are more than five hundred different kinds of sharks swimming in oceans all over the world," it clicked.

Juno pointed at a shark with a long pointy nose. "That one looks like my triceratops horn!"

Milo laughed. "Sharks aren't dinosaurs, silly. But they sure do look wild."

A gray shark with sharp triangle teeth cruised past, hunting fish far, far away from the kids. "That's a great white," Milo whispered. "It can grow almost twenty feet long, nearly as long as a school bus!"

The brick clicked twice, sounding proud. Milo counted the different shark shapes zooming by: round ones, flat ones, speckled ones, striped ones.

"It's like a whole LEGO set made of sharks," he said, "and nobody built two exactly the same!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Sandpaper Skin and Endless Teeth
chapters.text:
Milo reached toward a shark gliding past, then stopped his hand just before touching. "Can I pet it?" he asked.

The brick clicked a gentle warning. "Better to just look. Shark skin feels rough, like sandpaper, covered in tiny little bumps."

"Whoa, skin with bumps?" Juno gasped, eyes huge.

"Not biting teeth," Milo said, "just bumpy ones, to help it swim fast and smooth."

A shark opened its mouth, and Milo spotted rows and rows of teeth lined up like a zipper. "Why so many?" he asked.

"Sharks lose teeth all the time," the brick clicked, "and new ones keep moving forward to replace them, their whole life long."

"So it never runs out?" Juno asked.

"Never!" said the brick. Milo grinned. "I wish my LEGO bricks did that when I lost one under the couch!"

Juno laughed so hard a bubble popped right out of her mouth.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Shark With a Hammer Head
chapters.text:
Something strange swam toward them, a shark with a head shaped like a hammer! Juno pointed, eyes wide. "That shark is broken!"

"Not broken," Milo laughed, "that's just how it's shaped!"

The brick clicked happily. "That's called a hammerhead shark. Its wide head spreads its eyes far apart, so it can see almost all the way around itself."

Milo waved one hand near the side of his head, then the other side. "Like seeing behind you without even turning around!"

Down on the sandy floor, a small spotted shark used its fins like tiny legs, walking right across the sand.

"IT'S WALKING!" Juno shouted, bouncing in the water.

"Like a dinosaur!" she added.

"That one can even hold its breath a long time, resting quietly in little puddles when the water pulls back," the brick clicked.

Milo tried wiggling his arms like fins. "I want fin-legs too!"

Juno copied him, and the two of them wiggle-walked together through the bubbles, giggling the whole way.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Giant Shark from Long Ago
chapters.text:
The water turned a little darker, and something huge drifted down from above, landing softly in the sand in front of them: a tooth bigger than Milo's whole hand.

Juno picked it up carefully. "A dino tooth!"

"Not quite," the brick clicked. "That's from megalodon, a giant shark from millions and millions of years ago. It's not swimming anywhere anymore. We call that gone-forever extinct."

"Bigger than a dinosaur?" Juno gasped.

"It actually swam before most dinosaurs ever did," said the brick.

Juno's mouth made a perfect round O. "SHARKS ARE OLDER THAN DINOSAURS?!"

"Way older," Milo said. "Sharks have been swimming around for more than four hundred million years!"

"How do we even know about megalodon if it's gone?" Milo asked, turning the giant tooth over in his hands.

"Teeth don't disappear like the rest of the body does," the brick clicked. "So teeth like this one are almost all we have to learn from. We call an old, old thing turned hard like stone a fossil."

Juno hugged the giant tooth like a stuffed animal. "I'm naming you Chomper."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Shark Lady
chapters.text:
A woman in a diving mask swam up smiling, bubbles trailing behind her, sharks gliding calmly all around her like old friends.

"That's Eugenie Clark," the brick clicked. "Everybody called her the Shark Lady."

"She's not scared at all!" Milo said.

"She studied sharks for years and years," said the brick, "and showed everyone that sharks are curious, and can even learn tricks, kind of like a puppy."

Juno reached out one hand, not touching, just waving hello. A little shark seemed to wave a fin right back at her.

"See?" the Shark Lady seemed to smile through her mask. "Sharks mostly just want to be sharks. They almost never bother people."

Milo nodded hard. "So they're not scary monsters at all."

"Nope," clicked the brick. "They're an important part of keeping the whole ocean happy and healthy."

Juno still held tight to Chomper, the giant tooth. "I'm gonna be a shark lady," she said, "AND a dinosaur lady. Both!"

The brick gave one last happy click, like it agreed completely.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The water spun into swirling bubbles, and WHOOOOSH, the carpet appeared under Milo's knees again.

His tall LEGO tower stood right where he had left it, every brick still holding strong.

Next to it sat one brand new thing: a smooth gray tooth, bigger than his whole hand.

"Chomper came home with us!" Juno cheered, hugging it tight against her pajamas.

The little red brick gave one last soft click, then dimmed down to a sleepy, glowing red, waiting quietly for next time.

Milo yawned a great big yawn. "Sharks are basically the LEGO bricks of the ocean," he said. "So many different kinds, and somehow they all fit together just right."

Juno was already snoring a tiny dinosaur snore, Chomper tucked safe under her arm like a stuffed shark.

Milo tucked the little brick safely by his pillow and lay down too, smiling up at the ceiling.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

story.title: Stumps, Arjun: The Night Cricket's Guide to Sleep
story.subtitle: A bedtime report from the world's strangest commentator.

chapters.heading: Over 1: The Boy Who Twitched (1953)
chapters.text:
Arjun was lying flat on his stomach, flashlight under the blanket, reading the newest issue of his favorite comic for the fourth time.

"Five more minutes," he whispered to no one, the way he did every single night.

Then the flashlight flickered green, and the comic's last panel began to glow like a firefly had moved in. Something small and shiny popped out of the page and landed on his pillow. It had wings like a cricket — the chirping kind — and tiny sunglasses pushed up on its head.

"Nibs," it said, bowing. "Night Cricket. I commentate on sleep, the way your telly commentates on actual cricket. Fancy a look at tonight's match?"

Arjun sat up so fast the comic slid off the bed. "Sleep has a *match*?"

"Every night," said Nibs. "First ball's in **1953**, University of Chicago. Two scientists, Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman, were watching a boy sleep."

"That's... creepy?" Arjun guessed.

"Science," corrected Nibs. "They noticed the boy's eyes twitching back and forth under his eyelids, fast, like he was watching a rally. They called it **REM sleep** — Rapid Eye Movement. Eyes racing, even though the boy looked totally still."

Arjun pressed his own eyes shut, trying to feel them move. Nothing happened, obviously — you can't catch yourself dreaming.

"Kleitman spent his whole life watching people sleep," Nibs said. "People still call him the father of the whole science of it."

"So I've got a secret eye-match going on every night?" Arjun said. "Nobody told me!"

"Lean in," said Nibs, "and I'll show you the whole innings."

chapters.heading: Over 2: The Ninety-Minute Over
chapters.text:
A glowing line now rippled across the dark like a scoreboard. It dipped low, then spiked, then dipped again.

"Every sleep is divided into rounds," Nibs said, "about **ninety minutes** each — roughly one half of a football match, if that helps."

Arjun squinted at the spikes. "They're like overs. Quiet, quiet, quiet, then — action!"

"Close enough," said Nibs. "The quiet part is called **non-REM** — your body resting, heart slowing down. Then it flips into REM, where you dream hardest and your brain gets almost as busy as when you're awake."

"But I don't sleepwalk every night," Arjun said. "So what stops me acting it out?"

"Good question — the exact one scientists asked," Nibs said. "During REM, your muscles basically switch off. Go floppy. Your brain can run around all it wants. Your body just lies there like a sack of kit bags."

Arjun tried to imagine his arms gone totally limp while his brain played test cricket inside his own skull. "That's either amazing or terrifying."

"Bit of both," Nibs agreed. "Now — count the spikes with me. How many rounds in a normal night?"

Arjun counted along the glowing line. "Four? Five?"

"Four or five," Nibs confirmed. "A whole tournament, every single night."
chapters.shout_line: A WHOLE TOURNAMENT, EVERY SINGLE NIGHT!

chapters.heading: Over 3: The Clock Behind Your Eyes
chapters.text:
Nibs led him through a corridor shaped like the inside of a comic panel, until they reached a glowing knot of light shaped like a tiny stadium clock, nestled right behind Arjun's own eyes.

"That," said Nibs, "is the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**. Say it three times fast and you win a prize."

Arjun tried. He did not win a prize.

"Everyone just calls it the master clock," Nibs said. "It sits exactly where the nerves from your two eyes cross over, and it keeps your whole body on schedule — sleepy at night, awake in the day."

"So that's why I get tired at the same time every night," Arjun said, "even on holiday, even with no clock in the room."

"Exactly. Scientists have a word for a clock that runs about once a day: **circadian**. It comes from old Latin words that basically mean 'about a day.'"

"Circa-day," Arjun repeated, liking the sound of it. "Like a day-shaped boomerang."

"Not far off," said Nibs. "It keeps coming back whether you want it to or not — which is bad news for anyone hoping for five more minutes."

Arjun groaned. The clock had clearly heard that joke before.

chapters.heading: Over 4: Three Scientists and a Fly (2017)
chapters.text:
A tiny fly buzzed past Arjun's ear and landed, dead still, on the scoreboard clock.

"Is it... sleeping?" Arjun asked. "It's a fly. Its brain's the size of a comma."

"Even flies go still like they're asleep," Nibs said. "Scientists think sleep might be one of the oldest tricks in the whole animal game — older than cricket, older than comics, older than pretty much everything alive."

Arjun looked at the fly with new respect.

"The clock behind your eyes runs on tiny genes," Nibs went on, "switches inside your cells that tick off the hours. In **2017**, three scientists — Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young — won the **Nobel Prize**. That's basically the gold medal of science. They won it for finding those very genes."

"They won a medal," Arjun said slowly, "for other people's bedtimes."

"For *everyone's* bedtimes," said Nibs. "Fly bedtimes included."

The fly gave what might have been a shrug, and went straight back to sleep.

chapters.heading: Over 5: The Lights-Out Hormone (1958)
chapters.text:
The stadium floodlights began to dim on their own, dropping from white to orange to a sleepy purple.

"Who's doing that?" Arjun asked.

"A little chemical messenger called **melatonin**," said Nibs. "Scientists call it a hormone — basically a note your body sends itself. This note says: lights out."

"Where does it even come from?"

"A pea-sized part of your brain makes it, as soon as the room goes properly dark. In **1958**, a scientist named Aaron Lerner led the team that first managed to pull it out and study it closely."

Arjun watched the lights fade almost to nothing, like a stadium after the last ball of the day.

"So melatonin's basically an umpire," he said, "calling stumps on the whole day?"

"Best comparison I've heard all night," said Nibs, sounding genuinely impressed.

"I have good ones sometimes," Arjun said, trying not to look too pleased with himself.

chapters.heading: Over 6: The Rinse Cycle and the Growth Spurt
chapters.text:
They moved to a part of the stadium where everything looked freshly mopped, pipes gurgling overhead.

"Every night your brain runs its own rinse cycle," Nibs said. "Scientists call it the **glymphatic system** — think of it as a cleaning crew flushing out waste while you're deep asleep."

"Gross," said Arjun, "but also kind of great."

"During the deepest part of non-REM sleep," Nibs went on, "your body releases the most **growth hormone** — the stuff that helps you grow taller. One reason kids need more sleep than grown-ups."

Arjun perked up. "So sleep makes me taller? For cricket?"

"Partly," said Nibs. "It also sorts your memories, filing the important stuff into long-term storage. Like that bowling grip you practiced today."

"So if I sleep well tonight," Arjun said, working it out loud, "I'll remember it better tomorrow?"

"That's the theory," said Nibs. "Sleep's basically doing your homework while you're unconscious."

Arjun decided, right there, that sleep was extremely underrated.

chapters.heading: Over 7: The Sleep Scoreboard
chapters.text:
A glowing scoreboard rose up, shaped like the ones at the cricket ground, except it listed animals instead of teams.

"Sleep records," Nibs announced. "Pick one."

Arjun pointed straight at the dolphin. "Dolphins can't fully fall asleep, right? They'd drown."

"They solve it by sleeping with half their brain at a time," Nibs said. "One eye stays open, watching for danger, while the other half rests. Seals do something similar."

"Next," said Arjun, scanning down. "Giraffe — only two hours?"

"Sometimes under two, in short naps, standing right up," Nibs confirmed. "Shortest sleeper of any big animal."

"And bats pull the opposite stunt," Nibs added before Arjun could even ask. "Some small ones sleep up to **twenty hours** a day. Laziest mammals on record."

"What about baby humans?" Arjun asked, thinking of his cousin's new little sister.

"Newborns sleep **fourteen to seventeen hours**, in short bursts, nearly half of it in REM," said Nibs. "All that dreaming helps build a brand-new brain."

Arjun did some quick math in his head. "So by the time I'm old, I'll have slept through, what, a third of my whole life?"

"Just about," said Nibs. "Which means you're basically a professional at this already."

chapters.heading: Over 8: The Boy Who Stayed Awake (1964)
chapters.text:
"One more player," said Nibs, the lights dropping low, almost stumps. "In **1964**, San Diego — a seventeen-year-old called Randy Gardner stayed awake for about **eleven days** straight, for a school science project."

Arjun's mouth fell open. "ELEVEN DAYS? That's basically a whole series!"

"It's one of the longest stretches anybody's ever properly recorded," Nibs said. "But listen close — doctors do not want anyone trying to break that record. Go without sleep that long and your mood crashes, your attention goes to pieces, you forget everything. Randy turned out fine, but nobody recommends the stunt."

Arjun thought about his own nightly argument for five more minutes, multiplied by eleven days, and felt a little ill.

"Message received," he said. "Five more minutes is my absolute limit."

"Good," said Nibs, folding his wings. "Stumps."

The stadium lights dimmed to nothing. The comic slid shut on its own, its glowing edge fading back to ordinary paper. Nibs hopped onto the last panel and gave a small salute.

"Same time tomorrow?" Arjun whispered.

"Every innings needs a tomorrow," said Nibs, and blinked out.

Arjun set the flashlight down, pulled the blanket up, and for once did not ask for five more minutes.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow's nets could wait; tonight was for letting that bowling grip settle in, rested and ready to remember itself.
