story.title: Mia and the Scorebook That Remembers Everything
story.subtitle: One pencil, one glowing page, and the real history of soccer, stat by stat.

chapters.heading: Kickoff in Han China
chapters.text:
It was 11:40 on a school night, and Mia had three windows open: her homework, a spreadsheet of her club team's shot-conversion rates — how many of their shots actually went in — by half, and a chat with herself that just said *you should be asleep*.

She closed exactly none of them.

On the shelf above her desk sat her grandfather's old scorebook, scuffed green at the corners, the kind of relic from someone who tracked every stat by hand because there was no app for it in his day. She'd been meaning to compare his 1970s numbers to hers for weeks. Pencil out, she opened to a blank taped-in page at the back and wrote a real stat from tonight's match: **14 shots, 3 goals**.

The pencil mark turned the color of a stadium floodlight.

The page didn't just glow. It opened — the way a door opens, not the way a book does — and a cold gust of dust and distant shouting rolled out across her bedroom carpet.

Mia did the math on that for exactly one second before she climbed in after it.

She landed on hard-packed dirt under a wide gray sky, next to a wall with a round hole cut high into it. A crowd of teenagers in loose tunics were kicking a stitched leather ball back and forth, trying to put it through that hole without using their hands.

"Okay," Mia said, to nobody, "where and when am I."

"Han China," said a voice from the scorebook, somehow still under her arm, its pages flipping like a fan. "Somewhere past **2,000 years ago**. They call this game **cuju** — 'kickball.' Through the hole counts. Hands don't."

Mia watched a boy miss three times running, then catch the rhythm on his fourth try and thread it clean through the gap. The crowd roared.

"Wait," Mia said, the stats part of her brain waking up before the rest of it. "He missed because he rushed his setup touch. Fourth time he slowed down before the shot."

"Go tell him that," said the scorebook.

She did — badly, in three words and a lot of pointing — and the boy, confused but game, tried it her way next turn. Setup touch, pause, strike. **Through the hole, clean.**

He turned and yelled something at her that didn't need translating. It meant *again*.

"Is this the earliest soccer there is?" Mia asked.

"Earliest anyone's found," said the scorebook. "People have been obsessed with 'kick thing through gap' since before most of history got written down. Good, extremely old company."

Mia grinned and wrote it down. **CUJU. 2,000+ YEARS. STILL WORKS.**

chapters.heading: The Mob and the Missing Ball
chapters.text:
The scorebook's pages whipped forward hundreds of years, and the smell of dust turned into the smell of mud, smoke, and a whole lot of yelling.

Mia stumbled into a street crammed with people — not a stadium, a street — kicking, shoving, and occasionally full-on tackling each other over something that might once have been a ball. Shutters slammed shut up and down the road.

"This can't be soccer," Mia said, ducking an elbow.

"Technically it's an ancestor," said the scorebook. "**Mob football**. Whole villages against whole villages, barely any rules at all. Shins: not optional cushioning."

A man in fine robes pushed through the crowd and unrolled a scroll, reading loudly enough to quiet half the street. Mia caught a date stamped at the bottom: **1314**.

"**King Edward the Second**," the scorebook translated. "Banning the game in **London**, this very year, because it wrecks the city faster than anyone can fix it."

"They banned soccer because it was too much fun?" Mia said.

"They banned it because nobody had invented a referee yet," said the scorebook. "Same problem. Different solution."

Mia crouched by a flattened market stall and counted the broken crates out loud, working out how many games it must have taken to make a king this annoyed. The stallholder, grudgingly impressed by a stranger who'd shown up mid-riot just to count his wreckage, pressed a battered leather ball into her hands before the crowd swept her away.

The next page landed her somewhere quieter: a cold stone room high in a castle, centuries later. A servant was shoving a stitched leather ball — old, round, handled to death — up into the rafters above a doorway.

"Why's he hiding it?" Mia whispered.

"Not from anyone in this room," said the scorebook. "He's hiding it from time. That ball stayed up there, forgotten, until workers found it during repairs at **Stirling Castle** — and it may go all the way back to the **1540s**, which would make it the oldest football anyone's ever found."

Mia looked at the beat-up ball under her own arm, then up at the one vanishing into the rafters, four hundred years apart and somehow the same idea.

"Everybody just keeps kicking the same thing forward," she said.

"That's basically the whole book," said the scorebook.

chapters.heading: Cambridge, and the Man Who Wrote It Down
chapters.text:
Next page, next century. Mia landed in a wood-paneled room above a tavern in **London**, where a dozen serious men in suits argued across a long table like it was a penalty shootout.

"You can't just pick the ball up and run with it!" one shouted.

"Every school's always done it that way!" another shot back.

Mia leaned toward the scorebook. "Let me guess. Everyone's playing a slightly different game and calling it the same sport."

"Exactly the problem," said the scorebook. "Different schools, different rules — handling, tripping, all of it up for grabs. Back in **1848**, some Cambridge students tried writing down one shared rulebook. Didn't quite stick everywhere. Tonight, this room tries again."

A tall man with a serious mustache — **Ebenezer Cobb Morley**, the scorebook whispered — was scribbling furiously, crossing out lines, starting over. Mia peered over his shoulder at a half-finished rule and caught the contradiction before he did: one line banned carrying the ball, two lines down, another allowed catching it under certain conditions.

"Those two rules fight each other," Mia said, pointing.

Morley stopped mid-sentence, read it twice, and struck the second line out entirely.

"No hands. Full stop," he muttered, and wrote it down for good.

By the end of the night the room had a name — the **Football Association**, founded that very evening, **26 October 1863** — and Morley walked out with the first official Laws of the Game, the sport's actual rulebook, folded in his coat pocket, cross-outs and all.

"One contradiction," Mia said, "and I basically co-wrote the rules of soccer."

"Don't let it go to your head," said the scorebook. "You fixed a typo. He wrote the other four hundred lines."

chapters.heading: The Cup and the Goalless Draw
chapters.text:
The next jump smelled like cut grass and nerves.

Mia landed pitchside at a real match, real stakes, real crowd, somewhere in England. A brass band was playing badly. A man with a stopwatch kept checking it like it owed him money.

"What's the occasion?" Mia asked.

"First-ever **FA Cup**," said the scorebook. "Started the **1871-to-'72** season. Oldest football competition still running anywhere in the world, played every single year since."

Mia watched two teams fight out a scrappy match, tracking shots and misses under her breath the way she always did at her own games. "Nobody's scored in twenty minutes," she said. "That's not bad luck, that's two very good defenses."

"Write that down," said the scorebook. "You've basically just invented sports commentary."

A few pages later, same kind of stadium, different jerseys: **Scotland against England**, in **Glasgow**, the air thick with noise and absolutely nobody scoring a single goal.

"**First official international match ever played**," the scorebook said. "**1872**. Ends **nil-nil** — zero to zero."

"A world-first match," Mia said, "and it's the most boring scoreline possible."

"Zero-zero isn't boring," the scorebook sniffed. "Zero-zero is two teams playing perfect defense for ninety straight minutes. You of all people should respect a clean sheet."

Walking back through the crowd afterward, Mia heard schoolboys arguing over what to even call the sport — "football" sounded plain, somebody wanted something snappier, and one of them, laughing, shortened "**association** football" down to "**assoc**," then "soccer," like a joke that got away from him.

"That word's going to stick around for about a hundred and fifty years," the scorebook said. "Mostly in America. It'll start arguments at every family dinner."

"Finally," Mia said, "a stat I can win with my dad."

chapters.heading: Tables, Leagues, and a World Governing Body
chapters.text:
The next page dropped Mia into a cramped office that smelled like pipe smoke and panic, paper covering every surface.

A stressed man named **William McGregor** was trying to schedule a season's worth of matches between a dozen clubs, by hand, with no spreadsheet, no app, and clearly no idea how badly he needed one.

"You're trying to rank twelve teams," Mia said, looking over his shoulder, "and your fixtures are written in the order you thought of them instead of a rotation. That's why it's not working."

McGregor looked up, exhausted. "Go on, then."

Mia grabbed a blank sheet and built him a simple grid — every team plays every other team, home and away, results logged as they happen. It wasn't fancy. It was just a table. McGregor stared at it like she'd handed him a trophy.

"**1888**," the scorebook said quietly. "McGregor organizes the **Football League** — the first football league anywhere in the world. You just helped lay out the first league table in history. No pressure."

"I build tables for my own club's youth division for fun," Mia said. "This is just that, with worse record-keeping."

Sixteen years later, new room: **Paris**, officials from **seven** different European countries around one table, signing paper after paper.

"What's this one?" Mia asked.

"**1904**," said the scorebook. "Seven countries just founded **FIFA** — football's world governing body. One organization, every country's teams, one set of rules everyone agrees to follow."

Mia scanned the signatures. "So in forty-one years we went from arguing about handling a ball in a tavern to an entire planet agreeing on rules."

"Give it time," said the scorebook. "You haven't even met the trophy yet."

chapters.heading: Montevideo, 1930
chapters.text:
The next page roared before it even opened — actual crowd noise leaking out through the paper like a held breath finally let go.

Mia stepped into blinding sun and a stadium packed to the rafters, flags everywhere.

"**1930**," said the scorebook. "**Uruguay**. The first-ever **FIFA World Cup**, final match, right now, host country against **Argentina**."

A man in a sharp suit paced the sideline like he'd invented the whole thing himself, mostly because he had. "That's **Jules Rimet**," the scorebook said. "FIFA's president. The reason this tournament exists at all. Tonight's trophy will carry his name."

Mia watched Uruguay pull ahead, lose the lead, then claw it back in the second half, the crowd rising and falling like one enormous animal breathing. She found herself shouting with them without meaning to.

"**URUGUAY WINS IT!**" she yelled as the final whistle cut through the noise, and the stadium erupted so hard she felt it in her chest.

"Host nation," said the scorebook, "beating Argentina, in the very first World Cup there ever was. Not a bad game to catch live."

Mia watched the small gold **Jules Rimet Trophy** get carried out onto the pitch, gleaming under lights that, this far back, were honestly not that bright.

"That little thing," she said, "is going to get fought over by the entire planet for the rest of history, isn't it."

"You have no idea," said the scorebook. "Wait till you see what happens to it in thirty-six years."

chapters.heading: The Dog Who Found the World Cup
chapters.text:
The scorebook's page landed her on a gray London afternoon, sirens somewhere in the distance, newspaper headlines practically shouting off the stands.

"What happened?" Mia asked.

"**1966**," said the scorebook. "Someone just stole the actual World Cup trophy, right off its display stand, right here in London, days before the tournament it's supposed to be handed out in."

"They stole the trophy," Mia repeated, "before the tournament it's for."

"Entire country's in a panic," the scorebook confirmed. "Except for one dog."

A small, scruffy mutt trotted past, nose down, tail going like a metronome, and stopped hard at a hedge near a garden wall. His owner tugged the leash, annoyed, until he saw what the dog had found wrapped in old newspaper under the bush: the missing trophy, completely unharmed.

"That," said the scorebook, with real reverence, "is **Pickles**. Found the entire World Cup trophy, a week after it vanished, sniffing around a hedge like it was just another walk."

"A dog solved the biggest sports crime of the decade," Mia said, "and I bet he didn't even get a trophy of his own."

"He got better than a trophy," said the scorebook. "He got to watch **England** actually win the thing a few weeks later. Hosted the tournament, won the final. Only World Cup title England's picked up so far."

Mia watched the celebration from a safe distance, a sea of scarves and noise, and thought about how close that whole party had come to opening with an empty display case and a very awkward apology.

"Good dog," she said.

"Best stat in the whole book," the scorebook agreed. "Zero trophies stayed missing. One hundred percent recovery rate."

chapters.heading: Three Stars and a Pocketful of Cards
chapters.text:
Four more pages, four more World Cups blurring past in flashes of color and noise, and somewhere in the middle Mia started noticing the same number seventeen jersey turning up again and again.

"Okay, who is that," she said, pointing at a Brazilian forward doing things with a soccer ball that looked faintly illegal.

"**Pele**," said the scorebook. "**1958**. Then **1962**. Then **1970**. Three World Cup wins, three different squads, and he's still the only player in history who's managed that."

"That's not a stat," Mia said. "That's a glitch."

By 1970 the referees had clearly had enough of arguing with players, because one of them — a calm Englishman named **Ken Aston**, sitting at a traffic light waiting for it to change — apparently had the idea right there in his car, and started carrying two cards in his pocket. Yellow for a warning. Red for sending someone off.

Mia watched him flash a yellow card at a furious midfielder who looked ready to argue and then, faced with an actual piece of colored card, simply didn't.

"Traffic lights," Mia said. "He built the simplest conflict-resolution system in sports out of **traffic lights**."

"**1970 World Cup**," the scorebook confirmed. "First time anyone ever saw those cards. Every match since."

By the time that tournament's dust settled, Brazil had lifted the trophy for a third time — their results across those decades adding up to **five World Cup titles** altogether, more than any other country — and because they'd now won it three times, FIFA let them keep the original gold trophy for good. A brand-new one, built specifically to replace it, showed up in **1974**.

"They won so much," Mia said, "they broke the trophy case."

"They earned a new one," the scorebook said. "Try not to sound too impressed. It encourages them."

chapters.heading: The Fifty-Year Foul
chapters.text:
The next page felt different before it even opened — quieter, like the scorebook itself was choosing its words carefully.

Mia stepped into a packed stadium in England, thousands of people crammed in to watch women's teams play, a tall, confident forward in the middle of the pitch who clearly scared every defender near her.

"That's **Lily Parr**," said the scorebook. "Star player for the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**, one of the most popular teams in the country right now. Crowds this size, for women's football. Remember that part."

"Why do I need to remember it specifically," Mia said, already suspicious of the scorebook's tone.

"Because the people running English football are about to ban women from playing on their grounds at all," said the scorebook. "And the ban is going to last **fifty years**."

Mia felt something sharp and unfair sit in her stomach, watching Parr sprint past a defender like the game belonged to her. "Fifty years is most of a lifetime," she said.

"It's unfair, and it's also not the ending," said the scorebook. "Turn the page."

She did. The stadium changed, the jerseys changed, decades folded past under her hand — and there it was: **1971**, the ban finally lifted, women's football legal again on the grounds that had shut it out for half a century. Then another jump, further still: **1991**, a packed stadium, a brand-new tournament banner reading **Women's World Cup** for the very first time, and the **United States** lifting the trophy at the end of it.

"They waited fifty years," Mia said, watching the celebration, "and then just — kept going."

"That's most of the good parts of history," said the scorebook. "People get told to stop. A lot of them don't."

chapters.heading: Final Whistle
chapters.text:
The last page didn't glow so much as settle, quietly, like a long final whistle.

Mia found herself back on her bedroom floor, laptop still open to her shot-conversion spreadsheet, exactly four minutes later than when she'd left — which felt, frankly, like bad accounting for several thousand years of soccer.

Grandad's scorebook sat closed in her lap, warm at the edges in a way old leather books generally aren't. She opened it to the blank taped-in page where she'd first written tonight's score.

Underneath her own handwriting, in ink that definitely hadn't been there before, someone had added: **2,000+ YEARS AND COUNTING. STILL YOUR MOVE.**

Mia closed the laptop. She looked at her own stat line again — **14 shots, 3 goals** — and thought about a boy in Han China slowing his touch down before a shot, a man in a tavern crossing out his own contradiction, a dog sniffing out a hedge, a stadium full of people who kept showing up no matter who tried to stop them.

She picked up her pencil one more time and, underneath the glowing note, wrote her own: **conversion rate needs work.**

The page didn't glow this time. It didn't need to. Some stats just needed practice, not magic.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow's match would have to prove it.

story.title: Mia and Number Nine: A History of the Beautiful Game
story.subtitle: One scuffed soccer ball, four thousand years of football, and a stats nerd who finally gets the receipts.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Cuju, China — Around 200 BCE
chapters.text:
Mia had the laptop open to a spreadsheet of her own team's shot conversion rate, rows of green and red cells stretching well past midnight. She should have been asleep two hours ago. Instead she was arguing with a pivot table about whether her left foot was actually weaker than her stats said it was.

On the shelf behind her sat the beaten-up size-4 ball her first coach had given her, scuffed down to gray, laces long gone. She'd kept it because the numbers were still legible — a 9 inked on in marker from the season she'd worn that number three years straight.

She reached over without thinking, meaning to toss it onto the bed, and the seams lit up gold under her fingers. Not a trick of the desk lamp. Stitches, actually glowing, rearranging themselves into a string of digits: -200.

"That's not a year," she said out loud, because arguing with a soccer ball felt marginally less insane than believing it. "There's no year zero. You'd need—"

"Four hundred BCE-ish, give or take a century," the ball said, in a voice like a sports commentator reading a final score. "Welcome to the all-time stat sheet, Mia. I'm Number Nine. I've been keeping tabs since before anyone called this sport anything at all."

She should have dropped it. She bounced it instead, because some part of her — the part that color-coded spreadsheets for fun — wanted to see where the data went.

The room dissolved into dust and lantern light. A dirt court. Men in long tunics kicked a stuffed leather ball between two bamboo poles, no hands allowed, roaring every time it sailed through.

"Cuju," said Number Nine, spinning lazily in her grip. "A kicking game, played in Han China **over 2,000 years ago**. A lot of historians call it the oldest ancestor soccer's got."

Mia watched a player flick the ball up with his heel, juggle it twice, then thread it dead center between the poles. The crowd completely lost it.

"That's a better first touch than half my varsity team," Mia muttered.

"Write it down," said Number Nine. "I keep the receipts. You're just visiting them."

She grinned, and bounced the ball again before she could talk herself out of it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: A King's Ban and a Castle's Secret
chapters.text:
The next bounce landed her mid-riot.

Mud, noise, and about forty men hauling an inflated pig's bladder — the squishy, air-filled sac that used to get stitched inside old leather balls — down a London street like it owed them money. Mia ducked an elbow that wasn't aimed at her but might as well have been.

"This is **mob football**," said Number Nine, sounding delighted. "Whole villages against each other. No ref, barely any rules, and absolutely no sideline."

"This is a riot with a ball in it," Mia said, watching a man get shouldered straight into a fruit cart.

"King Edward II thought so too. He banned it in London in **1314** — too much property damage, not nearly enough actual football."

Mia laughed despite herself. "So the first rule in soccer history is basically 'please stop.'"

"Pretty much."

The scene blurred, and when it settled she was standing in a quiet stone room lined with tapestries — somebody's castle, judging by the drafts coming off the walls. Number Nine nudged her attention toward a dusty rafter overhead, where something round and leathery had been wedged for who knew how long.

"Stirling Castle, Scotland," said the ball. "That thing up there might be the oldest football in the world — leather stitched around a pig's bladder for bounce, hidden away sometime in the **1540s**."

Mia reached up and turned it over in her hands. Lopsided, soft with age, nothing like the machine-stitched spheres crammed in her gear bag. "Might be?"

"Nobody's got a receipt for that one. History doesn't always keep score as neatly as I do."

"That's the most honest thing you've said all night."

"I'm always honest. I'm just not always certain." Number Nine's stitches flickered, almost like a shrug. "Put it back gently. That one's close to five hundred years old and doesn't owe you a juggling trick."

Mia set it back in the rafter exactly where she'd found it, careful as she'd be with a trophy, and felt, for a second, like she'd shaken hands with the game's great-great-great-grandfather.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: One Rulebook to Settle an Argument
chapters.text:
They landed in a courtyard full of shouting, except this argument had no ball in it at all.

Young men in university gowns stood in two clumps, each side insisting their old school's version of football was the only correct one. One side wanted to carry the ball. The other wanted it kicked only, no hands, ever, under any circumstances.

"Cambridge, **1848**," said Number Nine. "Every school had brought its own rules from home, and nobody agreed on anything. Shin-kicking was legal in some versions. That tells you how bad it had gotten."

Mia watched two students nearly come to blows over whether tripping an opponent counted as clever defending or just plain mean. "This is like three different stats sites reporting three different numbers for the exact same game."

"Close enough. So a handful of Cambridge students sat down and tried to write one shared rulebook — the **Cambridge Rules**."

"Tried?"

"The full details didn't all survive, and historians argue about exactly what it said. But it's generally agreed they made the attempt, and other people borrowed from it later. That part mattered, even if the paper itself is fuzzy."

Mia liked that answer more than a tidy one would have. Real data was messy too; she'd spent enough nights reconciling two conflicting box scores to know a suspiciously clean story usually meant somebody hadn't checked it hard enough.

She watched one young man finally slap a sheet of paper down on the table, silencing the group, at least for a minute. "Somebody just needs to write it down properly and make everyone agree to disagree less," she said.

"That's the next stop, actually," said Number Nine. "Bounce me."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Tavern Meeting
chapters.text:
They landed in a smoky room above a London tavern, a dozen serious-looking men arguing over a sheet of paper like it was a contract worth a fortune.

"October 26th, **1863**," said Number Nine. "The **Football Association** — the FA — gets born tonight. Right here."

A man at the head of the table, thin and precise-looking, was writing fast, crossing things out, writing again. "That's Ebenezer Cobb Morley," said Number Nine. "He's about to personally write the first official **Laws of the Game** — the rulebook that practically everyone after this one copies."

Mia leaned over his shoulder, careful not to actually touch anything four centuries of ghost-rules apparently didn't want touched. One line stood out, underlined twice: no carrying the ball with your hands.

"That's the rule that splits it from rugby forever," she said.

"Correct. Before tonight, 'football' meant about six different games wearing a trench coat. After tonight, this version finally gets its own name."

"Which is?"

"Association football. Give it twenty years and some English schoolboys will get bored of saying the whole thing."

Mia's eyebrows went up. "Let me guess. They shortened it."

"To 'assoc.' Then to 'soccer.' Both words — **soccer** and **association football** — are the same sport in different jerseys, both from about the same decade, just **1880s** England being lazy with syllables."

Mia grinned. She'd spent her whole life hearing American commentators get side-eyed for saying "soccer," never once knowing the word was English through and through. "Wait till I tell my coach that one."

"Tell Morley first. He's still writing."

She watched him finish the page, set down his pen, and exhale like a man who'd just solved a very long equation. Mia knew that exhale. She made the exact same one closing a spreadsheet at one in the morning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Nil-Nil in Glasgow
chapters.text:
The next stop smelled like cut grass and nerves.

"FA Cup, **1871-72**," said Number Nine, as men in long shorts jogged onto a pitch ringed by a modest, hopeful crowd. "First tournament of its kind. Still running today, which makes it the oldest football competition on Earth."

"A hundred and fifty-some years and it's never once stopped?" Mia asked.

"Wars, pandemics, nothing's killed it yet. Somebody always finds a pitch."

They didn't stay for the final whistle. Number Nine spun her forward a few months, into colder air and a bigger, louder crowd — Glasgow, a banner reading SCOTLAND somewhere up in the stands.

"**1872**," said the ball. "First official international match ever played. Scotland versus England."

Mia watched ninety minutes of genuinely committed effort produce exactly nothing. The final whistle blew on a flat, featureless scoreline.

"0-0," she said, checking twice like the number might change on her. "The first international match in the history of the sport, and it's a scoreless draw."

"Welcome to football."

"As a stats person, I respect it. As a fan, I would like a refund."

"Nobody asked for a refund in **1872**. They just agreed to do it again."

Mia watched the two captains shake hands, completely unbothered, like 0-0 was a perfectly respectable outcome between gentlemen. Somewhere down the line, she thought, some future version of herself would build an entire personality around arguing that shot quality mattered more than final scorelines — and this flat, boring draw was the very first entry in a database that was about to get extremely long.

"Keep the receipt," she told Number Nine.

"Already have it. I have all of them."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: A League, Then a World
chapters.text:
They landed inside an office that smelled like pipe tobacco and ambition.

A man was sketching columns onto a chalkboard — teams, listed vertically, points scrawled beside each one.

"William McGregor," said Number Nine. "**1888**. He's organizing the Football League — the world's first — so that instead of one-off matches, clubs play each other all season long, building a table that actually means something at the end of it."

Mia stared at the chalk columns like she'd come home. Wins, losses, points. "That's literally a leaderboard."

"It's the ancestor of every leaderboard you've ever refreshed at midnight."

She almost laughed. Her entire spreadsheet habit, it turned out, had a great-great-grandfather, and his name was William McGregor, and he'd built it out of nothing but chalk and stubbornness.

The scene shifted again, this time to a room in Paris, men from seven different countries signing papers around a long table, none of them fully agreeing on the language they were arguing in.

"**1904**," said Number Nine. "FIFA. Soccer's world governing body, born right here, from seven countries that wanted one shared set of rules — not just for one league, but across borders entirely."

"So first it's one club against another," Mia said slowly, working it out loud the way she worked out a formula. "Then it's a league. Then it's whole countries. It's just... scaling up, over and over."

"That's exactly what it is. You're basically watching a spreadsheet grow more tabs."

"Please never say the word 'tabs' to me again."

"Noted. Bounce me."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Ban Nobody Could Justify
chapters.text:
The crowd noise hit her before the picture did — actual roaring, thousands of voices, for a game Mia hadn't expected to find at all.

Women in long shorts and buttoned jerseys tore down a muddy pitch while a packed stadium howled their names.

"Dick, Kerr Ladies," said Number Nine. "English women's team, early twentieth century. Their best player's right there — **Lily Parr**. She helped make this team one of the most popular sides in the whole country, full stop, not just in women's football."

Mia watched Parr strike a ball with a left foot that looked, even across decades, genuinely unfair to defend against. The stands were packed tighter than half the men's matches she'd seen on television. "Then why have I literally never once heard of her?"

Number Nine's glow dimmed, just slightly. "Because in **1921**, the FA banned women's football in England. Said it wasn't suitable. No real reason that held up under any scrutiny — it just happened, and that was that, for a very long time."

Mia's jaw tightened. "That's not fair."

"No. It wasn't."

She didn't say anything for a second, just watched Parr take a corner, drop it perfectly onto a teammate's head, and the crowd come apart.

"How long did the ban last?"

"Fifty years. The FA finally lifted it in **1971**."

"Fifty years." Mia did the math without meaning to — more than three times her own age, of a sport simply not letting people play it. "And after that?"

"After that, it built back, slower than it should have had to. In **1991**, China hosted the first official Women's World Cup. The United States won it."

Mia looked at Parr once more before the scene faded, filing the name away like a stat too important to ever misplace again. "Keep her on the sheet," she told Number Nine. "Permanently."

"She was never off it. Some records just get buried longer than they should be."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Thirteen Teams and a Boat Ride
chapters.text:
Heat hit her first, thick and bright, a stadium under a sun that didn't do subtlety.

"Montevideo, **Uruguay**, **1930**," said Number Nine. "The first FIFA World Cup. Thirteen teams total, most of Europe's best declining the boat trip, so it's mostly the Americas represented. Uruguay's the host."

Mia watched the host team work the ball with controlled chaos, defenders overlapping like they'd rehearsed it, which, apparently, they had. "Home advantage is a real stat, you know. Crowd noise genuinely changes decision-making on the field."

"Then you'll like the final. Uruguay versus Argentina."

The whistle blew; the stadium detonated into noise before the ball had even crossed the line once. Mia couldn't follow every pass through the roar, but she didn't need the play-by-play to read the scoreboard at the end: Uruguay had won it, the very first champion the sport ever crowned.

A man in a suit stood near the trophy presentation, looking exactly as relieved as a tournament organizer should.

"Jules Rimet," said Number Nine. "FIFA's president. He's the one who pushed this whole tournament into existing in the first place. They name the trophy after him."

Mia studied the small gold statue being handed over, unglamorous by modern standards, nothing like the gleaming thing she'd seen lifted on television every four years of her life. "That's it? That's the whole trophy?"

"That's the start of it. Trophies get better sequels. Bounce me — this one's got a plot twist."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: A Stolen Cup and a Very Good Dog
chapters.text:
They landed in London, gray skies, a glass display case standing conspicuously, suspiciously empty.

"Somebody's missing something," Mia said.

"In **1966**, somebody stole the World Cup trophy. Right off its display, days before England was due to host the whole tournament."

Mia blinked. "They just... took it?"

"For about a week, yes. Then a dog named **Pickles** found it, wrapped in newspaper, under a garden hedge, out on an ordinary walk with his owner."

"A dog solved it."

"A dog solved it. England got its trophy back in time, hosted the tournament, and then won it outright — their only title to date."

The scene rolled forward, and suddenly she was watching a different World Cup entirely, 1970 judging by the kits, a referee reaching into his pocket and holding up a small bright square of color at a player.

"Yellow card," said Number Nine. "A referee named Ken Aston invented the whole system — yellow and red — straight off a traffic light he happened to be sitting at when the idea hit him. It debuted at this tournament."

"Stop and go. That's such an obvious idea I'm genuinely annoyed nobody thought of it sooner."

"Most good ideas are, in hindsight."

She watched a player in yellow and green dismantle an entire defense in three consecutive touches, the crowd rising before the shot had even gone in.

"Brazil," said Number Nine. "They'll finish with five World Cup titles total, more than anyone — **1958**, 1962, this one in **1970**, plus two more down the line. And that man right there has been on three of the winning squads himself. First player ever to manage it."

"Pele," Mia said, like naming a fact she'd always half-known but never actually watched happen in front of her.

"Brazil kept this particular trophy for good after that third win — tournament rules at the time. FIFA had to make an entirely new one in **1974** for everybody else to fight over."

Mia watched Pele get lifted onto someone's shoulders, grinning, and thought that out of everyone she'd met tonight, he looked the most like he was genuinely having fun doing something that mattered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Final Whistle
chapters.text:
The seams dimmed, and the roaring crowd noise thinned back into the ordinary hum of her bedroom, laptop fan still running, spreadsheet still glowing faintly on the screen like it had never once blinked.

Mia sat up straight, the ball warm and quiet in her hands again, just an old size-4 with a marker 9 and no laces. She turned it over out of habit, checking the seams. No glow now. Just leather.

"You still there?" she asked, feeling slightly ridiculous saying it out loud.

"Always," said Number Nine, voice barely above a whisper now, like a commentator signing off after extra time. "I don't go anywhere. I just wait for someone who actually checks the stat sheet."

Mia glanced at her spreadsheet — her own tidy little percentages — and thought about Lily Parr's name sitting unrecorded for fifty years, and a man writing rules by candlelight, and a dog finding a trophy under a hedge, and a scoreless draw that somehow mattered more than most 5-0s ever would.

She opened a new tab and started a second sheet. Not stats this time. Names. Dates. The whole long chain of people who'd built the game she played every single Saturday without ever once wondering who'd come before her.

"You're going to fall asleep at your desk," said Number Nine.

"In a minute."

"That's what you said an hour ago."

Mia smiled, set the ball gently back on the shelf, number-side out, and kept typing a little longer before she finally closed the laptop. Somewhere past the window, the sky was already turning the pale gray that meant morning wasn't far off, and she had a match to play in a few hours that suddenly felt like it carried a little more history on its shoulders than it had the night before.

story.ending_line: Saturday's match couldn't come soon enough.

FA founder Ebenezer Cobb Morley personally wrote the first official Laws of the Game in 1863.
The FA Cup, first played in 1871-72, is the oldest football competition still running in the world.
The first official international match, a 0-0 draw between Scotland and England, was played in Glasgow in 1872.
In 1888, William McGregor organized the Football League in England, the world's first football league.
FIFA, football's world governing body, was founded in Paris in 1904 by seven European countries.
A pig's-bladder ball found hidden at Stirling Castle in Scotland may date to the 1540s, making it the world's oldest football.
The first FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, with host Uruguay beating Argentina in the final.
FIFA president Jules Rimet drove the creation of the World Cup, and its original trophy was named after him.
In 1966 the World Cup trophy was stolen in London, then found safe a week later by a dog named Pickles.
England hosted and won the 1966 World Cup, its only title so far.
Brazil has won the World Cup a record five times: 1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, and 2002.
Brazilian forward Pele is the only player ever on three World Cup-winning squads: 1958, 1962, and 1970.
Referee Ken Aston invented yellow and red cards, inspired by traffic lights, debuting at the 1970 World Cup.
Since Brazil kept the original trophy for good after their third title, FIFA introduced a new World Cup Trophy in 1974.
In 1921 the FA banned women's football from its grounds in England, despite crowds over 50,000 at women's matches.
Star player Lily Parr helped make the Dick, Kerr Ladies one of England's most popular teams before that ban.
The FA finally lifted its ban on women's football in England in 1971, fifty years after it began.
The first official Women's World Cup was held in China in 1991 and won by the United States.

story.title: Maya and the Race to the Stars
story.subtitle: A splashy bedtime trip through the Space Race, with Barnacle the seal along for the ride.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Bathtub Liftoff
chapters.text:
Maya sat in the bathtub with her waterproof crayons. She drew a round ball with a wiggly antenna on the foggy tile.

It had been one whole week since Barnacle waved his flipper at the last rivet on that humming bridge. Tonight the water felt extra fizzy.

"Five more minutes, Maya!" called her mom from the hallway.

Maya kept drawing. She liked drawing best right before bedtime, when the tub was warm and quiet.

SPLOOSH! A round, whiskery face popped up between her knees.

"All aboard, Maya!" said Barnacle, the harbor seal, shaking water off his nose.

"Barnacle!" Maya laughed. "Look what I drew."

The little ball on the tile began to glow. It lifted off the wall and floated into the bathwater. Then it started to beep.

BEEP. BEEP. BEEP.

"Why is it beeping?" Maya asked, because asking why was her favorite thing to do.

"That's **Sputnik 1**," said Barnacle. "The very first **satellite**. A satellite is just a little metal moon that circles a planet instead of falling down."

"When was it?" Maya asked.

"**October 4, 1957**," said Barnacle. "It was only **fifty-eight centimeters** wide. About the size of a beach ball."

Maya held her hands apart to show how small that was. "That tiny? And everyone heard it beep?"

"On ordinary radios, everywhere," said Barnacle. "People pointed their antennas at the sky just to listen."

Maya reached out and touched the glowing ball. The bathwater shivered. Then it turned into a thousand tiny stars, swirling like bubbles.

The tub tipped back like a rocket on a launchpad.

"Hang onto your crayons!" shouted Barnacle.

WHOOOOSH! The little boat Maya had drawn rose up out of the water. It grew big enough to sit in, with Maya and Barnacle aboard, zooming through a tunnel of starlight.

"Where are we going?" Maya asked, gripping the sides.

"Back to 1957," said Barnacle. "The year two countries, America and the Soviet Union, started racing each other to space."

Maya looked down. The bathroom was gone. Below them, Earth spun, blue and round, with the little beeping satellite looping around it.

"It beeps," Maya whispered, "like it's saying hello to everybody."

Barnacle smiled his whiskery seal smile. "I'd say hello back. But I'm a seal. I only know how to say SPLOOSH."

Maya giggled so hard she nearly let go of the boat.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Laika's Brave Ride
chapters.text:
A soft bark echoed through the starlight.

Maya sat up. "Was that... a dog?"

The little boat drifted toward a silver capsule — a kind of sealed space car — tumbling gently through the dark.

"That's Sputnik 2," said Barnacle. "Launched **November 3, 1957**, just one month after the first satellite. And yes, there's a dog inside."

"A dog? In space?" Maya pressed her nose to the boat's rail.

"Her name was **Laika**," said Barnacle. "She was the first living creature ever to circle the Earth."

Maya peered through the capsule's little window. Two big brown eyes peered back.

"She looks lonely," Maya said. "Can I draw her something?"

"Go ahead," said Barnacle. "Nobody rushes anybody around here."

Maya flipped to a clean page. She drew a soft, round cushion with a bone on it. The picture glowed, lifted off the page, and floated straight through the capsule wall, landing beside Laika with a gentle plop.

Laika pressed her paw to the window. A little foggy paw print bloomed on the glass.

"Why did they send a dog instead of a person?" Maya asked.

"Because nobody knew yet if a living creature could survive up here," said Barnacle. "Laika went first, so braver trips could follow."

Maya waved at the window. "Thank you for going first, Laika."

The paw print on the glass shimmered brighter. Tiny silver sparkles floated off the capsule, drawing a trail through the stars like a path to follow.

"Looks like she's pointing the way," said Barnacle.

"Where to?" asked Maya.

"Follow the sparkles and find out," said Barnacle, paddling his flippers like oars.

The little boat turned, caught the glittering trail, and sailed on, leaving Laika's capsule tumbling peacefully behind, her paw print still glowing warm on the glass.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: America Catches Up
chapters.text:
A buzzer rang out, loud and urgent, like a school bell gone wild.

"Uh oh," said Maya. "Someone's in a hurry."

The boat floated down past a building full of blinking lights and scribbling scientists.

"Sputnik gave the United States a scare," said Barnacle. "So on **October 1, 1958**, they started a brand-new space team called **NASA**."

Maya looked at a chalkboard covered in numbers and arrows. "What are they trying to find?"

"Watch," said Barnacle, pointing a flipper at a thin, pencil-shaped ship on the launchpad. "That's **Explorer 1**, America's first satellite. It went up **January 31, 1958**."

The little ship roared off the pad and climbed high above Earth. Maya watched its dials wiggle and spike on a screen nearby.

"Why's it doing that?" she asked.

"It just found something nobody knew was there," said Barnacle. "An invisible ring of fizzy space weather, circling the whole planet like a giant hula hoop."

Maya's eyes went wide. "A ring you can't even see?"

"Not with your eyes," said Barnacle. "But Explorer 1's instruments felt it."

Maya grabbed her sketchbook. She drew her own little satellite, with the same thin antennas as the real one, and a dotted loop all around Earth to show where the hidden ring sat.

The drawing glowed and zipped off the page, joining Explorer 1 in **orbit** — the word for circling all the way around a planet.

On the screen, the dotted loop lit up gold, matching Maya's picture exactly.

"FOUND IT!" Maya shouted, pointing.

The scientists below cheered. One of them taped a copy of her drawing right onto the chalkboard.

"Nicely spotted," said Barnacle. "Next stop, the big one — the year humans finally leave the ground."

The boat rose through the cheering room and out into the stars once more.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Gagarin's Giant Loop
chapters.text:
A streak of silver shot past the boat so fast it rocked side to side.

"Whoa!" Maya grabbed the rail. "What was that?"

"That was Vostok 1," said Barnacle. "Inside it is a very brave pilot named **Yuri Gagarin**."

"Is he going in a loop?" Maya asked, watching the silver ship curve around the blue Earth below.

"The whole way around," said Barnacle. "On **April 12, 1961**, he became the first human ever in space. One full orbit took about **108 minutes**."

Maya counted on her fingers, then gave up. "That's a long time!"

"Not even two hours," said Barnacle. "Shorter than a movie."

Maya grabbed her crayons. She drew a big looping racetrack around a picture of Earth, to show the whole path Gagarin had flown. The loop glowed gold where his ship had already passed.

"Who else is racing?" Maya asked.

Right on cue, a stubby little capsule zoomed by below them, going up and straight back down, like a diver doing a quick bounce.

"That's **Alan Shepard**," said Barnacle. "On **May 5, 1961**, he became the first American in space, aboard Freedom 7. His trip was short. He didn't make it all the way around like Gagarin did."

Maya drew a short dashed line next to her big loop, to show Shepard's quicker bounce.

Then a deep voice rang out across the stars, like a speech from a podium.

"We choose to go to the Moon," the voice said, "and do the other things, because they are hard."

"Who's that?" Maya whispered.

"**President John F. Kennedy**," said Barnacle. "On **May 25, 1961**, he dared his whole country to land someone on the Moon, and bring them home safe, before ten more years had passed."

Maya's eyes lit up. "It's a race to the Moon! Like a boat race, but with rockets!"

"Exactly like that," said Barnacle, and together they watched Kennedy's words sparkle across the sky like a finish line waiting to be drawn.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Valentina's Vostok
chapters.text:
Crackly static buzzed from a little radio bolted to the boat's dashboard. Then, through the static, came a woman's voice, calm and clear.

"Who's that?" Maya asked, turning the dial.

"**Valentina Tereshkova**," said Barnacle. "She used to work in a factory. Then she trained to fly. On **June 16, 1963**, she became the first woman ever in space."

A silver ship called Vostok 6 sailed past, circling Earth again and again.

"She's going around and around," said Maya, watching it loop. "Like me doing laps at swim practice!"

"A bit faster than swim practice," said Barnacle, chuckling.

Maya tore a page from her sketchbook and drew a little checkered racing flag. "For her," she said. "Since it's a race."

She held the flag up out of the boat and waved it as hard as she could.

The moment she waved, Vostok 6 dipped one wing, almost like a wave back. A shower of silver sparkles drifted from its hull toward the little boat.

"She saw you," said Barnacle softly.

Maya beamed, tucking her flag into her sketchbook like a prize. "Why did it take so long for a woman to go?" she asked. "Gagarin went first, and that was two whole years before."

"Lots of people had to say yes first," said Barnacle. "But once Valentina got her chance, she circled this whole planet again and again, proving she belonged up here just as much as anyone."

The sparkles gathered into a swirling silver trail, curling away through the dark like a ribbon.

"Follow that?" Maya asked, already steering.

"Follow that," said Barnacle, and the little boat chased the glittering ribbon deeper into the stars.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Floating Free
chapters.text:
Something — or someone — floated right outside the boat's window, tumbling slowly in the dark.

Maya gasped. "Barnacle! A person!"

A figure in a big, puffy white suit drifted at the end of a long cord, like a kite on a string.

"That's **Alexei Leonov**," said Barnacle. "On **March 18, 1965**, he opened his hatch and stepped outside his ship. Nobody had ever done that before."

"Stepped outside?" Maya pressed close to the glass. "Isn't that scary? Won't he float away?"

"That's what the cord is for," said Barnacle. "It kept him tied to the ship, so he couldn't drift off. A bit like how you wear a pool noodle at swim practice, so you always float back to the edge."

Maya grinned. "I love floating in the pool."

"Leonov floated for about ten minutes," said Barnacle, "then climbed carefully back inside."

Maya grabbed her crayons and drew her own cord, stretching from the little boat all the way to Leonov's drifting boots, just to be extra safe.

The drawn cord glowed. It stretched across the stars and gently tugged Leonov back toward his open hatch, right on schedule.

He gave a thumbs-up through his visor before disappearing inside.

"Nice knot," said Barnacle.

"I learned it tying up our rowboat," said Maya proudly.

The hatch sealed with a soft clunk. A comet streaked by overhead, trailing a long tail of light.

"That comet's headed somewhere," said Maya, pointing.

"Then let's follow it," said Barnacle, and the little boat turned to chase the comet's glowing tail into the dark.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Earthrise
chapters.text:
The boat slid around the gray, bumpy edge of the Moon, and Maya gasped out loud.

There, rising over the Moon's horizon, hung the whole Earth — blue, white, and small enough to cover with her thumb.

"Barnacle," Maya whispered. "It's rising. Like a sunrise. But it's Earth."

"They call it **Earthrise**," said Barnacle. "In **December 1968**, three astronauts aboard **Apollo 8** became the first people ever to circle the Moon. One of them took a photo of exactly this."

"Can I draw it?" Maya asked, already flipping to a fresh page.

"Nobody's rushing you," said Barnacle.

Maya drew carefully: the gray Moon ground in front, the small blue Earth hanging above it, swirled with white clouds. She colored the ocean her favorite shade of boat-blue.

When she finished, her drawing glowed softly. So did the real Earth outside the window, as if the two pictures were shaking hands.

"It's so small," Maya said quietly. "Everyone I know is on that little ball."

"Every boat, every bathtub, every bed," said Barnacle.

Maya tucked her drawing into her sketchbook, right next to her racing flag. "What happens next?" she asked.

"Next," said Barnacle, "people stop circling the Moon, and finally land on it."

A bright dotted line sparked to life across the sky, leading off toward a nearby crater glowing gold.

"That way?" Maya asked, already steering the boat toward the light.

"That way," said Barnacle, and off they sailed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: One Giant Leap
chapters.text:
A rocket stood on a distant launchpad, so tall it poked through the clouds.

"That's a **Saturn V** rocket," said Barnacle. "**363 feet** tall. Taller than the Statue of Liberty."

Maya tipped her head all the way back. "That's HUGE."

"Two men built rockets like it," said Barnacle. "**Wernher von Braun** led the American team. In the Soviet Union, a quiet genius named **Sergei Korolev** led theirs. It was such a secret that almost nobody knew his name until after he died, in 1966."

"That's sad," Maya said softly.

"It is," said Barnacle. "But his rockets flew on without him."

The Saturn V roared off the pad in a sheet of fire and smoke. The little boat shot forward in time, all the way to **July 20, 1969**.

A ladder unfolded from a spindly spacecraft. A boot touched gray dust.

"**Neil Armstrong**," Barnacle said. "The first person to ever walk on the Moon."

"That's one small step for man," crackled a radio voice, "one giant leap for mankind."

Maya watched, barely breathing, as a second astronaut climbed down to join him.

"That's **Buzz Aldrin**," said Barnacle. "And up above, circling all alone, waiting for them, is **Michael Collins**, flying the ship called Columbia."

"He's all by himself?" Maya asked.

"For a while," said Barnacle. "But he knew exactly what he was doing, and exactly when his friends were coming back."

Maya pulled out her sketchbook one more time. She drew two bootprints in gray dust, side by side.

The drawing glowed, and real bootprints appeared beside Armstrong's and Aldrin's, right there on the Moon.

"They're not alone," Maya grinned.

"Over the next few years," said Barnacle, "ten more astronauts followed those very first footprints, across five more landings."

Maya traced her bootprints with one finger. "Twelve people," she whispered. "Twelve people on the Moon."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Splashdown and a Handshake
chapters.text:
The boat rocked suddenly, hard, and a warning light flashed red on the dashboard.

"What's wrong?" Maya grabbed the rail.

"This is **Apollo 13**, in **1970**," said Barnacle. "An air tank on board just had a problem. It gave the astronauts quite a jolt."

Maya's stomach dropped. "Are they okay?"

"They are," said Barnacle quickly. "Clever engineers back on Earth figured out a fix, step by step. The whole crew splashed down safely. Nobody was hurt."

Maya let out a breath she didn't know she was holding. "Good," she said firmly. "That's the most important part."

"Always is," said Barnacle, patting her hand with one flipper.

The warning light faded. The boat drifted on, calm again, toward one last glowing date: **July 17, 1975**.

Two spacecraft, one American and one Soviet, floated nose to nose in the quiet dark.

"After all that racing," Barnacle said, "the two sides finally decided to meet instead."

A hatch opened. An American hand reached through. A Soviet hand reached back, and the two shook, right there above the Earth.

"They're not racing anymore," Maya said. "They're friends."

"The Space Race was over," said Barnacle, "and everybody had won."

Maya pulled out her sketchbook one last time. She drew the two hands shaking, with Earth glowing blue behind them. The picture shimmered, and the stars around the boat began to melt back into warm, soapy bathwater.

SPLOOSH!

Maya blinked. She was back in the tub, water gone lukewarm, her sketchbook open on her knees to a brand-new page: two hands, shaking, in crayon.

"Five minutes was actually fifteen," called her mom, "but I'll let it slide tonight."

Barnacle winked one whiskery eye before sliding beneath the bubbles. "All aboard, Maya," he said. "Same time next sleep?"

Maya hugged her damp sketchbook to her chest and grinned all the way to her pajamas.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya — all aboard for dreamland.

true_facts.text: **Sputnik 1** was the first **satellite**, launched by the Soviet Union on **October 4, 1957**.

fact_pack.summary: The Space Race was a Cold War contest between the United States and the Soviet Union to achieve firsts in spaceflight, from Sputnik in 1957 to a joint mission in 1975. It brought the first satellite, first human in orbit, and first footsteps on the Moon.

facts.text: The Space Race was a Cold War contest between the US and USSR to achieve spaceflight firsts, lasting roughly 1957 to 1975.
On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a beach-ball-sized satellite that became the first man-made object to orbit Earth.
Sputnik 1 was about 58 centimeters wide and sent out a simple radio beep that people around the world could pick up on ordinary radios.
On November 3, 1957, the Soviets launched Sputnik 2 carrying a dog named Laika, the first living creature to orbit Earth.
Shocked by Sputnik, the United States created NASA, which began operating on October 1, 1958.
The first US satellite, Explorer 1, launched January 31, 1958, and discovered the Van Allen radiation belt.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, orbiting Earth once aboard Vostok 1 in about 108 minutes.
On May 5, 1961, Alan Shepard became the first American in space aboard the Freedom 7 capsule, though his short flight did not orbit Earth.
On May 25, 1961, President Kennedy challenged the US to land a man on the Moon and return him safely before decade's end.
On June 16, 1963, Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth aboard Vostok 6.
On March 18, 1965, Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, floating outside his Voskhod 2 capsule for about ten minutes.
On January 27, 1967, astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee died in a fire during a launch pad test of Apollo 1.
In December 1968, Apollo 8 astronauts became the first to orbit the Moon, and William Anders took the famous Earthrise photo.
On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronaut Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap for mankind.
Buzz Aldrin joined Armstrong on the Moon while crewmate Michael Collins orbited alone above in the command module Columbia.
In 1970, an oxygen tank explosion crippled Apollo 13 on its way to the Moon, but the crew safely returned to Earth after engineers improvised a fix.
Between 1969 and 1972, twelve American astronauts walked on the Moon across six successful Apollo landing missions.
The Saturn V rocket that carried Apollo astronauts to the Moon stood 363 feet tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty.
Soviet chief designer Sergei Korolev secretly led the USSR's rocket program, and his identity was kept a state secret until after his death in 1966.
Wernher von Braun, who earlier built rockets for Germany, led the NASA team that developed the Saturn V rocket.
The Space Race ended in a spirit of cooperation on July 17, 1975, when American and Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit and their crews shook hands.

story.title: Maya and the Star-Sailing Boat
story.subtitle: A bedtime voyage through the real race to space.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep in the Puddle
chapters.text:
It had been three whole nights since Barnacle waved his flipper from the water, right after the last rivet went in on that hummy bridge. Maya was still drawing boats about it.

She lay on her bedroom floor with her best green crayon, drawing a little paper boat on thick paper. Outside her window, one rain boot sat on the sill, half full of rainwater. The water began to glow, soft and green, like a nightlight under the sea.

**POP!** A whiskery nose popped out of the boot. It was Barnacle the harbour seal, dripping and grinning.

"All aboard, Maya," he said. "Tonight we're not going under the waves. We're going up, up, past the clouds, to the stars."

"Boats don't fly," said Maya, giggling.

"This one might," said Barnacle, and he tapped her paper boat with one flipper.

The paper boat shivered, then grew warm under her hands. The glow from the puddle poured into it like water filling a cup. Maya climbed aboard, and Barnacle hopped up beside her.

**WHOOOOSH!** The little boat shot out the window into a sky gone sparkly and dark, sailing on starlight the way it once sailed on bathwater.

They landed with a soft bump on a round, quiet little moon of rock. Below them, a beach-ball-sized silver ball floated past, beeping.

"What is THAT noise?" asked Maya, cupping her ears.

"That little ball is called **Sputnik 1**," said Barnacle. "On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union — that's a country, part of what's now Russia — sent it zooming around Earth. It was the very first machine ever to circle our whole planet from space, which is called going into **orbit**."

Maya watched it spin. "It's not much bigger than a beach ball!"

"Exactly right," said Barnacle. "About as wide as your bicycle is long. And that beep you hear? People all over the world could catch it on their ordinary radios at home."

Maya pressed her ear near the glow as it passed. **BEEP. BEEP. BEEP.** She grinned so wide her cheeks hurt.

"It sounds like a tiny robot saying hello," she said.

"Seal of approval," said Barnacle, which was not even close to a real joke, but Maya laughed anyway.

She reached out and gave the little silver ball a gentle wave as it sailed by, and it beeped once more, almost like it waved back.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Laika's Brave Ride
chapters.text:
A bark echoed across the dark, and Maya sat up straight. "Was that a DOG? In space?"

"Good ears," said Barnacle, steering the little paper boat closer to a second silver capsule — that's the little round pod something rides inside — drifting by. "Just one month after Sputnik 1, on **November 3, 1957**, the Soviets launched **Sputnik 2**. Inside rode a small dog named **Laika**."

"She was the first living creature ever to circle the Earth from way up here," Barnacle went on.

Maya pressed her nose to the glowing window of their boat, hoping for a glimpse. "Was she scared?"

"Maybe a little," said Barnacle gently. "But people everywhere loved her for it. She became famous all around the world."

Maya thought about her own dog snoring at the end of her bed and felt a soft little ache for brave Laika, orbiting so far from home.

Then a bright building rose up ahead of them, all glass and antennas, humming with excitement.

"What's THIS place?" Maya asked, already reaching for her crayon to sketch its tall tower.

"That excitement you hear?" said Barnacle. "Sputnik gave the United States such a surprise that they built a brand-new space team. It started working on **October 1, 1958**. They called it **NASA**."

Maya drew a quick picture of the tower, adding little sparks around it. "Like a new team getting ready for a big race," she said.

"Precisely," said Barnacle, bobbing his whiskers proudly. "Fin-tastic drawing, by the way."

Maya rolled her eyes at the pun, but she tucked the drawing into her boat's little paper pocket anyway, right next to her sketch of Sputnik.

"Two down," she said, patting her growing stack of drawings like a captain checking her log. "Where next, Barnacle?"

"Wherever the stars point us," said Barnacle, and the little boat tilted upward again, chasing a bright streak of light across the dark.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The First Riders
chapters.text:
The boat rocked gently, and Maya spotted two round capsules racing side by side, trailing fire.

"Someone's INSIDE those?" she asked, eyes wide.

"People, this time," said Barnacle. "On **April 12, 1961**, a Soviet pilot named **Yuri Gagarin** became the very first human being to fly in space. He circled Earth once, in about **108 minutes** — barely longer than your favorite movie."

"That's so fast!" said Maya. "What do you call a space pilot from Russia?"

"A **cosmonaut**," said Barnacle. "That's simply their word for astronaut."

Maya rolled the word around in her mouth. "Cosmonaut," she said again, liking the sound of it.

The second capsule zoomed past them, trailing a little American flag.

"And that one?" Maya asked, pointing.

"Just a few weeks later, on **May 5, 1961**," said Barnacle, "an American named **Alan Shepard** became the first American in space, riding a capsule called **Freedom 7**. His ride was shorter and didn't circle the whole planet, but up he went all the same."

Maya leaned way out over the edge of their little boat, which made Barnacle hum a worried note, though he never rushed her back.

"Careful now," he said softly, and waited while she looked her fill before settling back down on her own.

"Two firsts in one chapter," Maya said, counting on her fingers. "First person ever, and first American."

"You're keeping very good count," said Barnacle.

Maya grabbed her crayon and sketched two little capsules racing side by side, with a tiny flag on one, and underneath she wrote, in wobbly letters, FIRST AND FIRST.

"That's going right next to Laika," she said, tucking it away.

Barnacle chuckled. "At this rate, Maya, you'll run out of paper before we run out of sky."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: A Dare and a Flight
chapters.text:
A booming voice rolled across the stars like far-off thunder, and Maya jumped.

"Who's SHOUTING?" she asked.

"Just a president, making a promise," said Barnacle, floating them closer to a glowing patch of starlight shaped almost like a podium. "On **May 25, 1961**, President **John F. Kennedy** dared his whole country to land someone on the Moon, and bring them safely home, before the end of that decade — that's ten years."

Maya looked up at the pale, round Moon glowing above them. "That's a BIG dare," she said.

"The biggest," agreed Barnacle.

They sailed on, and soon a third capsule zipped past, this one painted with a small flower on its side.

"Who's flying THAT one?" Maya asked, already reaching for her crayon.

"That's **Valentina Tereshkova**," said Barnacle. "On **June 16, 1963**, she became the first woman ever to fly in space, orbiting Earth aboard a capsule called **Vostok 6**."

"Was she a pilot before, like Gagarin?" Maya asked.

"She'd worked in a factory," said Barnacle, "then trained hard to earn her seat among the stars."

Maya grinned and quickly sketched a girl in a round helmet, flying past a little flower. "She worked hard and then she flew," Maya said. "That's like practicing swimming until you finally win the race."

"A very fine comparison," said Barnacle.

Maya tucked her newest drawing in with the others, now four pictures deep. She patted the stack like a treasure chest.

"At this rate," she said, echoing Barnacle from before, "I'll need a bigger boat."

"Or a bigger ocean of stars," said Barnacle, and steered them onward into the glittering dark.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Floating Free
chapters.text:
Something small and round floated right past their little boat's window, trailing a long silver cord.

"Is that a PERSON?" Maya gasped, nose pressed to the glow.

"That's **Alexei Leonov**,” said Barnacle. "On **March 18, 1965**, he became the first person ever to leave his spacecraft and float outside it, all alone in his space suit. That's called a **spacewalk**. He floated out there for about **ten minutes**."

Maya watched the tiny figure drift, turning slow and weightless, tethered only by that long cord.

"Wasn't he scared he'd float away forever?" she asked, her voice small.

"That cord kept him tied safely to his ship the whole time," said Barnacle gently. "And after ten minutes, he floated right back inside, safe and sound."

Maya let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding, and smiled.

"I want to try floating," she said, and before Barnacle could answer, she unbuckled her little paper seatbelt and pushed gently off the bench.

**WHOOOSH.** Maya drifted up, slow as a bubble, her hair floating around her face like seaweed.

"Just like swimming," she laughed, "except there's no water to push against!"

"Better hold my flipper," said Barnacle, "unless you'd like to float all the way to the Moon without me."

Maya grabbed his flipper, giggling, and he towed her gently back down to the bench, patient as ever, not the littlest bit rushed.

"Thanks, Barnacle," she said, settling back in.

"Anytime,” he said. "Though I'll admit, out here, I'm a bit more at home in the water."

Maya patted the little paper boat beneath them. "Me too," she agreed. "But this is pretty great, too."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Whole Blue Marble
chapters.text:
Their boat crested a curve of dark sky, and suddenly Maya gasped so loud Barnacle nearly dropped his pun.

"BARNACLE. Look."

There, hanging in the blackness above the gray edge of the Moon, hung a small blue and white ball, glowing soft as a nightlight.

"That's home," said Barnacle quietly. "The whole Earth, from way out here."

"It's so SMALL," Maya whispered.

"In **December 1968**, three astronauts aboard **Apollo 8** were the first people ever to fly all the way around the Moon," said Barnacle. "One of them, **William Anders**, looked back and saw exactly what you're seeing now. He snapped a photo of it rising over the Moon's edge."

"What did he call it?" Maya asked.

"Earthrise," said Barnacle.

Maya reached for her crayon without even looking, her eyes still fixed on the little blue ball. She drew it quickly: a small round Earth, peeking up over a gray curve of Moon.

"It looks so soft," she said. "Like it could fit in my hand."

"That's rather the point of the photo," said Barnacle. "It reminded everyone down there just how small and precious home really is."

Maya held her drawing up next to the real thing, comparing them carefully, tongue poking out in concentration.

"Close enough," she decided, satisfied, and tucked it in with the others.

"You know," said Barnacle, "out of everyone who's ever lived, only a tiny few have seen that sight with their own eyes."

Maya looked at her drawing one more time before folding it carefully.

"Then I'm glad I got to see it too," she said. "Even if it's just from a paper boat."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Giant Leap
chapters.text:
A tall, silver tower rose ahead of them, taller than anything Maya had ever seen, trailing smoke and fire at its base.

"What IS that?" she breathed.

"A rocket called the **Saturn V**,” said Barnacle. "It stood **363 feet tall** — taller than the Statue of Liberty. Two rocket masterminds helped make rockets like it possible: an American named **Wernher von Braun**, who led the team that built it, and a Soviet genius named **Sergei Korolev**, whose name was kept secret by his own country until after he died in **1966**."

"A SECRET genius?" said Maya, eyes huge. "Like a superhero with a mask?"

"A bit like that," Barnacle agreed, chuckling.

The rocket's top glowed, and a tiny ladder appeared, leading down onto gray, dusty ground.

"On **July 20, 1969**, astronaut **Neil Armstrong** climbed down that very kind of ladder and became the first person to ever walk on the Moon," said Barnacle. "He said it was a giant leap for everyone back home."

Maya squinted at the dusty gray ground below. "Can I try a leap too?" she asked.

"Go ahead," said Barnacle, "the Moon won't mind."

Maya hopped down from the boat and bounced, light as a feather in the low gravity, landing with a soft little **THUD** of moon dust.

"Buzz Aldrin walked here too, right beside Armstrong," said Barnacle, "while their crewmate, **Michael Collins**, circled alone above in their ship, named **Columbia**, waiting to bring everyone home."

"That's a big job, waiting all by yourself," Maya said thoughtfully.

"The biggest kind of patient," said Barnacle.

Maya took one more giant bounce across the dust, laughing the whole way, then scrambled back aboard, breathless and grinning, moon dust still on her shoes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Handshake and the Way Home
chapters.text:
Their little boat shuddered suddenly, and a warning light blinked on the dashboard.

"Uh oh," said Maya. "Is something WRONG?"

"Something went wrong once, for real astronauts," said Barnacle calmly. "In **1970**, a tank aboard **Apollo 13** had trouble on the way to the Moon. But the crew and their helpers on the ground worked together and fixed things up, and everyone made it safely home."

Maya let out a breath. "That's good," she said. "I'm glad they figured it out."

"So am I," said Barnacle, patting her shoulder with one flipper.

Their own little warning light blinked off on its own, and the boat steadied again, sailing smooth.

Ahead, two spacecraft drifted toward each other, slow and careful, like two puzzle pieces lining up.

"On **July 17, 1975**, an American ship and a Soviet ship met up in orbit and **docked** together," said Barnacle. "That means they joined up, nose to nose. The astronauts and cosmonauts climbed through and shook hands."

Maya watched the two crews shake hands through the glow, grinning at each other like old friends.

"After all that racing," she said, "they just... shook hands?"

"The whole race ended in a handshake," said Barnacle. "Sometimes that's the very best finish line."

Maya smiled and leaned her head on Barnacle's warm, damp shoulder, suddenly sleepy, her stack of drawings held tight in her lap.

"All aboard for home, then," said Barnacle softly, and the little paper boat turned, gliding back down through the glittering dark.

**SPLOOSH.** They landed right back in the rain boot on her windowsill, gentle as a bath.

Maya climbed into bed, her stack of space drawings fanned out on the carpet below: Sputnik, Laika, Gagarin, Tereshkova, Leonov, Earthrise, the giant leap, and the handshake.

Barnacle's nose poked once more from the glowing puddle. "Goodnight, Maya," he said. "Play well, and dream of stars."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. Play well, and dream of stars.

facts.text: The Space Race was a Cold War contest between the US and USSR to achieve spaceflight firsts, lasting roughly 1957 to 1975.
On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a beach-ball-sized satellite that became the first man-made object to orbit Earth.
Sputnik 1 was about 58 centimeters wide and sent out a simple radio beep that people around the world could pick up on ordinary radios.
On November 3, 1957, the Soviets launched Sputnik 2 carrying a dog named Laika, the first living creature to orbit Earth.
Shocked by Sputnik, the United States created NASA, which began operating on October 1, 1958.
The first US satellite, Explorer 1, launched January 31, 1958, and discovered the Van Allen radiation belt.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, orbiting Earth once aboard Vostok 1 in about 108 minutes.
On May 5, 1961, Alan Shepard became the first American in space aboard the Freedom 7 capsule, though his short flight did not orbit Earth.
On May 25, 1961, President Kennedy challenged the US to land a man on the Moon and return him safely before decade's end.
On June 16, 1963, Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth aboard Vostok 6.
On March 18, 1965, Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, floating outside his Voskhod 2 capsule for about ten minutes.
On January 27, 1967, astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee died in a fire during a launch pad test of Apollo 1.
In December 1968, Apollo 8 astronauts became the first to orbit the Moon, and William Anders took the famous Earthrise photo.
On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronaut Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap for mankind.
Buzz Aldrin joined Armstrong on the Moon while crewmate Michael Collins orbited alone above in the command module Columbia.
In 1970, an oxygen tank explosion crippled Apollo 13 on its way to the Moon, but the crew safely returned to Earth after engineers improvised a fix.
Between 1969 and 1972, twelve American astronauts walked on the Moon across six successful Apollo landing missions.
The Saturn V rocket that carried Apollo astronauts to the Moon stood 363 feet tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty.
Soviet chief designer Sergei Korolev secretly led the USSR's rocket program, and his identity was kept a state secret until after his death in 1966.
Wernher von Braun, who earlier built rockets for Germany, led the NASA team that developed the Saturn V rocket.
The Space Race ended in a spirit of cooperation on July 17, 1975, when American and Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit and their crews shook hands.
