story.title: Maya and the Race to the Moon
story.subtitle: A splashy trip through the Space Age, with Barnacle the seal along for the ride.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep in the Water Cup
chapters.text:
Maya had swim practice that morning, and now her arms ached in a good, floppy way. She sat cross-legged on her bed, painting a little rowboat, her paintbrush dipped in a cup of water on the nightstand.

It had been a whole week since the glow from the hum-bridge had faded off her windowsill. Tonight the glow was back, but this time it came from her water cup.

**BEEEEP.** The water fizzed like soda. Up popped a round, whiskery head.

"All aboard, Maya!" said Barnacle the seal, water sloshing onto her sketchbook.

"Barnacle! You're in my cup!"

"Technically," he said, "I'm in a little slice of outer space. Listen." The beep came again, steady as a heartbeat.

"That sounds like boat code," Maya said. "Like when ships blink their lights."

"Close! On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union launched something called **Sputnik 1** — the first satellite ever to fly around the Earth." Barnacle explained a satellite is just a machine that circles a planet, around and around, like a toy on a string with no string at all.

"Sputnik was only about as wide as a **beach ball**," he went on, "and all it did was send out that simple beep, over and over. Anybody with an ordinary radio could hear it."

Maya grinned. "People all over the world heard a little beach ball beeping from space?"

"Paws-itively true," said Barnacle.

Maya cupped her hands around the glowing water. It spun into a tiny whirlpool, bright as stars.

"Hold on tight," said Barnacle.

**SPLOOSH.** The cup swallowed them whole.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Laika and the New Space Team
chapters.text:
They landed with a soft *thump* on something cold and metal. Above them hung a shiny silver ball with a tiny round window.

Maya pressed her face close. Inside sat a small, bright-eyed dog.

"Why is there a dog in space?" Maya asked.

"On **November 3, 1957**," said Barnacle, "the Soviets launched **Sputnik 2**, and a brave dog named **Laika** became the very first living creature to circle the Earth."

Maya waved through the window, careful not to touch the glass. "Hi, Laika. You're so brave."

"The whole world fell in love with her," Barnacle said. "She became famous everywhere."

A siren of sorts wailed in the distance — not scary, just busy and important, like a school on the first day.

"Everyone over in America got a big surprise," Barnacle said. "They didn't want to be left behind, so they built a brand-new space team."

"What's it called?"

"**NASA**. It started working on **October 1, 1958**."

Maya thought about her own swim team, how they'd all gotten matching caps once. "Did they get a cool name because of Sputnik?"

"Exactly because of Sputnik," said Barnacle, clapping his flippers. "You could say Sputnik beeped, and NASA answered."

Maya giggled. "That's a good one. For a seal."

"I have my moments," said Barnacle, and the silver ball above them began to spin into a new, glowing circle of light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Invisible Belt
chapters.text:
This time they landed on a launch pad with a tiny satellite shaped like a long pencil.

"This one's American," said Barnacle. "**Explorer 1**. Launched **January 31, 1958**."

Maya tilted her head. "What did it find?"

"Something nobody could see before. An invisible ring of fizzy energy wrapped all the way around the Earth. Scientists named it the **Van Allen belt**, after the man who figured it out."

"A belt made of energy, not for pants?" Maya asked.

"Not for pants," Barnacle agreed. "Just a glowing ring, circling our whole planet, like a hula hoop made of light."

Maya loved this. She flipped open her sketchbook and started drawing: Earth in the middle, a glowing ring looping around it.

"Can I keep this drawing?" she asked.

"You'll want to," said Barnacle, with a wink that seals probably shouldn't be able to do. "It might come in handy."

Maya tucked her pencil behind her ear. "Where next?"

"Somewhere a person finally gets to go, not just a satellite," said Barnacle, and the drawing in her lap began to glow at the edges.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The First Person Up There
chapters.text:
They tumbled out beside a tall rocket, steam hissing from its sides.

A man in a round white helmet waved from a hatch, grinning so big his whole face seemed to smile.

"That's **Yuri Gagarin**," said Barnacle. "On **April 12, 1961**, he became the very first human to fly in space. He zoomed all the way around the Earth once, in about **108 minutes**."

"That's faster than my whole swim practice!" Maya said.

"Much faster," said Barnacle.

Maya asked, "Was he scared?"

"He smiled the entire way," said Barnacle. "That's why people loved him so much."

Then the scene shifted, quick as a wave, to a smaller capsule bobbing nearby.

"And that one?" Maya asked.

"**Alan Shepard**. On **May 5, 1961**, he became the first American in space. His trip was shorter — he didn't make it all the way around the Earth like Gagarin did."

Maya thought of boat races back home, how sometimes one boat went all the way around the buoy and another just went partway.

"So Gagarin did the whole lap," she said, "and Shepard did half?"

"A fair way to think about it," said Barnacle, clearly impressed.

Maya grinned. "I want to see who finishes the whole race."

"Funny you say that," said Barnacle. "Someone's about to announce exactly that."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: A Dare to the Moon
chapters.text:
A crowd gathered around a podium. A man in a dark suit stood tall, speaking in a clear, booming voice.

"That's President **Kennedy**," Barnacle whispered. "Listen."

"We choose to go to the Moon," the voice rang out, "and to do it before this decade is out."

Maya's mouth fell open. "The actual Moon? Like, land on it?"

"On **May 25, 1961**, he dared his whole country to do exactly that," Barnacle said.

Maya grabbed her pencil and, right under her drawing of the glowing belt, wrote one big word: MOON.

"What's that for?" Barnacle asked.

"It's our mission plan," Maya said. "If we're going to see everything, we need to know where we're headed."

Barnacle looked at the word, then at Maya, clearly delighted. "A captain who plans ahead. I like it."

"All boats need a destination," Maya said proudly.

"Then let's follow your map," said Barnacle, and the word MOON on her page began to shimmer like moonlight on water.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Valentina's Forty-Eight Laps
chapters.text:
They landed beside yet another rocket, smaller flags painted along its side.

A woman climbed out, hair pushed back, eyes bright with excitement.

"On **June 16, 1963**," said Barnacle, "**Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman ever to fly in space. She circled the Earth aboard a ship called **Vostok 6**."

Maya's eyes went wide. "A whole lady astronaut? Like, by herself?"

"All by herself," said Barnacle. "She used to work in a factory before this. Then she went and orbited the Earth **forty-eight times**."

Maya tried to picture swimming forty-eight laps of her pool and nearly fell over giggling. "That's SO many laps!"

"She never got tired of the view," Barnacle said.

Maya waved up at Valentina, who waved right back before her rocket rumbled off the pad.

"I want to go around the whole Earth someday too," Maya said.

"One lap at a time," said Barnacle gently. "You've already got the forty-eight-lap spirit. That's the important part."

Maya beamed, tucking that thought away like a shell in her pocket.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Secret Superhero
chapters.text:
The next landing was quiet and dark, stars thick overhead.

A spaceship floated nearby, and a figure in a puffy suit drifted slowly outside it, tethered by a long cord, like a balloon on a string.

"That's **Alexei Leonov**," said Barnacle. "On **March 18, 1965**, he became the first person ever to float outside his spaceship. That's called a **spacewalk**. He floated out there about **ten minutes**."

"Why doesn't he fall?" Maya asked.

"No gravity up here to pull him down," said Barnacle. "Nothing to fall toward. He just floats."

Maya watched, amazed, as Leonov tumbled gently, slow as a leaf in a pool.

"Who built all these rockets, anyway?" Maya asked. "Somebody has to design them."

"Ah," said Barnacle, lowering his voice like it was a secret — which, it turned out, it was. "On the Soviet side, one man led it all: **Sergei Korolev**. But nobody outside his country even knew his name until after he died, in **1966**. It was kept completely secret."

Maya gasped. "A secret superhero behind everything?"

"Exactly that," said Barnacle. "And on the American side, a rocket builder named **Wernher von Braun** led the team that built the giant rockets for NASA."

Maya nodded slowly, piecing it together like puzzle edges. "So there were two secret rocket wizards, racing each other."

"You found it," said Barnacle, clearly proud. "Nobody told you that. You worked it out yourself."

Maya grinned so wide her cheeks hurt.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Whole Earth in a Photo
chapters.text:
They drifted now, not toward a planet but around one. Through a round window, Earth hung small and blue and swirled with white clouds, like a marble floating in black water.

"This is **Apollo 8**," Barnacle said. "In December **1968**, these astronauts became the first people ever to circle the Moon. And look — right there."

An astronaut lifted a camera to the window.

"That's **William Anders**," said Barnacle, "taking what people now call the **Earthrise** photo — our whole Earth, rising over the edge of the Moon."

Maya pressed her hands to the glass, awestruck. "It looks so small. And so pretty."

"From up here," Barnacle said softly, "it's the only home anybody has."

Maya didn't say anything for a moment. Then she grabbed her pencil and began to draw it exactly as she saw it — round, blue, rising over gray Moon dust.

"Keep that one safe," said Barnacle. "It's a good one to bring home."

Maya folded the drawing carefully into her sketchbook, right next to her glowing belt and her MOON plan.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: One Giant Leap
chapters.text:
The ground shook. A rocket taller than any building Maya had ever seen stood waiting, smoke curling from its base.

"That's the **Saturn V**," said Barnacle. "**363 feet tall** — taller than the Statue of Liberty!"

Maya craned her neck all the way back. "That's bigger than my whole street."

**WHOOOOSH.** The rocket climbed into the sky, and the scene swept forward to a dusty gray surface, a ladder, and a boot stepping down.

"On **July 20, 1969**," Barnacle said, "**Neil Armstrong** became the first person to ever walk on the Moon. He called it a giant leap."

Maya watched Armstrong's boot press into the dust, leaving a perfect print.

"**Buzz Aldrin** walked there too," Barnacle added, "while their friend **Michael Collins** stayed up above, all alone, flying the ship called **Columbia** in circles around the Moon."

"Wasn't he lonely?" Maya asked.

"Maybe a little," said Barnacle. "But somebody had to keep the ship safe for the ride home. That's its own kind of brave."

Maya thought of staying home to keep a boat tied up steady, while others went ashore. "That's a good job too," she decided.

She looked at the boot print, perfect and still, and whispered the words right along with Armstrong.

"ONE GIANT LEAP!" Maya shouted, and her voice echoed clear across the quiet gray Moon.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Splashdown, and Shaking Hands
chapters.text:
The next rocket did not look right. A bang, far off and muffled, rattled the little ship, and a warning light blinked red.

"Uh-oh," said Barnacle, calm as ever. "This is **Apollo 13**, **1970**. An oxygen tank broke, way out past the Moon."

Maya's stomach tightened for one second. "Are they okay?"

"They are," Barnacle said right away. "Everybody on the ground worked together and figured out a fix using only what the astronauts already had on board. The whole crew made it safely home."

Maya let out a breath. "Like patching a torn sail with whatever's in the boat."

"Exactly like that," Barnacle said, and the worry melted off Maya's shoulders like morning fog.

"By the end of it all," Barnacle went on, "**twelve** astronauts had walked on the Moon."

"Twelve whole people!" Maya said, wiggling with delight.

Then the sky filled with two ships, one Soviet, one American, drifting slowly toward each other.

"**July 17, 1975**," said Barnacle. "The last chapter. American and Soviet spaceships **docked** together, right there in orbit, and the crews climbed through and shook hands."

Maya watched the astronauts grin at each other, shaking hands in space the way she shook hands after a swim meet.

"That's a nice way to end a race," she said.

"The nicest way," said Barnacle, and the stars around them began to swirl and fold, pulling gently back toward home.

**SPLOOSH.** Maya landed softly on her own bed, paintbrush still in her hand, her water cup calm and still beside her.

On her sketchbook sat a drawing she didn't remember finishing: the whole Earth, rising blue over gray Moon dust, with a tiny paper rocket tucked beside it.

Barnacle's flipper-print glistened, just once, on the rim of the cup, and then the water went quiet.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. The stars are still up there, circling along, same as always. SPLOOSH, and play well, little astronaut.

facts.text: The Space Race was a Cold War contest between the US and USSR to achieve spaceflight firsts, lasting roughly 1957 to 1975.
On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a beach-ball-sized satellite that became the first man-made object to orbit Earth.
Sputnik 1 was about 58 centimeters wide and sent out a simple radio beep that people around the world could pick up on ordinary radios.
On November 3, 1957, the Soviets launched Sputnik 2 carrying a dog named Laika, the first living creature to orbit Earth.
Shocked by Sputnik, the United States created NASA, which began operating on October 1, 1958.
The first US satellite, Explorer 1, launched January 31, 1958, and discovered the Van Allen radiation belt.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, orbiting Earth once aboard Vostok 1 in about 108 minutes.
On May 5, 1961, Alan Shepard became the first American in space aboard the Freedom 7 capsule, though his short flight did not orbit Earth.
On May 25, 1961, President Kennedy challenged the US to land a man on the Moon and return him safely before decade's end.
On June 16, 1963, Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth aboard Vostok 6.
On March 18, 1965, Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, floating outside his Voskhod 2 capsule for about ten minutes.
On January 27, 1967, astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee died in a fire during a launch pad test of Apollo 1.
In December 1968, Apollo 8 astronauts became the first to orbit the Moon, and William Anders took the famous Earthrise photo.
On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronaut Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap for mankind.
Buzz Aldrin joined Armstrong on the Moon while crewmate Michael Collins orbited alone above in the command module Columbia.
In 1970, an oxygen tank explosion crippled Apollo 13 on its way to the Moon, but the crew safely returned to Earth after engineers improvised a fix.
Between 1969 and 1972, twelve American astronauts walked on the Moon across six successful Apollo landing missions.
The Saturn V rocket that carried Apollo astronauts to the Moon stood 363 feet tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty.
Soviet chief designer Sergei Korolev secretly led the USSR's rocket program, and his identity was kept a state secret until after his death in 1966.
Wernher von Braun, who earlier built rockets for Germany, led the NASA team that developed the Saturn V rocket.
The Space Race ended in a spirit of cooperation on July 17, 1975, when American and Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit and their crews shook hands.

story.title: Theo and the Sputnik Signal
story.subtitle: A midnight build turns into the real race to space.

chapters.heading: Level 1: Sputnik's Beep (1957)
chapters.text:
Theo was belly-down on his bedroom carpet at 11:52 p.m., laptop propped on a pillow, headphones clamped over his ears like he was defusing a bomb.

On the screen, a little rocket sat on a launchpad he had spent two hours building in Roblox Studio. Every time he hit Play, the rocket sank through the floor like it was made of wet sand.

"Come ON," Theo muttered, dragging the collision box wider for the ninth time. "You're a rocket. Rockets don't fall through the ground."

He hit Play again. The rocket sank. Again.

He yanked his headphones off to rub his eyes — and that was when he heard it anyway, thin and tinny, leaking out of the speakers even though the game wasn't making a sound.

Beep. Beep-beep. Beep.

The screen flickered. Not a normal flicker — a green-and-black flicker, like someone had reached back in time and dragged an old computer terminal into his bedroom.

A shape blinked into the corner of the screen: a small pixel satellite, round as a beach ball, with four thin antennas trailing off it like whiskers. A chat bubble popped up beside it.

BEEP. BEEP. HELLO, it read.

Theo did not scream, which he would like on the record. He did lean back about a foot.

"...Hello?" he said. "Are you a glitch?"

I AM NOT A GLITCH, the bubble said, sounding faintly offended for something made of pixels. I AM PIP. YOU HAVE BEEN BUILDING ROCKETS ALL NIGHT. DO YOU KNOW WHERE THE FIRST ONE ACTUALLY WENT?

Theo blinked. "...Into orbit?"

CLOSE, Pip beeped. TUNE ME IN AND I'LL SHOW YOU.

A little dial appeared, like an old radio. Theo — who had spent enough nights messing with audio settings in Roblox Studio to know a frequency slider when he saw one — nudged his mouse slowly until the beeping outside his headphones lined up with the beeping inside them.

CLICK.

The screen opened, like a loading screen, into a black sky scattered with stars, and a silver ball the size of a beach ball sailing through it, trailing a thin radio signal like a kite string.

"That's..." Theo squinted. "That's Pip. That's literally you."

NOT ME, said Pip. MY GREAT-GREAT-GRANDFATHER. **SPUTNIK 1.** **OCTOBER 4, 1957.** THE SOVIET UNION LAUNCHED HIM — THE FIRST MAN-MADE OBJECT EVER TO GO AROUND THE EARTH.

"Around the Earth," Theo repeated. "Like, going in circles forever?"

AN **ORBIT**, Pip explained, is just a big circle a thing makes around a planet because it keeps falling and missing the ground, over and over. SPUTNIK WAS ONLY **58 CENTIMETERS WIDE.** SMALLER THAN YOUR DESK CHAIR. ALL IT DID WAS GO BEEP.

"That's it? It just beeped?"

THAT'S IT. AND PEOPLE ALL OVER THE WORLD PICKED UP THE BEEP ON ORDINARY RADIOS.

Theo looked at the little silver ball sailing through the dark, beeping its heart out, and suddenly his glitchy rocket didn't feel so embarrassing. "Okay," he said. "That's actually unbelievably cool."

ROUND ONE, said Pip, and the stars rearranged into a corridor of glowing doors. THERE ARE MORE LEVELS. TRY TO KEEP UP.

chapters.heading: Level 2: Laika's Orbit (1957)
chapters.text:
The next door didn't open so much as ping, the way a Roblox server does when a friend joins.

Theo stepped through — or whatever you call it when your brain is apparently inside a loading screen — into a close, round little chamber with padded walls and a tiny window. Wagging in the middle of it, impossibly calm, sat a brown-and-white dog with her ears pricked forward.

"That is a dog," Theo said. "In space. Please tell me that's a hologram."

SHE IS **LAIKA**, Pip beeped. **NOVEMBER 3, 1957.** ONE MONTH AFTER SPUTNIK, THE SOVIETS LAUNCHED **SPUTNIK 2** — AND SHE WAS INSIDE. FIRST LIVING CREATURE TO ORBIT EARTH.

Theo crouched by the little window, careful not to touch the glass. "She just... went around the whole planet. By herself."

NOT ALONE, Pip said. SCIENTISTS ON THE GROUND WATCHED OVER HER THE WHOLE TIME. SHE BECAME FAMOUS AROUND THE WORLD — A SMALL DOG WHO DID SOMETHING NO LIVING THING HAD EVER DONE BEFORE.

Theo studied the capsule itself — round, snug, no steering wheel, nothing to grab onto. It looked nothing like his Roblox rocket, which was basically a cylinder standing on a flat plate.

"Why's it round?" he asked. "Shouldn't it be pointy? Aerodynamic?"

ASK YOURSELF, Pip said, WHICH SHAPE SURVIVES A CRASH LANDING BETTER — A CORNER, OR A CURVE?

Theo thought about every Roblox build that had ever fallen off a cliff. The sharp-edged ones always snapped apart. The round ones bounced.

"...A curve," he said slowly. Then, faster: "Wait. My rocket's been falling through the floor because the bottom's a flat square. If I round the edges—"

HE'S CATCHING ON, Pip told the dark, like he was narrating to an audience only he could see.

Theo grinned and waved at Laika's little window, and the pup tilted her head, like she was waving back from decades and a few hundred miles up.

"Good girl," Theo said softly. "You did something nobody had ever done."

The chamber faded, the way a loading bar finishes, and the corridor of doors reappeared.

ROUND TWO, said Pip. NEXT STOP — AMERICA PANICS.

"That's an oddly specific level name," Theo said.

IT'S HISTORICALLY ACCURATE, said Pip, which is somehow worse.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Invisible Belt (1958)
chapters.text:
The next door opened onto a cramped room full of people in short-sleeved shirts, staring at a chart that jumped and spiked like a heart monitor having a bad night.

"Okay, this looks like a glitchy leaderboard," Theo said.

IT'S BETTER THAN A LEADERBOARD, said Pip. SPUTNIK SCARED THE UNITED STATES SO BADLY THEY BUILT A WHOLE NEW SPACE AGENCY. **NASA** STARTED WORKING ON **OCTOBER 1, 1958.**

"Because of one beeping ball?"

BECAUSE OF ONE BEEPING BALL, Pip confirmed. AND EVEN BEFORE NASA OFFICIALLY EXISTED, THE U.S. LAUNCHED ITS OWN FIRST SATELLITE — **EXPLORER 1**, ON **JANUARY 31, 1958.**

The jumpy chart filled the screen again, lines spiking every time a little animated satellite crossed a certain patch of sky.

"What's making it spike like that?" Theo asked. "Is the satellite lagging?"

NOT LAGGING. Explorer 1 found something nobody knew was there — an invisible ring of charged particles wrapped around the Earth, held in place by the planet's own magnetism. Scientists later named it the **Van Allen radiation belt**.

"So it's like an invisible wall," Theo said, "that you'd only find by accident. By flying straight into it."

EXACTLY LIKE THAT, Pip said. WHICH REMINDS ME.

A thin, shimmering line appeared across the floor, right where Theo would have walked if he'd kept moving. He stopped just short of it.

"Is that—"

AN INVISIBLE WALL. YES. TRY NOT TO WALK THROUGH HISTORY. IT GETS MESSY.

Theo laughed and stepped around it — and froze. "Wait. That's it. That's why my rocket keeps falling through the floor. I never added a collision wall under the pad. I just assumed the floor would catch it."

YOU CAN'T SEE GRAVITY EITHER, Pip pointed out. DOESN'T MEAN IT ISN'T THERE.

"You're surprisingly wise for a beach ball," Theo said.

I CONTAIN MULTITUDES, said Pip, and the room folded away like a tab closing.

chapters.heading: Level 4: One Hundred Eight Minutes (1961)
chapters.text:
The new room was snug and round again, but bigger, with a single curved seat and a porthole showing the whole blue curve of Earth outside.

A man in a white helmet grinned through the glass of the capsule, like he was having the best day of his life, which, as it turned out, he kind of was.

"Who's that?" Theo asked, already liking him.

**YURI GAGARIN.** SOVIET PILOT. **APRIL 12, 1961** — THE FIRST HUMAN BEING TO FLY INTO SPACE, RIDING A CAPSULE CALLED **VOSTOK 1** ALL THE WAY AROUND THE EARTH. ONE FULL LOOP. ABOUT **108 MINUTES.**

Theo, who had spent roughly eleven hundred Saturdays on a soccer field, did the math automatically. "That's longer than a whole match. He went around the entire planet in less time than it takes my team to lose in overtime."

PUT YOUR SKILLS TO USE, said Pip, and a glowing stopwatch appeared, already counting down from 108:00.

Theo watched it tick, picturing it like a match clock — first half, second half, the whistle. By the time it hit zero, Gagarin's capsule was already arcing back toward the ground, parachute blooming.

"That's insane," Theo breathed. "One lap and you're already a legend."

THREE WEEKS LATER, ANOTHER PILOT WENT UP TOO — **ALAN SHEPARD**, THE FIRST AMERICAN IN SPACE, ON **MAY 5, 1961.** HIS FLIGHT WAS SHORTER AND NEVER WENT ALL THE WAY AROUND. BUT IT STILL COUNTED.

"Sounds like Gagarin got the full match and Shepard got a penalty shootout," Theo said.

THAT'S UNFAIRLY ACCURATE, said Pip.

The scene shifted to a podium, a man in a dark suit speaking to a crowd that stretched farther than Theo could see.

ON **MAY 25, 1961**, said Pip, more quietly, PRESIDENT **JOHN F. KENNEDY** STOOD UP AND TOLD HIS COUNTRY TO LAND A PERSON ON THE MOON — AND BRING THEM HOME SAFE — BEFORE THE DECADE ENDED.

"That's like telling your whole team you're winning the championship before the season even starts," Theo said, "when you don't even have the players yet."

PRETTY MUCH. AND BEHIND THE SCENES, TWO DESIGNERS WERE RACING TO MAKE IT HAPPEN. ON THE SOVIET SIDE, **SERGEI KOROLEV** RAN THE WHOLE ROCKET PROGRAM — BUT HIS NAME WAS KEPT SECRET UNTIL HE DIED IN 1966. NO ONE EVEN KNEW HIS FACE.

"A secret genius," Theo said slowly. "Like a modder who builds the best game on the platform and never puts their name on it."

ON THE OTHER SIDE, **WERNHER VON BRAUN** LED THE AMERICAN TEAM BUILDING THE ROCKET THAT WOULD EVENTUALLY TRY FOR THE MOON.

Theo looked at the stopwatch, frozen at 00:00, and felt something tighten pleasantly in his chest — the same feeling he got when a build finally, finally worked. "Okay," he said. "I need to see if they actually did it."

PATIENCE, said Pip. THERE ARE STILL LEVELS LEFT.
chapters.shout_line: HE WENT AROUND THE ENTIRE PLANET?!

chapters.heading: Level 5: Forty-Eight Laps (1963)
chapters.text:
The next door opened on a woman strapped into a capsule, grinning the exact same unstoppable grin Gagarin had worn.

**VALENTINA TERESHKOVA**, said Pip. **JUNE 16, 1963.** FIRST WOMAN IN SPACE. SHE FLEW ABOARD **VOSTOK 6** AND WENT AROUND THE EARTH NOT ONCE, BUT **FORTY-EIGHT TIMES.**

Theo whistled. "Forty-eight? That's not a flight, that's a whole season."

A little counter appeared beside the capsule, ticking upward: 1... 2... 3...

"Hang on," Theo said, watching it climb, "let me guess where it stops." He thought about laps around a soccer pitch, about how his legs usually started complaining after ten, and multiplied it out in his head. "Forty-eight."

The counter stopped. 48.

THAT'S CORRECT, said Pip, sounding almost smug on Theo's behalf. SHE HAD BEEN AN ORDINARY FACTORY WORKER BEFORE SHE TRAINED TO FLY. NOT A TEST PILOT. NOT MILITARY. JUST SOMEONE WHO WANTED IT ENOUGH.

"So she just... leveled all the way up," Theo said. "From the factory floor to actual orbit."

PUT LIKE THAT, said Pip, IT SOUNDS EASY. IT WAS NOT EASY.

Theo watched her capsule sail past the window forty-eight invisible times in his mind and felt oddly proud of a woman he'd known about for exactly ninety seconds. "She's basically the final boss of persistence," he said.

A GOOD WAY TO PUT IT, said Pip, and for once didn't argue.

chapters.heading: Level 6: Ten Minutes Outside (1965)
chapters.text:
The next room had no walls at all — just a capsule floating in black space, and, drifting just outside it at the end of a long cord, a figure in a bulky white suit.

Theo's stomach did a small flip. "Is he just... out there? With nothing around him?"

**ALEXEI LEONOV**, said Pip. **MARCH 18, 1965.** FIRST HUMAN EVER TO LEAVE HIS CAPSULE AND FLOAT FREE IN SPACE — WHAT WE CALL A **SPACEWALK.** HE WAS OUTSIDE FOR ABOUT TEN MINUTES.

"Ten minutes doesn't sound that long," Theo said, eyeing the thin cord connecting the floating man to the capsule, the only thing between him and absolutely nothing. "But that cord is doing a LOT of work."

THAT'S THE **TETHER**, said Pip. A STRONG LINE THAT KEEPS AN ASTRONAUT ATTACHED TO THEIR SHIP SO THEY DON'T DRIFT AWAY FOR GOOD.

Theo stared at it, and something clicked in his brain. "That's an anchor point," he said. "My rocket keeps wobbling because I never anchored the fuel tank to the frame. It's just balanced there. One bump and it's gone."

HISTORY: STILL HELPFUL, said Pip.

Leonov drifted gently back toward the capsule, hand over hand along the tether, and climbed back inside, safe. The whole thing had lasted ten minutes and ended exactly the way it was supposed to.

"Ten minutes floating in actual space and he just climbs back in like he's done on the trampoline," Theo said. "Unbelievable."

MOST OF HISTORY, said Pip, IS PEOPLE BEING BRAVER THAN THEY HAD ANY RIGHT TO BE, AND THEN GOING HOME FOR DINNER.

chapters.heading: Level 7: Earthrise (1968)
chapters.text:
The next door didn't open onto a room at all. It opened onto nothing — then, suddenly, onto everything: a dusty gray horizon curving away below, and above it, impossibly, a small blue marble rising into a black sky.

Theo forgot to say anything for a second, which almost never happened.

**DECEMBER 1968**, said Pip, quieter than usual. **APOLLO 8.** THE FIRST ASTRONAUTS TO FLY ALL THE WAY TO THE MOON AND ORBIT AROUND IT. ONE OF THEM, **WILLIAM ANDERS**, LOOKED OUT THE WINDOW AND SAW THAT.

"That" was Earth, rising over the Moon's gray edge like a sunrise, except blue and white and swirled with cloud, smaller than Theo had ever imagined a whole planet could look.

"He just... saw it happen?" Theo said. "Nobody had ever seen that before?"

NOBODY. HE GRABBED A CAMERA AND TOOK THE PICTURE RIGHT THERE. IT'S CALLED **EARTHRISE**, AND IT'S ONE OF THE MOST FAMOUS PHOTOS EVER TAKEN.

Theo thought about every screenshot he'd ever taken of his own builds — the little camera icon he mashed the second something finally looked right. "I get that," he said. "You build this whole thing and then one angle just... makes you stop."

He raised an imaginary camera, framed the rising Earth exactly the way Anders must have, and mimed the click.

NOT BAD, said Pip. YOU'D HAVE MADE A DECENT ASTRONAUT.

"I'd have made a decent photographer," Theo corrected. "Let's not get ahead of ourselves."

The little blue Earth kept climbing silently over the gray horizon, and for a moment neither of them said anything else, because some things don't need a joke after them.

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Giant Leap (1969)
chapters.text:
The next door thundered open — actual thunder, a wall of sound and fire, the biggest rocket Theo had ever seen standing on a pad like a skyscraper that had decided to go somewhere.

"How big IS that thing?" Theo shouted over the roar.

THE **SATURN V**, Pip beeped back. **363 FEET TALL.** TALLER THAN THE STATUE OF LIBERTY. IT'S THE ROCKET THAT GOT THEM THERE.

The rocket climbed, impossibly, almost gently, trailing fire — and the scene jumped, the way levels do, straight to a gray dusty surface, a ladder, and a boot, reaching down.

"Wait," Theo said. "Is this—"

**JULY 20, 1969.** **APOLLO 11.** AND THAT'S **NEIL ARMSTRONG**, ABOUT TO BECOME THE FIRST PERSON EVER TO WALK ON THE MOON.

The boot touched down. Dust puffed up around it in complete silence, because there's no air on the Moon to carry a sound.

"That's one small step for man," crackled a voice, "one giant leap for mankind."

Theo didn't say anything clever. For once, he just watched.

BUZZ ALDRIN CLIMBED DOWN AFTER HIM, said Pip. THEY WALKED AROUND TOGETHER DOWN THERE. MEANWHILE THEIR THIRD CREWMATE, **MICHAEL COLLINS**, STAYED UP IN THE COMMAND MODULE — NAMED **COLUMBIA** — ORBITING THE MOON ALL ALONE, WAITING TO BRING THEM ALL HOME.

"He didn't even get to walk on it?" Theo said. "That's rough."

SOMEBODY HAD TO FLY THE SHIP, Pip said. NOT EVERY HERO GETS THE SCREENSHOT. SOME OF THEM JUST KEEP EVERYONE ELSE ALIVE.

Theo thought about every multiplayer build he'd ever done where he was the one holding the server together while a friend grabbed the glory — and decided Michael Collins was, in fact, the real MVP.

The two boots on the dust kept walking, bouncing slightly in the lighter gravity, and Theo watched with his mouth slightly open, feeling like he'd just watched the final level of the best game ever made — except it was real, and it had happened before his own parents were even born.

"They actually did it," Theo said. "Kennedy's whole deadline thing. They actually did it."

BEFORE THE DECADE ENDED, said Pip. WITH TWO YEARS TO SPARE.

chapters.heading: Level 9: The Fix and the Handshake (1970–1975)
chapters.text:
The next room started calm — a capsule gliding smooth and quiet toward a gray dot that was obviously the Moon — and then, without warning, something inside it went BANG, and warning lights flooded the little cabin red.

Theo flinched. "Whoa — what happened?"

**1970.** **APOLLO 13.** AN OXYGEN TANK EXPLODED ON THE WAY TO THE MOON AND CRIPPLED THE WHOLE SHIP. THEY HAD TO TURN BACK.

"Are they okay?" Theo asked immediately, because that mattered more than anything else in the room.

THEY'RE OKAY, said Pip, fast and firm, like it wanted that part understood before anything else. ENGINEERS BACK ON EARTH WORKED OUT A FIX USING WHAT THE ASTRONAUTS ALREADY HAD ON BOARD, AND TALKED THEM THROUGH IT, STEP BY STEP. THE WHOLE CREW MADE IT HOME SAFE.

Theo let out a breath he hadn't noticed he was holding. "So it's like — the server crashes, but instead of losing everything, somebody figures out how to rebuild it out of spare parts while you're still inside it."

THAT'S UNCOMFORTABLY EXACT, said Pip. AND KIND OF THE WHOLE POINT. SOMETIMES THE BEST PART OF A STORY ISN'T THAT NOTHING WENT WRONG. IT'S THAT PEOPLE FIGURED IT OUT ANYWAY.

The battered little capsule splashed safely into blue ocean, and the scene dissolved into one last room — two spacecraft, docked nose to nose in orbit, a hatch sliding open between them.

**JULY 17, 1975**, said Pip. **APOLLO-SOYUZ.** AN AMERICAN SHIP AND A SOVIET SHIP MET UP IN ORBIT AND DOCKED TOGETHER. THE CREWS OPENED THE HATCH AND SHOOK HANDS. THAT'S HOW THE SPACE RACE ENDED.

Two astronauts floated through the hatch and clasped hands in midair, grinning, upside down relative to each other, which in zero gravity didn't matter at all.

"After everything," Theo said slowly, "beeping satellites and secret rocket designers and a guy floating in actual space on a rope — it just ends with a handshake?"

IT ENDS WITH A HANDSHAKE, Pip agreed. SEEMED LIKE A GOOD PLACE TO STOP RACING AND START WAVING.

The corridor of doors folded up behind them like a closing tab, and the green-black flicker rose around Theo's room again, and then — ordinary lamplight. His carpet. His laptop, still open, the cursor blinking in Roblox Studio exactly where he'd left it.

He looked at his rocket. Rounded base now. An invisible wall under the pad. A tether holding the fuel tank to the frame.

He hit Play.

The rocket sat on the pad for one heart-stopping second — and then it lit, and climbed, smooth and steady, all the way up past the render distance.

"YES," Theo said, loud enough that it was lucky nobody else was awake to hear it. "YES. FINALLY."

In the corner of the screen, for just a second, a tiny pixel satellite blinked once, beeped twice, and faded out.

"Night, Pip," Theo said to the empty screen, grinning like an idiot. Then he saved his file, like a sensible astronaut radioing home, and finally — finally — went to bed.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there'd be a new level to build — and somewhere, Theo figured, Pip would already be listening for his next beep.

story.title: Theo and the Space Race Server
story.subtitle: One glowing block, one very late bedtime, and a race across the stars.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Beep in Orbit (1957)
chapters.text:
Theo was still awake, which was exactly the plan.

His tablet threw blue light across the ceiling. In Roblox Studio, he was building a rocket for his new game, and the launch effect was all wrong — flat, no shake, no WHOOOOSH. He tapped the fire button for the ninth time. Nothing.

Then the screen flickered black and green, like an old computer waking up from a long nap. A block appeared on his baseplate that he hadn't placed — a glowing green cube, humming faintly, stamped with one word: LAUNCH.

"That's not mine," Theo said.

He clicked it anyway.

The hum turned into a WHOOOOSH, and his bedroom dropped away. He landed somewhere that felt like outside, except there was no sound at all — just stars, a glowing dial, and a voice.

"New player detected," the voice said, sounding exactly like a loading screen. "Welcome to the Space Race server. I'm Nova. I run this place."

Nova turned out to be a blocky figure in a dented silver suit, hovering on a jetpack that didn't seem to be doing much work at all. "You're a little early for the Moon," Nova said. "We've got years of history to get through first. Buckle in."

Below them, something spun slowly in the dark — a silver ball with four thin legs, like a spider that had given up on two of them.

"What is that?"

"The first thing humans ever put into orbit," Nova said. "Orbit just means it travels around something, instead of falling back down. This one travels around Earth."

"It's kind of small," Theo said.

"About 58 centimeters wide. Roughly beach-ball sized — maybe two soccer balls stacked on top of each other. It launched **October 4, 1957**, from the Soviet Union. They called it **Sputnik 1**."

Static crackled from a speaker Theo hadn't noticed. Beep. Beep. Beep.

"That's it talking," Nova said. "A simple radio beep. People everywhere could pick it up on ordinary radios — no fancy equipment, just a dial and some patience."

Three channels glowed faintly in front of Theo. "Can I find it?" he asked.

"Try."

He turned the first dial — static. The second — silence. On the third, the beep locked in clean and steady.

"There it is," Nova said, and the silver ball flashed bright, like it knew it had been heard. "Nice tuning."

"It's basically a tiny radio ball in space," Theo said.

"Basically," Nova agreed. "But in 1957, nobody had ever heard anything like it. People everywhere stopped what they were doing just to listen to a sound falling out of the sky. Sputnik started the whole race. Once it was up there, everybody wanted to go further."

A little score counter ticked upward somewhere in the dark.

chapters.heading: Level 2: A Passenger for Sputnik (1957)
chapters.text:
Nova led Theo toward a second capsule, smaller, with a round window and a hatch that hadn't sealed yet.

"One month after Sputnik 1," Nova said, "the Soviets launched again. This one wasn't empty."

Theo pressed close to the window. A shape curled in the corner, dark eyes blinking back at him.

"Is that a dog?"

"Her name was Laika," Nova said. "**November 3, 1957**. She became the first living creature to ever orbit Earth."

Theo flattened his hand against the glass. "She looks pretty calm about it."

"She was a good traveler," Nova said. "Before her, nobody knew for sure if a living creature could survive a launch, or floating weightless, or any of it. Laika was how they found out it could be done."

A panel on the hatch blinked red, waiting for a code — three slots, each needing an icon. A tray beside Theo held a paw print, a rocket, and a star.

"I guess I seal her in properly," Theo said, sliding the paw print into the first slot.

CLICK. The hatch glowed green. The rocket and star slid into place after it on their own, and a small animation played — the capsule lifting off, trailing orange light.

"Good call," Nova said. "You just sealed the hatch for one of the most famous dogs in history."

"People made a dog famous for going to space?"

"There's a statue of her in Moscow," Nova said. "People still send her letters, if you can believe it."

"People send letters," Theo repeated slowly, "to a dog. From decades ago."

"People are like that about Laika," Nova said, managing a shrug despite being made entirely of blocks.

Theo watched the little capsule shrink into a dot of light, joining Sputnik 1's faint beeping somewhere out past the dark. It felt, for a second, like two tiny players finally on the same server.

"Next stop," Nova said, "is where the United States finally gets off the bench."

Theo laughed. "Took them a whole year?"

"A very busy year," Nova said, and the stars around them began to blur sideways, like a loading bar sweeping across the sky.

chapters.heading: Level 3: Mission Control Comes Online (1958)
chapters.text:
The stars snapped back into focus around a room full of blinking control panels and men in short-sleeved shirts, all of them staring at a single screen.

"Sputnik scared the United States badly," Nova said. "So badly that they built a brand-new space agency almost overnight. NASA started running on **October 1, 1958**."

"Just like that?" Theo asked.

"Just like that. And three months before NASA even opened its doors, the US had already launched its first satellite — **Explorer 1**, on **January 31, 1958**."

A glowing globe floated in front of Theo, wrapped in a faint ring of colored light he hadn't noticed at first. It pulsed, almost like a loading icon that wouldn't finish.

"What's that ring doing there?" Theo asked.

"That's what Explorer 1 found," Nova said. "Count the bands. Tell me what you see."

Theo leaned close, squinting. "One... two. Two rings, both kind of glowing."

"Correct," Nova said. "Two bands of invisible energy wrapped around the Earth, like belts nobody could see until Explorer 1 flew straight through one. Scientists named them the **Van Allen radiation belt** — belt, like you'd wear, except made of energy instead of leather."

"So the satellite found something nobody even knew was there?"

"Exactly. A tiny satellite, barely bigger than your arm, discovered something wrapped around the whole planet."

A tall man in the corner of the control room leaned over a drafting table covered in rocket sketches. "That's Wernher von Braun," Nova said. "He led the team that would eventually build the rocket big enough to reach the Moon. Keep that name in your head — you'll want it later."

Theo tapped the glowing globe, and the two rings locked into place with a soft chime, like a level clearing.

"Ring count: confirmed," Nova said, in the voice of someone reading an achievement banner. "You just discovered something the whole world didn't know was circling it."

"Not bad for a Tuesday," Theo said, though he had no idea if it was actually a Tuesday, in 1958 or anywhere else.

chapters.heading: Level 4: One Hundred Eight Minutes (1961)
chapters.text:
The control room melted away into a launchpad, steam hissing off a rocket taller than any building Theo had ever stood next to.

"This is it," Nova said. "**April 12, 1961**. A pilot named Yuri Gagarin is about to become the first human being ever to leave the ground and not come back down."

A capsule sat at the rocket's tip, round as a ball, with one small window. Inside, a man in a white suit gave a thumbs up through the glass, grinning like he was about to win something.

"How long is he up there?" Theo asked.

"About 108 minutes," Nova said. "Long enough to circle the entire planet once."

A panel beside Theo lit up with a jumble of switches, clearly out of order. "Launch sequence needs sorting," Nova said. "Fuel, ignition, release. Get it wrong and we just waste a lot of very expensive steam."

Theo studied the switches like he was reading a script in Roblox Studio — find the order, test it, see what breaks. Fuel first. Then ignition. Then release.

He flipped them in that order. The rocket shuddered, then roared upward in a column of fire and smoke.

"We have liftoff," Nova said.

As the rocket shrank into the sky, Theo noticed something odd — a blank spot on a wall of photographs nearby, where a name plate should have been.

"Who's missing?" he asked.

Nova's voice dropped, almost conspiratorial. "The chief designer behind this whole program. A man named Sergei Korolev. He planned nearly everything the Soviets achieved in space — but his name was kept completely secret. Most people didn't even know he existed until he died in **1966**."

"They hid the guy who built it?"

"For years," Nova said. "Imagine making the biggest thing in the world and nobody's allowed to know it was you."

Theo looked at the blank name plate for a long moment. "That's wild," he said finally. "He's basically the best player on the server and nobody knew his username."

Nova actually laughed at that one — a small, surprised, static-crackled laugh. "Best way I've ever heard it put."

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Ten-Year Dare (1961)
chapters.text:
Two capsules floated side by side, one small and round, one slightly different in shape. A single glowing arrow pointed at each.

"Less than a month later," Nova said, "the United States sent its own pilot up. Alan Shepard, **May 5, 1961**, aboard a capsule called Freedom 7."

"Did he go all the way around, like Gagarin?" Theo asked.

"No," Nova said. "His flight was suborbital — meaning it went up and came back down without circling the Earth. Shorter trip. Still the first American ever in space."

"So which one is his?" Theo looked between the two capsules.

"You tell me. One flew in a straight line up and down. One flew all the way around the planet."

Theo pointed to the smaller, boxier capsule. "That one. Looks built for a quick trip, not a lap."

"Correct," Nova said, and the capsule glowed in confirmation.

The scene shifted again — a podium now, a man speaking to a crowd Theo couldn't quite see the edges of. A single sentence floated in glowing letters above his head.

"President Kennedy," Nova said. "**May 25, 1961**. Just twenty days after Shepard's flight, he stood up and dared the entire country to land a person on the Moon — and bring them home safely — before the decade was over."

"Before 1970," Theo said, doing the math fast. "That's not very long."

"Nine years, give or take," Nova said. "A countdown clock for an entire country."

A big red button sat under Theo's hand, labeled simply: ACCEPT.

"Is this actually my call?" he asked.

"Someone's got to push it," Nova said. "Might as well be you."

Theo pressed it. A countdown clock blinked to life above them, ticking down toward the end of the decade, numbers scrolling fast like something out of his own game's loading screen.

"Nine years to build a rocket that can reach the Moon," Theo said. "That's a bigger project than anything I've ever built in Studio."

"Funny you should say that," Nova said. "Wait until you see the size of the thing."

chapters.heading: Level 6: Two Firsts, One Hatch (1963–1965)
chapters.text:
Two glowing doors appeared side by side, each with a blank card hovering in front of it, waiting for a name.

"Two more firsts before we get anywhere near the Moon," Nova said. "Your job: match the traveler to the record."

On a tray floated two photographs — a woman with a steady, confident smile, and a man in a bulky suit, tethered by a long cord that trailed off into darkness.

"Door one," Nova said, "**June 16, 1963**. First woman ever in space, orbiting Earth aboard a capsule called Vostok 6."

Theo slid the woman's photo into the first door. It locked with a soft chime. "Valentina Tereshkova," the panel read, glowing gold.

"She used to work in a factory," Nova added. "Then she went and orbited the entire planet."

"From factory floor to space," Theo said. "That's a pretty big level up."

"Door two," Nova said, nodding toward the man in the bulky suit. "**March 18, 1965**. First human to leave his spacecraft completely and float outside it in open space — a spacewalk, they called it. About ten minutes, tethered the whole time so he couldn't drift off."

Theo slid the second photo into place. CLICK. "Alexei Leonov," the panel confirmed.

"Ten minutes doesn't sound long," Theo said.

"Try floating outside a spacecraft for ten seconds," Nova said, "let alone ten minutes. Nobody had ever done it. He had no idea if his suit would even hold."

Theo studied the photo — the tether, the dark behind him, nothing but a thin line connecting him to anything solid. "That's either the bravest thing I've ever heard," Theo said, "or the scariest video game level of all time."

"Both," Nova said. "He got back inside fine, by the way. Suit held. Hatch worked. Totally fine landing after."

Both doors swung open at once, revealing nothing but more stars beyond them — which, Theo was starting to realize, was basically how every level on this server ended.

"First woman, first spacewalk," Theo said. "Both firsts, both huge. Why doesn't anybody talk about these as much as the Moon stuff?"

"They will tonight," Nova said. "Keep going. The Moon's close now."

chapters.heading: Level 7: Earthrise and the Giant Leap (1968–1969)
chapters.text:
The server shifted, and suddenly Theo was floating beside a small capsule window, Earth hanging below like a blue marble half in shadow.

"**December 1968**," Nova said. "Apollo 8. First humans ever to fly around the Moon. One of the astronauts, William Anders, looked up from his checklist and saw this."

A photo framed itself in front of Theo — Earth rising over a gray, cratered horizon, small and blue and completely alone in the black.

"He wasn't even supposed to take it," Nova said. "Not on the schedule. He just grabbed the camera."

"Can I line it up the same way?" Theo asked, already adjusting an invisible camera angle like he was setting up a cutscene in Studio.

"Try."

He nudged the frame until Earth sat exactly on the edge of the gray horizon, small and bright against all that dark. The shutter clicked on its own, and the photo locked into place, glowing faintly.

"Earthrise," Nova said. "Same shot. Nicely done."

The scene shifted again, faster this time — a rocket taller than anything Theo had seen yet, standing on a distant pad.

"Saturn V," Nova said. "**363 feet tall.** Taller than the Statue of Liberty. This is what finally got us there."

"**July 20, 1969**," Nova continued, as a ladder extended down from a spindly-legged lander toward gray dust. "Neil Armstrong is about to become the first person to ever stand on the Moon."

A single rung glowed at the bottom of the ladder, waiting.

"Last step's yours to confirm," Nova said. "Line him up."

Theo nudged the boot forward, millimeter by millimeter, until it touched the glowing rung exactly. Dust puffed outward in total silence.

"The Eagle has landed," crackled a voice from somewhere far above them — and then, a moment later: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

"Buzz Aldrin climbed down after him," Nova said, "while a third astronaut, Michael Collins, orbited alone above in the command module — the part of the ship that stayed circling the Moon the whole time, waiting to bring them home."

"So one guy just... waited up there? By himself? The whole time?"

"Somebody's got to fly the getaway ship," Nova said. "Not everyone gets to be the one on the dust."

Theo looked at the footprint glowing in the gray ground and grinned. "The Eagle has landed," he said quietly, mostly to himself.

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Fix and the Handshake (1970–1975)
chapters.text:
A warning light blinked red, and an alarm chirped somewhere close, sharp and insistent.

"**1970**," Nova said, voice suddenly brisk. "Apollo 13. An oxygen tank just exploded on the way to the Moon. Crew's fine. Ship's in trouble."

Theo's stomach dropped for exactly one second. "Are they okay?"

"They're okay," Nova said immediately. "Scared, cramped, cold — but okay. And they stayed okay, because engineers back on Earth spent days building a fix out of whatever the astronauts already had on board."

A tangle of wires and a cardboard-looking panel floated in front of Theo, three connectors dangling loose. "Help me finish it," Nova said. "Match the shapes. Round to round, square to square."

Theo worked through it the way he'd debug a broken script — slowly, checking each piece before locking it in. Round connector, round socket. Square to square. The last wire clicked home, and the panel hummed to life, a small green light blinking steady.

"Fix confirmed," Nova said. "That's basically what really happened — not you personally, obviously, but engineers on the ground, puzzling out a fix with cardboard, tape, and the manual. The crew made it home safe."

"They got better," Theo said, mostly to reassure himself. "Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon total, right? Across six missions?"

"Between 1969 and 1972," Nova confirmed. "All of them made it home."

The stars shifted one last time, and two spacecraft drifted toward each other in the dark, slow and careful, like two kids approaching a handshake they'd been practicing all week.

"**July 17, 1975**," Nova said. "American and Soviet spacecraft, docking together in orbit — meaning their hatches connected and locked, so the crews could float between them."

A hatch creaked open between the two ships. Two gloved hands reached through, found each other, and shook.

"That's the end of the whole race," Nova said softly. "Not a winner. A handshake."

Theo watched the two ships hang there, joined together, lit gold by a sun with no up or down. "That's a pretty good ending screen," he said.

"Best kind there is," Nova said. "Speaking of — your server's calling you back."

The stars folded inward, and Theo's bedroom rushed up to meet him. His tablet sat exactly where he'd left it, screen glowing ordinary blue again. The green LAUNCH block was gone — except for one small gold badge now sitting in the corner of his rocket build, shaped like two tiny hands shaking.

His launch effect, when he tested it, finally worked. WHOOOOSH, with a shake and everything.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there was soccer practice — but first, he had a server update to finish.

true_facts.text: **Sputnik 1** launched on **October 4, 1957**, the first thing people ever sent to circle Earth.
It was about **58 centimeters wide** — roughly beach-ball sized — and sent out a simple beep anyone could hear on an ordinary radio.
On **November 3, 1957**, a dog named **Laika** became the first living creature to orbit Earth.
Shocked by Sputnik, the United States started a new space agency, **NASA**, on **October 1, 1958**.
The first American satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched **January 31, 1958**, and found a hidden ring of invisible energy wrapped around Earth.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space, circling Earth once in about **108 minutes**.
On **May 25, 1961**, President Kennedy dared the country to land someone on the Moon and bring them home safely before the decade ended.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth aboard Vostok 6.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** became the first person to float outside his spacecraft, for about ten minutes.
In **December 1968**, Apollo 8 astronauts flew around the Moon, and one of them snapped the famous **Earthrise** photo.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap for mankind.
In **1970**, an oxygen tank explosion crippled **Apollo 13**, but engineers on the ground helped the crew fix it and get home safely.
The **Saturn V** rocket that carried astronauts to the Moon stood **363 feet tall** — taller than the Statue of Liberty.
On **July 17, 1975**, American and Soviet spacecraft docked together in orbit, and the crews shook hands, ending the Space Race.

new_recurring.name: The Launch Block
new_recurring.rule: A glowing green cube stamped LAUNCH appears unasked on Theo's Roblox Studio baseplate when a story should begin. Clicking it pulls him into the Space Race server, guided by Nova. It fades at the story's end, leaving one small gold badge…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Theo returned to his ordinary bedroom to find the glowing Launch Block gone, replaced by a tiny gold handshake badge on his Roblox rocket build, and his launch effect finally worked.

request.care_notes: Focus on the achievements, inventies, and human courage of space exploration. The story should emphasize the scientific breakthroughs and the collaborative spirit that followed, avoiding detailed Cold War politics, weapons development, or the ideological conflict between the nations.

fact_pack.summary: The Space Race was a Cold War contest between the United States and the Soviet Union to achieve firsts in spaceflight, from Sputnik in 1957 to a joint mission in 1975. It brought the first satellite, first human in orbit, and first footsteps on the Moon.

facts.text: The Space Race was a Cold War contest between the US and USSR to achieve spaceflight firsts, lasting roughly 1957 to 1975.
On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a beach-ball-sized satellite that became the first man-made object to orbit Earth.
Sputnik 1 was about 58 centimeters wide and sent out a simple radio beep that people around the world could pick up on ordinary radios.
On November 3, 1957, the Soviets launched Sputnik 2 carrying a dog named Laika, the first living creature to orbit Earth.
Shocked by Sputnik, the United States created NASA, which began operating on October 1, 1958.
The first US satellite, Explorer 1, launched January 31, 1958, and discovered the Van Allen radiation belt.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, orbiting Earth once aboard Vostok 1 in about 108 minutes.
On May 5, 1961, Alan Shepard became the first American in space aboard the Freedom 7 capsule, though his short flight did not orbit Earth.
On May 25, 1961, President Kennedy challenged the US to land a man on the Moon and return him safely before decade's end.
On June 16, 1963, Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth aboard Vostok 6.
On March 18, 1965, Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, floating outside his Voskhod 2 capsule for about ten minutes.
On January 27, 1967, astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee died in a fire during a launch pad test of Apollo 1.
In December 1968, Apollo 8 astronauts became the first to orbit the Moon, and William Anders took the famous Earthrise photo.
On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronaut Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap for mankind.
Buzz Aldrin joined Armstrong on the Moon while crewmate Michael Collins orbited alone above in the command module Columbia.
In 1970, an oxygen tank explosion crippled Apollo 13 on its way to the Moon, but the crew safely returned to Earth after engineers improvised a fix.
Between 1969 and 1972, twelve American astronauts walked on the Moon across six successful Apollo landing missions.
The Saturn V rocket that carried Apollo astronauts to the Moon stood 363 feet tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty.
Soviet chief designer Sergei Korolev secretly led the USSR's rocket program, and his identity was kept a state secret until after his death in 1966.
Wernher von Braun, who earlier built rockets for Germany, led the NASA team that developed the Saturn V rocket.
The Space Race ended in a spirit of cooperation on July 17, 1975, when American and Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit and their crews shook hands.
