story.title: Theo and the Glowing Launch Button
story.subtitle: One click, one giant leap.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Beep in the Dark (1957)
chapters.text:
Theo had exactly four bricks left to place in his newest Roblox Studio build: a rocket launchpad, copied stud for stud from a video he'd watched three times. It was past ten. His door was shut. His headset sat crooked on one ear.

He clicked **Play** to test the countdown script.

The screen didn't flicker. It went black, then a flat green, the green of an old computer screen that still works but barely. A single word blinked where his rocket used to be: LAUNCH?

Theo frowned. He hadn't coded that.

He clicked it anyway.

The laptop screen stretched like fabric, swallowing the desk lamp's light, swallowing Theo, pulling him through a tunnel of falling green numbers. He landed hard on packed dirt, under a sky full of stars he'd never get in his bedroom.

A silver ball sat on a metal stand nearby, about the size of a beach ball, bristling with four thin antennas like a spider that skipped leg day. It was beeping. Steady. Rhythmic. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP.

"That's the same beep as my Play button," Theo said out loud, to nobody.

"Good ear," said a voice behind him. A woman in a heavy coat was checking a clipboard. "That's **Sputnik 1**. First man-made thing to ever circle the Earth. We sent it up **October 4, 1957**."

Circle the Earth — Theo filed that one away. "You mean it's going around and around up there, like a marble in a bowl?"

"Exactly like that," she said. "Round and round, forever falling, never landing. We call that an **orbit**."

Theo stepped closer to the silver ball before it was lifted onto the rocket. "It's small."

"About **fifty-eight centimeters** wide," the woman said. "Smaller than your beach ball at the pool. Big enough to change the world."

The beeping, she explained, wasn't a message. It was just a simple radio signal, so plain that regular people with regular radios back on Earth could tune in and hear it themselves. No special equipment. Just a beep, bouncing down from space, proving something was really up there.

Theo grinned. In his own game he'd spent weeks trying to make one sound effect feel important. This one had done it by accident, with four antennas and a sense of humor.

"Can I touch it?" he asked.

"Once it's on the rocket, nobody touches anything," she said. "Rule one of launch day."

The ball was lifted, bolted in, sealed. Somewhere behind Theo a countdown began, in a language he didn't speak but somehow understood anyway. Countdowns are basically the same everywhere.

Then the green tunnel yanked him sideways again, and the launchpad melted into static.

chapters.heading: Level 2: Sputnik 2 and a New Team (1957–1958)
chapters.text:
Theo landed next in a cold room full of humming machines, a month deeper into the same green blur.

A dog with sharp, curious eyes watched him from behind a window, sitting calmly in a small harness.

"Her name is **Laika**," said a man adjusting dials, not looking up. "**November 3, 1957.** She's about to become the first living creature to orbit the Earth."

Theo crouched by the window. The dog tilted her head at him, like she was sizing up a new player who'd just joined her server.

"She's... a dog. In space." Theo said it slowly, like saying it twice might make it make more sense.

"The Soviets wanted to know if a living thing could survive a launch and an orbit," the man said. "Laika's flight helped answer that."

Theo didn't ask what happened after. He had a feeling the man wouldn't want to talk about it, and honestly, Theo didn't either. He just pressed his palm flat on the glass, the way you'd fist-bump a teammate before kickoff, and the dog pressed her nose to the same spot from her side.

"Good luck up there," Theo said.

The green tunnel grabbed him again — gently this time, like a loading screen rather than a yank — and dropped him somewhere entirely different: a sunny parking lot outside a brand-new building with fresh paint and a sign that still smelled like glue.

**NASA**, the sign read. Underneath, smaller: **October 1, 1958**.

A man in short sleeves was hanging the second half of the letter S, slightly crooked.

"You're off by like, two inches," Theo said, before he could stop himself.

The man laughed and straightened it. "Rookie mistake. We only just started this agency. Sputnik gave everybody a scare, so the country decided it needed one team, one plan, instead of a bunch of separate ones all doing their own thing."

Theo understood that completely. He'd once tried to build a soccer stadium in Roblox with three friends who each built a different-sized goal, in three different corners, with three different color schemes. Nothing had matched. The whole thing had collapsed into a pile of mismatched bricks until they agreed on one plan and one leader.

"So NASA's like... the team captain," Theo said.

"Something like that," the man said, climbing down the ladder. "Though we've got a lot more rockets than soccer balls."

Theo looked up at the fresh sign, glowing a little in the afternoon sun, and felt the floor tilt under him again as the green tunnel came back for its next delivery.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Belt Nobody Could See (1958)
chapters.text:
The tunnel spat Theo out into a control room jammed with people cheering, papers flying, somebody's coffee tipping over and nobody caring.

A thin, silver rocket shape sat on a screen, climbing a wobbly line upward.

"**January 31, 1958**," a woman said, grinning so wide it looked like it hurt. "**Explorer 1.** Our first **satellite** — something that circles the Earth, the same way Sputnik did. Finally."

Theo clocked the date instantly. "That's after Sputnik. You guys were behind."

"Four months behind," she admitted. "But watch this."

A different machine on the desk was ticking out numbers nobody seemed to expect. The woman's grin faded into something sharper — more curious than happy.

"That's strange," she muttered. "The readings keep maxing out the gauge, then dropping to nothing, then maxing out again."

Theo leaned over the paper. The pattern looked familiar — like the lag spikes in a laggy Roblox server, on, off, on, off, for no obvious reason.

"Is it broken?" Theo asked.

"Or," she said, "there's something out there we didn't know was there."

It turned out to be real: a wide, invisible belt of charged particles — tiny bits of electric energy — looping around the Earth high above the sky, too high to see or feel, found by accident because Explorer 1 happened to fly straight through it.

"We're calling it the **Van Allen radiation belt**," the woman said, "after the scientist who figured out what the gauge was actually showing us."

"So it's like... an invisible ring around the whole planet," Theo said. "A force field nobody built."

"Nobody built it, and nobody knew it was there until a satellite flew through it and got confused," she said. "Space had secrets. We only just started finding them."

Theo thought about every secret room he'd ever hidden in a build, behind walls players never thought to check. Earth had been hiding one in plain sight, in a spot nobody had bothered to look, until something flew through it by accident.

He wanted to stay and watch the numbers some more, but the tunnel was already humming behind him, and the room dissolved into green static before he could ask a single follow-up question.

chapters.heading: Level 4: Two Men, Two Flights (1961)
chapters.text:
Theo landed on grass this time, next to a launch tower taller than anything near his house, and a man in a bright orange suit was climbing a ladder toward a hatch.

"**April 12, 1961**," said a voice beside Theo. It belonged to a technician holding a stopwatch like it owed him money. "**Yuri Gagarin.** About to become the first human being to leave the Earth."

The hatch sealed. The countdown rolled. Fire and smoke and noise Theo felt in his teeth.

Then, quiet.

"How long's he up there?" Theo asked.

"**One hundred and eight minutes**," the technician said. "One full **orbit** — all the way around the planet — then back down."

Theo did the math out loud, the way he did everything out loud when he was thinking. "That's less than two soccer matches."

"Less than two soccer matches," the technician agreed, "to go all the way around the entire world."

Gagarin landed safely, smiling in photos that would later hang in a thousand classrooms, and the green tunnel barely let Theo catch his breath before yanking him to a different launch pad, this one with a smaller rocket and a different flag.

"**May 5, 1961**," said a new voice — an engineer in a headset, chewing gum fast. "**Alan Shepard.** First American in space."

"Wait," Theo said, watching the numbers on a nearby screen. "This flight's way shorter than Gagarin's."

"Good eye," the engineer said. "Shepard went straight up, came straight back down. No full orbit — just up, out past the edge of the sky for a few minutes, then home. We call that **suborbital**. Gagarin went all the way around. Shepard didn't, not yet."

"So it's like... Gagarin scored the full goal, and Shepard just got a really good shot on target," Theo said.

The engineer snorted gum through his nose, which was, Theo decided, the single funniest thing he had seen all night. "Something like that, kid. We caught up fast, though. Give us a minute."

Theo didn't get a minute. The tunnel was already pulling at his sneakers.

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Dare and the Secret Designer (1961)
chapters.text:
The next room was a stage, with flags and a podium and a man speaking to a huge crowd, his voice carrying clean across a field Theo couldn't see the end of.

"**May 25, 1961**," read a nearby sign. "President **John F. Kennedy**."

"...land a man on the Moon," Kennedy was saying, "and return him safely to Earth — before this decade is out."

The crowd roared. Theo's jaw actually dropped, a little, in a way he'd deny later if anyone asked.

"He just... said that? Out loud? To everyone?" Theo asked a man standing near him with a clipboard and a pencil stub behind his ear.

"He did," the man said. "Now a few thousand of us have to go figure out how."

Before Theo could ask who "us" was, the green tunnel dropped him somewhere colder and much more secretive: an office with blacked-out windows, and a man bent over blueprints who refused to look up.

"You're not supposed to be in here," the man said.

"Who are you?" Theo asked.

"Nobody," the man said. "Officially, I don't exist."

Theo had definitely never heard anyone say that about themselves before, not even the most dramatic kid in his Discord server. "That's... not a real answer."

The clipboard man from before had followed him in, apparently used to this. "That's **Sergei Korolev**," he said quietly. "Chief designer of the entire Soviet rocket program. His name was kept a total secret, even inside his own country, until after he died in **1966**. The government didn't want anyone to know who to target."

"So he's like a modder who builds the best game on the server," Theo said slowly, "but never once puts his username on it."

Korolev almost smiled at that, just barely, before going back to his blueprints.

The tunnel dragged Theo once more, this time to a sunnier workshop full of massive rocket parts, where a broad-shouldered man with a thick accent was sketching something enormous on a chalkboard.

"**Wernher von Braun**," the clipboard man said. "Built rockets back in Germany, years ago. Now he's leading the team building the rocket that's actually going to get us to the Moon."

"Two different countries," Theo said. "Two secret geniuses. Both just... building the biggest thing they can think of."

"That's the whole race," the man said, "in one sentence."

chapters.heading: Level 6: First Woman, First Walk (1963–1965)
chapters.text:
Theo's next landing spot smelled like jet fuel, and a woman in a flight suit was signing a photograph for a little girl at the fence.

"**Valentina Tereshkova**," said the clipboard man, suddenly back at Theo's side. "**June 16, 1963.** About to become the first woman in space."

"She used to work in a factory," he added, before Theo could ask. "Now she's about to orbit the Earth **forty-eight times**."

Tereshkova caught Theo staring and grinned. "Something wrong?"

"No," Theo said quickly. "Just — that's a lot of laps."

"Forty-eight," she agreed. "I'll let you know how many I've got left when I land."

She didn't wait for his reply. She walked straight to the rocket like she had somewhere to be, which, Theo supposed, she did.

The tunnel's next stop made Theo's stomach drop in a way that had nothing to do with traveling through green static.

A man in a bulky white suit floated outside a small spacecraft, tethered by a single cord, Earth curving enormous and blue beneath his boots.

"**Alexei Leonov**," the clipboard man said. "**March 18, 1965.** First person to ever leave his spacecraft and float free in open space. We call that a **spacewalk**."

"Is the cord... enough?" Theo asked. The cord looked impossibly thin against all that empty dark.

"It's enough," the clipboard man said. "It's attached to the capsule. He's not going anywhere he doesn't choose to go."

Theo watched Leonov tumble slowly, weightless, grinning through his visor at nothing and everything.

"How long's he out there?" Theo asked.

"About ten minutes," the clipboard man said. "Then back inside, safe and sound."

Ten minutes didn't sound like very long at all, until Theo pictured himself floating outside anything, tethered by one thin cord, with nothing underneath him but the whole planet. Then ten minutes sounded like plenty.

"I wouldn't do that," Theo admitted.

"Most people wouldn't," the clipboard man said. "That's sort of the whole point of doing it first."

Leonov climbed back inside. The hatch sealed. Somewhere, Theo imagined, people exhaled all at once.

The green tunnel swept him away again before he could ask whether Leonov had liked it.

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Photo That Changed Everything (1968)
chapters.text:
The tunnel let Theo out somewhere with no floor at all — just a window, and beyond the window, the Moon's gray surface sliding by close enough to touch.

"**December 1968**," the clipboard man said. "**Apollo 8.** First humans to ever orbit the Moon."

Three astronauts floated near the window, cameras in hand, arguing cheerfully about something.

Then one of them went still.

Theo followed his gaze. Over the edge of the gray Moon, impossibly small and impossibly blue, Earth was rising.

Nobody said anything for a second. Not the astronauts, not the clipboard man, not Theo.

"Camera — quick, color film, hurry," said the astronaut, scrambling.

"**William Anders**," the clipboard man murmured, as the camera clicked. "That photo's going to be called **Earthrise**. People are going to hang it on walls for the rest of history."

Theo understood that feeling completely. Every time he finished a build he was proud of, he took a screenshot before touching another brick, just in case the moment never looked quite that good again.

"It's just... Earth," Theo said. "We live there. Why's it such a big deal to see it from here?"

"Because nobody's ever seen their whole home like that before," the clipboard man said. "Every person who's ever lived, right there, in one little blue marble, floating in all that black."

Theo pressed his face near the glass, careful not to actually touch it. The Moon's surface looked close enough to walk on. Earth looked small enough to hold.

"Next time," the clipboard man said, "somebody's actually going to walk on that gray ground down there."

"Who?" Theo asked.

The clipboard man smiled like he already knew, and wasn't telling.

The tunnel pulled Theo in before he could push the question, and the last thing he saw through the glass was Earth, rising.

chapters.heading: Level 8: One Giant Leap (1969)
chapters.text:
Theo's boots hit real ground this time — gray, dusty, crunchy underfoot, like walking on a beach made of flour.

Above him, a rocket the length of a soccer field stacked on end still smoked faintly on a pad miles behind, though Theo had clearly skipped straight to the good part.

"**363 feet**," the clipboard man said, pointing back at where the **Saturn V** had stood before launch. "Taller than the Statue of Liberty. That's what it took to get here."

"**July 20, 1969**," he added, as two figures in bulky white suits bounced across the gray ground ahead.

Theo recognized the moment before anyone said the name. He'd seen the photo a hundred times, on posters, on the cover of a library book he'd renewed twice.

"**Neil Armstrong**," Theo whispered.

Armstrong planted one boot, then stepped down fully, his voice crackling through a radio Theo could somehow hear perfectly.

"That's one small step for man," Armstrong said, "one giant leap for mankind."

"**IT'S REAL**," Theo shouted, and nobody told him to be quiet, because out here, there was nobody around for a few hundred thousand miles to hush him.

A second astronaut bounced down after Armstrong. "**Buzz Aldrin**," the clipboard man said. "Joined him down here. Their crewmate, **Michael Collins**, is orbiting alone up above, in the **command module** — the part of the spacecraft that stayed in space the whole time — named **Columbia**."

"Alone up there? While they're down here?" Theo asked.

"Somebody had to stay with the ship while the other two went for a walk," the clipboard man said.

Theo bounced once, experimentally, on the gray dust, the way Armstrong and Aldrin were bouncing. Low gravity made every step feel like a video game glitch where you forgot to turn off the jump height.

"Between **1969 and 1972**," the clipboard man said, "**twelve** astronauts are going to walk on this same gray ground, across six separate trips."

"Twelve," Theo repeated. "That's basically a whole starting squad."

"Give or take," the clipboard man said, grinning. "With a very strange away kit."

Theo looked up. Earth hung in the black sky above him, small and blue and perfect, exactly like it had looked through that other window. He didn't want to leave. The tunnel, predictably, didn't care.

chapters.heading: Level 9: The Flight That Almost Wasn't (1970)
chapters.text:
The next room had no windows at all — just screens, and every single one of them showing numbers that made grown adults go pale.

"**1970**," the clipboard man said, quieter than before. "**Apollo 13.** On the way to the Moon when something went wrong."

"What happened?" Theo asked.

"An oxygen tank exploded," the clipboard man said. "Damaged the spacecraft badly, on the way there. Suddenly getting to the Moon didn't matter anymore. Getting three astronauts home did."

Theo's stomach tightened. This was the part of every story where something bad was allowed to happen.

"Are they okay?" he asked, straight out, because he needed to know before he could listen to anything else.

"They made it home safe," the clipboard man said immediately. "Every single one of them. That's the end of this story, so you can relax into the middle of it."

Relieved, Theo turned back to the screens, where engineers were staring hard at a small pile of spare parts and odds and ends already sitting on board, like a puzzle with no instructions.

"They need to fix an air problem," the clipboard man explained, "using only whatever already happens to be inside the spacecraft. Nothing extra. No trip to the store."

Theo knew this feeling better than almost anyone on Earth. Every time he'd run out of the right block in Roblox Studio halfway through a build, he'd had to solve it with whatever was already sitting in his inventory. "That's exactly like finishing a level when your good pieces glitched out," he said. "You use what you've got. You make it work anyway."

"That's precisely what they did," the clipboard man said. "Spent hours figuring it out with nothing but what was already on board. Then they built it for real, inside the actual spacecraft, piece by piece."

Theo watched the astronauts assemble something clunky and strange-looking, fitting it together by hand, and the room around him finally exhaled.

"Made it home safe," the clipboard man repeated, like he knew Theo needed to hear it twice.

"Made it home safe," Theo echoed, and this time, when the tunnel grabbed him, it didn't feel so rough.

chapters.heading: Level 10: The Handshake in Orbit (1975)
chapters.text:
Theo landed in space this time — properly in space, floating, no gravity at all, two spacecraft drifting slowly toward each other against a wall of black.

One had Russian letters on the side. One had American ones.

"**July 17, 1975**," the clipboard man said. "Last stop. This is where the whole race ends."

Theo watched the two crafts line up, nose to nose, a connector sliding into place with a soft mechanical CLUNK that echoed through Theo's bones even though there was supposedly no sound in space.

"That's called **docking**," the clipboard man said. "Joining two spacecraft together, in orbit."

A hatch opened. An American astronaut reached through into the Russian spacecraft. A Soviet crew member reached back.

They shook hands.

Theo had watched plenty of soccer matches end with a handshake line, winners and losers filing past each other, hands out, respect intact either way. He'd never thought about it meaning much beyond good manners.

This felt different. This felt like the actual final whistle on something that had lasted eighteen years.

"Eighteen years," Theo said slowly. "From a beeping ball, to a dog, to a secret guy who wasn't allowed to have a name, to a guy walking on the Moon in front of the whole planet. And it ends with... a handshake."

"Started as a race," the clipboard man said. "Ended as a team-up."

Theo thought that sounded like the best possible ending to any match he could imagine — two different squads, each playing as hard as they possibly could, finally meeting in the middle once the real work was done.

The green tunnel opened one last time, gentler than ever, and Theo tumbled back through falling numbers into his own dark bedroom, landing soft in his desk chair instead of hard on dirt.

His laptop screen glowed ordinary blue again. His half-finished rocket build sat exactly where he'd left it.

Except for one thing.

A tiny block sat in the corner of his build, shaped like a silver ball with four thin antennas, one he definitely hadn't placed there himself. Underneath it, a small label blinked: **SEE YOU NEXT LAUNCH.**

Theo saved the file. Twice, just to be safe.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a two-player rocket level to finish — and a launch button that might not be done with him yet.

true_facts.text: A beach-ball-sized satellite called **Sputnik 1** became the first man-made thing to circle the Earth, launched on **October 4, 1957**.
**Sputnik 1** was about **fifty-eight centimeters** wide and sent out a simple beep that regular radios on Earth could pick up.
A dog named **Laika** became the first living creature to orbit the Earth, on **November 3, 1957**.
Shocked by Sputnik, the United States started a brand new space team called **NASA**, which began work on **October 1, 1958**.
The first American satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched on **January 31, 1958**, and stumbled onto an invisible ring of radiation now called the **Van Allen belt**.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human being in space, circling the Earth once in about **108 minutes**.
On **May 5, 1961**, **Alan Shepard** became the first American in space, though his flight went straight up and down instead of all the way around.
On **May 25, 1961**, President **John F. Kennedy** challenged the country to land someone on the Moon and bring them home safe before the decade ended.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** became the first person to float freely outside his spacecraft, for about **ten minutes**.
In **December 1968**, the **Apollo 8** crew became the first humans to orbit the Moon, and astronaut **William Anders** snapped the famous **Earthrise** photo.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it 'a giant leap for mankind.'
The **Saturn V** rocket that carried the astronauts to the Moon stood **363 feet** tall — taller than the Statue of Liberty.

new_recurring.name: The Launch Button
new_recurring.rule: A glowing green Play button appears inside Theo's Roblox Studio build. Clicking it opens a tunnel of falling green numbers that drops him into a real moment of science or history, then pulls him home again when the scene ends.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Theo landed back in his desk chair to find a tiny silver Sputnik-shaped block sitting uninvited in his save file, with a blinking label that read SEE YOU NEXT LAUNCH.

request.care_notes: Focus on the achievements, inventies, and human courage of space exploration. The story should emphasize the scientific breakthroughs and the collaborative spirit that followed, avoiding detailed Cold War politics, weapons development, or the ideological conflict between the nations.

fact_pack.summary: The Space Race was a Cold War contest between the United States and the Soviet Union to achieve firsts in spaceflight, from Sputnik in 1957 to a joint mission in 1975. It brought the first satellite, first human in orbit, and first footsteps on the Moon.

facts.text: The Space Race was a Cold War contest between the US and USSR to achieve spaceflight firsts, lasting roughly 1957 to 1975.
On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a beach-ball-sized satellite that became the first man-made object to orbit Earth.
Sputnik 1 was about 58 centimeters wide and sent out a simple radio beep that people around the world could pick up on ordinary radios.
On November 3, 1957, the Soviets launched Sputnik 2 carrying a dog named Laika, the first living creature to orbit Earth.
Shocked by Sputnik, the United States created NASA, which began operating on October 1, 1958.
The first US satellite, Explorer 1, launched January 31, 1958, and discovered the Van Allen radiation belt.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, orbiting Earth once aboard Vostok 1 in about 108 minutes.
On May 5, 1961, Alan Shepard became the first American in space aboard the Freedom 7 capsule, though his short flight did not orbit Earth.
On May 25, 1961, President Kennedy challenged the US to land a man on the Moon and return him safely before decade's end.
On June 16, 1963, Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth aboard Vostok 6.
On March 18, 1965, Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, floating outside his Voskhod 2 capsule for about ten minutes.
On January 27, 1967, astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee died in a fire during a launch pad test of Apollo 1.
In December 1968, Apollo 8 astronauts became the first to orbit the Moon, and William Anders took the famous Earthrise photo.
On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronaut Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap for mankind.
Buzz Aldrin joined Armstrong on the Moon while crewmate Michael Collins orbited alone above in the command module Columbia.
In 1970, an oxygen tank explosion crippled Apollo 13 on its way to the Moon, but the crew safely returned to Earth after engineers improvised a fix.
Between 1969 and 1972, twelve American astronauts walked on the Moon across six successful Apollo landing missions.
The Saturn V rocket that carried Apollo astronauts to the Moon stood 363 feet tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty.
Soviet chief designer Sergei Korolev secretly led the USSR's rocket program, and his identity was kept a state secret until after his death in 1966.
Wernher von Braun, who earlier built rockets for Germany, led the NASA team that developed the Saturn V rocket.
The Space Race ended in a spirit of cooperation on July 17, 1975, when American and Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit and their crews shook hands.

story.title: Eli and the Eighteen-Year Race
story.subtitle: A busted homemade radio, a voice called Control, and the whole Space Race live on the dial.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep in the Static (1957)
chapters.text:
Eli had been awake since eleven, chasing one sound through the homemade shortwave radio he'd built for his physics fair project, the one due in six days and still three resistors short of actually working.

Then the noise found a rhythm.

Beep. Beep. Beep. Evenly spaced, nothing random in it anywhere. Static doesn't repeat. A signal does.

He turned the dial a hair, and a green light flared behind the glass tube like something inside had been waiting for exactly that movement.

"Carrier wave," said a voice, flat and unbothered, like it had said this a thousand times before. A carrier wave, Eli knew, was just the steady background hum a radio signal rides on top of — and this one had something riding it. "You found it on the first try. Most people take longer."

Eli's hand froze on the dial. "Who—"

"Control," the voice said. "Hang on to something."

The room folded the way a picture folds when you close a laptop too fast, and then Eli was standing on open scrubland at night, cold enough to see his breath, a rocket lit up white under floodlights half a mile off.

"Where—"

"Baikonur Cosmodrome. Kazakhstan. **October 4th, 1957**," said Control. "You're about to hear the sound you were just chasing, except live."

The rocket lifted on fire with no sound at first — the light always gets there before the noise does — and then the roar arrived and shook Eli's chest. A small sphere, not much bigger than a beach ball, rode the tip of it into the dark.

"**Sputnik 1**," Control said. "First man-made object ever to make it to orbit."

Eli did the math without meaning to. The sphere was tiny, maybe **58 centimeters** wide, polished metal and antennas and nothing else. "That's the whole satellite?"

"That's the whole satellite. It doesn't need to be big. It needs to broadcast." Control's voice carried something that might have been pride, carefully disguised as boredom. "Every radio on the planet that could tune to its frequency could hear it beep. Yours included, a few minutes ago."

Eli looked up. Somewhere above the floodlights, invisible now, a beach-ball-sized machine was already circling the Earth, saying *here I am* to anyone who'd listen.

"That's the signal I built my whole radio to find," he said.

"Copy that," said Control. "Took you long enough."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Dog and the Agency (1957–1958)
chapters.text:
Eli found himself behind a glass wall, looking into a cramped capsule with padded sides, barely big enough for the dog curled inside it.

"Her name's **Laika**," said Control. "**November 3rd, 1957**. One month after Sputnik 1. She's about to become the first living creature to make it to orbit."

Eli had been expecting more hardware, more switches. He hadn't expected something with a heartbeat. "She's not scared?"

"She's trained for it. Full life support, temperature control, enough food for the mission." Control didn't elaborate further, and Eli understood the conversation was supposed to move on, so he let it.

The capsule sealed. A dull roar somewhere behind the glass. Then nothing but readouts.

"Up she goes," Control said. "Around the world, and around it again."

Eli exhaled slowly. "One satellite that beeps, and one with a passenger. That's two shocks in a month."

"Try living in Washington D.C. that fall," said Control, and the scene dissolved into fluorescent light and a long hallway full of men in narrow ties, carrying boxes marked with three stacked letters.

"N-A-S-A," Eli read off a freshly painted door. "Let me guess."

"**October 1st, 1958**," Control confirmed. "The United States needed an agency built specifically to catch up, and fast. Sputnik did that. One beeping ball rearranged an entire government's org chart."

Eli grinned. "A ball beat the Pentagon."

"A ball **and** a dog," said Control. "Don't shortchange Laika. Copy that?"

"Copy that," Eli said, and found he liked the way it sounded.

He flipped to a blank page in his notebook and wrote two words at the top: ESCAPE VELOCITY — the speed something needs to hit so gravity can't drag it back down. He didn't know the number yet. He wrote the question anyway. Questions were usually the first useful thing in any physics problem.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Belt Nobody Expected (1958)
chapters.text:
Control dropped him into a room wallpapered in dials, every needle twitching, cigarette smoke doing a passable impression of fog.

"**January 31st, 1958**," Control said. "**Explorer 1**. America's answer, four months late and still catching up."

On a screen, a thin trace jumped and spiked with no clean rhythm Eli could find.

"That's not just a counter miscounting?" he asked, because something that irregular felt wrong for a brand-new satellite nobody had flown before.

"Look again," said Control. "What do spikes like that usually mean, in a Geiger counter?"

Eli had used a Geiger counter exactly once, during a radioactivity unit, and he remembered the rule well enough. "Radiation. If it's hitting so hard the counter can't keep up, it can actually look like it's dropping instead of climbing."

"Correct." For once Control sounded almost impressed. "Explorer 1 had just flown straight into something nobody had mapped: a doughnut-shaped ring of charged particles trapped by Earth's own magnetic field, way out past where the air runs out. They'd call it the **Van Allen radiation belt**, after the scientist running the instrument."

"So the counter wasn't broken. Space was just radioactive somewhere nobody expected."

"Space usually is," Control said. "You're going to want to remember that belt. Everything you fly through it later has to deal with it."

Eli scribbled *Van Allen = particles + magnetic field, not a glitch* into the notebook he was somehow still carrying, pencil and all, despite having just teleported across two decades.

"First satellite finds a new part of the solar system by accident," he said. "Not bad for a four-month delay."

"Second-best isn't nothing," Control agreed. "It's usually how real discoveries happen."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: 108 Minutes and a Name No One Would Say (1961)
chapters.text:
Control brought him to a dim room full of headsets, men hunched over consoles, voices low and urgent in a language Eli didn't speak but somehow understood anyway.

"**April 12th, 1961**," Control said. "**Yuri Gagarin**. Vostok 1. About to become the first human being in space."

On the console, a dot crawled along a curved line — an orbit.

"One trip around," Control said, "roughly **108 minutes**, and then back down."

Eli watched the room hold its breath every time the signal dropped out, then exhale when it returned.

He noticed something odd: nobody in the room ever said the name of the engineer who'd designed the rocket, even though they clearly revered him. He was only ever "the Chief Designer."

"Why doesn't anyone just say his name?" Eli asked.

"Because the Soviet government decided his name was a state secret," said Control. "**Sergei Korolev** ran their entire rocket program from the shadows. Nobody outside a small circle knew who he was until after he died, in **1966**."

"A secret genius hiding behind a classified title. That's either really cool or really unfair."

"Both, usually," said Control, and didn't elaborate, which told Eli the subject was closed for tonight.

Three weeks later by the room's clocks, Control confirmed, on **May 5th, 1961**, a different console, a different flag. A capsule marked FREEDOM 7 sat on a different pad.

"**Alan Shepard**," Control said. "First American in space. Shorter flight — an up-and-down arc, not a full orbit — but it counted."

"The Soviets got the orbit. We got fifteen minutes and a splash."

"For now," Control said. "Catching up usually starts small."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Decade Clock (1961)
chapters.text:
Control set him down in sunlight this time, a crowd outside a building, a voice carrying over speakers.

"**May 25th, 1961**," Control said. "Listen."

The voice on the speakers was steady, unhurried, the kind of calm that made outrageous things sound reasonable. Eli caught the phrase: land a man on the Moon, and return him safely, before the decade is out.

"That's **President Kennedy**," Control said. "He just gave the country about eight and a half years to go from fifteen-minute hops to the Moon and back."

Eli did the arithmetic in his head without trying, the way he always did with any number that had a deadline attached. "They'd just barely gotten a guy above the atmosphere for fifteen minutes. Now there's a countdown to the Moon."

"Going to orbit is one problem," Eli went on, turning it over the way he turned over every other impossible physics problem. "Landing something on the Moon and then getting it back off the surface afterward is three or four hard problems stacked on top of each other."

"Which is why nobody serious thought the timeline was easy," Control said. "They thought it was possible. That's a different claim entirely."

Eli watched the crowd applaud, slow and uncertain, like people deciding whether to believe what they'd just heard.

"I want to see how this turns out," he said.

"You will," said Control. "Patience looks good on you. Copy that?"

"Copy that."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The First Woman in Orbit (1963)
chapters.text:
Control's next doorway opened onto launch-pad quiet, a woman in a flight suit walking toward a gantry alone, like she'd done it a hundred times even though nobody ever had.

"**June 16th, 1963**," Control said. "**Valentina Tereshkova**. Vostok 6. First woman in space."

Eli watched her climb in, unhurried, like it was a normal Tuesday. "Wait — she used to work in a factory?"

"Textile factory," Control confirmed. "No pilot's license, no engineering degree. She applied, trained, and got picked anyway."

"So the first guy in space was a fighter pilot, and the first woman just... showed up and won the job."

"People do that, when the door's actually open," Control said. "She went around the planet **48 times** before she came back down. Longer than every American flight up to that point, combined."

Eli whistled low. "That's not a token flight. That's a record."

"It never was a token flight," Control said, something sharper than usual in the voice. "It just got remembered like one, for a while. Takes some digging sometimes to get the credit lined up with the achievement."

Below them, the capsule's hatch sealed with a sound like a vault closing. Eli leaned toward the glass without thinking, the way he always leaned toward big displays at the planetarium.

"Three days up there alone," he said. "No one to talk to but mission control."

"She managed," said Control. "Turns out people adapt to practically anything, given a reason big enough."

Eli made a note in his notebook, underlining her name twice. "Noted."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Ten Minutes Outside (1965)
chapters.text:
Control placed him near a monitor showing a grainy black-and-white feed, a figure floating outside a capsule.

"**March 18th, 1965**," Control said. "**Alexei Leonov**. About to become the first human being to float outside a spacecraft in open space."

The figure drifted, tethered by a thin line, turning slow circles against black nothing.

Eli's pulse ticked up despite himself — there was no sound up there, no air, nothing between Leonov and raw vacuum except a suit holding pressure in. "How long's he out there?"

"**About ten minutes**," Control said.

Ten minutes didn't sound like much until Eli pictured being the guy inside the suit, a thin layer of fabric standing between him and literally nothing. "That's either the bravest ten minutes in history or the longest."

"Both, probably," Control said. "His suit puffed up out there — stiffened enough in the vacuum that getting back through the hatch took some real doing. He made it back inside with time to spare, which is the only part of this you need to lose sleep over, and you don't, because it worked."

Eli exhaled, the tension draining the moment Control said *worked*. "Ten minutes to be the first person ever to just float there and look at the whole planet with nothing between you and it."

"Most people don't get ten seconds of a view like that," Control said. "He got ten minutes. Not bad."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Photograph That Changed the View (1968)
chapters.text:
The next stop had no gravity to speak of — Eli felt the lightness in his stomach before he saw anything, floating half an inch off an imaginary floor until Control muttered something about compensating and he settled.

Through a small window, gray ground scrolled past, cratered and colorless, closer than any Moon Eli had ever seen with his own eyes.

"**December 1968**," Control said. "**Apollo 8**. First humans to orbit the Moon. Keep watching that window."

The gray horizon rolled by, and then, impossibly, a blue and white marble came up over the edge of it — small, bright, alone against black.

"That's—" Eli didn't finish the sentence. There wasn't a word ready for it.

"Earth," Control said quietly. "**William Anders** took the photo that's about to become one of the most reproduced images in human history. They're calling it 'Earthrise.'"

"We came all the way out here," Eli said slowly, "to take a picture of home."

"Turns out that's what a lot of space exploration is actually for," Control said. "You go out to look at everything else. You come back having mostly learned something about the place you started."

Eli kept his eyes on the window until the blue marble rolled out of frame again. He thought of his own backyard, his own radio, small as that marble must have looked from here. He didn't write anything in the notebook this time. Some things didn't need notes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Giant Leap (1969)
chapters.text:
Control's next doorway came with heat and noise before anything else — a launch pad so vast Eli had to tilt his head back to find the top of the rocket standing on it.

"**363 feet**," Control said, before Eli could even ask. "Taller than the Statue of Liberty, torch and all. The **Saturn V**."

"Who builds something that size and expects it to fly?"

"**Wernher von Braun**," Control said. "Led the NASA team that designed it. He'd built rockets before, for a different government entirely, years earlier — not a part of the story anyone tells proudly, but it's the truth of where some of this engineering came from."

Eli filed that away without comment, the way you file a fact that's complicated enough to need more room than tonight had.

The Saturn V lit and climbed, and the ground shook under Eli's sneakers even though he was fairly sure his sneakers weren't technically present. Then the scene jumped, the way Control's jumps always did, straight to a gray surface, a ladder, a boot coming down toward dust that had never once been stepped in.

"**July 20th, 1969**," Control said. "Watch. **Neil Armstrong**, about to become the first person to walk on the Moon."

The boot touched down. Eli realized he was holding his breath for no reason at all, since he already knew how this part ended, and let it out slow.

"A giant leap," Control said, quoting the line everyone quotes, "though he was just a few feet off his own ladder when he said it."

"**Buzz Aldrin** joined him down there a bit later," Control added. "**Michael Collins** stayed up above the whole time, alone in the command module — the part of the ship that never actually touches down — orbiting by himself while the other two got all the cameras."

"That sounds like the worst job on the mission," Eli said.

"Try explaining that to the twelve astronauts who walked on the Moon across the six landings that followed, between **1969** and **1972**," Control said. "Someone always has to mind the ship. Collins never once complained about it on the record."

Eli watched the flag go up, stiff with a wire frame because there was no air to let it hang properly, and thought that was somehow the most practical detail in the whole story.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Splashdown, Handshake, Home (1970–1975)
chapters.text:
Control's last jump landed Eli in a cramped capsule interior, warning lights blinking amber, three astronauts moving with the unhurried calm of people who'd rehearsed disaster a hundred times in simulators.

"**1970**," Control said. "**Apollo 13**. An oxygen tank just exploded on the way to the Moon."

Eli's stomach dropped, old instinct kicking in before he remembered who was telling him this story. "Are they—"

"Alive," Control said immediately, cutting the worry off before it could grow legs. "Every one of them. Engineers on the ground redesigned their return plan from scratch, improvised a fix for the air filters out of spare parts and tape, and flew them home safe. That's the whole headline: crisis, then rescue, then home."

Eli let his shoulders drop. "So it's not actually a disaster story."

"It's a story about what a good engineer does when the plan breaks," Control said. "Which, given your hobby, you might want to remember."

One more jump — gentler this time, sunlit, two spacecraft nose to nose in orbit, hatches open, hands reaching across.

"**July 17th, 1975**," Control said. "American crew, Soviet crew, docked together on purpose, shaking hands in orbit. Eighteen years after a beeping ball started the whole contest, this is how it ended."

"Not with someone winning," Eli said slowly. "With everyone just... deciding to stop keeping score."

"That's usually how the good endings work," said Control.

The static rose around them like a tide coming in, and the launch pads and capsules and footprints blurred back into dial-light and bedroom shadow. Eli blinked, and he was sitting cross-legged on his own carpet, the homemade radio warm under his hands, headphones around his neck instead of on his ears.

The dial had gone dark. On the notepad beside him, in handwriting he didn't fully remember producing, was a string of dots and dashes he recognized immediately — the exact rhythm of the first beep he'd ever caught, copied out like a souvenir.

"Copy that," Eli said quietly, to no one, and found he meant it as a kind of thank-you.

Outside his window, it was still dark, still a school night. His physics fair project had just gotten a much better title.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, his science fair project had a new title: How to Build a Radio That Hears History.

true_facts.text: **Sputnik 1**, the first man-made object to orbit Earth, launched from Baikonur on **October 4th, 1957** — just **58 centimeters** wide, yet its radio beep could be picked up on ordinary radios everywhere.
A dog named **Laika** rode Sputnik 2 into orbit on **November 3rd, 1957**, the first living creature to get there.
The Sputnik shock pushed the United States to start a brand-new space agency, **NASA**, on **October 1st, 1958**.
America's first satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched **January 31st, 1958**, and its instruments found a ring of radiation now called the **Van Allen belt**.

**Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space on **April 12th, 1961**, circling Earth once in about **108 minutes**; **Alan Shepard** followed on **May 5th, 1961** as the first American in space, on a short up-and-down hop rather than a full orbit.
The USSR's chief rocket designer, **Sergei Korolev**, worked in total secrecy — his name wasn't made public until after his death in **1966**.
On **May 25th, 1961**, President **Kennedy** challenged the country to land a person on the Moon and bring them home safely before the decade was out.
**Valentina Tereshkova**, once a factory worker, became the first woman in space on **June 16th, 1963**, orbiting Earth **48 times**.
**Alexei Leonov** made the first spacewalk on **March 18th, 1965**, floating outside his capsule for about **ten minutes**.
In **December 1968**, Apollo 8 astronauts became the first to orbit the Moon, and **William Anders** took the famous 'Earthrise' photo of Earth rising over the lunar horizon.
On **July 20th, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, with **Buzz Aldrin** beside him and **Michael Collins** orbiting alone above in the command module.
The **Saturn V** rocket that carried them stood **363 feet** tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty, built by a NASA team led by **Wernher von Braun**.
In **1970**, an oxygen tank explosion crippled Apollo 13 on its way to the Moon, but engineers improvised a fix and brought the whole crew home safe.
The Space Race ended in cooperation on **July 17th, 1975**, when American and Soviet crews docked their spacecraft and shook hands in orbit.

fact_pack.summary: The Space Race was a Cold War contest between the United States and the Soviet Union to achieve firsts in spaceflight, from Sputnik in 1957 to a joint mission in 1975. It brought the first satellite, first human in orbit, and first footsteps on the Moon.

facts.text: The Space Race was a Cold War contest between the US and USSR to achieve spaceflight firsts, lasting roughly 1957 to 1975.
On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a beach-ball-sized satellite that became the first man-made object to orbit Earth.
Sputnik 1 was about 58 centimeters wide and sent out a simple radio beep that people around the world could pick up on ordinary radios.
On November 3, 1957, the Soviets launched Sputnik 2 carrying a dog named Laika, the first living creature to orbit Earth.
Shocked by Sputnik, the United States created NASA, which began operating on October 1, 1958.
The first US satellite, Explorer 1, launched January 31, 1958, and discovered the Van Allen radiation belt.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, orbiting Earth once aboard Vostok 1 in about 108 minutes.
On May 5, 1961, Alan Shepard became the first American in space aboard the Freedom 7 capsule, though his short flight did not orbit Earth.
On May 25, 1961, President Kennedy challenged the US to land a man on the Moon and return him safely before decade's end.
On June 16, 1963, Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth aboard Vostok 6.
On March 18, 1965, Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, floating outside his Voskhod 2 capsule for about ten minutes.
On January 27, 1967, astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee died in a fire during a launch pad test of Apollo 1.
In December 1968, Apollo 8 astronauts became the first to orbit the Moon, and William Anders took the famous Earthrise photo.
On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronaut Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap for mankind.
Buzz Aldrin joined Armstrong on the Moon while crewmate Michael Collins orbited alone above in the command module Columbia.
In 1970, an oxygen tank explosion crippled Apollo 13 on its way to the Moon, but the crew safely returned to Earth after engineers improvised a fix.
Between 1969 and 1972, twelve American astronauts walked on the Moon across six successful Apollo landing missions.
The Saturn V rocket that carried Apollo astronauts to the Moon stood 363 feet tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty.
Soviet chief designer Sergei Korolev secretly led the USSR's rocket program, and his identity was kept a state secret until after his death in 1966.
Wernher von Braun, who earlier built rockets for Germany, led the NASA team that developed the Saturn V rocket.
The Space Race ended in a spirit of cooperation on July 17, 1975, when American and Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit and their crews shook hands.

story.title: Eli and the Beacon
story.subtitle: One long night, eighteen years of history, and a radio that should not have worked.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Static
chapters.text:
Eli was supposed to be asleep. Instead he was on the floor of his room, soldering iron warm in one hand, trying to get the igniter wire on his model rocket to sit flush against the terminal. The rocket was a B6-4 motor job, nothing fancy, but he'd been chasing a stable flight for three weekends and tonight felt like the night.

His grandfather's old radio sat on the shelf above his desk, dead for as long as Eli had owned it — a boxy, wood-cased shortwave set that was supposed to be decoration. It had never once turned on. Tonight, with no warning, its dial light flickered green, and a sound came out of it that was not static.

**Beep. Beep. Beep.** Steady, metronomic, patient.

Eli set down the iron. He knew Morse code the way most kids his age knew a TikTok sound — not fluently, but enough to notice this wasn't Morse. It was simpler than that. A single tone, on, off, on, off, like a pulse.

"That's not a real transmission," he said out loud, to nobody. "That's a carrier wave with nothing on it."

"Wrong," said the radio. The voice was dry, a little tinny, like it was coming through sixty years of wire. "That is the realest transmission in human history. You're listening to a satellite the size of a beach ball, talking to the whole planet at once, and it's only saying one word. *Here.*"

Eli's mouth went dry. "Radios don't talk."

"This one does. Call me the Beacon. I pick up signals other radios can't — because I'm not picking them up now. I'm picking them up *then*. Dial's yours if you want to find out when."

Eli looked at the tuning dial. There was a date etched beside it, faint with age: **October 4, 1957.**

He turned it.

The beeping got louder, and louder, and the room around him folded away like a photograph curling in a flame — and then he was somewhere else, somewhere colder, standing on a dark field under a sky full of more stars than his city ever showed him, the beeping now coming from directly overhead.

"That," said the Beacon, floating beside him now as a dim green glow, "is **Sputnik 1**. Launched by the Soviet Union tonight, **October 4, 1957**. First man-made object ever to circle the Earth."

"How big?" Eli asked, squinting up at a bright point crossing the stars.

"**About 58 centimeters wide** — smaller than your bike wheel. No camera, no weapons, no instruments worth mentioning. Just a radio, a battery, and that beep, built simple enough that any ham radio operator on the planet could pick it up on an ordinary receiver."

"So the first satellite in history," Eli said slowly, working it out, "wasn't a spy tool or a science lab. It was a flex. A proof of concept, broadcast on repeat."

"Now you're getting it," the Beacon said. "Welcome to the Space Race, Eli. It's going to get a lot less simple from here. **Signal acquired.**"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: A Dog Named Laika
chapters.text:
The dial spun on its own this time, and the cold field became a different kind of cold — a launch pad lit by floodlights, steam venting off a rocket that looked thrown together out of welded pipe.

"**November 3, 1957**," the Beacon said. "One month after Sputnik 1. The Soviets wanted a second first before anyone caught up."

Eli heard something small bark, once, from inside the capsule stacked on top of the rocket.

"There's a dog in there," he said, and it wasn't a question.

"**Laika**," the Beacon confirmed. "A stray picked up off the streets of Moscow. She became the first living creature to orbit the Earth, aboard **Sputnik 2**."

Eli watched the rocket go, a long tongue of fire unzipping the dark, and felt something twist in his chest that was not excitement. "Did she make it back?"

The Beacon didn't dodge it. "No. She didn't survive the flight. It's one of the harder chapters in this story, and people have argued about it for sixty years. But she went up first, and because of her, the people who came after her — human people — had better odds."

Eli was quiet for a second, watching the light shrink to a star among stars. "Okay," he said eventually. "Where next?"

"Less than a year later," the Beacon said, and the scene dissolved into a sunlit lawn in front of a very official-looking building, flags out front, men in narrow ties walking briskly between doors. "**October 1, 1958**. The United States, badly rattled by Sputnik, stood up a brand-new agency to catch up in a hurry."

"NASA," Eli said, reading a sign being bolted to the wall by a man on a ladder.

"**NASA**," the Beacon agreed. "Founded that day. Before Sputnik, America's rocket programs were scattered across different branches of the military, barely talking to each other. Sputnik was the wake-up call that got them all under one roof."

Eli watched the sign go up — four letters, no logo yet, nothing to suggest it would end up on jackets and coffee mugs for the next seventy years. "One beach ball," he said, "and an entire country reorganizes its government."

"That's fear for you," said the Beacon. "Good motivator. Terrible long-term strategy. Luckily for them, it worked anyway."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Belt Nobody Expected
chapters.text:
The next stop smelled like jet fuel and nerves. Eli found himself in a crowd of engineers standing well back from a floodlit gantry, all of them staring at a thin white rocket with their arms folded like they were bracing for bad news.

"**January 31, 1958**," the Beacon said. "America's answer. **Explorer 1**, their first satellite — four months behind Sputnik, and they knew it."

Eli watched the countdown tick down on a hand-lettered sign one of the engineers was holding, and the rocket went up clean, no hesitation, a tight white line climbing into a sky that was just starting to go pink at the edges.

"They got something Sputnik didn't," the Beacon said, once the cheering below had died down. "A real instrument on board this time — a detector built by a physicist named James Van Allen."

"Detecting what?" Eli asked.

"Radiation. And it found way more of it than anyone expected — a whole belt of charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetic field, invisible, wrapped around the planet like a donut nobody knew was there."

Eli's brain, which lit up for exactly this kind of thing, caught fire a little. "So Earth's magnetic field is basically a force field, and it's been grabbing charged particles out of space this whole time, and nobody noticed until they flew an instrument through it?"

"Exactly. They named it the **Van Allen radiation belt**, after the guy who found it. First real scientific discovery of the Space Race, and it happened by accident, because somebody thought to point a Geiger counter at the sky instead of just waving a flag."

Eli watched Explorer 1's light climb and vanish, turning that over. "That's the part nobody tells you about," he said. "Everyone remembers the flags. Nobody remembers the guy who found an invisible donut of radiation around the entire planet."

"Write that on a T-shirt," said the Beacon. "I'd wear it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: One Hundred and Eight Minutes
chapters.text:
The dial clicked forward three years in an instant, and the air changed completely — warmer, louder, a crowd somewhere cheering in a language Eli didn't speak but understood anyway.

"**April 12, 1961**," the Beacon said, and above them a tiny silver sphere rode a pillar of fire into a blue morning sky. "Vostok 1. On board: a twenty-seven-year-old pilot named **Yuri Gagarin**."

"First human in space," Eli said. He'd known that one since he was eight.

"First human in space," the Beacon agreed. "One full orbit of Earth, about **108 minutes**, start to finish. He came back smiling — there's a famous photo of it, missing a shoe from the landing, grinning like he'd just gotten away with something."

"How fast would he have needed to be going to stay in orbit instead of falling back down?" Eli asked, already doing the math in his head out of habit.

"Fast enough that you'd need your own rocket to find out," the Beacon said dryly. "Which, incidentally, is the entire reason this is hard. Point straight up and you come straight back down. Go sideways fast enough and the ground curves away from you just as quick as you're falling toward it. That's an orbit. Gagarin's capsule did it at roughly **17,000 miles an hour**."

Eli let out a breath. "That's not flying. That's falling and missing."

"Astronaut humor got there before you," the Beacon said. "Less than a month later, the Americans answered."

The scene shifted to a launch pad in Florida, swampy heat instead of Russian cold. "**May 5, 1961**. **Alan Shepard**, aboard Freedom 7. Didn't orbit — his flight was short, up and back down, no full lap around the planet. But he made history too: first American in space."

"Second place," Eli said. "But first for his country."

"There's a lot of that in this story," the Beacon said. "Firsts come in more flavors than you'd think."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Dare
chapters.text:
The next scene put Eli in a packed hall, wood paneling, a podium, a man with a Boston accent gripping both sides of it like he meant every word.

"**May 25, 1961**," the Beacon said. "Twenty days after Shepard's flight. President **John F. Kennedy**, addressing Congress."

"I believe this nation should commit itself," the man at the podium said, "to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the Earth — before this decade is out."

Eli stared. "He just... said that. Out loud. With no idea if it was even possible."

"That's the dare," the Beacon said. "America had put one man in space, for fifteen minutes, and couldn't even get him into orbit yet. And the President just bet the entire country's reputation on reaching the Moon within nine years. Pure nerve."

"Did it work?"

"Patience," said the Beacon. "You'll see. But first — two years on, the Soviets had one more surprise in them."

The hall dissolved into a launch field again, and this time the pilot climbing into the capsule wore her hair pinned under her helmet, and the crowd around her was quieter, more intent, like they knew they were watching something that mattered.

"**June 16, 1963**. **Valentina Tereshkova**. Former textile factory worker, amateur skydiver, about to become the first woman in space."

Eli watched the capsule go up, trailing fire. "How long was she up there?"

"Long enough to orbit Earth **48 times**. Longer, in total flight time, than every American astronaut who'd flown before her, combined."

"So while the US is still figuring out how to get a guy into orbit for one lap," Eli said, "the Soviets just put a woman up there for forty-eight."

"The Space Race," the Beacon said, "was never a straight line. Keep that in mind. It's about to get stranger."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Secret Designer
chapters.text:
The Beacon's dial this time didn't glow toward a launch pad. It pointed somewhere darker — an office with the shades drawn, a man bent over blueprints by lamplight, his face deliberately never quite in view.

"Who's that?" Eli asked.

"**Sergei Korolev**," the Beacon said. "Chief designer. The man behind Sputnik, behind Gagarin, behind almost every Soviet triumph in this story so far. And almost nobody outside a tight circle knew his name while he was alive."

"Why hide him?"

"State secret. The Soviet government was terrified that if the West knew who their chief rocket designer was, he'd become a target — of rivals, of foreign agents, of anyone who wanted to slow the program down by taking him out of it. So they simply never printed his name. He died in **1966**, and only then did the world learn who'd been running the show the whole time."

Eli looked at the bent shoulders in the lamplight, turning that over. "That's wild. You can build the machines that start a whole space race and the public doesn't even get your name."

"History's full of people like that," the Beacon said. "Now — look up."

The office vanished, and Eli found himself staring at the black curve of Earth from somewhere that was very obviously not the ground. A capsule floated nearby, and tethered to it, drifting slowly against a backdrop of stars, was a man in a bulky white suit.

"**March 18, 1965**," the Beacon said. "**Alexei Leonov**, Voskhod 2. First human to leave a spacecraft and float free in space — what they'd start calling a spacewalk."

"How long was he out there?"

"**About ten minutes.**" The Beacon paused. "His suit puffed up in the vacuum so badly he almost couldn't fit back through the hatch. He had to bleed air out of his own suit to squeeze back in. Nobody watching from the ground could do a single thing to help him. He just had to solve it, alone, floating above the planet."

Eli watched the tiny white figure drift, utterly calm against all that black. "And he did."

"He did. Ten minutes that must have felt like ten years, and then he was back inside, and the hatch sealed, and everyone on the ground finally breathed again."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Earthrise
chapters.text:
"**December 1968**," the Beacon announced, and this time there was no launch pad at all — just the inside of a cramped capsule, three men strapped into seats no wider than Eli's desk chair, a small round window in front of them.

"Apollo 8," Eli said, recognizing the mission patch stitched on a sleeve.

"First crewed spacecraft to leave Earth's orbit entirely and circle the Moon. They didn't land — that wasn't the plan yet — but they went all the way around it and came back, which nobody in history had ever done."

One of the astronauts leaned toward the window, camera in hand, and went still.

"That's **William Anders**," the Beacon said quietly. "Watch."

Over the gray, cratered horizon of the Moon, a small blue marble rose into view — half-lit, swirled with white cloud, achingly bright against the black.

"Oh my God, look at that picture over there!" Anders said. "There's the Earth coming up. Wow, is that pretty."

He took the photo. Eli didn't say anything for a second.

"That's Earthrise," the Beacon said. "One of the most reproduced photographs in human history. Taken by three men who went to look at the Moon and came back having really seen their own planet for the first time."

"Who built the rocket that got them there?" Eli asked, because his brain always circled back to the hardware.

"Good question. Come look." The scene shifted to a hangar the size of a football stadium, a white rocket lying on its side like a sleeping giant. "**Wernher von Braun**. Built rockets in Germany before the war, then led the NASA team that built this — the **Saturn V**. **363 feet tall.** Taller than the Statue of Liberty, base to torch."

Eli walked the length of it in his mind, doing the math on thrust and mass ratios without meaning to. "That's not a rocket," he said. "That's a skyscraper that's decided to leave."

"Best way anyone's put it yet," the Beacon said. "And in seven months, it's going to do exactly that — with the whole world watching."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Giant Leap
chapters.text:
The hangar fell away, and Eli stood on a dark, dusty plain under a black sky with no air to soften the stars at all. A ladder stretched down from a spindly four-legged lander beside him.

"**July 20, 1969**," the Beacon said, and its voice, for the first time all night, had gone very quiet. "You're standing on the Moon. Or close enough to it that it won't matter."

A boot touched the dust below the ladder, kicking up a small, slow-motion cloud that drifted and settled strangely in the low gravity.

"That's one small step for man," said the figure on the ladder, "one giant leap for mankind."

"**Neil Armstrong**," the Beacon said. "First human being to stand on another world."

Eli realized he was holding his breath, and let it out slowly. "Who else is down here?"

"**Buzz Aldrin**, right behind him — second man on the Moon, twenty minutes later. And up there" — the Beacon tipped an invisible hand toward the black sky — "orbiting alone above you both, is **Michael Collins**, flying the command module **Columbia**, keeping it ready for the ride home. He never set foot on the surface. Spent the whole mission circling overhead, further from another human being than anyone in history ever had been."

"That's got to be the loneliest job in the entire program," Eli said, looking up at a sky with no Collins visible in it at all, just stars.

"He said as much, later. Also said he wouldn't have traded it. Somebody had to fly the ride home."

Eli crouched down and pressed his palm flat against the dust, feeling nothing through the dream of it, but trying anyway. "Eight years," he said. "Kennedy said nine, and they did it in eight. From a guy who couldn't even get fifteen minutes of suborbital flight, to this."

"**1969 to 1972**," the Beacon said. "Six landing missions, in total. **Twelve astronauts** walked on the Moon in that stretch — and nobody's done it since."

Eli looked at the footprints leading away across the dust, perfectly sharp-edged with no wind or rain to ever soften them. "They're still up there, aren't they. The footprints."

"Still up there," the Beacon said. "Waiting for somebody to add more."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Splashdown and a Handshake
chapters.text:
"Not every mission went the way this one did," the Beacon said, and the Moon dust dissolved into the cramped interior of a different capsule, warning lights blinking red, three men working fast and calm in a space the size of a car's interior.

"**1970**," the Beacon said. "Apollo 13. An oxygen tank exploded on the way to the Moon."

Eli's stomach dropped. "Did they—"

"They made it home," the Beacon said immediately, before the thought could even finish. "Every one of them. Engineers on the ground, working with whatever the astronauts had on board — duct tape, cardboard, a checklist rebuilt from scratch — figured out a fix in time. The mission to the Moon turned into a mission to just get three men back alive. It worked."

Eli let his shoulders drop. "That's — okay. Good. That's really good, actually."

"It's one of the best stories in the whole program," the Beacon agreed, "precisely because nobody died telling it."

The capsule scene faded, and the last stop arrived gently, without any drama at all — two spacecraft, one American, one Soviet, drifting toward each other against the curve of the Earth, slow as two hands reaching across a table.

"**July 17, 1975**," the Beacon said. "Apollo-Soyuz. The race ends here — not with one side winning, but with both sides docking together in orbit, and the crews climbing through the hatch to shake hands."

Eli watched an American astronaut grip a Soviet cosmonaut's hand through the open hatchway, both of them grinning the exact same grin Gagarin had worn fourteen years earlier.

"Eighteen years," Eli said. "From a beeping beach ball to that handshake."

"Eighteen years," the Beacon agreed, "and you watched most of it in one night. Not bad."

The dial spun backward on its own, fast, and the stars and capsules and dust all poured away like water down a drain — and Eli was on his bedroom floor again, soldering iron cold now in his hand, his half-finished rocket sitting exactly where he'd left it.

The old radio sat dark and silent on its shelf, dial light out, looking exactly like the dead decoration it had always pretended to be. Except the date dial, which had read October 4, 1957 when he started, now read a different date entirely — tonight's.

Eli looked at his model rocket for a long moment. Then he picked the soldering iron back up, finished the last joint clean, and set it down to cool properly this time.

Somewhere out past the ceiling, past the roof, past the sky his model would never reach, twelve sets of footprints sat undisturbed in gray dust, waiting.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, the rocket would finally fly — and so, probably, would he, eventually.

Sputnik's shock pushed the US to found **NASA**, which started operating on **October 1, 1958**.

facts.text: The Space Race was a Cold War contest between the US and USSR to achieve spaceflight firsts, lasting roughly 1957 to 1975.
