story.title: Maya and the Glowing Porthole of the Titanic
story.subtitle: A bedtime voyage through the biggest ship of her time

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Porthole
chapters.text:
Maya lay on her bedroom floor, pencil in hand, drawing a boat with three funnels and tiny flags. It was way past bedtime, but the drawing was almost done.

Her pencil gave a tiny **CLICK**, and the page glowed gold.

A round brass porthole shimmered on her wall, like a window made of water and sunshine. A kind, crackly voice came through it. "Evening, sailor. Fancy seeing something real?"

"Who's there?" Maya whispered.

"Call me Pip," said the porthole. "I show boats. Real ones. Want to see the start of the biggest one ever built?"

Maya grinned and climbed through.

She landed in a noisy **shipyard** — a place by the sea where workers build ships — in Belfast, Ireland. Hammers banged. Sparks flew like tiny orange stars.

"This is where Titanic was born," said Pip. "Built right here at the **Harland & Wolff** shipyard."

Maya looked up at a giant metal beam stretching along the ground like a spine.

"That's the **keel**," said Pip. "The very first bone of the ship. Workers laid it down on **March 31, 1909**."

Maya traced its shape with her finger. "It's so long!"

"When she's done," said Pip, "Titanic will stretch **882 feet** — almost three football fields. The biggest ship afloat."

Maya spotted two more half-built ships nearby, shaped just the same.

"Wait," she said. "Are those her sisters?"

Pip chuckled. "Sharp eyes. Titanic was the middle sister of three — **Olympic** came first, **Britannic** after."

Maya grinned, already sketching all three in a row. "Triplets. Just bigger."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Four Smokestacks, Sixteen Boxes
chapters.text:
Two years later, Pip brought Maya back for the loudest **CLANG** she'd ever heard.

Grease covered the launching ramp. Thousands of people cheered. On **May 31, 1911**, Titanic slid backward into the water with a **SPLOOSH**.

Maya counted the tall smokestacks poking the sky. "One, two, three, four!"

"Good counting," said Pip. "But only three ever puffed real smoke. The fourth was just for looks, to make her seem even grander."

Maya giggled. "A pretend chimney!"

Down below, a worker showed her inside the hull, where metal walls divided the ship into sealed rooms.

"These are **watertight compartments**," the worker explained. "Sixteen of them. If water gets into one, the rest stay dry, and the ship still floats."

"So she can't ever sink?" Maya asked.

"People called her **nearly unsinkable**," said Pip gently. "Nearly. Not the same as never."

Maya frowned, thinking hard. "What if a lot of them fill up at once?"

Nobody had a good answer. The worker just shrugged and went back to his rivets.

Maya tucked the question away, like a pebble in her pocket, and kept drawing little boxes inside her picture of the ship, just in case she needed them later.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Flags at Southampton
chapters.text:
Horns blasted so loud Maya covered her ears, then laughed.

It was **April 10, 1912**, and the dock at Southampton, England, was bursting with people waving handkerchiefs and hats.

"She's off to New York City," said Pip, "on her very first trip."

Maya waved an imaginary flag of her own. Sailors in crisp white shirts carried trunks and hatboxes up the gangway.

A small fluffy dog trotted past in someone's arms.

"Aw, a puppy gets to go too?" Maya said.

"A few lucky pets came aboard," said Pip. "Keep an eye out for that one."

Maya grinned and gave the little dog a wave as it bounced up the ramp, its owner laughing at how fast its tail wagged.

The ship's whistle let out one enormous **WHOOOOSH**, and slowly, slowly, Titanic pulled away from the dock, sliding into open water like the biggest toy boat in the world.

Maya hopped on her tiptoes, watching until the ship was just a dark shape on the horizon, getting smaller with every second.

"Next stop," said Pip, "the middle of the ocean."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Shape in the Dark
chapters.text:
Four days later, the night was quiet and very, very cold.

Maya peered through Pip's porthole at a flat black sea. It was **11:40 p.m. on April 14, 1912**.

Something pale drifted ahead, barely visible.

"Pip — there! A shadow on the water!" Maya pointed, her heart thumping.

High in the crow's nest, a lookout spotted it in that same moment and rang the warning bell, three sharp dings.

Too late to turn all the way, the ship's side scraped along a giant **iceberg** — a mountain of floating ice — with a long, low groan.

Maya held her breath. "Is it going to sink?"

"Not yet," said Pip steadily. "The compartments are doing their job. But water's getting into more of them than anyone hoped."

Down in the boiler rooms, crew worked fast, pumping water, keeping the lights and radios running.

Maya let her breath out slowly. "Okay. Okay. There's still time."

"There is," said Pip. "And time is exactly what they need."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Dot Dot Dot
chapters.text:
Up in the radio room, two operators named **Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride** tapped out messages as fast as their fingers could fly.

Maya watched the little sparks jump off their key. "What are they doing?"

"Sending a **distress call**," said Pip. "A radio message asking any nearby ship to come help. They used the old signal, **CQD**, and a brand new one too, called **SOS**."

Maya tapped the porthole frame herself, three short, three long, three short. "Like that?"

"Exactly like that," said Pip, sounding impressed.

Out on deck, passengers wrapped in blankets heard music drifting through the cold air. A small band, led by a man named **Wallace Hartley**, kept playing to help keep everyone calm.

"People always said they played right to the very end," said Pip. "Nobody's completely sure that part is true, but it's the kind of brave thing worth remembering."

Maya listened to the faint, brave little tune and found she wasn't quite so worried anymore either.

"Keep playing," she whispered. "Smooth sailing."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Not Enough Boats
chapters.text:
Crew began lowering lifeboats, one by one, down the ship's tall side.

Maya counted them swinging down. "There aren't very many."

"You're right," said Pip. "Titanic only carried enough lifeboats for about **1,178** people, far fewer than everyone aboard."

Maya's chest tightened. "That's not fair."

"No," said Pip. "It wasn't. People fixed that rule afterward, I promise."

In one boat, a passenger named **Margaret Brown** grabbed an oar and rowed hard alongside the crew, keeping everyone's spirits up. People later called her the **"Unsinkable Molly Brown."**

"She's not even a sailor and she's rowing!" Maya cheered.

Nearby, the same little fluffy dog from the dock got tucked safely inside someone's coat and lowered into a boat of its own.

"It's okay, it's okay," Maya murmured, as if the dog could hear her all the way from home.

On the bridge, Captain **Edward Smith** stayed at his post, helping guide passengers toward safety instead of saving a seat for himself.

"That's what a good captain does," said Pip quietly.

Maya nodded, suddenly very proud of a man she'd never even met.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: A Light on the Water
chapters.text:
The sky was turning from black to grey. Maya scanned the horizon hard.

"Pip — there! A tiny light, way out there!"

Pip's porthole zoomed in like a telescope. "Good eyes again, Maya. That's the **Carpathia**."

The steamship had raced through the night after hearing the distress call, and now she was close enough to help.

One by one, cold and tired passengers climbed aboard her decks, wrapped in warm blankets, handed steaming mugs of tea.

Maya watched a woman hug a little girl so hard she nearly knocked her over.

"They made it," Maya whispered. "They actually made it."

"Many did," said Pip, "thanks to that call for help, and a crew that didn't stop rowing."

The sun came all the way up, gold and warm, lighting a sea with nothing left on it but lifeboats, blankets, and very relieved people wrapped inside them.

Maya let out a long breath. "That was close."

"It was," Pip agreed. "Close enough that people made sure it would never happen quite that way again."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Deep, Deep Down
chapters.text:
Pip's porthole flickered, pages of calendar flipping fast.

"After that night," said Pip, "ships changed their rules forever. Every ship now has to carry enough lifeboats for every single person aboard. Boats started watching for icebergs too, so captains always get warned in time."

Maya nodded firmly. "Good. That pebble question I had, about too many compartments flooding, somebody finally fixed it."

"They did," said Pip. "Took a while. But they did."

Then the porthole glowed a deep, deep blue, the color of the very bottom of the ocean.

"On **September 1, 1985**," said Pip, "an explorer named **Robert Ballard** finally found her."

Maya gasped at a grainy, ghostly picture: a huge shape resting on the seafloor, **12,500 feet** down, further under the water than Maya could really imagine.

She squinted at the picture. "It looks like... two pieces?"

"Good eye," said Pip. "She broke into two main parts on the way down. She rests about **370 miles** off the coast of Newfoundland, Canada."

Maya pressed her hand flat against the porthole glass, as if she could touch the old ship goodnight.

"Sleep well down there," she whispered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The blue glow faded. The brass porthole shrank smaller and smaller, until it was just a shiny coin of light on Maya's wall.

"One more thing," said Pip, "before I go. People built a museum in Belfast, shaped like a giant ship's front, right where Titanic began. Years later, someone even made a movie about her, one of the most watched movies ever made."

"People still remember her," Maya said.

"They do," said Pip. "Stories like hers don't really sink. They just wait to be found again."

The porthole winked out completely.

Maya looked down at her drawing. The boat now had four funnels, sixteen little boxes drawn carefully along its side, and a tiny fluffy dog peeking over the railing.

She tucked the drawing under her pillow, climbed into bed, and listened to the quiet of her very own room.

Outside, somewhere far off, a real boat horn gave one soft, sleepy **toot**, almost like it was saying goodnight too.

Maya smiled and closed her eyes.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. Smooth sailing, always.

true_facts.text: Titanic was built by workers at the **Harland & Wolff** shipyard in **Belfast, Ireland**.
Her very first beam, the **keel**, was laid down on **March 31, 1909**, and she slid into the water on **May 31, 1911**.
Titanic stretched **882 feet** long, making her the biggest ship of her time.
Titanic was the middle sister of three ships, alongside **Olympic** and **Britannic**.
Titanic had **four** tall funnels, but only three ever puffed real smoke.
Inside, Titanic had **sixteen watertight compartments**, sealed rooms that led people to call her **nearly unsinkable**.
Titanic left **Southampton, England** on **April 10, 1912**, heading for New York City.
At about **11:40 p.m. on April 14, 1912**, Titanic struck an iceberg in the dark.
Radio operators sent out calls for help using the old signal **CQD** and the brand new **SOS**.
Passenger **Margaret 'Molly' Brown** grabbed an oar and helped row her lifeboat, earning the nickname "**Unsinkable Molly Brown**."
The steamship **Carpathia** raced through the night and rescued survivors from the lifeboats the next morning.
On **September 1, 1985**, explorer **Robert Ballard** finally found the wreck, resting **12,500 feet** down on the seafloor.
After the disaster, new rules meant every ship had to carry enough lifeboats for everyone aboard.

fact_pack.summary: The RMS Titanic was a huge new ocean liner that sank on its first voyage after hitting an iceberg in April 1912. Its story of bravery, mistakes, and mystery still fascinates people, especially since the wreck was found on the seafloor in 1985.

facts.text: RMS Titanic was a British liner built for the White Star Line by the Harland & Wolff shipyard in Belfast, Ireland.
Titanic's keel was laid on 31 March 1909, and she was launched on 31 May 1911.
Titanic left Southampton, England, on 10 April 1912 on her first voyage, bound for New York City.
At about 11:40 p.m. on 14 April 1912, Titanic struck an iceberg in the icy North Atlantic Ocean.
Titanic sank at around 2:20 a.m. on 15 April 1912, less than three hours after hitting the iceberg.
At about 882 feet (269 meters) long, Titanic was the largest ship in the world at the time.
More than 1,500 of the roughly 2,224 people aboard died, while about 700 survived.
Titanic had lifeboats for only about 1,178 people, far fewer than the total number aboard.
Captain Edward John Smith, one of White Star's most experienced commanders, stayed aboard as the ship went down.
Titanic had four funnels, but only three carried real smoke; the fourth was mostly for looks.
Titanic's hull had 16 watertight compartments, leading people to call her nearly unsinkable before the iceberg proved otherwise.
The steamship Carpathia raced through the night and rescued Titanic's survivors from their lifeboats the next morning.
Wireless operators Jack Phillips and Harold Bride sent distress calls using both the old CQD signal and the newer SOS.
Legend says the ship's band, led by Wallace Hartley, kept playing music on deck as Titanic sank; survivors did report hearing music, though exact songs are debated.
Third-class passengers had far lower survival rates than first-class passengers, reflecting the ship's unfair class divisions.
A few small pet dogs, including two Pomeranians, survived because owners carried them into lifeboats.
Passenger Margaret 'Molly' Brown helped row her lifeboat and later earned the nickname 'the Unsinkable Molly Brown.'
The wreck was found 1 September 1985 by Robert Ballard's expedition, about 12,500 feet (3,800 m) deep.
The wreck sits about 370 miles (600 km) off Newfoundland, Canada, split into two main pieces.
After the disaster, the International Ice Patrol was formed and the SOLAS treaty required enough lifeboats for everyone aboard.
Titanic was the second of three sister ships built for White Star Line, alongside Olympic and Britannic.
Titanic Belfast, a museum shaped like a ship's prow, opened in 2012 on the old shipyard site for the disaster's 100th anniversary.
James Cameron's 1997 film 'Titanic' became one of the highest-grossing movies ever made.
Many objects recovered from the wreck, from dinner plates to shoes, are now displayed in museums worldwide.

story.subtitle: A bedtime voyage through the real story of the Titanic

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Porthole Lights Up
chapters.text:
Maya lay on her bedroom floor with a flashlight under her chin, drawing a little sailboat on her pad.

Her night light was a small brass porthole, round like a ship's window, a gift from Grandpa. Tonight the glass fogged up green, and tiny ripples moved across it like real water.

"Permission to come aboard?" said a cheerful voice from inside the glass.

A round, friendly face blinked at her. "I'm Pip," it said. "I show people ships. Want to see the biggest one ever built?"

Maya grinned and reached out. **WHOOOOSH!** The porthole swallowed her flashlight beam, her crayons, and her, and the bedroom melted into salty sea air.

She landed on wooden scaffolding, towering over a half-built ship. Hammers banged. Sparks flew.

"Where are we?" Maya asked, hugging her drawing pad.

"**Belfast, Ireland**," said Pip. "The year is **1909**. Workers just laid the **keel** — that's the long backbone at the very bottom of a ship."

Maya counted windows along the hull. "It's HUGE."

"You bet," said Pip. "When she's finished, she'll be about **882 feet long** — nearly three soccer fields end to end."

Two years later, crowds cheered as the ship slid into the water for the first time, built by workers at the **Harland & Wolff** shipyard.

"They call her **Titanic**," said Pip.

Maya drew the huge hull sliding down the ramp, bubbles everywhere. "I want to see the rest!"

"Climb aboard, artist," said Pip. "There's plenty more ship to draw."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Four Funnels, Three Smokers
chapters.text:
Maya stood on the deck, neck craning up at four giant smokestacks painted bright orange and black.

"Why does that back one look different?" she asked, squinting.

"Good eye," said Pip. "Titanic had **four funnels**, but only **three of them carried real smoke** from the engines below."

"So the fourth is just... pretend?" Maya giggled.

"Pretty much," said Pip. "It made her look even more powerful. Big and bold, like a drawing with extra sparkle."

Maya flipped to a blank page and drew all four funnels, marking a tiny star on the fake one.

"That's my secret code," she said. "Star means fibber funnel."

Pip laughed so hard the porthole glass fogged right up. "I'm stealing that joke, Maya."

A sailor walked by, counting funnels on his fingers, and Maya waved her drawing at him. He tipped his cap and laughed too, pointing right at her starred funnel as if she'd caught him out.

"Four funnels, three smokers, one big fibber," Maya sang under her breath, skipping along the deck to see what else she could find to draw before the ship set sail.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Sixteen Floaty Boxes
chapters.text:
Down a steep staircase, Maya found herself inside the ship's belly, surrounded by tall metal walls and heavy doors.

"Why are there so many doors down here?" she asked, running her hand along cold steel.

"These separate the hull into **sixteen watertight compartments**," said Pip. "Like sealed boxes inside the ship."

"Watertight... water can't get in?" Maya asked.

"Exactly," said Pip. "If one box got a leak, the others would stay dry, and the ship would still float."

Maya thought about her bath toys, the ones with air trapped inside that always bobbed back up no matter how she pushed them under.

"So people thought she couldn't sink," Maya said slowly.

"That's right," said Pip. "Everybody called her 'nearly unsinkable.' Remember that word, Maya. It matters later."

Maya drew sixteen little boxes in a neat row, labeling each one with a tiny wave. Underneath she wrote, in careful crayon letters, "Floaty boxes."

She tapped the metal wall gently, listening to it ring like a bell.

"Let's go meet her sisters," said Pip, tugging her sleeve toward the stairs.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Three Sisters Set Sail
chapters.text:
Back on deck, two other enormous ships steamed past in the busy harbor, their horns blasting.

"Those look just like Titanic!" Maya said, pointing.

"They're her **sisters**," said Pip. "**Olympic** and **Britannic**. Same shipyard, same family, three ships total."

A deep horn sounded right beneath their feet. Sailors scurried along the ropes, shouting cheerful orders.

"It's **April 10, 1912**," said Pip. "Titanic is leaving **Southampton, England**, on her very first trip, heading for **New York City**."

Maya leaned over the rail and waved at the crowds on the dock, waving back with handkerchiefs and hats.

"Can I draw the flags before we go too fast?" she asked, crayon already moving.

"Draw quick," said Pip, grinning. "She's picking up speed."

The horn blew once more, deep and proud. **WHOOOOSH**, the water churned white and foamy behind them as Titanic slid out past the harbor wall into the open sea, gulls wheeling overhead like excited exclamation marks.

Maya tucked her finished drawing safely under her arm and watched the land shrink away behind them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Night the Ice Came
chapters.text:
Four nights later, the sea turned glassy and still. The air smelled like frost.

Maya shivered on deck, pulling her sleeve down over her cold hand.

"It's **April 14, 1912**," said Pip quietly. "Around **11:40 at night**, lookouts spotted something ahead."

A huge pale shape loomed out of the dark, taller than a house. The ship turned hard, but its side brushed the ice, and a long scrape shuddered through the deck.

Maya grabbed the railing. "Are we okay?"

"The crew acted fast," said Pip gently. "**Captain Edward Smith** gave calm orders. He stayed at his post the whole night, helping everyone he could."

Lifeboats swung down into the dark water, one by one, lanterns glowing on their sides.

"There weren't quite enough boats for everyone," said Pip. "Only about **1,178 seats**. That's a lesson we'll come back to."

A passenger named **Molly Brown** rowed hard in one boat, keeping everyone around her calm and warm.

Maya watched the little lifeboats drift safely away from the ship, bobbing like candles on black water.

"They're going to be okay," Pip said softly. "Help is already coming."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Dots, Dashes, and Carpathia
chapters.text:
In a tiny radio room, two men worked fast by lantern light, a little machine clicking under their fingers.

"What's that noise?" Maya asked.

"That's **Morse code**," said Pip. "**Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride**, the wireless operators, are calling for help."

"CQD! CQD!" Maya tried tapping the pattern on the table herself. "What does that mean?"

"The old signal for 'come quickly, danger,'" said Pip. "They tried the newer one too."

"SOS! SOS!" Maya shouted, grinning, dot dot dot, dash dash dash, dot dot dot.

Far across the dark water, a ship called **Carpathia** turned hard and raced through the night, engines roaring, to answer the call.

By morning, Carpathia reached the lifeboats and pulled everyone aboard, wrapping them in warm blankets and hot tea.

"Not everyone could be saved that night," Pip said gently, "and it's still remembered as a sad night at sea. But so many people made it home safely, because of boats like this one, and brave people who didn't give up."

Maya nodded quietly, then drew Carpathia steaming through the gold morning light, wrapped in a little blanket of her own crayon strokes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Lifeboats for Everyone
chapters.text:
Back on calm water, Maya noticed something odd: the ships nearby now carried extra lifeboats, stacked high along their decks.

"Why so many now?" she asked, counting them on her fingers.

"After that night," said Pip, "people made new rules. Every ship must now carry **enough lifeboats for every single passenger and crew member** aboard."

"That seems obvious," Maya said, wrinkling her nose.

"It wasn't, before," said Pip. "They also started the **International Ice Patrol**, ships and planes that watch for icebergs and warn everyone nearby."

Maya drew a little patrol boat with a flag that read "ICE AHEAD!" in big crooked letters.

"So next time, ships get warned early?" she asked, holding up her drawing proudly.

"Exactly," said Pip. "That's how we learn, Maya. Something hard happens, and smart people fix it, so it's safer for everyone who sails after."

Maya tucked the drawing into her pad. "I like fixing things."

"Me too," said Pip, the porthole glass glowing warm and gold, like a little sun was tucked inside it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Twelve Thousand Feet Down
chapters.text:
The scene shifted, and Maya floated in inky blue water, lit only by a small round light.

"Where's the ship now?" she asked, voice echoing softly.

"Resting on the seafloor," said Pip, "about **12,500 feet** down. That's deeper than ten tall buildings stacked on top of each other."

A shape loomed out of the dark, Titanic's broken bow, quiet and rusted, draped in soft ribbons of sea growth.

"In **1985**, an explorer named **Robert Ballard** finally found her," said Pip. "She rests in two big pieces, far out in the ocean."

Maya pressed her palm flat against the glass. "She looks sleepy."

"She's been resting a long time," said Pip. "People have brought up plates, shoes, all sorts of things, kept safe in museums now, so nobody forgets."

Maya sketched the broken ship gently, adding soft curls of seaweed drifting all around it like a blanket.

"Goodnight, big ship," she whispered, tapping the glass once, softly, like a knock.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home Again
chapters.text:
Light swirled, and suddenly Maya stood before a huge silver building shaped like a ship's pointed front.

"This is **Titanic Belfast**," said Pip. "A museum that opened in **2012**, right where she was built, a hundred years later."

Inside, children pressed their noses to glass cases full of drawings, tools, and tiny lifeboat models.

Maya pinned her own drawings up beside them, the funnels, the floaty boxes, the glowing lifeboats, the ice patrol flag.

"I helped tell her story," Maya said proudly, smoothing the edges flat.

"You sure did," said Pip, glass glowing soft and warm. "Now, time for bed, artist."

**WHOOOOSH** — the museum melted away, and Maya blinked, back on her bedroom floor, flashlight dim, crayons scattered everywhere.

On her pad lay a fresh drawing she didn't remember finishing: a brass porthole, glowing soft green, with tiny letters underneath that read, "Smooth sailing."

The porthole night light on her shelf gave one last friendly wink, then settled into its ordinary quiet gold glow, waiting for the next adventure.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. Smooth sailing until tomorrow.

story.title: Maya and the Ship Called Titanic
story.subtitle: A gentle voyage to the biggest ship in the world — and the people who helped each other home.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Boat That Woke Up
chapters.text:
Maya lay on her bedroom floor, feet drumming the carpet, pencil scratching fast. It was way past bedtime. She wanted one more boat.

She drew a big one. Three tall chimneys. A sharp front, like a shark's nose. She wrote TITANIC across the hull in big wobbly letters.

The pencil line glowed blue.

"Whoa," Maya whispered.

The little paper boat lifted right off the page. It hummed like a kettle and grew bigger and bigger, until a real wooden boat sat glowing on her carpet.

A soft voice came from its bow. "Permission to come aboard, Maya?"

She had drawn boats a hundred times. None of them had ever talked back. She climbed in anyway.

"Where are we going?" Maya asked.

"Back to where the real Titanic began," said the boat. "Belfast, Ireland. The year is 1909."

The window turned to fog, then to gray sky and hammering sounds. When it cleared, Maya floated above a giant shipyard full of sparks and clanging metal. A ship's long metal spine stretched out below, longer than her whole street.

"That spine is called a **keel**," said the boat. "It's the very first part builders put down. Everything else gets built on top of it, like the first line you draw before a whole picture."

Maya spotted a sign nailed to a post. "It says **31 March 1909**," she read. "Is that today?"

"That's the very day workers laid this keel," said the boat. "Good eye."

Maya reached for her pencil, already itching to draw what came next.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Biggest Ship in the World
chapters.text:
The boat zoomed forward through swirling fog. "Hold on," it said. "Skipping ahead two years."

They landed by a river packed with cheering people. A huge ship slid down into the water with a giant splash.

"That's called a **launch**," said the boat. "**31 May 1911**. It just means the finished ship touches water for the very first time."

Maya counted the smokestacks poking up from the deck. "One, two, three, four!"

"Good counting," said the boat. "But here's a secret. Only three of those ever had real smoke coming out. The fourth was just for looks, so the ship would seem even grander."

Maya giggled. "A fake chimney? That's sneaky."

"A little bit," the boat agreed.

Later, they floated alongside the finished ship. Maya tilted her head back and back and still couldn't see the top.

"How long is she?" Maya asked.

"About **882 feet**," said the boat. "Picture almost three soccer fields end to end. When Titanic was built, she was the biggest ship anyone had ever floated."

Maya pulled out her sketchbook and tried to fit the whole ship on one page. It didn't fit. She had to tape on a second sheet.

"Even my paper isn't big enough," she laughed.

The boat's little bell chimed, like a laugh of its own.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Sixteen Boxes That Should Have Kept Her Safe
chapters.text:
"Come below," said the boat, dipping through a doorway that shouldn't have fit a boat at all.

Inside, Maya saw the ship sliced open like a cake, so she could see every floor at once.

"Look at the bottom," said the boat. "See those walls splitting it into boxes?"

Maya counted along a row. "...fourteen, fifteen, sixteen!"

"**Sixteen compartments**," said the boat. "Each one has its own **watertight** door, which just means water can't sneak through it. If water ever got into one box, the others would stay dry, and the ship would keep floating."

"So nothing could ever sink it?" Maya asked.

"That's what people thought," said the boat, a little quieter. "People even called her 'nearly unsinkable,' which means almost impossible to sink. We'll see how that idea gets tested."

Maya frowned a little. "That sounds like trouble is coming."

"A little," said the boat gently. "But remember, you're safe with me the whole time."

Maya reached out and touched one of the heavy metal doors. It didn't budge.

"Strong," she said.

"Very strong," said the boat. "Now let's go meet the ship on her very first trip."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Away From Southampton
chapters.text:
Horns blasted. Paper streamers flew through the air like confetti snow.

"We've landed in **Southampton, England**," said the boat. "**10 April 1912**. Titanic's very first trip. She's heading across the ocean to New York City."

Maya waved at the crowd, even though nobody could see her.

On the top deck stood a tall man with a white beard and a captain's hat.

"That's **Captain Edward Smith**," said the boat. "One of the most experienced captains in the whole White Star Line. He's sailed more ships than you've drawn boats."

"That's a LOT of ships," Maya said.

The captain gave a calm nod to his crew. The great ship began to move. Maya felt the deck hum beneath her sneakers.

"Where does she go now?" Maya asked.

"West," said the boat. "Out into the cold, deep ocean."

Maya pulled her sketchbook close and drew Captain Smith's tall hat, humming along with the engines as the shore slid away behind them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Something in the Dark
chapters.text:
Four nights later, the ocean turned quiet and still.

"It's so dark," Maya whispered, looking out at black water and a sky full of stars.

"Cold nights like this make icebergs hard to spot," said the boat. "No moon to light them up."

Maya pressed her nose to the rail, watching.

Then, far ahead, something pale slid out of the dark.

"ICEBERG!" Maya shouted, pointing.

Up on the ship, a bell clanged three times. Sailors spun the wheel hard.

At **11:40 p.m. on 14 April 1912**, the ship's side scraped against the ice, deep below the waterline.

Maya grabbed the rail. "Are we okay?"

"We're safe," said the boat softly. "We're watching from just above the water, remember? Nobody on our little boat can be hurt."

The scraping stopped. The night went quiet again.

"But the big ship?" Maya asked.

"The scrape let water sneak into more of those sixteen boxes than anyone expected," said the boat. "Let's go see what the crew does about it."

Maya held tight to the rail, brave and curious instead of scared, watching lantern lights begin to move across Titanic's deck.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Calling for Help
chapters.text:
Down in a tiny room, two men sat hunched over a crackling machine.

"Those are the **wireless** operators, **Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride**," said the boat. "A wireless machine sends messages through the air without any wires at all, like an old-fashioned radio."

Jack's fingers tapped out short beeps. "What's he saying?" Maya asked.

"First he sent the old distress call, **CQD**," said the boat. "Then he tried a brand new one too: **SOS**. Three short beeps, three long, three short. Easy to remember, easy to hear."

Maya tapped her own fingers on the rail, copying the rhythm. "SOS," she whispered.

Up on deck, sailors helped people into small boats hanging off the ship's sides.

"There are only enough lifeboats for about **1,178 people**," said the boat quietly. "Fewer than everyone aboard."

Maya's eyes went wide. "That's not enough boats!"

"You're right," said the boat. "It's one of the biggest lessons this ship ever taught the world."

A woman in a big hat rowed hard at the oars of one lifeboat, calling out cheerfully to keep spirits up.

"That's **Molly Brown**," said the boat. "People later called her 'the Unsinkable Molly Brown,' because she rowed and helped and never gave up."

Somewhere above, music drifted across the water, calm and steady.

"Legend says the ship's band kept playing, led by a man named **Wallace Hartley**," said the boat. "Nobody's completely sure which songs. But survivors really did remember hearing music, right until the end."

Maya listened to the faint, brave little tune and felt her chest go warm instead of scared.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Ship That Came Running
chapters.text:
Hours passed. Maya's boat bobbed gently near the little lifeboats, waiting.

Then, far off, a light appeared.

"That's the **Carpathia**," said the boat. "Another ship. She heard the SOS and raced all night long to reach the lifeboats."

By sunrise, the Carpathia was pulling people up one by one, wrapping them in warm blankets.

Maya watched a small dog get lifted aboard inside someone's coat. "A puppy!"

"A couple of little dogs made it too," said the boat. "Tucked safe the whole time."

Maya smiled, then turned a little serious. "Did everyone get saved?"

The boat's glow dimmed, gentle and honest. "Not everyone could fit in a lifeboat, and the ship was lost that night. It made the whole world very sad. Captain Smith stayed aboard to help others right to the end. But many people were saved, because the Carpathia came, and because people like Molly Brown kept rowing."

Maya was quiet a moment, watching families hug on Carpathia's deck.

"That's good," she said softly. "That they came for them."

"After that night," said the boat, "people made new rules. Every ship had to carry enough lifeboats for every single passenger, and a new ice patrol started watching the ocean, so captains would always know where the ice was."

Maya nodded slowly. "So next time, everyone gets a boat."

"Exactly," said the boat. "Every time."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Found Again
chapters.text:
The boat's glow flickered, and fog rolled in once more.

"One more stop," it said. "Far into the future. The year is **1985**."

They sank down and down, through water so dark Maya couldn't see her own hands, until bright lights cut through the gloom below. A small yellow submarine glided past, cameras blazing.

"That's **Robert Ballard**," said the boat. "An ocean explorer. He searched for years, and on **1 September 1985**, he finally found Titanic resting on the sea floor."

Maya peered down. Below them lay the huge ship, quiet and still.

"How deep is she?" Maya whispered.

"About **12,500 feet** down," said the boat. "Deeper than ten tall buildings stacked up. She broke into two big pieces on the way down, resting near a place called Newfoundland, in Canada."

Maya opened her sketchbook, hands a little shaky in the cold dark, and drew the broken shape anyway, because even broken things deserve a careful drawing.

"People still visit her story," said the boat. "Plates, shoes, all sorts of things from the ship are kept safe in museums now, so nobody forgets. There's even a museum shaped like a ship's front, built in **Belfast** in **2012**, right where she was born."

"She came home," Maya said. "Sort of."

"Sort of," agreed the boat. "Speaking of home..."

The fog swirled bright blue, and the cold sea floor melted away. Maya blinked. She was back on her bedroom carpet, pencils scattered everywhere.

The little paper boat lay flat on her sketchbook page again, glowing faintly, then not at all.

Maya looked at her drawing. Beside the big ship she'd scribbled, there was now a tiny lifeboat, sixteen tiny doors along the hull, and a tiny dog peeking over the edge.

"Fair winds," the boat whispered, so quiet she almost missed it.

Maya traced the hull with one finger and climbed into bed, already dreaming of the next boat she'd draw.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. Fair winds and calm seas.

story.title: Hana and the Titanic's True Course
story.subtitle: One brass compass, one old chart, and a ship that still has stories to tell.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Compass That Would Not Point North
chapters.text:
Hana was supposed to be asleep an hour ago. Instead she sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with a ruler, tracing a line across an old chart of the North Atlantic Ocean pinned above her desk. It had belonged to her grandfather, a merchant sailor, and so had the brass compass sitting next to her knee.

The compass had never worked right. Its needle never settled on north. Tonight it spun faster than ever, then stopped dead and glowed a soft, sudden green.

Hana leaned closer. The needle began to twitch in a pattern — short, short, long, short — like it was tapping out a message in some code she almost recognized. A thin ribbon of green light unrolled from the compass's open lid, and inside that light, a chart drew itself: a shipyard, a river, the shape of a half-built hull.

"Belfast," Hana whispered, reading the tiny glowing letters. "Ireland."

The light swallowed her bedroom whole.

When it let go, she was standing on a wooden platform above a river, under a sky loud with hammering. Below her, a steel spine as long as a city block lay propped on wooden blocks, men crawling over it like ants.

"That's not a ship," Hana said to a passing workman, pointing at the giant backbone of steel. "That's just... a beam."

"That's her keel, miss," the workman said, wiping his hands on his apron. "The spine we build everything else onto. We laid the first piece of it back in **March of 1909**. Build the spine first, then the ribs, then the skin."

Hana looked past him and counted — not one hull taking shape on the slipways, but two, side by side, nearly identical.

"There are two of them," she said slowly, tracing the twin shapes with her finger the way she traced coastlines on her own maps. "They're the same ship. Built twice."

The workman grinned, impressed. "Sharp eyes. That one's to be called **Olympic**. This one — the one you're standing over — will be **Titanic**. Built right here at **Harland & Wolff**, for a company called **White Star Line**. There's a third sister coming after, too, name of **Britannic**. Three ships, cut from the same plan."

Hana grinned back. Her grandfather's map had never shown her a city where ships were born in twins and triplets. She was starting to like Belfast.

"When does she get to go in the water?" Hana asked.

"Patience," said the workman. "A ship this size doesn't rush."

The compass in Hana's pocket buzzed, as if it agreed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Launch Day
chapters.text:
Two years disappeared in a single green flash, and Hana found herself jammed into a crowd on the Belfast dockside, everyone craning their necks at the same enormous black hull.

"That's the same ship," Hana said, amazed. "It's finished. It's huge."

A woman beside her, holding a parasol against the sun, laughed. "Finished enough to float, dear. Not finished enough to sail. Today she only launches."

Hana checked the compass, which had gone warm and still in her pocket, like it trusted her to work this one out herself. She studied the hull from bow to stern, counting four tall smokestacks rising above the deck.

"Four funnels," she murmured. Then she noticed something — the fourth one, at the very back, had no soot streaking its paint. "Wait. That one's fake?"

The woman peered where Hana pointed. "Clever girl. Three funnels carry smoke from her boilers. The fourth is mostly there to look grand and let out extra air. A ship this size needs to look the part."

Somewhere, a bottle did not smash — White Star Line ships launched without the champagne ceremony other companies used — and instead a cannon of grease and tallow sent the hull sliding down the slipway on its own enormous weight.

**SPLOOOOSH!**

Spray exploded upward as nearly **882 feet** of steel hit the river for the first time, afloat for the first time in its life. The crowd roared.

"SHE FLOATS!" Hana shouted, along with everyone around her, and for once nobody told her to be quiet.

When the cheering settled, the woman explained the part Hana's map could never have shown her: below the waterline, the hull was divided into **sixteen separate watertight compartments** — rooms with doors that could seal shut so that water flooding into one wouldn't spread to the rest.

"That's why people are already calling her nearly unsinkable," the woman said.

Hana looked at the huge black hull floating calmly on the river, and believed it completely. She didn't know yet how much weight that word "nearly" was carrying.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Southampton, 10 April
chapters.text:
The green light set Hana down on a crowded pier, gulls wheeling overhead, a brass band somewhere playing loud enough to be heard over the crowd. The ship towering beside the dock was finished now — painted, polished, flags snapping from every mast.

"She sails today," said a woman in a wide hat, checking a small travel case at her feet. She had a brisk, cheerful voice, like someone used to being listened to. "**10 April, 1912**. Southampton to New York. My first time crossing on anything this grand."

"I'm Hana," said Hana, and because the woman seemed like someone worth asking, she asked: "Are you nervous?"

"Nervous? I once rowed myself out of worse scrapes than an ocean crossing." The woman winked. "Margaret Brown. Friends call me Maggie. You'll hear people call me other things eventually, after this trip — something about being unsinkable myself." She laughed at her own joke before Hana even understood it.

A whistle shrieked, long and deep, shaking the planks under their feet. Hana watched ropes thick as her arm get hauled in, watched the gap between hull and dock widen into open water.

She pulled her grandfather's compass from her pocket and lined it up with the ship's bow, the way she lined up her ruler on a chart at home. "New York's that way," she said, pointing west across the water.

"Not quite yet," Molly said. "We stop first in France, then Ireland, to pick up more passengers. Then it's open ocean, all the way across."

Hana watched the English coastline shrink behind them, green light humming faintly in her pocket like a held breath. She thought of her own bedroom map, the thin blue line she'd traced so many times between Europe and America, never quite able to picture how big that empty space really was until she was standing in the middle of it, deck thrumming under her sneakers, the whole Atlantic stretched out ahead like a chart waiting to be filled in.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Night of the Fourteenth
chapters.text:
Four days later, Hana stood at the rail in the dark, breath showing in the cold air. The sea around the ship had gone glassy and still, and the stars overhead were almost too bright to be real.

"Too calm," Molly Brown said beside her, pulling her coat tighter. "My grandmother always said still water hides things."

Hana checked her compass. The needle, usually lazy, was spinning in slow, uneasy circles.

Then, far ahead in the blackness, something pale slid past the edge of sight — gone before Hana could point at it.

A bell rang out from high in the ship, three sharp strikes, and a voice somewhere above shouted down to the bridge.

Hana felt the whole deck shiver, a long, grinding shudder she felt through her shoes more than heard. It passed in a few seconds. The ship didn't stop. It didn't even seem to slow.

"What was that?" Hana asked.

"Ice," said Molly, frowning now, all the cheerfulness gone quiet. "We've grazed an iceberg."

It was **11:40 at night**, on **14 April, 1912**, and Hana realized with a small cold jolt that nothing around her looked frightened yet — stewards were still smiling, the band was still tuning up somewhere below. Just a bump in the night, everyone seemed to think. A story to tell at breakfast.

Hana's compass had stopped spinning. It simply glowed, steady and green, pointing — not north, not anywhere on a map — straight down, toward the hull, toward the sea below the waterline where nobody could see what the ice had really done.

She didn't know yet how much those sixteen watertight rooms were about to be tested. But she knew, the way she always knew when a map was about to show her something new, that the next part of this voyage would not be dull.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: CQD, SOS
chapters.text:
Hana followed the glow of her compass down a narrow companionway and found a small room crackling with static, two men hunched over a brass machine covered in dials.

"Is that a telephone?" Hana asked.

"Wireless," said the nearer man, not looking up, fingers tapping a small lever in short, sharp bursts. "Sends messages through the air, no wires needed, to any ship close enough to listen."

Hana recognized the rhythm instantly — dots and dashes, the same pattern her compass had tapped out in her bedroom.

"That's Morse code," she said. "What are you saying?"

"**CQD**," he answered. "Old distress call — means 'all stations, danger.' We're sending the newer one too, just in case. **SOS**. Easier to tap out fast when your hands are shaking."

Hana looked at his hands. They were shaking.

"Is it bad?" she asked.

He paused just long enough to answer honestly. "Bad enough. We're asking every ship within reach to come now."

Hana thought of the sixteen sealed rooms below the waterline, built to stop water from spreading. She thought of the long grinding shudder she'd felt through her shoes.

"Will someone hear you?" she asked.

"Someone's already answering," he said, and for the first time he smiled, pointing at a scribbled line of dots and dashes on his notepad. "Ship called **Carpathia**. Fifty-eight miles off. Turning around, full speed, heading straight for us."

Hana let out a breath she hadn't noticed holding. Fifty-eight miles had sounded enormous a minute ago. Now, with a ship already turning through the dark toward them, it felt more like a distance a determined friend could cross.

"Keep tapping," she told him, which was a silly thing to say to a man who clearly already knew his job, but he laughed anyway, just a little, and kept tapping.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Boats and Band
chapters.text:
Up on deck, the calm from before had cracked into something busier, though not yet frightened — crewmen swinging lifeboats out on their davits, passengers in coats and life belts being helped in, one by one, down the side of the tilting ship.

Hana counted the boats as they filled. She counted again, comparing against the crowd still waiting on deck, and didn't like the number she got.

"There aren't enough," she said to Molly, who was helping an older passenger into a boat with one strong arm. "The boats only hold about **eleven hundred seventy-eight** people. There are more than that still standing right here."

"I know," Molly said, grim for one second, then brisk again, because brisk was useful and grim wasn't. "Ships back then only had to carry enough boats for a ship half this size, not one this big. Nobody's updated the rule yet. Into the boat, Hana."

"Wait — I need to find the captain."

She found him instead on the bridge, a steady, grey-bearded figure giving quiet orders, the most experienced captain White Star Line had. **Captain Edward Smith** was staying with his ship, the way captains of his time believed they should.

Somewhere below, music was still playing — a hired band, led by a man named **Wallace Hartley**, keeping their instruments going on the sloping deck. Nobody could later agree exactly which songs they played, or for how long, but more than one survivor swore they heard music right until the very end, something steady to hold onto in the cold and the dark.

A small, indignant yip made Hana turn. A woman nearby was climbing into a lifeboat with a trembling Pomeranian tucked inside her coat. Another dog, just as small, was already curled in a different boat two rows down.

"Dogs get a seat too?" Hana asked, half laughing despite everything.

"If they're small enough and someone loves them enough," Molly said, and pulled Hana firmly toward the last open boat. "Now. In. You can ask questions from the water."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Lights on the Water
chapters.text:
The lifeboat rocked gently on black water, crowded and quiet, everyone's eyes fixed on the same dark horizon.

Hana held her compass tight. It had stopped glowing green. Now it simply sat warm in her palm, needle trembling very slightly, like it was holding its breath with her.

More than fifteen hundred people did not make it off the ship that night. Hana would learn that fact later, plainly, the way you learn something true and sad and important all at once. Right now, in the boat, nobody said numbers out loud. They watched the water and waited.

It was Hana who saw it first — a single light, low and steady, growing on the horizon where there had only been stars.

"There," she said, pointing, and her voice cracked a little with how much she wanted to be right. "That's not a star. Stars don't move."

Molly followed her finger and went very still, then let out a whoop that startled half the boat awake.

The light grew into a shape, and the shape grew into a ship — the **Carpathia**, exactly as the wireless man had promised, steaming through waters littered with ice that had slowed every other ship for miles, risking the same danger Titanic had met, to reach them anyway.

By morning, every lifeboat had been found and pulled alongside, passengers hauled up rope ladders onto Carpathia's deck, wrapped in blankets, counted, and counted again until the counting finally stopped.

Hana sat wrapped in a scratchy wool blanket, compass warm in her lap, and watched the empty horizon where the biggest ship in the world had been the night before.

"She's really gone," Hana said quietly.

"She is," said Molly, settling beside her. "But you're not. That's the part worth holding onto tonight."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Rule That Came After
chapters.text:
The green light pulled at Hana again, gentler this time, and set her down somewhere dry — a paneled office hung with ship's charts, a world map spread across a long table.

A man in a dark coat was marking a new line across the North Atlantic in red pencil.

"What's that line?" Hana asked.

"A patrol route," he said, barely looking up. "After what happened to Titanic, ships started watching for ice and warning each other. We call it the **International Ice Patrol**. Someone always keeping a lookout now, every spring."

Hana leaned over his map, tracing the red line with one finger the way she'd traced her own chart back home. "And the lifeboats?"

"New rule for that too," he said. "A treaty called **SOLAS** — ships now have to carry enough lifeboats for every single person aboard. No more counting on 'probably enough.'"

Hana thought of the boat she'd sat in, of counting heads and running out of room. It felt, suddenly, like the whole miserable night had at least taught the world something it couldn't un-learn.

"That's good," she said, and meant it completely.

The man finally looked up, noticing her properly for the first time, and smiled like someone meeting a question he enjoyed answering. "Would you like to see where she ended up?"

Hana's compass answered for her, flaring bright green before she could even say yes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Found Again
chapters.text:
The light set her down on the deck of a research ship, salt wind in her hair, a screen in front of her glowing with grainy green shapes from a camera somewhere far below.

"That's the seafloor," said a man watching the screen with total focus, headphones around his neck. "**Robert Ballard**, oceanographer — someone who studies what's down in the ocean. We've been looking a long time."

The screen flickered, and a shape swam into view that made the whole room go silent: a great dark hull, a rust-streaked bow, half-buried after seventy-three years on the bottom.

"That's her," Hana breathed. "That's Titanic."

"**1 September, 1985**," Ballard said, voice careful, almost reverent. "Nearly **twelve thousand five hundred feet** down — deeper than most ships could even reach her before now. About **370 miles** off the coast of Newfoundland, Canada. She broke into two main pieces on the way down."

Hana studied the wreck on the screen, matching its position against the chart burned into her memory from the beginning of the night. The math worked. The map and the mystery finally lined up.

"FOUND HER!" she said, and nobody on the research ship seemed surprised that a ten-year-old was the one to say it first.

The green light caught her gently this time, and the research ship dissolved into her own bedroom, lamp still on, chart still pinned to the wall, exactly as she'd left it.

On her desk sat one new thing: a small brass button, green with age, resting beside the compass. A keepsake from somewhere she had never technically been able to visit.

She thought of a museum built decades later on the very shipyard where the keel had first been laid, shaped like a ship's prow, opened for the hundredth anniversary of a voyage that never finished. She thought of a movie people still watched, of dinner plates and shoes pulled gently from the sea and placed behind glass so nobody would ever quite stop remembering.

Hana set the compass down, picked up her ruler, and drew one last careful line across her chart — not where the ship had been going, but where it had finally been found.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, Hana decided, she would draw a map of every ship still waiting to be found.

request.care_notes: Focus the story on the engineering marvel of the ship, how it was built, the safety systems of the time, and the rescue efforts. Avoid graphic descriptions of drowning, panic, or suffering. Emphasize human courage and the lessons learned that changed maritime safety forever.

fact_pack.summary: The RMS Titanic was a huge new ocean liner that sank on its first voyage after hitting an iceberg in April 1912. Its story of bravery, mistakes, and mystery still fascinates people, especially since the wreck was found on the seafloor in 1985.

facts.text: RMS Titanic was a British liner built for the White Star Line by the Harland & Wolff shipyard in Belfast, Ireland.
Titanic's keel was laid on 31 March 1909, and she was launched on 31 May 1911.
Titanic left Southampton, England, on 10 April 1912 on her first voyage, bound for New York City.
At about 11:40 p.m. on 14 April 1912, Titanic struck an iceberg in the icy North Atlantic Ocean.
Titanic sank at around 2:20 a.m. on 15 April 1912, less than three hours after hitting the iceberg.
At about 882 feet (269 meters) long, Titanic was the largest ship in the world at the time.
More than 1,500 of the roughly 2,224 people aboard died, while about 700 survived.
Titanic had lifeboats for only about 1,178 people, far fewer than the total number aboard.
Captain Edward John Smith, one of White Star's most experienced commanders, stayed aboard as the ship went down.
Titanic had four funnels, but only three carried real smoke; the fourth was mostly for looks.
Titanic's hull had 16 watertight compartments, leading people to call her nearly unsinkable before the iceberg proved otherwise.
The steamship Carpathia raced through the night and rescued Titanic's survivors from their lifeboats the next morning.
Wireless operators Jack Phillips and Harold Bride sent distress calls using both the old CQD signal and the newer SOS.
Legend says the ship's band, led by Wallace Hartley, kept playing music on deck as Titanic sank; survivors did report hearing music, though exact songs are debated.
Third-class passengers had far lower survival rates than first-class passengers, reflecting the ship's unfair class divisions.
A few small pet dogs, including two Pomeranians, survived because owners carried them into lifeboats.
Passenger Margaret 'Molly' Brown helped row her lifeboat and later earned the nickname 'the Unsinkable Molly Brown.'
The wreck was found 1 September 1985 by Robert Ballard's expedition, about 12,500 feet (3,800 m) deep.
The wreck sits about 370 miles (600 km) off Newfoundland, Canada, split into two main pieces.
After the disaster, the International Ice Patrol was formed and the SOLAS treaty required enough lifeboats for everyone aboard.
Titanic was the second of three sister ships built for White Star Line, alongside Olympic and Britannic.
Titanic Belfast, a museum shaped like a ship's prow, opened in 2012 on the old shipyard site for the disaster's 100th anniversary.
James Cameron's 1997 film 'Titanic' became one of the highest-grossing movies ever made.
Many objects recovered from the wreck, from dinner plates to shoes, are now displayed in museums worldwide.

story.title: Hana and the Compass That Remembers: The Titanic
story.subtitle: A night voyage across maps, water, and time

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Keel in Belfast (1909)
chapters.text:
Hana was supposed to be asleep.

She lay on her bedroom floor instead, flashlight tucked under her chin, tracing the ragged coast of Ireland in an old atlas. Maps were her favorite kind of story — ink coastlines, tiny compass roses, blue nothing where the ocean began.

On her shelf sat a brass compass her grandfather had once found in a flea-market box. Tonight its needle wasn't pointing north. It was spinning, slow and green, like it had somewhere better to be.

"That's not how compasses work," Hana said.

The compass clicked open. A beam of light shot straight up and unrolled across her ceiling — not stars, but lines. Decks. Portholes. A hull longer than her whole street.

"Correct," said a voice, low and dry, like an old sea captain reading a logbook. "Which is why I need a navigator who already knows how to read one."

Hana sat up fast. "Who are you?"

"Call me Fathom," said the compass. "I keep the charts nobody else remembers. Tonight's is a big one. Ready?"

She looked at the glowing hull stretching across her ceiling, every rivet drawn in. "What ship is that?"

"Climb aboard and find out."

The light swallowed her bedroom whole.

When it faded, Hana stood on a wooden platform above a half-built ship, so enormous her neck hurt from looking up at it. Workers crawled over its metal ribs like ants on a whale, and the air smelled of hot rivets and fresh paint.

"Her name's Titanic," said Fathom, bobbing beside her like a tiny glowing moon. "Built right here in **Belfast, Ireland**, by a shipyard called **Harland & Wolff**."

Hana checked a chart pinned to a nearby post. A date was stamped in the corner: **31 March 1909**.

"That's when they laid the keel," she said slowly. "The spine along the bottom of the ship. Right?"

"Exactly right," said Fathom. "And two years later —" the light fast-forwarded, cranes swinging, crowds gathering along the river — "she launched. **31 May 1911**. The whole city turned out to watch her hit the water."

Hana counted portholes along the hull and lost track somewhere past sixty. "How big *is* she?"

"**882 feet** long," said Fathom. "Bigger than anything else afloat. She even had two sister ships, built from the very same drawings — **Olympic** and **Britannic**."

Hana spotted something odd near the back: four tall funnels, but only three trailing smoke while workers tested the boilers.

"That fourth one's fake," she guessed, squinting up at it.

"Mostly for looks," Fathom admitted. "Made her seem even grander. Good eye, Navigator."

Hana grinned up at the enormous hull, already sketching its shape in her head the way she'd sketch a coastline. "Let's see the rest of her."

The chart glowed brighter, and the platform tipped forward into the light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Southampton Morning (1912)
chapters.text:
Hana landed on a crowded dock, bands playing, hats waving, steam hissing from an enormous black hull beside her.

"Where are we now?" she asked, dodging a trolley piled with trunks.

"**Southampton, England**," said Fathom. "**10 April 1912**. Titanic's very first voyage. Everyone wants a look before she sails for New York."

Hana scanned the crowd, found the gangway, and followed a sailor up and inside. Belowdecks, a staircase curled like a seashell, carpets thick as moss, chandeliers swaying gently as the engines began to hum beneath her feet.

A crewman was bolting shut a heavy metal door across a narrow hallway.

"What's that for?" Hana asked.

"Watertight door," the sailor said, patting it like an old friend. "Ship's split into **sixteen separate compartments**, bow to stern. Any one floods, we seal it off, and the rest stays dry."

Hana ran her hand along the cold metal. "So she really can't sink?"

Fathom's light dimmed, just slightly. "That's what people were saying back on the dock. 'Nearly unsinkable,' the newspapers called her. A ship this carefully built — it's easy to believe nothing could touch her."

Hana caught something careful in his voice. "You don't sound so sure."

"I sound like someone who's read ahead," said Fathom. "Four days of smooth sailing first, though. You've earned a calm chapter, Navigator."

Hana laughed and went looking for a porthole with a view of the open sea, already missing the smell of paint and rivets from the shipyard, and finding instead the smell of salt.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Four Days at Sea
chapters.text:
Four days blurred by in sunshine and salt spray. Hana spent most of them exactly where she wanted — leaning over a real paper chart in the officers' chart room, plotting Titanic's course across the Atlantic with a borrowed pencil.

"Due into New York in six days total," a navigating officer told her, tracing the curved line toward America. "Fastest crossing of her whole career so far, if she keeps up this pace."

Hana measured the distance with her fingers, the same trick she used on her own atlas back home. "She's racing."

"Everyone loves a speed record," said Fathom, bobbing near the chart table. "Even brand-new, nearly-unsinkable ships like to show off a little."

Hana traced the line further west, toward a patch of chart marked only in pale blue — deep ocean, no land for hundreds of miles in any direction.

"It's getting cold out here," she murmured, noticing frost forming at the edge of a porthole glass.

"Very cold," Fathom agreed. "Especially in April, this far north. Keep that pencil handy, Navigator. Tonight's where the chart gets interesting."

Hana looked up, suddenly uneasy. Outside, the sea had gone flat and black and strangely still, with no moon to light it.

"Try to get some rest," Fathom said, his light staying warm and steady beside her. "Big day tomorrow. Well — big night."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: 11:40 at Night
chapters.text:
Hana woke with a jolt before Fathom even spoke. A low shudder ran through the whole ship, like a giant exhaling.

"What was that?" she said, grabbing the compass tight.

"Listen," said Fathom.

Somewhere above, a bell rang three times, sharp and fast. Footsteps thumped across the deck overhead.

Hana scrambled to a porthole and pressed her face against the glass. A pale shape slid past in the darkness, taller than the deck rails, glowing faintly blue in what little moonlight there was.

"Ice," she breathed. "That's an iceberg."

"**11:40 p.m., 14 April 1912**," said Fathom quietly. "Titanic just struck it, along the side, below the waterline."

Hana felt the floor tilt, just barely, under her feet. "Is she going to be okay?"

Fathom's light flickered, honest instead of certain. "Some of those sixteen compartments you saw are already taking on water. More than her builders ever planned for, all at once."

Hana thought of the watertight doors she'd touched herself, the steel she'd believed in only hours before. "The 'unsinkable' ship."

"Ships don't sink all at once," said Fathom. "There's still time, and there's a lot still to be done with it. Let's go see what people are doing."

He glowed brighter, steady now, and led her toward the stairs, past passengers pulling on coats over their nightclothes, calm and quick, the way you move when someone has told you exactly what to do.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Boats Away
chapters.text:
On deck, chaos was turning into order. Officers called out into a night that smelled of salt and cold metal, helping women and children toward small wooden boats swinging on ropes.

Hana counted boats along the rail, then counted heads crowding the deck. The numbers didn't match.

"There aren't enough," she said, alarmed. "Fathom, there's barely enough boats for half of them."

"**Lifeboats for about 1,178 people**," Fathom confirmed. "Out of a much bigger crowd aboard. Shipbuilding rules simply hadn't caught up yet with ships this large."

Hana's stomach dropped, but she kept looking, kept counting — the way she counted anything that scared her, until the fear turned into a plan. A woman nearby refused to climb into a boat that wasn't full, stepping back out onto the deck to help row instead.

"Who's that?" Hana asked.

"**Margaret Brown**," said Fathom. "Passengers will later call her 'the Unsinkable Molly Brown' — for exactly what you're watching her do right now."

Somewhere behind them, violins played, steady and unhurried, the same tune circling back on itself again and again.

"Is that... the band?" Hana asked.

"Said to be led by a man named **Wallace Hartley**," said Fathom. "Survivors really did report hearing music that night. Nobody's certain of every song that was played — part of that story has grown into legend over a hundred years of retelling. But the playing seemed to calm people down. That much seems true."

A woman hurried past clutching a small fluffy dog to her chest, straight into a lifeboat.

Hana managed a tired laugh. "A dog gets a seat and I'm still counting boats."

"A couple of little dogs made it through that night," said Fathom. "Sometimes the smallest things survive the biggest stories."

Hana turned back toward the rail, steadier now, sleeves pushed up. "Then let's make sure the people do too."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: SOS
chapters.text:
Belowdecks, the wireless room hadn't gone quiet for a second.

**Jack Phillips** sat hunched at a brass key, tapping out message after message into the dark. **Harold Bride** leaned over his shoulder, checking each one before it went out.

"CQD," Hana read over their shoulders. "What's that?"

"Old distress signal," said Fathom. "Means 'come quick, danger.' They sent that first. Then somebody suggested trying the newer one instead."

Phillips's hand shifted rhythm: three short, three long, three short.

"**SOS**," Hana said. "I know that one."

"Barely used before that night," said Fathom. "Titanic helped make it famous the hard way."

Far off across the dark water, a smaller steamship called **Carpathia** had already turned, engines straining, racing through ice fields it had no business crossing so fast.

Hana looked back toward the bridge, where a composed, gray-haired man in uniform gave orders without ever once raising his voice.

"**Captain Edward Smith**," said Fathom, following her gaze. "One of the most experienced captains the company had. He stayed aboard to the very end, helping others into boats instead of saving a seat for himself."

Hana didn't say anything for a moment. "That's brave. Not loud-brave. Just... steady."

"The steady kind usually is," said Fathom.

Hana kept her eyes fixed on the horizon, refusing to blink, counting slow minutes the way she'd counted boats. Then she saw it.

"There!" she shouted, pointing at one small, steady light. "That's a ship!"

Fathom's light pulsed, warm and certain. "**Carpathia**," he confirmed. "Right on time."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Daylight and New Rules
chapters.text:
By full daylight, Carpathia had gathered every lifeboat, one by one, hauling blankets and hot drinks down to survivors who could finally stop rowing.

Hana helped pass a mug of something warm to a shivering boy not much younger than her. He managed a small, grateful smile.

"We made it," he whispered.

"You made it," Hana agreed, and meant it.

Not everyone aboard Titanic survived that night. But everyone in these lifeboats did — brought home across the water by Carpathia, and by people who simply refused to stop rowing.

Fathom's light drifted close, steadier than Hana had seen it all night. "People built better rules after this. Within a few years, two big changes."

"Like what?" Hana asked.

"First, the **International Ice Patrol** — ships that watch for icebergs every single year since, so captains always know what's ahead of them. Second, a treaty called **SOLAS**. One simple rule out of it: every ship must carry enough lifeboats for every single person aboard. No exceptions, ever again."

Hana nodded slowly, watching the last lifeboat empty onto Carpathia's deck. "So nobody has to count empty boats again."

"Nobody," Fathom agreed. "Sometimes the best thing to come out of a hard night is a rule that keeps the next one from happening at all."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Seventy-Three Years Later
chapters.text:
The light shifted again, and decades spun past like pages flipping. Hana found herself aboard a small, humming submarine, pressed close to a round window, staring into pitch-black water.

"Where now?" she asked.

"**1 September 1985**," said Fathom. "An explorer named **Robert Ballard** is about to find something nobody has seen in **seventy-three years**."

Outside the window, a shape emerged from the dark — a massive rusted hull, resting quiet on the seafloor, **about 12,500 feet down**, deeper than any mountain Hana had ever hiked.

"It's really her," Hana whispered. "Titanic."

"Split into two pieces," Fathom said, "resting about **370 miles off Newfoundland**, Canada. Nobody knew exactly where, for decades. Ballard finally worked it out."

Hana pressed her palm flat against the cold glass, wishing she could reach through and touch the hull itself.

"She's not lost anymore," she said.

"Never really was," said Fathom. "Just waiting for the right navigator. People went on to make films about her, and build museums shaped like her bow, so nobody would forget what she looked like."

"I won't forget," Hana said.

The light folded back in on itself, familiar now, and Hana's stomach did the small gentle flip it always did right before —

She landed, soft, on her own bedroom carpet.

The atlas lay open beside her, exactly where she'd left it. The brass compass sat closed on her shelf, needle pointing due north, like it had never done anything strange in its whole life.

Hana sat up and smiled anyway. Tucked between the atlas pages was something new: a small, hand-drawn chart of the North Atlantic, with a tiny X marked **370 miles off Newfoundland** — and beside it, in handwriting that wasn't hers, one word: *Found.*

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she'd start mapping the next wreck herself.
