story.title: Hana and the Compass That Would Not Point North
story.subtitle: A journey through the engineering marvel — and the real story — of the RMS Titanic

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Keel in Belfast
chapters.text:
Hana was supposed to be asleep an hour ago. Instead she lay on her bedroom floor with every map she owned spread out like a quilt, tracing shipping lanes across the Atlantic with one finger, the lamp turned down low so the hallway light wouldn't give her away.

On the rug beside her sat the brass compass she'd found at a flea market last month, the one that never quite pointed north. Tonight its needle spun in a slow, lazy circle, and the glass over its face began to glow a blue-green the exact color of deep ocean on a map.

"That's new," Hana said.

The compass hummed like a ship's bell struck underwater. Ink seemed to spill up out of her Atlantic map and swallow the room, and when it cleared, Hana was standing in a shipyard so loud her teeth buzzed. RAT-TAT-TAT-TAT went a thousand rivet hammers, driving hot metal into the ribs of something enormous.

"Belfast, Ireland," said the compass, its voice a dry little tick-tick-tick. "The year is **1909**. That skeleton in front of you doesn't have a name yet. It's about to get a very big one."

Hana walked the length of the dry dock, counting her paces the way she measured distances on her maps at home. She ran out of ground before she ran out of ship. "This is going to be huge," she said. "Bigger than anything."

A shipwright wiping grease from his hands overheard her and grinned. "Smart girl. This is the **Harland and Wolff** shipyard, and we're building for the **White Star Line**. Today we laid her keel — that's the long backbone at the very bottom that the whole ship gets built around. **March 31st, 1909.**"

"So the keel is like... the spine," Hana said, "and everything else hangs off it, like roads hang off a river on a map."

The shipwright laughed so hard he had to sit down on a crate. "Never heard it put that way, but you're not wrong, miss."

The compass warmed against Hana's palm, pleased with her, the way a dog is pleased when you throw the right stick.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Four Funnels, Three Real
chapters.text:
Two years slid by in a blink of blue light, and when the ink-fog cleared, Hana was gripping a rail above a crowd that stretched farther than she could map in her head.

"**May 31st, 1911**," the compass ticked. "Launch day."

Someone cut a rope. The great hull — still just a hull, no decks or funnels yet, dark and slick with grease to help her slide — began to move. Then she hit the water with a SPLOOOOSH that soaked the front three rows of spectators, and the whole crowd roared.

"She's not finished," Hana said, surprised. "Where are the rest of her insides?"

"They build the outside first, then finish her afloat," said the compass. "Come back in a year."

It did that thing again, where a year disappeared like a page turning, and now Hana stood on a finished deck under four enormous funnels, black smoke pouring from three of them into a gray sky.

Hana counted. Then she counted again. "That fourth one isn't smoking."

"Correct," said the compass, sounding almost proud of her. "**Only three of her four funnels carried real smoke.** The fourth was mostly there to look grand and keep her balanced to the eye."

"They built a whole fake smokestack because it looked better?"

"People have built stranger things for looks," said the compass. "At about **882 feet long**, she was the largest ship in the world — and she had two sister ships, **Olympic** and **Britannic**, built from almost the same plans. You could say she was the middle child."

Hana grinned, thinking of her own little brother, who also insisted on being taller than he actually was. "What's her name?"

The compass's needle finally settled, for just a second, on one word etched into the bow in gold letters.

"**Titanic**," it said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Sixteen Rooms That Don't Talk to Each Other
chapters.text:
The ink-fog swirled again, and this time it dropped Hana onto a gangway crowded with trunks, hatboxes, and a brass band somewhere playing something cheerful.

"**April 10th, 1912**," said the compass. "Southampton, England. She's leaving for New York City. First voyage. Everyone's favorite kind of nervous."

Hana loved this part — the part where a map stops being lines on paper and becomes an actual plan somebody is about to follow. She found a posted diagram of the ship's insides near the gangway and traced it with her finger the way she traced coastlines at home.

"There are walls down here that don't look like normal walls," she said, pointing at thick lines running crosswise through the lower decks.

"**Watertight compartments**," said the compass. "Sixteen of them. Picture the inside of the ship cut into sixteen separate boxes, each with doors that can seal shut. Flood one box, and in theory the rest stay dry and she keeps floating."

Hana counted the boxes on the diagram, the same careful way she counted countries on a map she hadn't memorized yet. "Sixteen," she confirmed. "That's why everyone's calling her —"

"—**nearly unsinkable**," the compass finished. "That word *nearly* is doing a lot of work in that sentence."

Hana looked up sharply. "What do you mean, *nearly*?"

The compass's glow flickered, almost like a shrug. "Sixteen strong rooms is a very good number. It is not an infinite number. Hold that thought."

Hana held it. She didn't love how it felt in her hands.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Night the Sea Went Flat
chapters.text:
Four days later — though for Hana it was the space between one blink and the next — the air turned sharp and cold, and the ocean outside the rail had gone strangely still, like a map with no waves drawn on it at all.

"Something's wrong," Hana said. "It's too quiet."

"**Eleven forty at night, April 14th, 1912**," said the compass, quieter than usual. "Keep watching."

Far ahead, something pale rose out of the dark — not a cloud, not a wave. A shape taller than the deck rail, drifting silent as a held breath.

"Iceberg," Hana breathed.

A bell rang three times somewhere above. The ship shuddered, one long scrape Hana felt through the soles of her shoes more than heard, and then — nothing. No crash, no alarm, no shouting. Just the engines going quiet, one by one, like a held note finally ending.

"That's it?" Hana asked. "That's the whole collision?"

"That's the whole collision," said the compass. "No drama you can see from here. The real trouble is happening below the waterline, where five of those sixteen rooms we talked about are filling up with water nobody invited."

"Five," Hana repeated. "You said sixteen could flood and —"

"I said she could take some flooding and keep floating. Five was more than *some*." The compass's tone stayed level, almost gentle. "Nobody on deck is panicking yet, Hana. Right now, it just looks like a very large, very calm ship, standing still under the stars."

Hana let out a breath she hadn't realized she'd been holding. Calm. For now, calm was true, and she decided to believe it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Dots, Dashes, and a Very Old Song
chapters.text:
Below deck, a small room clattered with a sound like hail on a tin roof — dots and dashes, fast and urgent, tapped out by two men hunched over a glowing dial.

"That's **Morse code**," the compass said. "A message made of short beeps and long beeps instead of letters. Those two are **Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride**, and they're using the **wireless** — a radio, basically, except in 1912 the word *wireless* still sounded like magic."

Hana leaned toward the dial, picking out a pattern she half recognized from an old scouting badge. "Dash-dot-dash-dot, dash-dash-dot-dash... that's C-Q-D, isn't it? Then... S-O-S?"

The compass actually sounded impressed. "Good ear. **CQD** was the old distress call. **SOS** was the brand-new one, simpler to send and simpler to hear. That night, Phillips and Bride sent out both, just to be sure every ship listening would understand."

"Belt and suspenders," Hana said, quoting her dad.

Up on the boat deck, faint over the clatter, came music — a violin, then more instruments joining in, steady and almost cheerful, as people climbed into lifeboats in the cold.

"Legend says the ship's band, led by a man named **Wallace Hartley**, kept playing right through all of this," said the compass. "Survivors really did report hearing music. Nobody's completely sure which songs, or for how long — that part's gotten polished up over a hundred years of retelling. But the music itself seems to be true, and it must have helped, a little, to have something ordinary playing while everything else turned strange."

Hana listened to the thin, brave little tune drifting up through the cold and found she believed every note of it, polished or not.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Not Enough Boats, Just Enough People
chapters.text:
On deck, ropes creaked as wooden lifeboats swung out over black water, lowering a few dozen people at a time while a thousand more still waited.

Hana did what she always did with a map she didn't like the shape of: she counted. Boat after boat, person after person, the same math turning uglier each time. "There aren't enough," she said. "Not even close."

"You're right," said the compass, no softening it. "The lifeboats on board had room for about **1,178 people** — nowhere near everyone aboard that night. It's one of the plainest lessons this whole voyage has to teach."

A woman in a fur-trimmed coat elbowed her way to an oar in one half-loaded boat, ignoring the sailor who tried to take it from her. "I can row as well as any man here," she announced, and started rowing.

"**Margaret Brown**," the compass said. "Everyone will end up calling her 'the Unsinkable Molly Brown' after tonight, and she will have earned every letter of it."

Hana grinned, already planning to steal that nickname for herself someday.

In the boat ahead, a woman settled two trembling, fluffy shapes under her coat before anyone could stop her.

"Pomeranians," the compass explained, before Hana could ask. "Small dogs. A couple of passengers tucked their pets right in with them, and nobody had the heart to argue. Not every small thing aboard that night was lost."

Hana reached down and scratched the glass over the compass's face, the closest thing it had to a head. "You'd have smuggled yourself into a lifeboat too, wouldn't you."

"I prefer to think I'd have been useful," said the compass. "A compass is exactly what a lifeboat needs."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Lights That Finally Came
chapters.text:
By the time the sky began to pale into gray, Titanic herself was gone from the water — she had gone down at about **2:20 in the morning**, not even three hours after that first quiet scrape against the ice.

"**Captain Edward John Smith** stayed aboard until the very end," the compass said simply. "He'd commanded ships for the White Star Line for years. That night, he chose not to leave."

Hana didn't ask any more questions about that part. Some facts don't need picking apart; they just need a moment of quiet, and she gave it one.

What she did instead was scan the horizon the way she scanned a map for a town she knew had to be there somewhere. "There," she said, pointing at a single light, steady where everything else was only gray water and gray sky.

"**Carpathia**," the compass confirmed, ticking faster now, almost excited. "She picked up the distress call and turned around, running flat out through an ice field in the dark to get here. By morning, she'd pulled every lifeboat's survivors up out of the cold."

From the lifeboats, a thin, ragged cheer went up — tired people finding just enough breath left to be glad.

Hana watched the little boats row toward that one steady light, and thought that if she ever drew a map of this night, that single dot of light would be the only thing she'd bother marking.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Finding Her Again
chapters.text:
The ink-fog swirled one last time, and Hana half expected the cold deck again. Instead she landed somewhere entirely different: a dim room full of screens, grainy footage crawling across every one of them, pale shapes drifting through water so dark it looked like ink itself.

"**September 1st, 1985**," said the compass. "An explorer named **Robert Ballard** finally found her, sitting on the seafloor about **12,500 feet** down — that's deeper than four Empire State Buildings stacked on top of each other."

Hana leaned toward a screen showing a long, dark shape split cleanly into two pieces. She pulled out her own folded map of the Atlantic from her pocket — she always kept one somewhere — and matched the coordinates scrolling past against the blank ocean near Newfoundland, Canada.

"Here," she said, tapping the spot. "About **370 miles** off the coast. That's where she's been this whole time."

"Exactly there," the compass agreed. "You'd have made a fine member of Ballard's crew."

"What happened after they found her? After all of it, I mean."

"People finally fixed what needed fixing," said the compass. "A new rule called **SOLAS** said every ship had to carry enough lifeboats for everyone aboard, no exceptions. An **Ice Patrol** started watching the North Atlantic for icebergs, so no other ship would be surprised the way she was. A museum shaped like a ship's bow opened in Belfast in **2012**, right on the old shipyard site. A film came out in **1997** that practically everyone on Earth has now seen. And plates, shoes, all sorts of ordinary little things pulled up from the wreck sit behind glass in museums, so people never quite forget."

The ink-fog rose one final time, soft as a held breath, and set Hana down gently back on her own bedroom floor, maps still spread around her, lamp still glowing low.

The compass sat quiet in her palm, its needle finally pointing somewhere steady — not quite north, but close enough.

On her map of the North Atlantic, in pencil, a small dot now marked a spot that hadn't been there before.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow she had a whole ocean left to chart.

story.title: Ben and the Pixel Time Machine
story.subtitle: One boy, one pixel sprite, and the whole history of video games, before bedtime.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Screen Glows Green (1958)
chapters.text:
Ben lay on his bedroom floor, feet kicking in the air. His tablet glowed in the dark. He was drawing a tiny blocky hero, one pixel at a time. Shirt red. Eyes black. Shoes yellow. It was way past bedtime, but the hero still needed a mustache.

Then the screen flickered. Black. Green. Black again.

Lines of green fuzz swirled across it, like TV snow, but glowing. Ben sat up fast.

"Um. Hello?" he said.

A tiny pixel person popped right out of the tablet. He was blocky and green, with a smile made of three little squares.

"Name's Bit," said the sprite. "Nice mustache, by the way."

Ben blinked. "You're... from my drawing?"

"Nope. From every game ever made," Bit said. "Want to see where games started? Before Minecraft. Before Mario. Before pixels were even a thing."

Ben didn't even think twice. "YES."

The green light swallowed them both. WHOOOOSH.

They landed in a room full of humming machines, each one bigger than a fridge. A round green screen sat on a desk, with two white blobs bouncing back and forth across it.

"That's an **oscilloscope**," Bit said. "A machine that draws wiggly lines with light instead of ink."

A man in glasses looked up and grinned. "Want to play tennis?"

"On that?" Ben said.

"In **1958**," the man said, "I'm William Higinbotham. I built this so visitors at my lab wouldn't get bored while they waited around."

Ben grabbed a little knob. He turned it, and his dot on the screen dipped down to meet the ball.

"You just hit it back," Bit said. "That's **Tennis for Two**. The very first video game people played just for fun."

Ben volleyed the ball back and forth, counting his hits out loud. "Six! Seven! Eight!"

"Not bad for your first game ever," Bit said.

"This is the OLDEST video game? It's just two dots!" Ben said.

"Every game starts somewhere," said Bit. "Even Minecraft started as just blocks."

"Fair," said Ben, grinning.

chapters.heading: Level 2: Spaceships on a Computer the Size of a Fridge (1962)
chapters.text:
The green light swirled again. WHOOOOSH.

They landed in a room cold as a freezer, full of blinking lights. A machine as big as a closet buzzed in the corner.

"That's a **PDP-1**," Bit said. "A computer so huge it filled a whole room, back when computers were new."

A young man typed fast, grinning at a round screen.

"What are you making?" Ben asked.

"Spaceships," the man said. "I'm Steve Russell. My friends and I are turning this giant computer into a game."

On the screen, two tiny spaceship shapes spun around, shooting little white dots at each other.

Ben leaned closer. "They're fighting! Is that a star in the middle?"

"Good eye," Steve said. "That star pulls your ship toward it. Fly too close, and you'll crash right into it."

Ben grabbed the controls and spun his ship hard, just missing the star.

"WHEW," he said. "That was close."

"In **1962**," Bit said, "Steve and his friends finished **Spacewar!**, one of the very first computer games ever made."

Ben kept dodging the star, grinning the whole time. "It's basically Minecraft, but with lasers and no crafting table."

Bit laughed so hard his pixels wobbled. "Not exactly the same. But I like how you think."

One more spaceship zipped past, and Ben whooped as his pilot looped clear around it.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Brown Box and the Bouncing Dot (1972)
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH. The green light dropped them in a cozy workshop, wires strung everywhere.

A man held up a plain brown box with switches on top, wired to a TV.

"I'm Ralph Baer," he said. "Folks call me the father of video games. Still makes me blush a little."

"This is a **prototype**," Bit explained. "A first try at something new, before it's all finished."

On the TV, two white squares batted a white dot back and forth.

"You can play games on a normal TV?" Ben asked. "Not just in a lab?"

"That's the whole idea," Ralph said. "Games you play right at home."

Ben grabbed a dial and bumped his square upward. The dot bounced off it. CLICK.

"In **1972**," Bit said, "Ralph's brown box turned into the **Magnavox Odyssey**, the very first video game console anyone could buy for their house."

The green light shimmered again, and suddenly they stood in a dim, noisy arcade. Machines beeped along every wall. A tall wooden cabinet glowed with that same bouncing dot.

"This one's called **Pong**," said a man with a mustache, leaning on the machine. "I'm Nolan Bushnell. My friend Ted Dabney and I started a company called Atari, the same year as the Odyssey, in **1972**."

Ben fed in a coin and grabbed the knob, batting the dot back with a satisfying CLACK.

"People loved this game so much," Bit said, "that one arcade machine supposedly got so stuffed with quarters it actually jammed shut! That part might be a bit of a tall tale, but it shows just how popular Pong got."

Ben laughed. "A game so good it ATE money?"

"Pretty much," said Nolan, grinning.

chapters.heading: Level 4: Cartridges, Aliens, and a Hungry Yellow Circle (1977-1980)
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH. They landed back in the arcade, but busier now, with new machines crowding every corner.

Bit held up a flat plastic rectangle. "This is a **cartridge**. You plug it into a console, and it loads a whole new game, like swapping out a Lego set inside a box."

"In **1977**," Bit went on, "Atari made a console called the **Atari 2600**. Instead of just one built-in game, you could swap cartridges and play all sorts of games on the same machine."

Ben turned the cartridge over in his hands. "So this is when you could finally pick which game to play?"

"Exactly," said Bit.

A machine buzzed nearby, rows of blocky aliens marching across its screen.

"I made this one," said a man beside it. "Tomohiro Nishikado. I call it **Space Invaders**. Made it in **1978**, and it started a whole craze for arcades everywhere."

Ben grabbed the controls and blasted the aliens, one row at a time. They marched faster and faster the fewer there were.

"They're speeding up! That's a little spooky!" Ben said.

"Just enough to keep you on your toes," Bit said. "Nothing scarier than that."

Across the arcade, a round yellow shape chomped glowing dots along winding lines, chased by colorful ghosts.

"That's **Pac-Man**," Bit said. "A designer named Toru Iwatani made it in **1980**. Some people say he got the idea from a pizza with one slice missing."

Ben squinted at the yellow shape. "He kind of DOES look like a pizza!"

"Nobody's totally sure that story's true," Bit admitted, "but it's a fun one."

Ben grabbed the joystick and guided Pac-Man around a tight corner, just missing a ghost. "WHEW. Close one!"

"You're getting good at this," Bit said.

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Big Quiet (1983)
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH. This time they landed somewhere much quieter. Empty shelves. Dusty store windows.

"Something's wrong here," Ben said. "Where did all the games go?"

"In **1983**," Bit explained, "so many rushed, not-very-good games got made that people stopped trusting video games for a while. Stores stopped buying them. People call it the video game **crash** — not a car crash, just a word for when something stops selling."

Ben frowned. "That sounds kind of sad."

"It was a rough patch," Bit agreed. "But don't worry. It gets better soon."

They passed a dusty truck loaded with boxes.

"People say a bunch of unsold game cartridges, including one called E.T., got driven out to **New Mexico** and buried in a big hole where trash goes," Bit said. "Diggers actually found them there in **2014**, so that part turned out to be true!"

Ben's eyes went wide. "There's buried TREASURE out there? Game treasure?"

"Buried cartridges, anyway," Bit said, smiling. "Not quite treasure. More like a time capsule nobody meant to bury."

Ben kicked gently at the dust. "Well, I bet somebody found something cool."

"They did," Bit said. "Proof that even a bad year can turn into a pretty good story."

Ben nodded slowly. "Like how my first pixel drawing looked like a potato, and now it's actually good."

"Exactly like that," Bit laughed.

chapters.heading: Level 6: Falling Blocks and a Jumping Plumber (1984-1985)
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH. Snow fell outside tall windows. Ben rubbed his arms.

"Where are we now?" he asked.

"**Moscow**, in **1984**," Bit said. "Home of a very clever puzzle."

A man sat at a computer, watching blocky shapes drop and lock into rows.

"I'm Alexey Pajitnov," he said. "I made a game where blocks fall, and you fit them together. I call it **Tetris**."

Ben watched a long yellow block tumble down. "Turn it sideways! It fits in that gap!"

Alexey spun the block. It slid into place. A whole row vanished with a soft FWOMP.

"You've got a good eye for this," Alexey said, impressed.

The green light swirled, and they landed in a bright toy store. A box on the shelf showed a mustached man in overalls, jumping over a turtle.

"In **1985**," Bit said, "Nintendo sold a new console called the **NES**, with a game called **Super Mario Bros.** built right in."

"A man named Shigeru Miyamoto designed Mario," Bit added. "He's still gaming's most famous character."

Ben grabbed a controller hooked to a store TV and pressed a button. The little pixel plumber jumped, bopped a question mark block, and a coin popped out, spinning. DING.

"That's basically my pixel art hero," Ben said, "just way older."

"Way, way older," Bit said. "But every hero needs a good jump."

Ben jumped Mario onto a turtle shell and did a little fist pump. "GOT IT."

chapters.heading: Level 7: A Blue Blur and a Shiny Disc (1991-1994)
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH. Blue light zipped past them so fast it left a streak in the air.

"Whoa, was that a blue blur?" Ben said.

"In **1991**," Bit said, "Sega made a fast blue hedgehog named **Sonic**, to race against Nintendo's Mario."

Sonic zoomed past again, curled into a spinning ball, and bounced clean off a loop. Ben tried to follow him with his eyes. "He's SO fast!"

"Speed was the whole point," Bit said.

The scene shifted to a living room. A gray box sat under a TV, a shiny silver disc resting beside it.

"In **1994**," Bit said, "Sony released the **PlayStation**. It used round discs instead of cartridges, which let games look and sound way more real."

Ben picked up the disc carefully, holding the edges. "It's like a mini DVD!"

"Exactly like that," Bit said.

Nearby, a row of computers sat connected by tangled wires, kids clustered around each screen.

"In **1993**," Bit said, "a game called **Doom** let friends plug their computers together and play against each other at the very same time. People called those get-togethers **LAN parties** — just a bunch of friends and their computers, all wired up in one room."

Ben grinned. "That sounds like a sleepover, but with more monsters on the screen."

"Close enough," Bit laughed. "The best part wasn't even the game. It was everybody playing together."

Ben high-fived a kid at the nearest computer, who high-fived him right back without even looking up.

chapters.heading: Level 8: Shaking Controllers and Blocky Hills (2006-2015)
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH. Ben nearly toppled over as the green light set them down in a bright living room.

A person waved a white remote, and on the TV, a tiny tennis player swung back in reply.

"In **2006**," Bit said, "Nintendo made the **Wii**. You moved the controller with your whole arm, and the game moved along with you."

Ben swung an invisible controller hard. Bit ducked just in time.

"Careful! You nearly beaned me!" Bit said.

"Sorry!" Ben laughed.

The room melted away into something very familiar: blocky green hills, a blocky sun, a blocky sheep baa-ing nearby.

Ben gasped. "Wait. I KNOW this place."

"In **2011**," Bit said, "a game maker named Markus Persson, people called him Notch, released **Minecraft**. It ended up the best-selling video game ever made."

Ben punched a blocky tree, and wood blocks popped right out. "This is literally my favorite place in the whole world."

"Figured you'd like this stop," Bit grinned.

One more WHOOOOSH, and they stood in a bright museum hall, glass cases glowing with old consoles and cartridges.

"This is the **World Video Game Hall of Fame**," Bit said. "It opened in **2015**, in **Rochester, New York**, to remember all the games that got us here."

Ben spotted a tiny glowing dot behind glass, right beside a picture of Mario. "It all really did start with just two dots, huh?"

"Every single pixel did," Bit said.

The green light swelled one more time. WHOOOOSH.

Ben landed back on his bedroom floor, tablet still glowing warm in his hands. His pixel-art hero sat finished on the screen, mustache and all. Beside it, one tiny new pixel blinked — a little green dot, winking, just like the very first game Ben had ever played.

Ben smiled and pulled his blanket up. "Night, Bit," he whispered.

Somewhere in the pixels, Bit whispered back. "Catch you next level, Ben."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ben. Catch you next level.

true_facts.text: The very first video game people played for fun was **Tennis for Two**, shown on a glowing round screen in **1958**.
In **1962**, a student named Steve Russell and his friends made **Spacewar!**, a spaceship game on a computer as big as a closet.
Ralph Baer's brown box, a first try at a home game, grew into the **Magnavox Odyssey**, the first video game machine you could buy for your TV, in **1972**.
That same year, **1972**, Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney started Atari and put the bouncing-dot game **Pong** in arcades.
In **1977**, the **Atari 2600** let players swap in plastic cartridges to play lots of different games on one machine.
In **1978**, Tomohiro Nishikado made **Space Invaders**, with marching aliens that sped up the fewer of them were left.
In **1980**, Toru Iwatani made **Pac-Man**, a hungry yellow circle some people say was inspired by a pizza missing a slice.
In **1983**, too many rushed games made stores stop trusting video games for a while — people call it the video game crash.
Some unsold game cartridges really did get buried in a big hole in **New Mexico**, and diggers found them there in **2014**.
In **1984**, Alexey Pajitnov made **Tetris** in Moscow, a game where falling blocks fit together into tidy rows.
In **1985**, Nintendo's **NES** came with **Super Mario Bros.** built in, starring a jumping plumber named Mario.
In **1991**, Sega made **Sonic**, a super-fast blue hedgehog, to race against Nintendo's Mario.
**Minecraft**, released in **2011** by Markus "Notch" Persson, became the best-selling video game ever made.
The **World Video Game Hall of Fame** opened in **2015** in Rochester, New York, to remember the games that led here.

new_recurring.name: Bit
new_recurring.rule: A small, blocky green pixel-sprite guide who steps out of any glowing screen to lead the child through a history adventure. Dry, a little sarcastic, warm underneath. Signs off every story with the catchphrase 'Catch you next level!'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Ben returned to his glowing tablet with his pixel-art hero finished, mustache and all, a tiny new blinking green dot beside it, and fell asleep after Bit's whispered goodnight.

fact_pack.summary: Video games grew from 1950s lab experiments into arcades, consoles, and phones played by billions today, giving us stars like Mario and Sonic.

In 1978, designer Tomohiro Nishikado created Space Invaders for Taito, sparking a worldwide arcade craze.

story.title: Ben and the Glitch Block: A Trip Through Game History
story.subtitle: One pixel cube, nine levels, and about sixty years of games.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Green Glow at Brookhaven
chapters.text:
Ben was lying on his bedroom floor, flashlight propped against a pillow, finishing a pixel-art dragon on his tablet. Pixel by pixel, he dragged each tiny square into place. It was way past bedtime, but the dragon only needed one more wing.

Then the desk lamp flickered green.

On his shelf, a blocky gray cube he'd built out of cardboard — leftover from an old Minecraft art project — started to hum. Static crackled across its sides like TV snow. Ben sat up so fast his tablet slid off his knees.

"Hello?" he whispered.

The cube blinked open like a tiny door, and green light poured out, the exact green of his dragon's eyes.

"Finally," said a small voice. Out popped a creature made entirely of square pixels, about the size of a guinea pig, with two blinking eyes. "I've been waiting for someone who likes **blocks** as much as I do. I'm Byte. Want to see where games came from?"

Ben looked at the glowing cube, then at his half-finished dragon. "Is this part of the art?"

"Nope," said Byte. "This is real. Grab my hand — well, my pixel."

The moment Ben's finger touched Byte's square hand, the room melted into green lines, and then — **WHOOOSH!**

They landed in a room full of humming machines the size of refrigerators, wires snaking everywhere. A man in a white coat squinted at a round glowing screen that showed nothing but wobbly green lines.

"That's a funny TV," Ben said.

"It's not a TV," the man said, smiling. "It's an **oscilloscope** — a screen scientists use to look at wobbly lines. I'm William. I thought, why not make the wobbles into a game?"

Ben leaned closer. The green line bounced back and forth like a tiny dot playing catch with itself. "Is that... tennis?"

William grinned. "Good eye. I call it **Tennis for Two**. Built it right here at **Brookhaven National Laboratory**, in **1958**. Turn that knob to hit the ball back."

Ben turned it. The dot bounced. **BOING!**

"I WIN!" Ben yelled, even though nobody had kept score.

Byte laughed, a sound like a dial-up modem giggling. "First game thousands of people ever played on a screen, and you already want a rematch."

"Obviously," said Ben. "Where next?"

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Fridge-Sized Computer
chapters.text:
**WHOOOSH!** Green lines spun again, and when they stopped, Ben stood in a room that smelled like hot metal. A machine as big as three refrigerators stacked together blinked rows of lights across one whole wall.

"Whoa," Ben breathed. "That's one computer?"

"One computer," said Byte. "Back in **1962**, computers didn't fit in your pocket. This one's called a **PDP-1**, and it needed its own room just to say hello."

A college student in glasses typed fast at a console, two blobs of light drifting on a round screen nearby.

"Steve Russell, at your service," the student said, not looking up. "Or I will be, once this works."

Ben squinted at the screen. Two triangle-shaped dots floated near a scatter of tiny dots. "Are those... spaceships? And that's stars?"

Steve looked up, surprised. "That's exactly what they are. My friends and I are building a game called **Spacewar!** You fly a ship, dodge the star's pull, and try to shoot the other ship."

"Can I fly one?" Ben asked.

Steve slid him a control box with one switch and one button. "Thrust and fire. Try not to fly into the sun."

Ben flicked the switch. His triangle swung wide around the little star, barely missing it. "Whoa, close one!"

"Too close," laughed Steve. "That star pulls ships in if you're not careful — but nobody really gets hurt, it's just pixels."

Byte floated beside Ben's shoulder. "This was one of the very first computer games anybody could actually play against a friend. Right here, on a computer that needed its own air conditioner."

Ben pressed fire. A tiny dot streaked across the screen and Steve's ship spun away, untouched.

"Missed," said Steve cheerfully.

"Next time," Ben said, already grinning at the screen like it was the best arcade machine he'd ever seen — even though arcades didn't exist yet.

Byte tugged his sleeve. "Speaking of which. Let's go meet the man who put games on an actual television."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Brown Box in the Basement
chapters.text:
Green light again, and this time Ben landed in a basement that smelled like solder and coffee. A man with thick glasses hunched over a tangle of wires connected to a plain brown wooden box, plugged into a small television.

"Who turned my TV into a drawing board?" Ben asked, pointing at two white squares bouncing a white dot between them on the screen.

"I did," said the man, not looking annoyed at all. "Ralph Baer. People are going to call me the **father of video games** one day, though right now I'm just the guy whose wife keeps asking when dinner's happening."

"You made a game come out of a regular TV?" Ben said. "That's not supposed to work."

"That's exactly the idea," Ralph said, flipping a switch. The dot bounced again. "I built this **Brown Box** in my basement in the late **1960s**. Before this, if you wanted to play a game on a screen, you needed a whole room full of machines like your friend here probably showed you."

Byte nodded proudly, like he'd personally built the PDP-1.

Ben leaned over the controls, two knobs that moved the paddles up and down. "People are gonna want this in their living rooms," he said. "You should sell it."

Ralph grinned like Ben had read his mind. "Funny you say that. A company called Magnavox thought the same thing."

**FLASH** — the basement blinked away, replaced by a toy-store shelf lined with boxes showing a family gathered around their TV, controllers in hand.

"In **1972**," Byte explained, "Ralph's basement invention became the **Magnavox Odyssey** — the first video game console anyone could buy for their own home."

Ben picked up a box, grinning at the cartoon family on the cover. "So before this, nobody could play a TV game at home at all?"

"Nobody," Byte confirmed. "Now everybody could."

Ben set the box back on the shelf carefully. "Byte, I think I just watched my living room get invented."

Byte snorted. "Wait till you see what happens in the arcades."

chapters.heading: Level 4: Quarters Everywhere
chapters.text:
The green light dropped them into a dim, noisy room full of beeping machines and the smell of popcorn. In the corner stood a wooden cabinet with a small screen showing two white paddles and a bouncing square ball.

"Now THIS looks like an arcade," Ben said, already reaching for the coin slot — empty.

Two men stood nearby, one holding a clipboard, the other grinning like he'd just won something.

"Nolan Bushnell," said the grinning one. "This is Ted Dabney. We started a company called **Atari**, and this little machine is called **Pong**. Table tennis, but electric."

Ben peered at the coin slot. It looked stuffed, like someone had tried to feed it way too many snacks. "Is it... broken?"

Ted laughed. "Story goes that this very machine got so popular, so fast, people shoved in quarters till it actually jammed shut. Couldn't fit one more coin."

Byte leaned in. "Nobody's totally sure that part's true — it might be a bit of a tall tale — but it tells you how wild people went for it."

Ben grinned, imagining a machine stuffed to bursting with coins like a birthday piñata. "Can I try it even without quarters?"

Nolan flipped a hidden switch. "For you? Free game."

Ben gripped the knob and spun it. The little square ball bounced off his paddle — **BOP!** — zipped across the screen, and bounced past Ted's paddle entirely.

"POINT!" Ben shouted, pumping his fist like he'd scored the winning goal.

"That's **1972** for you," said Nolan, shaking his head good-naturedly. "Two guys, one simple game, and suddenly everybody on the block wants a turn."

Byte tugged Ben toward the green glow waiting by the door. "Speaking of wanting a turn — wait till you see what happens when games start coming on little plastic cartridges you can swap like trading cards."

Ben was already following, rubbing his hands together. "Swap like Minecraft skins?"

"Kind of," said Byte. "Just plastic instead of pixels."

chapters.heading: Level 5: One Box, A Thousand Games
chapters.text:
They landed in a living room bathed in TV light, a stack of flat plastic cartridges fanned across the carpet like a hand of cards.

"Whoa, it's like a chest full of discs," Ben said, picking one up. It had a cartoon spaceship on the cover.

"Close," said Byte. "In **1977**, Atari released a console called the **Atari 2600**. Before this, most home games only had one or two built-in games. This one let you swap **cartridges** in and out, like changing which world you load up."

Ben slid a cartridge into the slot. **CLICK.** The TV flickered to a new game entirely — rows of blocky aliens marching sideways across the screen, slowly creeping down.

"Those guys look mad," Ben said, squinting at the screen.

"They're from **Space Invaders**," said a new voice. A man adjusting dials behind the machine bowed slightly. "Tomohiro Nishikado. I made this game in **1978**, for arcades in Japan. Aliens march down, you shoot up. Simple."

Ben grabbed the controller, counting the alien rows out loud — "one, two, three, four rows!" — as they inched closer, faster each time one got shot.

"They speed up the fewer there are," Tomohiro said. "Keeps everybody's heart pounding — in a fun way."

Ben fired. **PEW PEW!** Two aliens blinked out. The rest sped up, marching a little quicker.

"They're getting faster!" Ben said, grinning instead of worried, mashing the button with both thumbs.

The last alien dropped. **BZZT — victory jingle!**

"Cleared the whole screen," said Byte. "This game got so popular in arcades, some places ran out of coins for change."

Ben set the controller down, buzzing with pride. "Okay, that one's going straight to the top of my favorites list."

"Careful," said Byte, pixels flickering with a grin. "Your list is about to get a lot longer."

chapters.heading: Level 6: Pizza, a Glitch, and a Buried Treasure
chapters.text:
The green light dropped them outside a pizza parlor, the smell of melted cheese drifting into the alley. Byte pointed at a round pizza missing one triangle slice. "Look familiar?"

Ben looked at the pizza, then pictured the little yellow circle from his game memory. "Wait. Is that supposed to be—"

"**Pac-Man**!" said a man carrying a sketchpad, grinning as he circled the pizza outline with a napkin. "Toru Iwatani, nice to meet you. Some people say I got the idea for this shape from a pizza missing a slice — that part's a little fuzzy, but the shape sure looks right, doesn't it?"

Ben compared the pizza and his memory of the game. "Pretty much exactly."

"I made **Pac-Man** in **1980**," Toru said, "for a company called Namco. Little yellow circle, eats dots, runs from ghosts."

"Runs from ghosts but never gets actually caught, right?" Ben checked.

"Never for long," Toru said with a wink. "Just a quick time-out and tries again."

Byte tugged Ben's sleeve toward the green glow. "Fast forward a few years, and things get bumpy."

They landed in a warehouse stacked to the ceiling with boxes of game cartridges, dust thick on top.

"By **1983**," Byte explained, "so many rushed, not-very-good games had been made, people stopped buying as many. The whole business shrank for a while — kind of like a party that got too crowded and everyone went home early."

Ben picked up a cartridge labeled E.T. "What happened to all these, then?"

"Funny you ask," said Byte, grinning. "A famous story says a bunch of unsold cartridges, including this exact game, got buried out in a New Mexico landfill — basically a giant trash dump. For years, people thought it was just a rumor."

"Was it true?" Ben asked.

"In **2014**," said Byte, "diggers actually went out there and found them. Cartridges, buried for decades, dug right back up."

Ben grinned, holding the dusty cartridge up like buried treasure. "So the games didn't disappear. They were just waiting."

"Exactly," said Byte. "Good thing too, because the comeback's about to be huge."

chapters.heading: Level 7: A Plumber and Some Falling Blocks
chapters.text:
The green glow cleared into a toy store wrapped in a red-and-white cardboard display, a mustached cartoon plumber jumping across the box art.

"In **1985**," Byte said, "the video game business needed a comeback. Nintendo brought out a console called the **NES**, and it came packaged with a brand-new game."

Ben grabbed the controller, a rectangle with a cross-shaped pad and two round buttons. "This looks way simpler than that PDP-1 thing."

"Way simpler," agreed a cheerful man polishing the display, pencil tucked behind his ear. "Shigeru Miyamoto. I designed the game inside that box — **Super Mario Bros.** Press the pad to run, the button to jump."

Ben pressed. On the screen, a small mustached man in overalls hopped clean over a gap and landed on a floating brick.

"He just jumped over a hole like it was nothing!" Ben said.

"That's **Mario**," Shigeru said proudly. "Probably the most famous character in any video game, ever."

Ben jumped Mario onto another brick, grinning. "He's basically the mascot of all gaming, huh?"

"Pretty much," Byte confirmed. "A **mascot** — a character everybody recognizes the second they see him, kind of like your Minecraft skin."

A soft electronic melody chimed from the next aisle over — falling square blocks tumbling down a screen, stacking into neat rows that vanished when they filled completely.

"Oh, I know this one," Ben said, eyes lighting up. "Tetris!"

A man adjusting the screen smiled. "Alexey Pajitnov. Built it in **1984**, at a computer center in Moscow. Just falling shapes — turn them, stack them, clear the lines."

Ben grabbed the controls and rotated a falling L-shaped block, sliding it into a gap. The row filled and vanished with a satisfying **ZAP**.

"That's so satisfying," Ben said, already reaching for the next block.

"Careful," Byte said, pixels flickering with amusement. "People have lost entire afternoons to that sound."

Ben didn't look up. "One more row."

chapters.heading: Level 8: Faster, Shinier, Wavier
chapters.text:
The green light this time came with actual speed — a blue blur streaked past before Ben even landed.

"Whoa, who was that?" Ben said, spinning around.

"That," said Byte, "was **Sonic the Hedgehog**, released by Sega in **1991**. They built him fast and blue specifically to race against Nintendo's Mario."

A looping track unspooled nearby with a small blue figure zipping through it, curling into a ball to roll through loops.

"Race you," Ben told the screen, grabbing the controller. Sonic zipped through a loop so fast the screen blurred. "He's basically Mario but turbocharged."

"Exactly the plan," said Byte.

The scene shifted to a living room glowing with a different console, a shiny silver disc spinning inside.

"In **1994**," Byte explained, "Sony jumped into consoles with the **PlayStation**. It used **CDs** — shiny discs — instead of cartridges, which meant games could look and sound a lot fuller."

Ben held the disc up to the light, rainbow colors swirling across it. "It's like a tiny rainbow."

Next, a cluster of computers sat connected by a tangle of cables, kids typing eagerly at each one.

"**1993**," said Byte. "A game called Doom got people linking their computers together with cables — called a **LAN party** — just to play against each other in the same room."

Ben glanced at the tangle of wires. "That's basically a sleepover, but for games."

"Pretty much," Byte laughed.

Finally, the room shifted again — a cozy living room, and someone waving a white remote around like a tennis racket.

"**2006**," Byte said. "Nintendo's **Wii** used a controller you actually wave around, instead of just pressing buttons. Even people who'd never touched a game before wanted a turn."

Ben grabbed the remote and swung it like a bat. On screen, his tiny cartoon self swung a bowling ball down a lane. **CRASH!** Pins scattered everywhere.

"STRIKE!" Ben yelled, swinging the remote again just because it felt good.

Byte floated beside him, pixels glowing warm. "One more stop, player one. This one, I think you're really going to like."

chapters.heading: Level 9: Back to the Block
chapters.text:
Green light swirled once more, and this time Ben landed somewhere that looked almost exactly like... a giant cube world, blocky trees and blocky hills stretching to a blocky sunset.

"Wait," Ben said slowly. "This is—"

"**Minecraft**," Byte confirmed, grinning wide. "Released in **2011** by a developer named Markus Persson — everybody just calls him **Notch**. Built entirely out of blocks you can place and break."

Ben reached out and touched a blocky tree. It felt oddly familiar, like the cardboard cube back on his shelf. "This one's basically made of the same stuff as Byte."

"Fair point," said Byte, patting his own square chest. "This game ended up becoming the **best-selling video game ever made**. Billions of blocks, placed by millions of people."

Ben grinned, already itching to build something. "Can I just — five more minutes?"

"We'll see," said Byte. "One last stop first."

The scene shifted to a quiet museum hall, glass cases lined with old controllers, cartridges, and consoles Ben now recognized — the Brown Box, the Odyssey, an Atari cartridge, a Game Boy.

"In **2015**," Byte said, "a museum called The Strong, in Rochester, New York, opened the **World Video Game Hall of Fame** — a place that keeps all these old games safe, so nobody forgets where it all started."

Ben peered into a case holding a dusty cartridge that looked a lot like the one he'd pulled from the landfill pile. "So all of it — the TV tennis, the spaceships, the pizza guy, all of it — just kept building up to now?"

"Every single level," said Byte, "led to the next one."

The green light swirled one final time, softer now, and Ben blinked — back on his bedroom floor, flashlight still glowing, tablet beside him. The cardboard cube on his shelf sat dark and still again, just cardboard.

Except now, propped against it, sat one tiny pixel-art brick Ben hadn't built — painted brown, just like a certain basement prototype.

Ben picked it up, grinning, and set it carefully beside his dragon drawing before finally switching off the flashlight.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ben. Game over — for tonight. Sleep tight, player one.

story.title: Theo and the First Save File
story.subtitle: One night, one glitchy screen, and fifty years of video games.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Green Line That Played Tennis (1958)
chapters.text:
Theo was not asleep. He was in Roblox Studio, testing a double-jump script for the eleventh time, and it still made his character faceplant into a wall.

He hit play again. The screen flickered. Then it went fully green-and-black, like an old computer that time forgot.

A single glowing dot bounced out of the monitor and landed on his desk. It looked like a tiny ball of pixels, if a pixel could look smug.

"Name's Blip," it said. "You just loaded me up. Want to see where games actually started?"

Before Theo could answer, the green lines on the screen arranged themselves into a court with a net and a bouncing dot — tennis, but made of light.

"This is **Tennis for Two**," Blip said. "Built in **1958** by a scientist named William Higinbotham, on a machine called an **oscilloscope** — normally it just drew wiggly lines to check electricity, but he turned it into a tennis game instead."

Theo squinted at the screen. "The ball doesn't bounce off the net. It just disappears if it hits the middle line."

"Yep," said Blip. "No graphics budget for that yet."

"That's basically my first build," Theo admitted. "One platform, no art, still fun."

Blip spun in a happy little loop. "Exactly. You get it. Ready to load the next save?"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Two Ships and One Very Patient Computer (1962)
chapters.text:
The green court folded away, and a new screen buzzed to life — this one showed two little ships shooting at each other in space.

"**Spacewar!**," Blip announced. "Made in **1962** by a college student named Steve Russell and his friends, on a giant computer called a **PDP-1** — basically a refrigerator-sized box that took up a whole room just to run one game."

Theo watched the ships loop around a star in the middle, swapping fire. "Wait, it's two players? Against each other?"

"First one of its kind," Blip said.

"That's like me and my cousin playing soccer against each other instead of just kicking a ball at a wall," Theo said. "It's way better with somebody to beat."

"Funny you say that," said Blip. "Multiplayer was kind of the whole point."

One of the ships drifted too close to the star and got pulled in.

"Gravity well," Blip said. "It'll eat your ship if you're not careful."

Theo grabbed the mouse without thinking and nudged the surviving ship clear of the star, just like dodging a defender. It worked. The ship lived.

"Nice save," said Blip. "Ready for the next one? This one's got cardboard in it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Box Wrapped in Wood-Print Tape (1972)
chapters.text:
The screen now showed a cluttered workshop and a plain brown box covered in fake wood-grain tape.

"Meet Ralph Baer," Blip said. "An engineer who had one big idea: what if you could play a game right on your own TV?"

"That's it? That's the box?" Theo asked.

"That's the **prototype**," Blip said — "a rough first version you build to test an idea before the real thing."

"I've got, like, forty prototypes of my obby in Studio," Theo said. "None of them look that ugly, though."

"Ugly works," Blip said. "In **1972**, Baer's box became the **Magnavox Odyssey** — the first ever video game **console**, a machine built just for playing games, plugged straight into your TV."

Theo leaned closer. "So before this, games only lived on huge lab computers?"

"Exactly. Baer brought it home."

"What if you could play more than one game on it, though?" Theo asked. "Like swapping between my different Roblox places?"

Blip's glow brightened. "Funny you should ask. Hang on to that thought."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Machine That Choked on Quarters (1972)
chapters.text:
The scene shifted to a noisy arcade, lit by one buzzing bulb and a single cabinet in the corner.

"Also in **1972**," Blip said, "two guys named Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney started a company called Atari and put out an arcade game called **Pong**."

On the screen, two white paddles knocked a square dot back and forth. BEEP. BOOP. BEEP.

"That's it?" Theo said. "Just paddles and a square?"

"People went nuts for it," Blip said. "Story goes, one early Pong machine jammed completely — so stuffed with quarters it couldn't close. Might be a bit of an exaggeration, honestly, but it tells you how fast people fell in love with it."

Theo tapped the cabinet. A little coin slot rattled. "Let's find out," he said, and started dropping imaginary quarters in, counting under his breath like he was counting laps at practice.

At twenty he grinned. "Okay, I believe it could jam. This thing's basically a piggy bank with graphics."

Blip laughed, a sound like a dial-up tone. "Ready for cartridges?"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: One Box, Many Games (1977–1978)
chapters.text:
The arcade melted into a living room with a TV and a stack of flat plastic cases.

"**1977**," Blip said. "The **Atari 2600**. Instead of one game built in forever, you could plug in a **cartridge** — a little plastic case with a whole game stored inside, kind of like swapping SD cards."

Theo picked one up. "So it's like my Roblox places, except you need an actual physical thing to switch games?"

"Before the internet, yeah. You wanted a new game, you bought a new cartridge."

He slotted one in. The screen filled with rows of blocky aliens marching down, and a little cannon at the bottom.

"**Space Invaders**," Blip said. "Made in **1978** by a designer named Tomohiro Nishikado. It caused an absolute craze — arcades everywhere packed with kids trying to beat it."

The aliens sped up as they got lower, beeping faster and faster. Theo's thumb found the fire button on instinct, same reflex as a last-second penalty save.

He cleared the bottom row just before it reached him.

"Nice reflexes," said Blip. "Goalkeeper training pays off, huh."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Pizza, a Pile of Cartridges, and a Comeback (1980–1983)
chapters.text:
A yellow circle with a wedge missing chomped across the next screen, gobbling little dots.

"**Pac-Man**," Blip said. "Made in **1980** by Toru Iwatani. Story goes he got the idea from a pizza missing a slice — nobody's totally sure that's true, but it's a good story, so it stuck."

Theo watched Pac-Man dodge four colorful ghosts. "Okay, that's actually kind of genius. Simple shape, instant character."

Then the screen glitched, and a pile of plastic cartridges appeared, dumped in a messy heap.

"**1983**," Blip said, quieter now. "Too many rushed, low-quality games flooded the stores. People stopped trusting new releases, and the whole market in North America shrank fast. They call it the **crash**."

"That's rough," Theo said. "Like if everyone started uploading unfinished Roblox games and people just... stopped playing new stuff."

"Exactly like that," said Blip. "Some of those unsold cartridges — including a game based on E.T. — ended up buried in a landfill in New Mexico. People thought that one was just a legend too, until diggers found the actual cartridges in **2014**."

"So it was true the whole time?"

"That one was true the whole time," Blip said. "Good games always find a way back, though. Watch this."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: A Plumber, a Falling Block, and a Comeback (1984–1985)
chapters.text:
A small mustached man in overalls jumped over a mushroom-shaped enemy, bouncing a brick with his head.

"**1985**," Blip said. "**Nintendo** brought the market back with a console called the **NES**, bundled together with a game called **Super Mario Bros.**"

"Mario," Theo said. "Obviously. Everyone knows Mario."

"Designed by Shigeru Miyamoto," Blip said. "He imagined a jumping hero — turned out to be the most famous character games have ever made."

On the screen, Mario leapt a gap. Theo's hand jumped with him, same timing he used lining up a free kick.

"And a year earlier," Blip added, as the screen split into falling blocks, "a scientist in Moscow named Alexey Pajitnov made **Tetris**, in **1984**. Blocks fall, you fit them together, lines clear."

Theo watched a long I-shaped block drop. "Rotate it and drop it on the left," he said instantly. "That gap needs the long one."

The line cleared. Blip blinked in surprise. "You've literally never played this."

"I build puzzle levels in Studio," Theo said. "Shapes fitting together is kind of my whole thing."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Blue, Shiny, and Connected (1991–2006)
chapters.text:
A blue hedgehog zipped across the screen so fast it left a streak of color.

"**Sonic the Hedgehog**," Blip said. "Sega's answer to Mario, made in **1991** — fast mascot for a company that wanted speed to be the whole pitch."

The screen then flickered to a gray console with a disc tray sliding open.

"**1994**," Blip said. "Sony's **PlayStation**. It used **CDs** instead of cartridges — shiny discs that held way more space, so games suddenly had real voices and smoother video."

Next, two computers lit up side by side, connected by a cable.

"**1993**," Blip said, "a shooter called **Doom** got people wiring computers together in the same room just to play against each other. They called it a **LAN party** — like a sleepover, but everyone brought their own keyboard."

"We basically do that with Roblox," Theo said. "Minus the cables."

Last, a white remote appeared, and on screen a tiny tennis racket swung whenever Theo swung his arm.

"**2006**," Blip said. "Nintendo's **Wii**. **Motion controllers** — it reads how you actually move, so your arms do the work instead of just your thumbs."

Theo swung like he was heading a corner kick. The on-screen racket swung with him. "Okay," he said, "that one's just fun."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to the Room, Achievement Unlocked (2011–Now)
chapters.text:
The last screen Blip pulled up looked almost exactly like Theo's own desktop: blocky green hills, a blocky sun.

"**Minecraft**," Blip said. "Made in **2011** by a Swedish developer who went by Notch. It's gone on to become the best-selling video game ever made."

"Everybody's played Minecraft," Theo said. "Even my grandma's played Minecraft."

"That's kind of the point," said Blip. "Started with one guy building blocks on his own computer. Now it's basically everywhere."

The screen zoomed out to a glass building, shelves full of old consoles and cartridges behind glass cases.

"The **World Video Game Hall of Fame**," Blip said. "Opened in **2015**, at a museum called The Strong, in Rochester, New York. Every game you just saw tonight has a spot in there somewhere."

Theo looked at the whole lineup — the green tennis line, the two ships, the brown box, the paddles, the aliens, Pac-Man, Mario, Tetris, Sonic, the blocky hills — all of it leading, somehow, exactly to his own messy Roblox Studio window.

"So every game I build," he said slowly, "is just the next save file after all of this."

"Now you're getting it," Blip said, already fading back toward the screen. "Press start on your own, Theo."

The green-and-black flicker cleared. Theo's ordinary desktop was back, Roblox Studio still open, his double-jump script sitting there, unfinished, waiting.

He looked at it differently now.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a game to finish building.

story.title: Theo and the Pixel Who Remembered Every Game
story.subtitle: A midnight tour through the history of video games, one glowing screen at a time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: A Dot on a Round Green Screen (1958)
chapters.text:
Theo was not supposed to be awake. He was definitely not supposed to be in Roblox Studio at 11:47 p.m., placing a glowing soccer goal into his half-finished game.

He hit save. The screen flickered — green, then black, then green again, like it was blinking. A small square of pixels popped out of the corner of his monitor and hovered there, blinking too.

"Finally," it said. "Someone who builds games instead of just playing them. I'm Glitch. I'm made of leftover code from every game ever written, and I think you should see where all this started."

Before Theo could answer, the screen stretched wide and swallowed him whole.

He landed in a room full of humming machines the size of refrigerators, in front of a round glass screen that glowed green — not a monitor, something older. A man in glasses was fiddling with dials.

"That's an **oscilloscope**," Glitch said, "a lab machine that draws lines of light instead of numbers. Scientists used it to check equipment. This guy had a better idea."

On the round screen, a glowing dot bounced back and forth over a single curved line.

"Wait," said Theo, leaning in. "Is that... a net? Is this tennis?"

"In **1958**, physicist **William Higinbotham** built exactly that at **Brookhaven National Laboratory** — a bouncing dot of light, playable on an oscilloscope. He called it 'Tennis for Two.' Most people say it's the first video game anybody ever made."

Theo stared at the little green dot. "That's it? No graphics, no map, no — anything?"

"Every game you've ever built started here," Glitch said. "Somebody has to make the first dot bounce."

Theo grinned and reached out to bat the dot back himself. It worked. Somewhere, a scientist in glasses looked very pleased with his tennis net.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: A Computer the Size of a Room (1962)
chapters.text:
The next room was colder, and louder, and completely ridiculous.

A machine as big as a refrigerator-sized closet filled the whole space, blinking with rows of little switches. On its tiny round screen, two triangle-shaped spaceships chased each other around a star, firing.

"That computer," Glitch said, "is a **PDP-1**. It cost more than a house. And it can do less than your phone's calculator."

Theo laughed. "Then how are they playing a space battle on it?"

"In **1962**, an MIT student named **Steve Russell**, with some friends, programmed exactly this on that giant machine. They called it 'Spacewar!' — two players, two ships, one star pulling them in."

Theo watched the ships loop around the gravity well. "It's basically a two-player server," he said. "Like when me and a friend duel in a Roblox game I built — except instead of a loading screen, you've got..." he gestured at the room-sized computer, "this."

"Exactly like that," Glitch said. "Just slower internet. No internet, actually."

One of the switches on the console blinked invitingly. Theo flicked it. The ship on the left spun sideways and clipped the star's edge, and both students at the real controls yelped with laughter.

"You just invented a new way to lose," Glitch said.

"Every good game needs one," Theo said. "Trust me. I've built six."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Box With Wires and the Jammed Machine (1972)
chapters.text:
Theo expected the next stop to be another lab. Instead, it was a living room with wood-paneled walls and a television the size of a microwave oven.

A man was kneeling in front of it, connecting a plain brown box to the TV with wires.

"That's **Ralph Baer**," Glitch said. "People call him the father of video games. He spent the late 1960s building that thing — everyone just called it the 'Brown Box' — a way to play a game on a normal television."

Theo studied the dials on the box. "So before this, a TV could only show... TV?"

"That's the whole idea he was chasing," Glitch said. "And it worked. That Brown Box became the **Magnavox Odyssey**, the very first home video game console — a little machine that plugs into your TV and lets you play — released in **1972**."

The screen snapped again, and suddenly they stood in a dim arcade, lit by one buzzing machine with two white paddles bouncing a square ball.

"Same year,” Glitch said, “a man named **Nolan Bushnell**, with his partner **Ted Dabney**, started a company called Atari and put this game — Pong — in arcades."

A kid in flared jeans fed quarter after quarter into the slot. The machine made a strange clunking sound and stopped.

"People love to say," Glitch said carefully, "that an early Pong machine once jammed because it was so stuffed with quarters it couldn't hold any more. It's a fun story — nobody's totally sure it's true — but it tells you how fast people fell for this game."

Theo grinned. "A game so good it broke the coin slot. I'd take that review."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Cartridges and an Alien Invasion (1977–1978)
chapters.text:
The next room smelled like plastic and static electricity. Theo picked up a flat rectangular cartridge from a shelf and turned it over in his hands.

"Wait," he said. "Isn't this just one game? What if you want to play a different one?"

"That," Glitch said, "used to be the whole problem. The Magnavox Odyssey played games it already knew. Then in **1977**, Atari released a console called the **Atari 2600** that let you pop in different cartridges — like swapping out a different world in Roblox Studio instead of building a brand-new game from nothing."

Theo turned the cartridge over again, delighted. "So this is basically the first mod support."

"Sure," said Glitch. "Tell that to the engineers who had to invent the slot."

The room dissolved into flashing lights and a wall of sound — beeps, stomps, and dozens of kids crowded around glowing cabinets.

Rows of blocky aliens marched across a screen while a lone cannon fired up at them.

"In **1978**," Glitch said, "a designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado** made this for a company called **Taito**. Space Invaders. It started a worldwide arcade craze — lines out the door, pockets full of quarters."

Theo watched the aliens close in, row by row. "It's just you, versus all of them, forever creeping closer."

"Welcome to every tower-defense game you've ever built," Glitch said.

Theo stepped up to an open cabinet and fired off a round just to say he'd done it. The crowd around him cheered like he'd scored a goal.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: A Pizza With a Slice Missing (1980–1983)
chapters.text:
The arcade noise faded into a quieter hum, and a new machine glowed in front of them — a yellow circle chomping dots down a maze, chased by four colorful ghosts.

"Okay, I know this one," Theo said. "But why's he shaped like that?"

"Here's the story people tell," Glitch said. "In **1980**, a designer named **Toru Iwatani** made this game — Pac-Man — for a company called **Namco**. Some people say he got the idea from looking at a pizza with one slice taken out of it. Nobody's completely sure that's really how it happened, but it's a good story, and it stuck."

Theo laughed. "A snack-shaped hero. I respect that."

The scene shifted again — this time to a store, shelves stuffed with cartridges, half of them with covers that looked thrown together in an afternoon.

"By **1983**," Glitch said, "so many rushed, sloppy games had flooded the shelves that people stopped trusting video games at all. The whole market in North America shrank — hard. People call it the video game crash."

Theo, who had once spent three weeks polishing a single Roblox obstacle course, nodded slowly. "Yeah. If you rush a game and it's bad, people just... stop believing in the next one too."

"Exactly the lesson," Glitch said. "It's said that truckloads of unsold cartridges — including a famously bad E.T. game — ended up buried in a landfill in New Mexico. Diggers actually found some of them in **2014**, so that part, at least, turned out to be true."

"They buried the evidence," Theo said, grinning, "and it still got found. That's so on brand for the internet."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: A Plumber, a Puzzle, and a Comeback (1984–1985)
chapters.text:
Theo expected gloom after a crash. Instead, the next room was bright, loud, and shaped like a cartoon castle.

"The market needed a reason to trust games again," Glitch said. "In **1985**, Nintendo gave it one — a new console called the **NES**, bundled with a game that came in the box for free."

On the screen, a short mustached man in overalls ran across a row of bricks and leapt onto a mushroom-shaped enemy.

"Designer **Shigeru Miyamoto** made this," Glitch said. "Super Mario Bros. Mario's a plumber. He's also the single most famous character video games have ever produced."

Theo watched Mario clear a gap with a perfectly timed jump. "The jump arc is clean," he said. "I've spent hours tuning jump height in my own games. This guy nailed it on try one, probably."

"Probably not try one," Glitch admitted. "But close enough."

One more flicker, and they stood in a cold office in Moscow, where a man at a computer watched blocky shapes fall slowly down the screen, locking together row by row.

"**Alexey Pajitnov**, a Soviet scientist, made this in **1984**," Glitch said. "Tetris. Falling blocks, stack them, clear the line."

Theo rotated one in his head before Pajitnov even reached for the key. "Turn it sideways — it fits the gap."

On screen, the block rotated and slid home. The line cleared with a satisfying flash.

"You just out-thought the inventor," Glitch said.

"I didn't invent falling blocks," Theo said. "I just know a good gap when I see one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: A Fast Hedgehog and a Room Full of Cables (1991–1994)
chapters.text:
The next screen buzzed with speed — a blue streak looping through loops faster than Theo's eyes could track.

"In **1991**, Sega made this," Glitch said. "Sonic the Hedgehog. Fast, blue, built on purpose to go up against Mario."

Theo, who'd spent half his soccer season being told he was quick for his age, watched Sonic blur through a loop and grinned. "Finally, a mascot built for speed instead of jump height."

The next room was dim, with a dozen chunky computers shoved together on folding tables, thick cables snaking between them.

"In **1993**, a shooter called Doom came out," Glitch said, "and it made something huge popular: players linking their computers together in one room so everyone could play against each other at once. People called these **LAN parties** — a room full of cables instead of the internet."

Theo lit up. "That's literally what I do when my friends and I all join the same Roblox server — except you needed actual wires between actual houses."

"Same idea," Glitch said. "Much worse cable management."

One more flicker, and a sleek gray console sat under a TV, a disc spinning softly inside it.

"**1994**," Glitch said. "Sony steps in with the **PlayStation** — the first big console to use CDs instead of cartridges, which meant fuller sound and video than anyone had managed before."

Theo turned the disc over in the light. "So games went from a tiny cartridge to basically a whole shiny mirror."

"Progress," Glitch said, "is mostly just fitting more stuff onto smaller things."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Blocks, a Wand, and the Trip Home (2006–2015)
chapters.text:
The last room was bright and ordinary, except for the TV, and the white remote sitting on the couch in front of it.

"Pick it up," Glitch said.

Theo did. On the screen, a tiny tennis racket swung when he did.

"**2006**," Glitch said. "Nintendo's **Wii** — a console you moved instead of just pressed buttons on. It pulled in people who'd never really played a video game before. Grandparents. Parents. Entire living rooms."

Theo swung again, harder, and nearly knocked a lamp off the side table. "Okay, note to self — swing smaller."

The room dissolved one last time into something Theo actually recognized — a blocky, pixelated world of green hills and square trees, familiar in a way nothing else tonight had been.

"**2011**," Glitch said. "A developer in Sweden named **Markus Persson** — everyone calls him Notch — released this. Minecraft. Built entirely out of blocks you place yourself. It went on to become the best-selling video game of all time."

Theo looked around at the cube-shaped trees, the cube-shaped hills, and felt something click. "It's basically Roblox Studio's whole great-grandparent."

"Somewhere down the family tree, yeah," Glitch said. "And in **2015**, a museum called The Strong, in Rochester, New York, opened the World Video Game Hall of Fame — a place that keeps the games people never want to forget."

The screen flickered one final time, green then black then green, and Theo was back on his bedroom floor, laptop glowing, half-built soccer goal still sitting in his unfinished game.

On the desktop, a single new file had appeared, named simply: *Theo's Game.*

Glitch's voice was barely a whisper now, fading back into static. "Someone's always building the next dot. Might as well be you."

Theo looked at the blinking cursor in his file, and at the clock, and did not feel tired at all.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a game to finish.

true_facts.text: The first video game many people count is **Tennis for Two**, a bouncing dot of light shown on a round screen in **1958** by scientist **William Higinbotham** at **Brookhaven National Laboratory**.
In **1962**, an MIT student named **Steve Russell** and his friends built a two-player space battle called **Spacewar!** on a computer the size of a closet.
**Ralph Baer**, later called the father of video games, built a wired-up prototype called the **Brown Box** in the late 1960s.
Baer's Brown Box became the **Magnavox Odyssey**, the first home video game console, which came out in **1972**.
That same year, **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started a company called **Atari** and put the arcade game **Pong** into arcades.
A popular story says an early Pong machine once jammed because it got stuffed with too many quarters — nobody's totally sure it's true, but it shows how fast the game caught on.
The **Atari 2600**, released in **1977**, let players swap in different plastic cartridges instead of being stuck with one built-in game.
In **1978**, designer **Tomohiro Nishikado** made **Space Invaders** for a company called Taito, starting a worldwide arcade craze.
Designer **Toru Iwatani** made **Pac-Man** for Namco in **1980** — some say he got the idea from a pizza missing a slice, though that story isn't fully confirmed.
By **1983**, so many rushed, low-quality games had flooded store shelves that the North American video game market shrank sharply — the video game crash.
It's said that truckloads of unsold game cartridges got buried in a New Mexico landfill, and diggers really did find some of them in **2014**.
Nintendo brought the market back in **1985** with its new console, the **NES**, which came packed with **Super Mario Bros.**, designed by **Shigeru Miyamoto**.
In **1984**, a scientist in Moscow named **Alexey Pajitnov** invented the falling-block puzzle game **Tetris**.
In **1991**, Sega released **Sonic the Hedgehog**, a fast blue character built on purpose to compete with Mario.
