story.title: Zara and the Glowing Rock
story.subtitle: A sleepover trip to the fiery insides of the Earth

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Rock That Glowed
chapters.text:
Zara sat on her bedroom floor long after lights-out, sorting her rock collection by flashlight. Shiny ones here. Bumpy ones there. Sparkly ones in a pile all their own.

At the bottom of the box sat a smooth black rock she almost never noticed. Tonight it felt warm in her hand. Then it started to glow, soft and orange, like a tiny coal.

"Whoa," Zara whispered. "Rocks don't do that."

"This one does," said a small, crackly voice. The rock had a face now, barely there, like light flickering on glass. "I'm Glimmer. I used to be melted rock, bubbling hot underground. Down there we call it **magma**. The second I spilled out into the air and cooled down hard, I became something else — **lava** that turned to stone."

Zara grinned. "So you're a leftover splash?"

"A very old splash," Glimmer said. "Want to see where I came from?"

Before she could answer, the room filled with orange light. **WHOOOOSH!**

They landed on a black rocky slope in Hawaii, warm air pressing on Zara's cheeks. Below them, a lake of melted rock glowed and popped like soup left too long on the stove.

"This is **Kilauea**," Glimmer said. "A **volcano** — that's any spot where hot melted rock, ash, and gas escape up from under the ground."

Zara studied the mountain's shape. It wasn't pointy at all. It spread out low and wide, like an upside-down dinner plate.

"It's not a sharp mountain," she said slowly. "It's more like... a shield lying flat?"

"Exactly right," said Glimmer. "We call that a **shield volcano**, because that's just what it looks like. And Kilauea barely ever stops. It has been erupting on and off for decades — that's years and years."

The lava lake burped a bubble the size of a beach ball. Zara jumped back, then laughed so hard she snorted.

"Soup rock!" she shouted. "Bubbling SOUP ROCK!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ring Around the Ocean
chapters.text:
Glimmer floated them up high, above the clouds, until Hawaii shrank to a green speck in a huge blue ocean.

"Look down," Glimmer said. "See how the ocean has an edge, almost all the way around, shaped like a horseshoe?"

Zara traced it with her finger. Japan. The Philippines. Down to South America and back up to Alaska.

"People call this the **Ring of Fire**," said Glimmer. "It's the spot where most of the world's volcanoes live — about three out of every four."

"Why there, though?" Zara asked. "Why not just anywhere?"

"Good question," Glimmer said. "The ground under your feet isn't one solid piece. It's cracked into giant puzzle pieces called **plates**, and they're always moving, just super slowly. Where two plates push together, or pull apart, or scrape past each other — that's where volcanoes love to pop up."

Zara squinted at one crowded little country near the middle of the ring. "That one has a LOT of dots."

"Sharp eyes," Glimmer said. "That's **Indonesia**. It has more active volcanoes than anywhere else on Earth."

"More than anywhere?" Zara repeated, delighted. "Like, the champion?"

"The champion," Glimmer agreed.

Zara counted dots on the map until she lost track, giggling every time she had to start over. "This is better than counting sheep," she said.

"Just wait," said Glimmer, glowing a little brighter. "There's one spot that breaks the whole rule."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Hot Spot Under Hawaii
chapters.text:
They dropped back down toward Hawaii, and Zara noticed something odd right away.

"Wait," she said. "You said volcanoes are at the edges of those puzzle pieces. But Hawaii's way out in the middle of the ocean!"

"Caught me," Glimmer said, sounding pleased. "Hawaii's volcanoes don't sit on an edge at all. They sit over a **hotspot** — a place deep down where extra-hot rock keeps rising up, like a candle flame that never blows out, no matter where the puzzle piece drifts on top of it."

Zara looked out at a second mountain nearby, even bigger than Kilauea, its wide shoulders rolling for miles.

"That one's huge," she breathed.

"That's **Mauna Loa**," said Glimmer. "The biggest active volcano on the whole planet, over four thousand meters tall from the sea up to its top. Bigger than it looks from here, and it already looks enormous."

Zara spread her arms wide, trying to show how big that felt, then gave up and just flopped backward dramatically onto the warm black rock.

"I can't even arms it," she said.

"You can't even arms it," Glimmer agreed, in a very serious voice, and Zara laughed so hard she rolled sideways.

She sat back up and pointed between the two mountains. "They're both the same shape, though. Both shields."

"Right again," said Glimmer. "Wide and gentle, built from lava that flows a long way before it cools. Not every volcano looks like this one. Some are tall and pointy instead, built from thicker, stickier stuff. We're headed to meet one of those next — and it has quite a story."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Day the Sky Went Dark
chapters.text:
The light shifted. Zara blinked, and suddenly she stood on a hillside above a sparkling blue bay, ancient stone buildings dotting the shore below.

"Where are we now?" she asked.

"Italy," said Glimmer. "The year is **79**. That mountain across the water is **Vesuvius**."

It didn't look scary. It looked almost sleepy, green and quiet. Then a thread of gray smoke curled up from its top, and Zara's stomach did a little flip.

"Is it going to blow up?" she asked.

"It already did, a long time before your today," Glimmer said gently. "This is just us watching it happen, safe and far away, like a movie. Vesuvius erupted so hard it covered two whole towns, **Pompeii** and **Herculaneum**, under thick, heavy ash."

Zara watched the smoke thicken into a tall gray cloud, shaped almost like a tree. A man stood on a rooftop nearby, scribbling fast on a scroll.

"Who's that?" Zara asked. "Shouldn't he run?"

"He's far enough away to be safe," said Glimmer. "His name is **Pliny the Younger**, and he's writing down everything he sees, because nobody has ever described an eruption like this before."

Zara watched him writing and writing. "He's basically taking notes on a volcano."

"He did it so well," Glimmer said, "that scientists still use his name today. Any volcano that blasts a tall cloud like that one gets called a '**Plinian**' eruption, after him."

"So he got a whole kind of explosion named after him just for writing a good letter?" Zara said, grinning. "I should start writing letters."

"Start with your rock collection," Glimmer suggested, and Zara decided that was actually a wonderful idea.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Loudest Bang Ever
chapters.text:
Next, the air turned warm and salty, and Zara found herself standing on a faraway beach, staring at an island with smoke pouring from its middle.

"This is **Krakatoa**," Glimmer said. "The year is **1883**. Cover your ears, just in case."

Zara clapped her hands over her ears and waited. Nothing happened.

"When does it—"

**BOOM.**

Even far away, even just watching, the sound rolled through her chest like thunder with no end.

"That's one of the loudest sounds ever made on Earth," said Glimmer. "People heard this very bang almost **three thousand miles away**, on a tiny island called Rodrigues."

Zara's mouth fell open. "Three THOUSAND? That's like... that's so far I can't even picture it!"

"Picture your town," Glimmer said. "Now imagine someone on the very other side of the whole country hearing you pop a balloon."

"No WAY," Zara said, delighted and a little bit stunned. "That's the loudest pop in the history of pops."

"Pretty much," said Glimmer, glowing with what might have been a laugh.

Zara sat down right there on the sand, still a little wide-eyed, and asked Glimmer to say the number again, just to hear it twice.
chapters.shout_line: THE LOUDEST POP IN THE HISTORY OF POPS!

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Summer That Never Came
chapters.text:
They traveled again, this time to a quiet mountain in Indonesia, the year **1815** hanging in the air like a label.

"This is **Tambora**," said Glimmer. "It had the biggest eruption anyone has ever recorded."

The mountain let out a huge dark cloud that spread and spread, drifting up high into the sky until it wrapped halfway around the whole Earth.

"All that ash floated so high," Glimmer explained, "that it blocked some of the sun's warmth, far away, for a whole year."

"Wait," Zara said, counting on her fingers. "So people somewhere else just... didn't get a summer?"

"Exactly. The next year, **1816**, people in Europe and America called it the 'Year Without a Summer.' Snow in June. Crops that wouldn't grow properly."

Zara looked up at the drifting ash cloud, trying to imagine snow falling in the middle of summer vacation.

"That's wild," she said. "One mountain, way over here, messed with people's SUMMER way over there?"

"One mountain," Glimmer confirmed. "That's how big these things can be."

Zara shivered, even though the air around them was warm, and tucked that thought away carefully, like a rock worth keeping.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Mountain That Lost Its Top
chapters.text:
The scene changed to green forest and a tall, snow-capped mountain that looked almost too perfect, like a drawing.

"Washington State," Glimmer said. "**Mount St. Helens**. The date is **May 18, 1980**."

"It's so pretty," Zara said. "Why do I feel nervous?"

"Scientists felt it too," Glimmer said. "For weeks, they'd been watching this mountain closely, using machines called **seismographs** that feel tiny wobbles in the ground, way too small for people to notice on their own."

As Zara watched from a safe distance, far up in the clear sky with Glimmer, the whole side of the mountain suddenly slid away in a massive landslide — the biggest ever recorded. A second later, the mountain itself burst open behind it.

**CRACK — WHOOOOSH!**

When the dust and ash finally settled, the mountain's whole top was gone — about **thirteen hundred feet** of it, simply blown away.

"Whoa," Zara breathed, eyes huge. "It just... doesn't have a top anymore."

"It doesn't," Glimmer agreed softly. "The scientists who studied this mountain worked hard to understand it, so that towns nearby would know when to stay away and stay safe."

Zara looked at the strange, flat-topped mountain for a long moment, then reached out and patted the air near it, the way she'd pat a dog that had been in a fight and won.

"Good job healing," she whispered. "You look tough now."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Baby Island
chapters.text:
The last stop smelled like salt and steam. Gray ocean stretched in every direction, and right in the middle of it, smoke hissed up out of the waves.

"Iceland, nearby waters," Glimmer said. "The year is **1963**. Keep watching the water."

Zara watched. Steam. A rumble. Then, slowly, black rock began poking up out of the sea, piece by piece, like a shy animal peeking out of its den.

"Is that..." Zara gasped. "Is a volcano building an ISLAND?"

"It is," said Glimmer. "A brand new island, called **Surtsey**, rising right out of the ocean because an underwater volcano kept on erupting."

"From nothing? From just... water and fire?"

"From nothing," Glimmer said. "Iceland sits on a spot where two of those giant puzzle pieces are pulling apart from each other, which is exactly why it has so many volcanoes of its own."

Zara watched the baby island grow a little more rock, a little more shape. "It's like the ocean is hatching an egg," she whispered.

"There's one more volcano I should mention," Glimmer added, "so you don't worry later. There's a giant one sleeping quietly under a place called Yellowstone. Its last big eruption was about **six hundred forty thousand years** ago, and nothing right now says it's waking up soon."

"So it's basically just... napping. Forever."

"Forever napping," Glimmer agreed. "Some volcanoes build you a new island. Some just nap for hundreds of thousands of years. Earth keeps all kinds."

Zara nodded slowly, watching Surtsey's dark rock gleam in the sunset. "Earth's weird," she said happily. "The best kind of weird."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The glow folded in on itself, and Zara blinked — and there she was, back on her bedroom carpet, rock piles still sorted around her exactly as she'd left them.

Glimmer sat small and dark in her palm again, barely glowing now, just a faint ember-orange line along one edge.

"Did that really happen?" Zara whispered. "All of it? The soup lake, and the island being born, and the mountain that lost its top?"

"Every bit," Glimmer said. "You saw real places. Real mountains. Real splashes of me, a long, long time ago."

Zara turned the little black rock over in her fingers, looking at it completely differently now — not just a rock, but a tiny piece of something enormous, cooled down and carried all this way.

"You're basically a souvenir," she said. "From the whole entire Earth."

"I like that," said Glimmer, glowing just a touch brighter, pleased. "Keep me safe on your shelf. Next time your rocks start feeling warm, you'll know it's me, ready for another trip."

Zara set Glimmer gently on the very top of her tallest pile, right where she'd see it first thing, and pulled her blanket up to her chin.

"Goodnight, Zara," Glimmer murmured, glow fading to a whisper of orange, then nothing at all. "Sleep well, little rock hound."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Zara. Sleep well, little rock hound.

fact_pack.summary: Volcanoes are places where melted rock, ash, and gas escape from deep inside the Earth. Some erupt gently and often, like Hawaii's Kilauea, while others, like Vesuvius or Krakatoa, produced huge explosions that changed history.

facts.text: A volcano is an opening in Earth's crust where hot melted rock, ash, and gases escape from underground.
Molten rock is called magma underground, and lava once it flows out onto the surface.
Most volcanoes form along the edges of Earth's moving plates, where plates push together, pull apart, or slide past each other.
The 'Ring of Fire' is a horseshoe belt around the Pacific Ocean holding about 75% of the world's active volcanoes.
Indonesia has more active volcanoes than any other country on Earth.
Hawaii's volcanoes formed over a 'hotspot' of rising hot rock deep inside the Earth, not at the edge of a plate.
Kilauea in Hawaii is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth, erupting almost continuously for decades.
Mauna Loa in Hawaii is Earth's largest active volcano by volume, rising over 4,000 meters above sea level.
Shield volcanoes are wide with gentle slopes, like Hawaii's; stratovolcanoes are tall, steep cones, like Mount Fuji.
Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD, burying the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under thick ash.
Roman writer Pliny the Younger watched the Vesuvius eruption and described it in letters, so scientists now call this explosive type a 'Plinian' eruption.
Krakatoa's 1883 eruption made a sound so loud it was heard about 3,000 miles away on Rodrigues Island.
Krakatoa's eruption caused giant tsunami waves that struck nearby coasts, making it one of the deadliest volcanic disasters in history.
In 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia produced history's largest recorded eruption, and its ash helped make 1816 the 'Year Without a Summer' in Europe and America.
On May 18, 1980, Mount St. Helens erupted right after the largest landslide ever recorded slid off its side.
The Mount St. Helens eruption blew about 1,300 feet off the mountain's summit while scientists were studying the volcano up close.
Yellowstone sits atop a supervolcano whose last huge eruption happened about 640,000 years ago; scientists see no sign it will erupt soon.
In 1963, a new island named Surtsey rose from the sea near Iceland as an underwater volcano kept erupting.
Iceland has many volcanoes because it sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where two of Earth's plates pull apart.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest known volcano in the solar system, about 13.6 miles (22 km) high, nearly three times taller than Mount Everest.
Volcanologists use seismographs to detect tiny earthquakes and satellites to spot ground swelling, both early warning signs of an eruption.
Volcanic ash breaks down into very fertile soil, which is why many farmers live and grow crops near volcanoes despite the risk.

story.title: Juno, Milo, and Theo and the Rumbling Rock
story.subtitle: A sizzling, bubbling trip into the heart of a volcano

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Rock That Rumbled
chapters.text:
It was way past bedtime. Juno sat on the rug with her toy dinosaurs. Milo stacked LEGO bricks into a tower. Theo peeked at one more game on his tablet.

Then Juno's little toy volcano started to glow. It was supposed to be gray and still. Now it was orange and warm.

RUMBLE. The toy volcano shook on the rug.

CRACK! The top popped open. Out popped a tiny glowing fellow made of orange light.

"Hiya!" he said. "I'm Sizzle. I live in volcanoes. Want to see how they work?"

Milo grinned. "Is it like popping open a LEGO brick?"

"Kind of!" said Sizzle. "A **volcano** is a hole in the ground. Hot melted rock, ash, and bubbly gas sneak out of it."

"What's the hot rock called?" asked Theo.

"Down under the ground, it's called **magma**," said Sizzle. "Once it comes out on top, we call it **lava**."

Juno poked the warm little volcano. "Can we go inside?"

Sizzle winked. "Hold on tight."

The rug seemed to melt into mist. WHOOSH! The three kids shrank down, down, down — right into the rumbling rock.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Great Horseshoe
chapters.text:
They landed on a floating map, glowing like a video game screen. Theo's eyes went wide. "It looks like my Roblox world map!"

"Look closer," said Sizzle.

A curvy orange line glowed all around the edge of the ocean on the map. It curled like a horseshoe.

"Most volcanoes live where Earth's **plates** bump together," said Sizzle. "Plates are giant puzzle pieces that make up the ground we stand on."

Theo traced the glowing horseshoe with his finger. "It goes all the way around!"

"That's the **Ring of Fire**," said Sizzle. "About three out of every four volcanoes on Earth live right along it."

Milo counted little orange dots. There were so many near one country.

"That place has more volcanoes than anywhere else!" Milo shouted. "It's called Indonesia!"

"Milo found it!" cheered Sizzle. "You're right."

The map spun like a soccer ball, faster and faster, until it blurred into orange light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Bubbling Island
chapters.text:
SPLOOSH! They landed on a warm, black beach. Steam puffed up from cracks in the ground.

"Where's the plate edge here?" asked Theo, looking around.

"There isn't one," said Sizzle. "This volcano grew over a **hotspot** — a warm, bubbly spot deep inside the Earth, far from any edge."

Juno pointed at the bubbling red glow nearby. "Is that one awake right now?"

"Very awake," said Sizzle. "This volcano is called **Kilauea**. It's one of the busiest on Earth. It has been erupting almost nonstop for years and years."

Milo, who loved sharks, leaned toward the water. "Does the lava go all the way into the ocean?"

"Sometimes it does," said Sizzle. "HISSSS — that's the sound it makes when hot lava meets cool sea water."

Juno hissed back, giggling. "HISSSS!"

Theo hissed too. Soon all three kids were hissing like little teakettles, while Sizzle laughed so hard his glow wobbled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Biggest Mountain Ever
chapters.text:
Next they stood at the bottom of a mountain so wide, Theo couldn't see the edges.

"Whoa," he said. "That's not pointy like a normal mountain."

"This one is called **Mauna Loa**," said Sizzle. "It's the biggest active volcano on the whole planet, taller than four thousand of your soccer fields stacked straight up."

"Why is it so wide and flat on top?" asked Milo.

"Some volcanoes are wide and gentle, like this one," said Sizzle. "Others are tall and pointy, like a mountain called Fuji, far away in Japan."

Milo grabbed an invisible LEGO brick from the air and pretended to build. "I'm gonna build a wide one AND a pointy one!"

"Build both," laughed Sizzle. "Then you'll know every volcano shape there is."

Juno clapped her hands. The ground rumbled happily underneath them, like a giant cat purring.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Island That Was Born
chapters.text:
The scene swirled into cold mist and crashing waves.

"Brrr," said Juno. "Where are we now?"

"Iceland," said Sizzle. "Here, two big plates are pulling apart, slow as a stretchy toy."

Suddenly the sea began to boil. BOOM! Steam and rock shot up from under the water.

"Is a new island being made?" Theo asked, amazed.

"Yes!" said Sizzle. "In **1963**, this exact thing happened. A whole new island popped up from the sea. They named it **Surtsey**."

Juno watched the rock pile grow taller and taller, like a sandcastle building itself.

"It's making its own land!" Juno shouted.

"That's exactly right, Juno," said Sizzle. "No danger here — we're watching safely from far away."

The three kids cheered as the little island kept rising out of the fizzy, bubbling water.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Mountain on Mars
chapters.text:
CLICK. The world around them went dark and sparkly, full of stars.

"Are we in space?" Theo gasped. This was better than any game level.

"We are," said Sizzle. "Look down."

Below them sat a red, dusty planet with one enormous bump on it.

"That's **Mars**," said Sizzle. "And that bump is **Olympus Mons** — the biggest volcano anyone has ever found, anywhere."

"How big?" Theo asked, already knowing it would be huge.

"About thirteen and a half miles tall," said Sizzle. "Stack almost three of your tallest mountains and you still wouldn't reach the top."

Theo whistled. "That beats every level I've ever built."

Milo tried to imagine a LEGO tower that tall and just laughed. "We'd need ALL the bricks in the world."

Sizzle chuckled. "Every single one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Watching the Wobbles
chapters.text:
Back on Earth, they stood beside a cozy little hut. Inside, people watched glowing screens.

"Who are they?" asked Milo.

"Scientists who study volcanoes," said Sizzle. "They use special machines that feel tiny wiggles in the ground. That tells them a volcano might wake up soon."

Juno looked at the dark dirt outside the hut. It was super dark and soft.

"Why does everything grow so big here?" she asked, pointing at tall, leafy plants.

"Old volcano ash turns into **fertile** dirt," said Sizzle. "That means dirt that helps plants grow big and strong. That's why some people live near volcanoes, even sleepy ones."

Juno patted the soft dirt. "It's like volcano food for plants!"

"Exactly like that," said Sizzle, beaming. "Juno, you said it perfectly."

The hut lights blinked gently, like a goodnight wave.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Rug
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! The warm wind spun them around and around.

Then — THUMP. Juno, Milo, and Theo landed right back on their own living room rug.

The toy volcano sat quiet again, gray and still. But right beside it was something new: one tiny, shiny orange rock, still warm to the touch.

"Sizzle left us a souvenir," Milo whispered, turning it in his fingers.

Theo grinned. "Best field trip ever. Better than any level."

Juno yawned a huge yawn and hugged her toy dinosaur close.

Milo set the little orange rock on his nightstand, right next to his LEGO tower.

"Goodnight, volcano," Juno whispered to the toy. "Rumble on."

Outside, the real world was quiet and cool, full of sleepy stars — just like the ones over that red, bumpy planet far, far away.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Theo. Rumble on.

facts.text: A volcano is an opening in Earth's crust where hot melted rock, ash, and gases escape from underground.
Molten rock is called magma underground, and lava once it flows out onto the surface.
Most volcanoes form along the edges of Earth's moving plates, where plates push together, pull apart, or slide past each other.
The 'Ring of Fire' is a horseshoe belt around the Pacific Ocean holding about 75% of the world's active volcanoes.
Indonesia has more active volcanoes than any other country on Earth.
Hawaii's volcanoes formed over a 'hotspot' of rising hot rock deep inside the Earth, not at the edge of a plate.
Kilauea in Hawaii is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth, erupting almost continuously for decades.
Mauna Loa in Hawaii is Earth's largest active volcano by volume, rising over 4,000 meters above sea level.
Shield volcanoes are wide with gentle slopes, like Hawaii's; stratovolcanoes are tall, steep cones, like Mount Fuji.
Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD, burying the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under thick ash.
Roman writer Pliny the Younger watched the Vesuvius eruption and described it in letters, so scientists now call this explosive type a 'Plinian' eruption.
Krakatoa's 1883 eruption made a sound so loud it was heard about 3,000 miles away on Rodrigues Island.
Krakatoa's eruption caused giant tsunami waves that struck nearby coasts, making it one of the deadliest volcanic disasters in history.
In 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia produced history's largest recorded eruption, and its ash helped make 1816 the 'Year Without a Summer' in Europe and America.
On May 18, 1980, Mount St. Helens erupted right after the largest landslide ever recorded slid off its side.
The Mount St. Helens eruption blew about 1,300 feet off the mountain's summit while scientists were studying the volcano up close.
Yellowstone sits atop a supervolcano whose last huge eruption happened about 640,000 years ago; scientists see no sign it will erupt soon.
In 1963, a new island named Surtsey rose from the sea near Iceland as an underwater volcano kept erupting.
Iceland has many volcanoes because it sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where two of Earth's plates pull apart.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest known volcano in the solar system, about 13.6 miles (22 km) high, nearly three times taller than Mount Everest.
Volcanologists use seismographs to detect tiny earthquakes and satellites to spot ground swelling, both early warning signs of an eruption.
Volcanic ash breaks down into very fertile soil, which is why many farmers live and grow crops near volcanoes despite the risk.

story.title: Juno, Milo, and Theo and the Glowing Fire Mountain
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip inside the volcanoes of Earth—and one on Mars!

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The LEGO Volcano Wobble
chapters.text:
Milo stacked red and orange LEGO bricks into a tall cone. Juno roared like a dinosaur next to him. Theo watched a volcano pop on his tablet.

"Ten more minutes," Mom called from the hall.

Then Milo's LEGO volcano gave a tiny wobble. It glowed bright orange, right there on the carpet.

Out popped a tiny warm spark with a crackly voice. "Hello! I'm Pip," it said. "I live inside fire mountains."

"A volcano is a hole in the ground," Pip said. "Hot melted rock pushes up and out!"

Juno gasped. "Like dino soup!"

Milo poked his glowing LEGO volcano. "Can we go see a real one?" he asked.

Pip spun in a happy circle. "Hold on tight!"

WHOOOOSH! The carpet melted into orange light, and all three children swirled down, down, down.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Hawaii's Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
They landed on warm black rock. A glowing orange river oozed slowly downhill.

"That orange stuff underground is called magma," said Pip. "Once it comes out, we call it lava."

Juno pointed. "It's slow! Like dino soup cooling down."

Theo looked at the wide, flat mountain around them. "Why isn't it pointy like the ones on my screen?"

"Good eye," said Pip. "This is **Kilauea**, in Hawaii. It's wide and gentle, not steep and sharp."

Milo tugged Theo's sleeve. "Let's see the biggest one too!"

Theo grinned. "Yeah! Take us there, Pip!"

Pip zipped them over to an even bigger, wider mountain. "This is **Mauna Loa**," Pip said. "It's the biggest volcano on Earth, taller than four thousand of your Mom's steps stacked up!"

Milo whistled. "That's higher than my tallest LEGO tower ever!"

Juno giggled and hugged a warm rock.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Ring Around the Ocean
chapters.text:
Pip lifted them high into the sky. Below them, a huge circle of mountains glowed like tiny campfires.

Theo's eyes went wide. "That's shaped like a horseshoe! I built a map just like this in my game!"

"You're right," said Pip. "It's called the **Ring of Fire**. Most of the world's fire mountains sit inside it."

Milo started counting the glowing dots. "One, two, three... there's so many!"

Juno pointed at one cluster, bigger than the rest. "Why does THAT one have the most?"

"Sharp eyes, Juno!" said Pip. "That's **Indonesia**. It has more fire mountains than any other country on Earth."

"COOL!" all three children shouted together.

Pip chuckled, sparks fizzing happily. "Earth's ground is made of giant puzzle pieces. Where they bump and squeeze, fire mountains pop up."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Island That Was Born
chapters.text:
Next, cold wind whooshed past them. Steam hissed up from a gray sea.

"What if two puzzle pieces pulled apart," Milo wondered, "and let the fire sneak out between them?"

Pip clapped tiny sparks together. "Exactly right! This is **Iceland**. Two of Earth's puzzle pieces are pulling apart here, slowly, every year."

Suddenly, bubbles boiled under the waves. Rock poked up, smoking and sizzling.

"Whoa, a whole island is being BORN!" Theo yelled.

"In **1963**, that's just what happened," said Pip. "A new island popped up out of the sea."

Theo thought hard. "What do we call it?"

"It's called **Surtsey**," said Pip. "Named after a fire giant from old stories."

Juno clapped. "A baby island! Hi, baby island!"
chapters.shout_line: A whole island is being BORN!

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Sleepy Giant
chapters.text:
They landed in a steamy, bubbly valley with colorful pools.

Juno stopped walking. "Is THIS one gonna pop? Right now?"

"No, no," said Pip gently. "This is **Yellowstone**. It sits on top of a really, really big fire mountain, called a supervolcano."

"It had one giant blast a super long time ago," Pip went on, "about **640,000 years** back. Scientists watch it closely, and there's no sign it will blow soon. You're safe."

Juno breathed out and smiled. "Phew. Okay, baby giant, you can keep sleeping."

Milo patted a warm rock like it was a puppy. "Night night, sleepy mountain."

Theo laughed so hard he snorted, which made everyone laugh even harder.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Mountain on Mars
chapters.text:
Pip zoomed them up, up, past clouds, past stars, to a red, dusty place.

"Whoa, are we on MARS?" Theo gasped, bouncing in the low gravity.

A mountain rose in front of them, so tall its top vanished into pink sky.

"Guess how big," said Pip, sparking with excitement.

Theo squinted up. "Bigger than Mount Everest?"

"Way bigger," said Pip. "This is **Olympus Mons**. It's about **thirteen miles** tall — almost three Mount Everests stacked up!"

"THAT'S THE BIGGEST MOUNTAIN EVER!" Theo shouted, pumping his fist.

Milo looked down at his sneakers. "Glad we're not climbing that one."

Juno just roared at it, dinosaur-style, because it seemed like the right thing to do.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Listening to the Ground
chapters.text:
Back on Earth, they met a scientist crouched by a quiet mountain, headphones on.

"What's she doing?" Milo whispered.

"Listening for tiny shakes," said Pip. "A special machine feels little wiggles in the ground before a fire mountain wakes up. Satellites watch the ground bulge too."

Milo grinned. "Like when I build a listening gadget out of LEGO!"

"Just like that," Pip said.

Juno knelt by a patch of dark dirt and poked it. "This dirt looks yummy and soft."

"Old volcano dirt makes great food-growing dirt," said Pip. "Farmers plant crops near fire mountains because the ground is so good for growing."

Juno planted a pretend seed. "Grow, pretend flower, grow!"

Everyone giggled as Pip sprinkled a tiny spark over the spot, just for fun.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Carpet
chapters.text:
Pip twirled them home in one last WHOOOOSH.

They landed back on the bedroom carpet, right beside the LEGO volcano.

It glowed softly, one last time, then settled into a quiet little nightlight.

"Thanks, Pip," said Milo, patting the bricks.

"Come back soon," said Theo, already imagining a volcano level for his game.

Juno yawned a dinosaur-sized yawn. "Night night, fire mountains."

Pip's spark dimmed to a tiny glow, tucked safely inside the bricks. "Sleep well, you three. Play well."

Mom peeked in. "Lights out, you three!"

And under the soft orange glow of a small LEGO volcano, three sleepy explorers closed their eyes.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Theo. Play well.
